l061.intro:
He must increase, but I must decrease. (John 3:30)

Who, existing in the form of God, didn’t consider equality with God a thing to be grasped, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of men. And being found in human form, he humbled himself, becoming obedient to the point of death, yes, the death of the cross. (Philippians 2:6–8)

sections.heading: Introduction: A Lighthouse Is Most Successful When No One Is Looking at the Lighthouse
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, good morning.

I’d like to begin by asking you to picture something in your mind.

It’s a foggy night. On a rocky shore by the sea stands a lighthouse, its beam turning round and round at the top of the tower. Far out on the water, a ship is searching for its channel. You stand on the shore and watch that light — and what do you see? You don’t stop to work out how many watts the bulb is. Without even meaning to, your eyes follow the beam out across the water until they land on that ship.

A lighthouse is at its most successful precisely when no one is paying attention to the lighthouse.

Brothers and sisters, that one picture is the whole message of today’s lesson.

The focus of revival is always Jesus. Revival is not a display of how zealous, how capable or how gifted people are; it is people coming to “see Jesus”. When Jesus is lifted up and seen, his presence comes, and lives are changed. So what part do we play in revival? The key lies in one word — “selflessness”. Only when we lay ourselves down and let Jesus reign will the power of revival be released.

In the autumn of 1904, something happened in the coal-mining valleys of South Wales. Evan Roberts, twenty-six years old, had been a miner and had then gone to a preparatory school to train for the ministry. That autumn he went back to the little church in his home town of Loughor and put forward just four simple requests: deal with every known sin; put away every doubtful habit; obey the prompting of the Holy Spirit at once; confess Christ publicly.

Then he did something very unlike an evangelist — he would often sit below the pulpit with his head bowed in prayer, and let others speak. By the usual accounts, within a year about a hundred thousand people in Wales turned to Christ.

What makes us stop and think most are the people who came from all over to watch. When they went home, the thing they said most often was not, “Roberts is a wonderful preacher,” but, “I met God.” Brothers and sisters, notice the difference — what stands between those two sentences is “self”.

In the vision of Kingdom 321, we say it again and again: the root of humanity’s fall comes down to one word — “self”. Satan did not overcome humanity by force in the beginning. He did it with a sentence: “you will be like God, knowing good and evil” (Genesis 3:5). He moved people’s eyes off God and onto themselves, and from that moment humanity left its originally intended position and began wanting to take God’s place.

So the mark of the old self is the self-centred life, and the mark of the new self is selflessness. Self-centred people, whatever they do, will without noticing swing the camera back onto themselves; selfless people, whatever they do, will without noticing hand the camera over to Jesus.

We have to be honest. In church, hardly anyone would say out loud, “I want to be seen.” But we all know that feeling in our hearts: after preaching, what matters most to us is whether anyone comes up to praise us; when someone else gets a mention, something in us suddenly goes a little cold.

Brothers and sisters, that isn’t some monstrous sin. It simply shows one thing — “self” is still on the throne.

“Self” is a strange thing. Sin hurts, and when it hurts we turn back. But the self-centred life doesn’t hurt; if anything, it makes us feel valuable and needed. So what “self” is best at isn’t tearing down God’s work — it’s standing right in the middle of God’s work, blocking the light.

Today’s lesson takes us down a road called “the Road to Revival”. That road doesn’t begin with power, or gifts, or methods. It begins with a decision: I am willing to take a step back and let Jesus stand at the centre.

We’ll look at three things together: first, letting people see Jesus and not myself; second, Paul’s life — not living for himself, but living only for Jesus; third, the selfless life — laying down myself and having Jesus.

sections.heading: Scripture Background: Three Passages, One Shared Heartbeat
sections.html:
Today’s three theme passages come from Galatians, John and Philippians. The three books have different authors, were written at different times and to different readers, yet they share one heartbeat: let Christ have first place, and let “self” return to its originally intended position.

First, Galatians 2:20.

Galatians was written by the apostle Paul. It is generally reckoned one of his earliest letters, written around AD 48–49 to the churches of southern Galatia — the churches Paul founded on his first missionary journey in Pisidian Antioch, Iconium, Lystra and Derbe. At the time a group known as the “Judaizers” were following in Paul’s footsteps, teaching Gentile believers that they had to be circumcised and keep the law to be truly saved. They wanted to turn salvation into a human achievement, something people could boast about on the strength of their own deeds.

So Paul wrote this, the most impassioned of his letters. In 2:11–14 he records something shocking: even the apostle Peter, when he came to Antioch, drew back and separated himself from the Gentiles out of fear of the people who had come from James. What Paul opposed was not Peter the man, but the “self” hiding under a cloak of piety — fearing people’s eyes more than God’s heart.

Then, in 2:19–20, Paul makes the loftiest personal confession in the whole New Testament: “For I, through the law, died to the law, that I might live to God. I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me.”

“I have been crucified with Christ” is in the perfect tense in the original — a fact already accomplished, whose effect continues to this day. It isn’t that I strive every day to nail myself up there; it’s that in Christ I have already been put to death. What I have to learn is not to climb down off the cross, day after day.

Next, John 3:30.

John’s Gospel was written by John, the disciple whom the Lord Jesus loved. The consistent witness of church history is that in his later years he shepherded the churches around Ephesus, and wrote this Gospel some time between AD 85 and 95. The scene in chapter 3 is remarkable: Jesus’ ministry has just begun, and John the Baptist’s ministry is at its height. His disciples come running to John with “bad news”: “he baptizes, and everyone is coming to him” (John 3:26).

This is a moment of testing every servant of God meets sooner or later — when the crowds turn towards someone else, where will my heart turn?

John the Baptist’s answer comes in three layers. On gifts: “A man can receive nothing unless it has been given him from heaven” (John 3:27) — nothing I hold in my hands did I earn. On identity: “the friend of the bridegroom, who stands and hears him, rejoices greatly because of the bridegroom’s voice” (John 3:29) — I am not the bridegroom. On direction: “He must increase, but I must decrease.”

The Greek word for “increase” is αὐξάνω (auxanō), meaning to grow, to be added to; the Greek for “decrease” is ἐλαττόω (elattoō), meaning to become smaller, to be reduced. John wasn’t grudgingly putting up with it. He had seen the order of heaven: this is how it was always meant to be.

Finally, Philippians 2:6–8.

Philippians was written during Paul’s first imprisonment in Rome, around AD 60–62. Philippi was a Roman colony in Macedonia whose citizens prized their citizenship and their honour. Cracks had appeared in the church — 4:2 mentions two sisters, Euodia and Syntyche, who could not agree. The first thing Paul deals with is not the issue but the mindset: “doing nothing through rivalry or through conceit, but in humility, each counting others better than himself” (Philippians 2:3). And then he brings out the greatest mountain in the universe — Christ emptying himself.

The Greek for “emptied himself” is ἐκένωσεν (ekenōsen), from the root κενόω (kenoō), meaning to empty out. We need to be clear here: Christ emptying himself does not mean he emptied out his divinity. He never stopped being God. What he emptied himself of was the display of the rights and glory that belonged to his equality with God. The word behind “a thing to be grasped” is ἁρπαγμός (harpagmos), something clutched and held on to, seized as one’s own — he did not treat that equality as a trophy he had to keep clenched in his fist.

Brothers and sisters, set these three passages side by side. Paul says, “it is no longer I who live.” John the Baptist says, “I must decrease.” The Lord Jesus says it with his actions: “he emptied himself.” Three different positions, yet one direction — downward.

And Scripture goes on to tell us where that downward road ends: “Therefore God also highly exalted him, and gave to him the name which is above every name” (Philippians 2:9).

In the language of 321, this is “humility overcomes pride; selflessness overcomes Satan”. Pride is leaving our originally intended position, seizing rights and wanting to take God’s place; humility is laying down our rights and returning to our originally intended position — let man be man and let God be God.

Now let’s go together into the three key points of the lesson.

sections.heading: Key Point 1: Letting People See Jesus, Not Myself
1. The Sermon at Pentecost: What Three Thousand People Saw Was Not Peter
sections.html:
After Jesus ascended, the disciples resolved to preach nothing but Jesus and his cross.

On the day of Pentecost, Peter stood up to preach the first sermon. Brothers and sisters, look closely at what that sermon contains: Peter doesn’t talk about himself. He doesn’t boast that he had seen the risen Lord with his own eyes, nor does he offer any explanation for the failure of denying the Lord three times. He speaks of one thing only — Jesus is the Christ, and he has risen. His conclusion is: “Let all the house of Israel therefore know certainly that God has made him both Lord and Christ, this Jesus whom you crucified” (Acts 2:36).

And the result? “Then those who gladly received his word were baptized. There were added that day about three thousand souls” (Acts 2:41). It was the first great harvest in the history of the church.

What moved those three thousand people? The text puts it very precisely: “Now when they heard this, they were cut to the heart” (Acts 2:37). What cut them to the heart was not Peter’s eloquence but the Jesus who was crucified and rose again. They were not moved by Peter; they were moved because they “saw Jesus”.

A few days later, Peter and John healed a man lame from birth at the Beautiful Gate, and everyone stared at them. Peter immediately said, “Why do you fasten your eyes on us, as though by our own power or godliness we had made him walk?” (Acts 3:12). At the very moment of being praised, his first move was to turn the camera away. That wasn’t polite modesty; it was a spiritual reflex.

Brothers and sisters, whether we can take the applause is not the hardest test. Whether we can pass the applause on straight away — that is.

sections.heading: 2. John the Baptist: How Many People He Helped to See Jesus
sections.html:
In the same way, John the Baptist understood this spiritual principle.

As the crowds left the Jordan, wave after wave, to follow Jesus, John’s disciples couldn’t bear it, and there was a sour note in their words: “Rabbi, he who was with you beyond the Jordan, to whom you have testified, behold, he baptizes, and everyone is coming to him” (John 3:26).

John, though, starts from the order of heaven. First he says, “A man can receive nothing unless it has been given him from heaven”; then, “I am not the Christ”; and then he fixes his own position with a beautiful picture: I am the friend of the bridegroom. At a Jewish wedding, the “friend of the bridegroom” took care of all the preparations. On the day of the feast he stood outside the door and listened, and when he heard the bridegroom’s voice his task was done, and he rejoiced greatly.

Brothers and sisters, listen carefully to where this friend’s joy comes from — not from “people are coming to me”, but from “the bridegroom has come”.

So he speaks those undying words: “He must increase, but I must decrease.”

In the early sixteenth century, the German painter Matthias Grünewald painted the famous Isenheim Altarpiece. At its centre is Christ on the cross. On the right stands John the Baptist, stretching out a long, thin, out-of-proportion forefinger that points to Christ, and beside him is a line of Latin — “He must increase, but I must decrease.” The twentieth-century theologian Karl Barth kept a reproduction of this painting hanging above his desk for decades. When someone asked him why, he said that finger is what a theologian should do: stand to one side and point to Christ.

Brothers and sisters, that finger isn’t pretty. It’s too long, too thin, too out of proportion. Yet when people all over the world look at that painting, no one is looking at the finger. Everyone is looking at the one the finger points to.

That is where John’s life succeeded. His success lay not in how many people he attracted, but in how many people he helped to see Jesus. And how did the Lord Jesus assess him? “Among those who are born of women there has not arisen anyone greater than John the Baptizer” (Matthew 11:11). A man who was glad to become small — God himself said he was the greatest.

sections.heading: 3. The Mirror of Psychology: We Care About Ourselves Far More Than We Think
sections.html:
Today many servants of God have real zeal, yet easily let people see “me” rather than “him” without meaning to. Mostly this isn’t hypocrisy; it’s that we don’t realise it. Psychology holds up a very honest mirror to us here.

In 1979 the social psychologists Michael Ross and Fiorella Sicoly published a study of “egocentric bias” in the Journal of Personality and Social Psychology. They asked husbands and wives each to estimate what percentage of the household tasks they themselves contributed. When the two estimates were added together, the total came to clearly more than a hundred per cent. Not because anyone was lying, but because we remember what we’ve done especially clearly, and what others have done only hazily.

Human memory is naturally drawn with ourselves at the centre. So in ministry we quite naturally overestimate our own weight, underestimate what others put in — and underestimate what God has done even more.

Another study is just as worth pondering. In 2000, Thomas Gilovich of Cornell University and his colleagues described the “spotlight effect”. They had participants put on an embarrassing T-shirt and walk into a room, then asked them to guess how many people had noticed. The participants’ estimates were roughly double the actual number. We always think there’s a spotlight shining on us. There isn’t.

Brothers and sisters, what freedom that is! You think everyone is watching whether you speak well or sing in tune — they aren’t. There is only one real spotlight, and it shines on Jesus.

When we long to be praised, to be seen, to be affirmed by people, it shows that “self” is still in control. True revival doesn’t focus on people; the focus turns entirely to Jesus.

sections.heading: 4. Applying the 321 Vision: Hand Over the Camera
sections.html:
In the 321 vision, this is called “Jesus is the focal point” — not ourselves, not other people, not our circumstances.

The first of the Three Foundations is: Jesus is my role model. The road he took ran from heaven to the manger, and from the manger to the cross — downward all the way. The Two Core Values are: let Jesus be King, and let Jesus receive all the glory — and these two are really two sides of one thing. If Jesus truly reigns as King in my heart, the glory will naturally go to him; if the glory keeps circling back to me, it shows that the one sitting on the throne is still me.

We can ask ourselves a very concrete question: if my name were taken off every piece of service I do this week, and no one knew it was me, would I still do it just as well and just as gladly?

John chapter 12 records that some Greeks had come up to Jerusalem for the feast. They came to Philip and said something that ought to be carved on the back of every church pulpit: “Sir, we want to see Jesus” (John 12:21).

Brothers and sisters, when people come among us, the one they ultimately want to see is Jesus. May we all become that finger pointing to Christ.

sections.heading: Key Point 2: Paul’s Life — Not Living for Himself, but Living Only for Jesus
1. One Confession That Turned a Whole Life Around
sections.html:
Paul’s whole life was a selfless life. He said, “I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me” (Galatians 2:20).

Brothers and sisters, to feel the weight of these words, we need to remember who said them. Paul, originally named Saul, came from Tarsus. He was educated at the feet of Gamaliel, the most renowned rabbi of his day (Acts 22:3); he held Roman citizenship; and he had advanced in Judaism beyond many of his own age (Galatians 1:14). In terms of credentials, few in the first generation of the church could match him.

He lists that CV himself, and then says, “However, I consider those things that were gain to me as a loss for Christ … and count them nothing but refuse, that I may gain Christ” (Philippians 3:7–8). The Greek word for “refuse” is σκύβαλον (skybalon) — kitchen scraps, rubbish thrown out into the street. Paul isn’t saying his learning was useless. He is saying: when these things stand between me and Christ, they are worth no more than rubbish.

This is the moment the self-centred life turns to selflessness.

Notice: “it is no longer I who live” is not self-annihilation, because the very next words are “but Christ lives in me”. Paul was still Paul. His mind, his temperament, his way with words, his missionary passion — none of it was lost. What changed was who sat on the throne.

In the 321 vision we say: selflessness is not having nothing; it is entering into the infinite and living out the infinite. “I” no longer live, but Christ lives in me. A cup is emptied not so that it can stay empty for ever, but so that it can be filled with something better.

sections.heading: 2. He Gave Thanks in Plenty, Was Content in Want, and Still Sang in Prison
sections.html:
Paul did not seek his own glory, nor did he fear people’s opinion.

When he wrote to the church in Philippi, he was a prisoner in Rome. He said, “I have learned in whatever state I am, to be content in it. I know how to be humbled, and I also know how to abound. In everything and in all things I have learned the secret both to be filled and to be hungry, both to abound and to be in need” (Philippians 4:11–12).

The Greek for “content” is αὐτάρκης (autarkēs), a favourite word of the Stoics of that day, meaning “self-sufficient” — being enough on your own. But Paul turns it completely on its head: “I can do all things through Christ, who strengthens me” (Philippians 4:13). Not self-sufficient but Christ-sufficient. Selfless people are not people with no needs; it’s that their contentment no longer depends on their circumstances.

Do you remember how the church in Philippi began? There Paul and Silas had their clothes torn off them, were beaten with many blows of the rod and thrown into prison with their feet fastened in the stocks. Then Scripture records this line: “But about midnight Paul and Silas were praying and singing hymns to God, and the prisoners were listening to them” (Acts 16:25). Midnight, the inner cell, the stocks, the wounds of the beating — singing hymns in a place like that isn’t a matter of being in a good mood. It’s because the King in their hearts hadn’t been replaced.

Then came a great earthquake, the prison doors flew open, and the jailer was about to kill himself — but Paul cried with a loud voice, “Don’t harm yourself, for we are all here!” (Acts 16:28). That night the jailer and his whole household came to the Lord. A man who would not save himself saved another man’s entire family.

sections.heading: 3. The Aim of His Ministry: Not to Build His Own Name
sections.html:
Paul’s ministry to the churches was not about building his own name, but about helping the brothers and sisters in those churches grow to maturity in Christ.

He put it very plainly: “For we don’t preach ourselves, but Christ Jesus as Lord” (2 Corinthians 4:5). The aim of all his labour was “that we may present every man perfect in Christ Jesus” (Colossians 1:28). To the Galatian believers who had broken his heart, he used the picture of a mother: “My little children, of whom I am again in travail until Christ is formed in you” (Galatians 4:19).

Notice that Paul’s aim was “Christ formed in you”, not “Paul formed in you”. A self-centred leader makes people unable to do without him; a selfless leader makes people unable to do without Jesus.

Paul even tore down comparison between co-workers: “I planted. Apollos watered. But God gave the increase” (1 Corinthians 3:6). He never hid his past: “sinners, of whom I am chief” (1 Timothy 1:15). And he was crystal clear about who all his achievements belonged to: “But by the grace of God I am what I am … yet not I, but the grace of God which was with me” (1 Corinthians 15:10).

His resolve was simple and clear — not to live for himself, but to live his whole life for Jesus. A life like that is a life God can use greatly. When a person is willing to be selfless, God has room, and his power is put on display.

sections.heading: 4. Confirmation from Management Studies: The Highest-Level Leaders Don’t Talk About Themselves
sections.html:
This spiritual principle has left its fingerprints even on secular research.

In his 2001 book Good to Great, the American management writer Jim Collins published a five-year study. From more than 1,400 listed companies, his team singled out eleven that had genuinely leapt from “good” to “great” and gone on beating the market for fifteen years, and then looked back to find what they had in common.

They had expected to find charismatic star CEOs. What they found was the exact opposite: these leaders were almost all names the media had never heard of. Collins called them “Level 5 leaders” and pointed out that two seemingly contradictory qualities lived side by side in them — intense professional will and deep personal humility. He also said that in success these leaders “look out of the window”, giving the credit to others, and in failure they “look in the mirror”, taking the responsibility on themselves. Mediocre leaders do the very opposite.

Brothers and sisters, this is only a business study. It can’t take the place of Scripture, but it stands as a side witness to Scripture: wherever fruit lasts, there is someone in the middle who doesn’t steal the camera. Scripture said it long ago: “God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble” (James 4:6).

sections.heading: 5. Applying the 321 Vision: Life First, Then Relationships, Then Ministry
sections.html:
Paul’s order is exactly the order 321 speaks of: life first, then relationships, then ministry. First he had the life of “it is no longer I who live”; only then came the testimony of singing in prison, and only then the ministry that carried the gospel across the Gentile world. Turn the order upside down, and the bigger the ministry gets, the emptier the person becomes.

We also see 321’s “235 relationships” working vividly in Paul’s life. He had spiritual companions, his “2” — Barnabas, Silas, Luke. He had spiritual children, his “3” — he called Timothy “my true child in faith” (1 Timothy 1:2). And beyond that, he joined a group of people with the fivefold ministries into a team of comrades, “for the perfecting of the saints, to the work of serving, to the building up of the body of Christ” (Ephesians 4:12).

Brothers and sisters, a self-centred person builds a stage; a selfless person builds a system. Only one person can stand on a stage, but a system can hold thousands upon thousands, each in their own place. This is exactly 321’s Goal — establish God’s system.

sections.heading: Key Point 3: The Selfless Life — Laying Down Myself, Having Jesus
1. Selflessness Is an Active Choice, Not a Passive Emptiness
sections.html:
Selflessness is not some hollow or passive state; it is an active choice — the choice to lay myself down and let Jesus reign.

Brothers and sisters, this has to be made clear, because many people are frightened the moment they hear the word “selflessness”. They think it means turning people into empty shells with no views of their own and no worth. Not at all. Human beings are made in the image of God, and that dignity was given by God himself. Paul says, “not to think of himself more highly than he ought to think; but to think reasonably” (Romans 12:3) — not rating ourselves too high, nor too low, but seeing ourselves in the place God has assigned.

So selflessness doesn’t deny our worth as persons. It puts the self back in its proper place — the place of a “servant” — so that the Lord can have complete first place in us. Colossians 1:18 says that Christ is the head of the body, the church, “that in all things he might have the preeminence”. The Greek for “have the preeminence” is πρωτεύω (prōteuō), meaning to be first. The whole order of Scripture rests on that word: he is first, I am second.

In the 321 vision, this is called “let man be man and let God be God”. Satan’s fall was those five “I will”s: “I will ascend into heaven! I will exalt my throne above the stars of God! … I will make myself like the Most High!” (Isaiah 14:13–14). Christ’s road is the very opposite — five steps downward: from the form of God, to not grasping, to emptying himself, to taking the form of a servant, to death on a cross. Brothers and sisters, those two roads still lie before us, every single day.

sections.heading: 2. Jesus Is the Perfect Role Model
sections.html:
Jesus himself is the most perfect role model. “Who, existing in the form of God, didn’t consider equality with God a thing to be grasped, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of men. And being found in human form, he humbled himself, becoming obedient to the point of death, yes, the death of the cross” (Philippians 2:6–8).

He laid down the glory of heaven, authority on earth, even sovereignty over his own life, only to accomplish the Father’s will. Through his selflessness came eternal victory, and the fire of revival has spread through every generation since.

The Lord himself explained the principle of this road: “Unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains by itself alone. But if it dies, it bears much fruit” (John 12:24). Brothers and sisters, if a grain of wheat keeps itself safe and sound, stored in the prettiest glass jar, a hundred years later it is still one grain. To become thousands of grains there is only one way — to fall into the ground and let its husk split open.

So the Lord goes on: “If anyone desires to come after me, let him deny himself, take up his cross, and follow me” (Luke 9:23). The Greek for “deny himself” is ἀπαρνέομαι (aparneomai), meaning “to disown, not to know” — the very word used of Peter denying the Lord three times. What Peter disowned was Jesus; what the Lord wants us to learn is to say to the old self, “I don’t know you. You are no longer my master.” And notice the word “daily”, which the Chinese Union Version has here: denying of self is not one big decision made once, but a small decision made every morning.

sections.heading: 3. A Witness in Creation: Only by Denying Itself Can It Carry
sections.html:
God has written this principle into his creation, and written it very clearly.

The first example is in our blood vessels. The last step in a red blood cell’s maturing in the bone marrow is to push out its own nucleus — the mature red blood cells of mammals have no nucleus. The reason is simple: clearing the space lets it carry more haemoglobin and deliver more oxygen. Only a cell that has given up its “core” can become the supplier of life to the whole body. It circulates for about a hundred and twenty days, carrying oxygen to every corner, and then is quietly broken down, and nobody remembers its name. Brothers and sisters, this isn’t a metaphor; it’s a fact taking place in your body every second. God long ago wrote “only selflessness can supply life” into our very blood.

The second example is over our heads. Look up at the moon at night. The moon is beautiful, yet it cannot give off a scrap of light of its own. According to NASA, the moon’s average albedo is only about twelve per cent; it reflects little more than a tenth of the sun’s light, yet that is enough to light up the whole wilderness so that the traveller by night can see the way. The moon’s greatness lies not in shining, but in facing the sun.

Brothers and sisters, we don’t need to become the sun. We just need not to turn our backs on it. The thing to fear most is the third case — a total solar eclipse: the moon moves between the sun and the earth, and day turns into night. The moon hasn’t done anything wicked; it’s simply standing in the wrong place. May God have mercy on us, and not let our “self” become that eclipse between someone else and Jesus.

sections.heading: 4. God Is Looking Today for People Willing to Be Selfless
sections.html:
Today God is still looking for people willing to be selfless — people who no longer pursue being seen, but are willing for Christ to be seen; who no longer exalt themselves, but let Jesus be exalted.

Church history has left a beautiful confirmation of this. At Herrnhut in eastern Germany lived a group of Moravian refugees who had fled persecution, led by the young nobleman Count Nicolaus Ludwig von Zinzendorf (1700–1760). At first they quarrelled and split into factions. Then, on 13 August 1727, as they shared Communion together, the Holy Spirit was poured out; people wept, confessed their sins and were reconciled. After that they organised a round-the-clock relay of prayer, taking turns day and night, which went on unbroken for more than a hundred years. And from this little village of fewer than six hundred people, missionaries were sent out who within twenty-odd years had reached the West Indies, Greenland, North America and South Africa.

Their motto was a single sentence: “May the Lamb that was slain receive the reward of his suffering.” Brothers and sisters, there isn’t a word in it about themselves.

It is generally said that the British evangelist Henry Varley once told the young D. L. Moody, “The world has yet to see what God can do with a man fully consecrated to him.” When Moody heard it, he said: by God’s help, I will be that man.

What God wants is not a more capable person; what God wants is a more empty vessel. “But we have this treasure in clay vessels, that the exceeding greatness of the power may be of God, and not from ourselves” (2 Corinthians 4:7). When we learn Jesus’ selflessness and let him reign within us, our lives become vessels of revival.

sections.heading: Integrating the 321 Vision: The Selfless Walk a Road That Goes Down Yet Leads to Heaven
1. The Three Foundations: Selflessness Has Roots; It Doesn’t Run on Feelings
sections.html:
The first foundation: Jesus is my role model. Selflessness isn’t some ascetic discipline of self-suppression; it is following a Lord who walks ahead of us. He emptied himself first; only then do we learn to empty ourselves. He said, “learn from me, for I am gentle and humble in heart” (Matthew 11:29).

The second foundation: the Bible is my standard. The boundaries of selflessness are to be drawn by Scripture, not by other people’s expectations. Some call it humility when they can’t say no and try to please everyone about everything. That isn’t selflessness; it’s just another form of fearing people. True selflessness hands sovereignty to God, not to the eyes of the crowd.

The third foundation: the Holy Spirit is my guide. “Self” cannot see itself; only the Holy Spirit can shine light on it. The Lord said that when the Spirit comes, “He will glorify me” (John 16:14). So the clearest mark of someone truly filled with the Holy Spirit isn’t that they are very excited, but that they very rarely talk about themselves.

sections.heading: 2. The Two Core Values and the Goal
sections.html:
The Two Core Values are: let Jesus be King, and let Jesus receive all the glory.

Letting Jesus be King means asking the “I” on the throne to step down. Brothers and sisters, let’s be honest here: the throne has only one seat. It isn’t that Jesus takes the big seat and I take the little one; he sits, and I stand.

Letting Jesus receive all the glory means turning all the applause upward. “Not to us, Yahweh, not to us, but to your name give glory, for your loving kindness, and for your truth’s sake” (Psalm 115:1). The Hebrew word for glory is כָּבוֹד (kabod), whose basic meaning is “weight”. Human beings cannot bear God’s weight; insist on carrying it, and it will only crush you.

The Goal is: establish God’s system. The difference between a system and a stage is the difference between the self-centred life and selflessness. Self-centred people must stand in the middle, so all they can ever have is a stage; selfless people are glad to let others step up, so they can establish a system.

sections.heading: 3. The Fivefold Change: It Starts with the Mindset
sections.html:
321 says that change is fivefold: mindset, life, daily living, relationships and ministry. Change the mindset and you change the life; change the life and you change daily living. What today’s lesson attacks is the very top of that stream — the mindset.

The old mindset says: I have to be seen to have any value. The new mindset says: if Jesus is seen, I’m satisfied.

The old mindset says: if others increase, I decrease. The new mindset says: he must increase, but I must decrease — that is simply the order of heaven.

The old mindset says: if I lay myself down, I’ll have nothing. The new mindset says: if I lay myself down, I have Jesus.

At the same time this is a fourfold shift of perspective: from the human to the divine — no longer asking “What do people think of me?” but “How does God see this?”; from the earthly to the heavenly — no longer fighting over seats on earth; from the temporary to the eternal — applause is temporary, fruit is eternal; from the worldly to the godly — no longer measuring service by the world’s rules of success.

sections.heading: 4. The 920 Practice and the 235 Relationships
sections.html:
First, the 920 practice. Everyone we have a relationship with is our “2”. In front of every “2”, we practise living out a selfless (0) life and bearing the fruit of the Spirit in all nine (9) of its expressions — “love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith, gentleness, and self-control” (Galatians 5:22–23).

Brothers and sisters, notice that not one of these nine graces can be grown on your own. Patience needs someone hard to bear with; gentleness needs a situation that makes your blood boil. The person you’ll meet this morning — your spouse, your children, that co-worker who always has plenty of opinions — is today’s “2”. Selflessness isn’t perfected on a mountain with nobody around; it is lived out where people are.

Second, the 235 relationships. Become a “2”, a spiritual companion, to selfless people; build “3”, spiritual parents and spiritual children; and go on to become a “5”, a fivefold-ministry team of spiritual comrades. Notice that all three numbers share one precondition: selflessness. Self-centred people can’t find true companions, only an audience; self-centred people can’t raise spiritual children, only fans. Selflessness is the doorway to every genuine relationship.

sections.heading: 5. The Path of Serving
sections.html: 321 describes the Path of Serving in five stages: Spirit — the Holy Spirit is my guide; Understanding — the Bible is my standard; Life — Jesus is my role model; Service — let Jesus be King; God — let Jesus receive all the glory. Every step on this road dismantles something: my judgement, my ideas, my ways, my sovereignty, my glory. Dismantle all the way, and what remains is Christ living in me. This is the Road to Revival — a road that goes down, and leads to heaven.

sections.heading: Putting It into Practice: Walking It Through with the Eight Stages of Changing Our Mindset
sections.html:
The lesson gives us three practices. We’ll walk them all the way through using 321’s eight stages of changing our mindset — Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication.

Practice 1: In my service today, do I want people to see “me” or “Jesus”?

Information: The focus of revival is always Jesus. Write John 3:30 somewhere you’ll see it today.

Revelation: Information stays in the head; revelation reaches the heart. Ask the Holy Spirit to show you one concrete picture — when was the most recent time you actually wanted people to see you? Don’t justify it. Let that picture stay in front of you for thirty seconds.

Conviction: Say to God, “Lord, I admit that in that moment I wanted people to see me.” Conviction isn’t a feeling; it’s agreeing that God is right.

Implementation: From today, ask yourself just one question each night before you sleep: today, whom did people see in me?

Evaluation and Correction: After a week, look back over the seven days’ answers, pick out the situation that came up most often, and set a new action for it. For example: every time you’re praised, first say in your heart, “Lord, you did this,” and only then reply.

Repetition and Multiplication: Keep it up for forty days until it becomes instinct. Then find a brother or sister, teach them this practice, and ask each other how it’s going.

Practice 2: List three things you need to “lay yourself down” over

The lesson suggests four directions: glory, sovereignty, control and opinions. Actually take a sheet of paper and write three things down.

Information and Revelation: First read Philippians 2:6–8 and see what the Lord laid down — glory (existing in the form of God), rights (not counting equality a thing to be grasped), status (taking the form of a servant), sovereignty (becoming obedient to the point of death). Every single thing he laid down was far greater than anything we have to lay down.

Conviction and Implementation: Over each thing, say, “Lord, I’ve been clutching this one in my hand, because I’m afraid.” Then this week find one occasion for each where you really let go. Laying down glory — take one chance you have to tell your own story and use it to talk about Jesus instead. Laying down sovereignty — hand one matter you’ve always decided yourself to someone else to decide. Laying down opinions — in one discussion, listen to everything and speak last, or not at all.

Evaluation and Correction: Which one was hardest? The hardest one is the last stronghold of “self”. Don’t berate yourself; make it your prayer topic for this season.

Repetition and Multiplication: Ask the Holy Spirit to help you learn to surrender, and share in your small group how God has been dealing with you.

Practice 3: Practise, for real, “stepping back and letting the Lord reign” once

It can be very simple: give an opportunity to lead to someone else, and sincerely pray for their success; in an argument that’s about to lock up, be the first to say, “You have a point”; at home, give up the right to have the last word.

321 says: pride stirs up pride, and both sides lose; humility draws out humility, and both sides win. Arguments heat up not usually because of the issue itself, but because two “selves” are colliding. As soon as one person takes half a step back, the whole temperature drops.

When you evaluate, please don’t ask, “I stepped back — did the other person appreciate it?” That’s back to “self” again. Ask instead: “When I stepped back, was Jesus seen?”

Multiplication: When your family or your group members see that you really did step back, they’ll ask you why. That is the best moment you’ll ever have to speak about Jesus.

A Gentle Reminder

Selflessness isn’t losing yourself; it’s letting Jesus take the place of the self. Laying yourself down isn’t weakness; it’s where strength begins.

Brothers and sisters, remember what the Lord said to Paul: “My grace is sufficient for you, for my power is made perfect in weakness” (2 Corinthians 12:9). The place where we have stepped back as far as we can go is exactly the place where God’s power begins.

sections.heading: Closing and Call: When He Is Lifted Up, Revival Is Sure to Come
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, let’s go back to where we started.

The starting point of the Road to Revival is selflessness. When we are willing to lay ourselves down and let Jesus have first place, his life can flow out through us. True revival isn’t about what we have done; it is about Jesus being “seen” in us. When he is lifted up, revival is sure to come.

The Lord himself said, “And I, if I am lifted up from the earth, will draw all people to myself” (John 12:32). What draws people isn’t our programmes, our eloquence or our size; it is Christ lifted up.

So this morning we are going to make a decision. Not a decision to try harder, but a decision to step further back; not a decision to do great things, but a decision to be a nobody; not a decision to be seen, but a decision to let him be seen.

Let Jesus be King — King in my home, King in my service, King in the deepest room of my heart, the one even I’d rather not open. Let Jesus receive all the glory — not a share of it, but all of it given to him. Because the only praise in heaven is this: “Worthy is the Lamb who has been killed to receive the power, wealth, wisdom, strength, honor, glory, and blessing!” (Revelation 5:12).

Brothers and sisters, a lighthouse is at its most successful when no one is looking at the lighthouse. May we, all our lives, be that long, thin finger pointing to Christ; may people see in us only Jesus.

“For the earth will be filled with the knowledge of Yahweh’s glory, as the waters cover the sea” (Habakkuk 2:14). And this revival begins with one small step back that you take this morning.

keyVerses: I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me. That life which I now live in the flesh, I live by faith in the Son of God, who loved me, and gave himself up for me. (Galatians 2:20)
declarations: Lord, I am willing to learn your ways, to lay down my own rights and pride, and to let you reign completely in me. May everything I do let people see Jesus and not myself. Use me, I pray, as a vessel of revival, so that your glory fills the whole earth.
practices: List three things you need to “lay yourself down” over
prayer: Dear Heavenly Father, we thank you.

Lord, we confess that there is a very big “self” inside us. It doesn’t shout or make a fuss, yet it often sits on the throne; it doesn’t commit great sins, yet it often blocks your light. This morning we are willing to hand it over.

Lord Jesus, you existed in the form of God, yet you emptied yourself, took the form of a servant and became obedient to the point of death. You are our role model; put that heart of yours that emptied itself within us.
Holy Spirit, shine your light on us and let us see the parts of ourselves we cannot see; give us courage, day by day, to say to the old self: I don’t know you; you are no longer my master.

Lord, we are willing to decrease so that you may increase; we are willing to step back so that people may see you. Use us as vessels of revival, so that in our homes, our fellowship and our cities Jesus is lifted up, Jesus reigns as King, and Jesus receives all the glory.
In the holy name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen.
discussion: John 3:30 says, “He must increase, but I must decrease.” Share a “decreasing moment” you have truly experienced in your heart — when someone else was seen and you were overlooked. What was your first inner reaction at the time? Looking back today, what does God want to teach you through it?

Philippians 2:6–8 describes Christ’s five steps downward. Following the lesson’s suggestions, name the one thing you most need to lay down right now — glory, sovereignty, control or opinions. What concrete action will you take this week to practise it? Pray for one another, and ask each other how it went at the next meeting.
l061.title: Selflessness: The Road to Revival
l061.subtitle: Let People See Jesus, Not Me
l061.partTitle: Unit 5 · The Road to Revival — Selflessness

sections.heading: Introduction: The Mirror That Cannot See Itself
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, good morning. This morning, let’s begin with a picture.

A couple who have been married for twenty-seven years sit in front of their pastor. They have been arguing over something small, and they simply cannot talk it through. The husband says, “She has never once seen how much I give to this family.” The wife says, “I’ve put up with it for twenty-seven years, and my feelings have never been respected.” Both of them speak from the heart; both of them are in tears. The pastor listens quietly to the end and asks just one question: “In everything you’ve both just said, was there a single sentence that didn’t start with ‘I’?”

The room suddenly went quiet. In that moment the two of them finally saw it: they hadn’t been defeated by each other. They had both been defeated by the same thing — “self”.

That is the subject we face today: “self” is the root of our fall.

The human body has a wonderful design — and a wonderful limitation. On the retina of each of our eyes, at the place where the optic nerve leaves the eyeball, there are no light-sensitive cells. That small patch sees nothing at all; in medicine it is called the “blind spot”. Even more remarkable, we are normally completely unaware it exists, because the brain automatically “fills in” the hole with the surrounding image, so that we think we are seeing everything.

Brothers and sisters, that is exactly what “self” is like in our lives. It sits right in the middle of our line of sight. It makes us miss a whole piece of the truth, and we have no idea; we even think we see perfectly clearly. Other people’s faults we see in sharp detail, but our own “self” stays in the blind spot.

So if we want to understand why humanity lost the glory and authority God first gave it, we have to go back to the beginning. When God created human beings, he made them in his own image and likeness. At that time there was no “self” in them, only “the likeness of God”. People then were selfless — living entirely under God’s rule, of one heart with God and walking with him, working alongside God and walking with him.

But Satan used an extremely cunning lie to make humanity fall from selflessness into the self-centred life. He got people to start gazing at themselves, wanting to be like God, wanting to decide good and evil for themselves. From that moment, all of humanity’s suffering and corruption began.

In today’s lesson we’ll answer four questions together: What were the first human beings like? How did “self” get in? What did “self” bring with it? And how do we go back? May the Holy Spirit himself, this morning, remove the blind spot from before our eyes.

sections.heading: Scripture Background: Reading from the First Page of the Bible
sections.html:
Our theme passage comes from Genesis chapter 1. Genesis is the first of the five books of Moses, and both Jewish tradition and the Lord Jesus’ own citations point to Moses as the author of the Pentateuch. The Lord Jesus said to the Jews, “For if you believed Moses, you would believe me; for he wrote about me” (John 5:46). Moses wrote somewhere between the fifteenth and thirteenth centuries BC, and his first readers were the Israelites who had just come out of Egypt and were walking through the wilderness.

That background matters a great deal. These people had just left Egypt — a system that treated Pharaoh as a god, honoured idols and made humanity itself the ultimate authority. They had been slaves there for more than four hundred years, their heads full of Egypt’s view of the world. Moses was to lead them into Canaan, and the first thing he did was not to teach them how to fight but to tell them all over again: there is only one Creator of the universe; human beings are not gods; human beings are made in the image of God.

When we read Genesis against the background of the ancient Near East, the contrast is even more striking. In the Babylonian creation myth, the Enuma Elish, human beings are slaves the gods made to spare themselves toil — labourers mixed from the blood of a slain god. But Genesis says human beings are made in the image of God, are blessed, and are entrusted with ruling the whole earth. One says humanity is dregs; the other says humanity is a representative. One says we are born base; the other says we are born with dignity.

Brothers and sisters, please hold on to this point: from the very beginning, human dignity did not come from ourselves. It came from being made “in the image of God”. A person’s worth lies not in who they are, but in whom they reflect. That sentence is the key to today’s whole lesson.

Genesis chapters 1 to 11 read like a medical file on “self”. Chapters 1 and 2 record the original pattern — the healthy human being. Chapter 3 records the turning point of the fall — the moment the illness struck. From chapter 4 on, they record the spread of “self” — Cain killing his brother, Lamech boasting, the flood destroying the world, Babel’s tower being built. Read straight through, and we see that humanity’s problem doesn’t get more and more complicated; the same diseased root keeps copying itself.

The other half of our theme passage comes from Philippians. Paul wrote this letter around AD 60–62, while he was imprisoned in Rome. Philippi was a Roman colonial city in Macedonia, whose inhabitants were proud of their Roman citizenship and set great store by status, position and rank. And it was precisely there, in chains, that Paul wrote: “For to me to live is Christ, and to die is gain” (Philippians 1:21).

A man locked up in prison, still able to say “to me to live is Christ” — what kind of life is that? It is the most beautiful footnote there is to selflessness.

So Genesis answers “Where did ‘self’ come from?” and Philippians answers “Where should ‘self’ go?” One book was written in a tent in the wilderness, the other in a Roman prison, fifteen hundred years apart, yet they point to the same answer: let God be God and let man be man; live not for ourselves, but only for Christ.

sections.heading: 1. The Original Pattern: Human Beings Were Originally Selfless
sections.html:
Scripture says, “God created man in his own image. In God’s image he created him; male and female he created them” (Genesis 1:27).

Before this verse, God first declared his intention: “God said, ‘Let’s make man in our image, after our likeness. Let them have dominion over the fish of the sea, and over the birds of the sky, and over the livestock, and over all the earth, and over every creeping thing that creeps on the earth’” (Genesis 1:26). And once they were made, God blessed them: “Be fruitful, multiply, fill the earth, and subdue it” (Genesis 1:28).

Notice the order: first the “image”, then “dominion”; first “being like God”, and only then “ruling on God’s behalf”. Authority isn’t something human beings seize for themselves; it comes from “reflecting God”.

The Hebrew word for “image” is tselem, which originally meant a statue, a carved likeness, a representation; “likeness” is demut, meaning resemblance, correspondence. In the ancient Near East, when a king conquered a territory, he would often set up a statue of himself at its borders, announcing to everyone: this land has a lord, and the lord is me. When God placed human beings in this world, they were the “image” God set up. Standing among all created things, human beings are there to announce one thing: this land has a Lord, and the Lord is God.

So the original purpose of humanity’s creation was to reflect God’s glory, not to display ourselves. When people are selfless, they are filled with God’s image, and God’s life, God’s authority and God’s glory flow naturally from them. People like that can rule the whole earth, and can live out true contentment.

Paul makes it even clearer with another picture: “But we all, with unveiled face seeing the glory of the Lord as in a mirror, are transformed into the same image from glory to glory, even as from the Lord, the Spirit” (2 Corinthians 3:18).

Brothers and sisters, a mirror gives off no light. A mirror’s greatest glory is to show the sun. If one day a mirror decided, “I don’t want to reflect anyone else any more; I want to shine by myself,” what would happen? It wouldn’t become the sun. It would just become a cold sheet of glass. That is the story of humanity.

So the lesson puts it very precisely: selflessness is not blankness, nor weakness, but letting God fill us completely. Only selfless people carry the glory of God himself. It’s like clear glass: only when it has no colour and no shape of its own can light pass through it unhindered.

There’s a scientific basis behind this picture too. Ordinary clear float glass used in buildings lets through roughly ninety per cent of visible light; the purer, the more colourless and the freer of impurities the glass is, the higher its light transmission. Stained glass is beautiful, but it blocks part of the light; frosted glass has plenty of character, but the light loses its shape.

In this life we often spend a great deal of effort turning ourselves into glass with “colour, character and style”, hoping others will see our beauty. But God says: child, I made you to be a clear window, so that others can see me through you.

In Book 14 of The City of God, Augustine has a passage of great depth. He says there are two cities, formed by two loves: the earthly city by the love of self, even to the contempt of God; the heavenly city by the love of God, even to the contempt of self. Brothers and sisters, these two cities are fighting for territory in our hearts today.

At this point someone may ask: can people really not see their own problems? Psychology gives us an answer that cuts to the heart. The Swedish psychologist Ola Svenson, in a study published in Acta Psychologica in 1981, found that among the American drivers he surveyed, about ninety-three per cent believed their driving skill was above average. Statistically that’s impossible — ninety-three per cent of people cannot be above the median.

This phenomenon later came to be called the “better-than-average effect”. What does it show? It shows that we come fitted with a built-in magnifying glass that always enlarges ourselves, and a built-in reducing glass that always shrinks others. This isn’t a bad habit we picked up along the way; the factory settings are broken. And Scripture tells us when that fault occurred — in the Garden of Eden.

From the perspective of the 321 vision, this is exactly what the first of the Three Foundations answers: Jesus is my role model. Hebrews says, “His Son is the radiance of his glory, the very image of his substance” (Hebrews 1:3). The Lord Jesus is the one completely selfless human being — the prototype of humanity, and our map for the way home. We are not trying hard to become a better version of ourselves; we are being restored to the pattern we were first created in.

So remember: selflessness is not having nothing; it is entering into the infinite and living out the infinite. An empty cup isn’t useless — only an empty cup can hold water. An empty room isn’t desolate — only an empty room can be lived in. What God wants is not a you that has been emptied out, but a you that has been filled.

sections.heading: 2. The Appearance of “Self”: Where the Fall Began
sections.html:
When Satan tempted Eve, he said, “For God knows that in the day you eat it, your eyes will be opened, and you will be like God, knowing good and evil” (Genesis 3:5).

At its core, this sentence is the beginning of “self”.

Let’s look first at Satan’s method. Genesis chapter 3 opens: “Now the serpent was more subtle than any animal of the field which Yahweh God had made” (Genesis 3:1). The Hebrew for “subtle” is ‘arum, while at the end of chapter 2 we read that the man and his wife “were both naked, and they were not ashamed” — and that word “naked” is ‘arummim. The two words sound almost the same. Scripture uses a play on words to lay the scene out before us: naked humanity meets the cunning serpent. Innocence meets deceit. It is an unequal fight — unless humanity holds fast to God’s word.

Satan’s attack comes in three steps. Step one is to cast doubt on God’s word: “Has God really said, ‘You shall not eat of any tree of the garden’?” (Genesis 3:1). Step two is to deny God’s word: “You won’t really die” (Genesis 3:4). Step three is to take God’s place: “you will be like God, knowing good and evil” (Genesis 3:5).

Notice that last step. In Hebrew, “knowing good and evil” is not simply about “knowing”; it means deciding for yourself, ruling for yourself, what is good and what is evil. What Satan sold humanity was never a piece of fruit. What he was selling was a throne. He was saying: you don’t need to listen to God any more; you can be your own standard.

Brothers and sisters, that is the definition of “self” — I want to be my own god.

Eve had already been made in God’s image, yet because she wanted to “be like God”, she lost God’s likeness. What an irony! What was already in her hand, she reached out to steal; what she already had, she struggled to grab. She began to put herself at the centre, wanting to decide the standard for herself — what is good and what is bad, what is worth it and what isn’t. When “self” enters the human heart, people no longer treat God as God; they make themselves their own god.

From that moment, humanity’s relationship with God was broken; humanity lost its spiritual authority and came under the dominion of sin and the curse.

Satan had in fact walked this road himself first. Isaiah records: “You said in your heart, ‘I will ascend into heaven! I will exalt my throne above the stars of God! I will sit on the mountain of assembly, in the far north! I will ascend above the heights of the clouds! I will make myself like the Most High!’” (Isaiah 14:13–14). Five “I will”s in a row. The very road on which Satan himself fell, he sold to humanity unchanged — and humanity bought it.

The lesson says something well worth meditating on: if Eve had said at that moment, “I don’t need to be like God — I already have God’s image,” she would not have been deceived, and she would not have lost the blessing. This shows that “self” is often just a single thought away.

A single thought, a world of difference. Before she reached out her hand, she was still God’s daughter; after she reached out, she had become her own slave. Brothers and sisters, every day we stand at the same crossroads. In that one second, will you listen to God telling you who you are, or to yourself telling you who you want to become?

There is a well-known finding in psychology that helps us understand how frightening “self” is. In 1999, Justin Kruger and David Dunning published research in the Journal of Personality and Social Psychology showing that those who perform worst at a given skill often overestimate their own performance most severely — because the very ability needed to judge one’s own competence accurately is the ability they lack.

This became widely known as the “Dunning–Kruger effect”. Brothers and sisters, listen carefully: the most frightening thing about “self” is not that it makes us fall, but that after we have fallen, it makes us feel we have risen higher. After Eve ate the fruit, her eyes were indeed opened — but the first thing she saw was not the mysteries of God; it was that “they were naked” (Genesis 3:7). She thought she would gain wisdom; all she gained was shame.

Let me give another example, from the history of science. For more than a thousand years, people firmly believed that the earth was the centre of the universe, with the sun, the moon and the stars all revolving around us. Then, in 1543, Copernicus published On the Revolutions of the Heavenly Spheres and moved the earth out of the centre. At first that was seen as an insult to human dignity, but it was later proven true — and it brought modern astronomy its freedom and its breakthroughs.

Brothers and sisters, every one of our lives needs a “spiritual Copernican revolution”: move “me” out of the centre, and let God return to the centre. At first it will feel like being hurt, like being wronged, like being demoted. But once you really move aside, you’ll find the whole universe suddenly lines up.

In terms of the 321 vision, here is the most important sentence: pride is leaving our originally intended position, seizing rights and wanting to take God’s place; humility is laying down our rights and returning to our originally intended position — let man be man and let God be God. Eve’s tragedy was not that she wasn’t good enough, but that she wasn’t willing to be properly human. Our tragedy today is the same: we are often defeated not by weakness, but by “refusing to return to our originally intended position”.

So remember: once “self” is exalted, God is displaced; once “self” is enlarged, authority is taken away. Humanity’s fall began with seeing itself; humanity’s revival begins with “seeing no one else but Jesus”.

sections.heading: 3. The Root of Sin and Suffering: Born of “Self”
sections.html:
Adam and Eve were driven out of the Garden of Eden because of “self”; Cain, because of “self”, envied his brother and shed his blood; the strife, wars and divisions of every age have all arisen from “self”.

Let’s take it step by step. After the fruit was eaten, God came into the garden and called to the man: “Where are you?” (Genesis 3:9). This is the first question God asks a human being in the Bible. Of course God knew where Adam was. What God was asking was: how did you get to this point?

And how did Adam answer? “The man said, ‘The woman whom you gave to be with me, she gave me fruit from the tree, and I ate it’” (Genesis 3:12).

Brothers and sisters, look closely at how that sentence is built. First he blames the woman, then he blames God — “the woman whom you gave”. The first fruit wasn’t even digested, and the first shifting of blame was already out of his mouth. “Self” doesn’t just sin; “self” is very good at defending itself. “Self” doesn’t just hide from God; “self” will take God to court along with everyone else.

Then comes the second generation. “But he didn’t respect Cain and his offering. Cain was very angry, and the expression on his face fell” (Genesis 4:5). God didn’t condemn him straight away; instead he reasoned with him: “If you do well, won’t it be lifted up? If you don’t do well, sin crouches at the door. Its desire is for you, but you are to rule over it” (Genesis 4:7).

God gave Cain a chance — a door to turn around. But “self” would not be persuaded. And the result? “Cain said to Abel, his brother, ‘Let’s go into the field.’ While they were in the field, Cain rose up against Abel, his brother, and killed him” (Genesis 4:8).

The first baby ever born in human history grew up to become the first murderer. The first death was not from old age; it was a man struck down by his own older brother. And the starting point of it all was simply, “My offering wasn’t accepted.”

Brothers and sisters, aren’t our quarrels today stamped from the very same mould? Marital conflict, broken families, church disputes, power struggles at work — every one of them begins with “my feelings, my views, my rights”.

James puts it very bluntly: “Where do wars and fightings among you come from? Don’t they come from your pleasures that war in your members?” (James 4:1). The war outside comes from the war inside; the fire in the home is a fire that has spread from the heart.

The apostle John lists the three faces of “self” in one go: “For all that is in the world, the lust of the flesh, the lust of the eyes, and the pride of life, isn’t the Father’s, but is the world’s” (1 John 2:16).

The lust of the flesh is “I want to enjoy”; the lust of the eyes is “I want to have”; the pride of life is “I want to be seen”. Three different wrappings, and inside each the same word — I.

If people keep seeking to satisfy themselves, they will only become emptier and emptier. Why? John goes on: “The world is passing away with its lusts, but he who does God’s will remains forever” (1 John 2:17). Try to fill an eternal heart with things that pass away, and of course it never gets full.

There is a weighty piece of scientific support for this. In 2003 the psychologist Roy Baumeister and his colleagues published a large-scale review of the literature in Psychological Science in the Public Interest. Having examined decades of research on “self-esteem”, they concluded that high self-esteem does not really improve academic results or job performance, nor does it reduce violence, bullying or antisocial behaviour; many aggressors in fact rate themselves quite highly.

In other words, lifting “me” higher has not made people healthier, kinder or happier.

Furthermore, the psychologists Jean Twenge and Keith Campbell, drawing on long-term data, have shown that American college students’ average scores on the Narcissistic Personality Inventory rose markedly from the late 1970s to the mid-2000s. This generation values the self more than the last — but is not necessarily any happier than the last.

Brothers and sisters, the curve that science has measured, the Bible wrote down in chapter 3 more than three thousand years ago.

So the lesson says: “self” is the root of sin; selflessness is the path of holiness. When we enlarge “self”, the problems grow too; when we lay “self” down, the problems fade away with it.

Today’s world exalts “the self” and “human rights”, yet forgets that “God’s rule” is the foundation of everything. Please note: we are not against human dignity and rights — human dignity is exactly what the very first chapter of the Bible proclaims. What we are saying is this: if human rights are not built on the foundation that “humanity is made in the image of God”, they become a contest in which whoever shouts loudest wins. If people make themselves the centre, then however many rights they win, they will only bring deeper confusion and harm.

In the chapter “The Great Sin” in Book 3 of Mere Christianity, C. S. Lewis says that pride is “the complete anti-God state of mind”, the chief of all the vices. He reminds us that other sins make people fall, but pride makes people think they are standing — and precisely because it can’t be seen, it is the hardest to cure.

The Reformer Martin Luther, in his Lectures on Romans of 1515–1516, used a vivid phrase to describe fallen humanity — “curved in on itself”. Like someone bent over at the waist, eyes fixed on the tips of their own shoes, walking a whole lifetime without once looking up at the sky. Brothers and sisters, that is the posture of “self”.

The Bible’s definition of “sin” is really the same picture: “All we like sheep have gone astray. Everyone has turned to his own way; and Yahweh has laid on him the iniquity of us all” (Isaiah 53:6). You see, “sin” here is defined not as committing some monstrous evil, but as “turning to his own way”. The way of self is the way of sin. That’s why Paul says, “for all have sinned, and fall short of the glory of God” (Romans 3:23). The moment people go their own way, a piece of God’s glory goes missing.

The Lord Jesus takes this to its root: “Most certainly I tell you, everyone who commits sin is the bondservant of sin” (John 8:34). Those bound by “self” look like the freest people of all — I do whatever I want. In reality they are the least free — the very things I don’t want to do, I keep on doing.

From the perspective of the 321 vision, this section gives us a very practical reminder: life first, then relationships, then ministry; people matter more than tasks, relationships matter more than things. How many families have hurt “people” over “tasks”, and ruined “relationships” over “things”? At the end of all the fighting, the task gets done but the people have scattered; the things are kept but the relationship is gone.

Remember this saying: pride stirs up pride, and both sides lose; humility draws out humility, and both sides win. Our quarrels are seldom because the other person is so bad; mostly it’s because two “selves” have collided. When two stones crash together, both are damaged; but if one is willing to become cotton wool, the fire goes out.

sections.heading: 4. Returning to God’s Intention: From the Self-Centred Life to Selflessness
sections.html:
The starting point of revival is not outward reform but inward surrender. If people are to regain God’s authority, they must first return to the pattern of creation — selflessness.

Paul says, “For to me to live is Christ, and to die is gain” (Philippians 1:21). This is the definition of selflessness. When what is within us is no longer “me” but “him”, we regain the authority to rule and to overcome.

Elsewhere Paul says it more fully: “I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me. That life which I now live in the flesh, I live by faith in the Son of God, who loved me, and gave himself up for me” (Galatians 2:20).

Notice those last words: “gave himself up for me”. Selflessness turns out not to be a virtue we invented; it is something the Lord did for us first. He gave himself up first, and so we can give ourselves up; he emptied himself first, and so we dare to be emptied.

Philippians chapter 2 draws this road most clearly: “Have this in your mind, which was also in Christ Jesus, who, existing in the form of God, didn’t consider equality with God a thing to be grasped, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of men. And being found in human form, he humbled himself, becoming obedient to the point of death, yes, the death of the cross” (Philippians 2:5–8).

The Greek word behind “emptied himself” is kenoō, which literally means “to empty oneself out”. Brothers and sisters, set these two pictures side by side:

In the Garden of Eden, a human being who had no divine status to boast of reached out to seize God’s place. In heaven, the Lord who existed in the form of God did not count equality with God a thing to be grasped, but emptied himself, came down, took on human likeness, and walked all the way to the cross.

One grabbed upward; the other poured himself out downward. The wrong step Eve took in Eden, the Lord Jesus retraced, step by step, at Golgotha.

So the Lord said to his disciples, “If anyone desires to come after me, let him deny himself, and take up his cross, and follow me. For whoever desires to save his life will lose it, and whoever will lose his life for my sake will find it” (Matthew 16:24–25).

The Greek for “deny himself” shares its root with the word used of Peter denying the Lord three times. What does it mean to deny ourselves? It means that when “self” leaps up again to fight for the throne, we say just one thing to it: I do not know this man.

Some people grow frightened when they hear this: won’t there be nothing left of me? The Lord himself answered that fear: “Most certainly I tell you, unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains by itself alone. But if it dies, it bears much fruit” (John 12:24).

When a grain of wheat falls into the ground, it isn’t destroyed; it is set free. What it loses is the shape of one grain; what it gains is a whole field of wheat. This is what 321 means: selflessness is not having nothing; it is entering into the infinite and living out the infinite; “I” no longer live, but Christ lives in me.

Let me illustrate with a picture from everyday life. Suppose that in a symphony orchestra there is a violinist of outstanding technique who insists on his own tempo, his own volume, his own interpretation. What happens? The whole piece is ruined. A truly mature musician keeps his ears open — he listens to others, he watches the conductor, he places himself within the whole. And the wonderful thing is that when no one is grabbing for attention, everyone’s voice is actually heard.

The church is an orchestra, and the conductor is Jesus. A family is a small orchestra too. If you and I are willing to lay down our own beat, the music will be so beautiful it moves people to tears.

Let me give you one more picture from science. On 14 February 1990, the Voyager 1 spacecraft, about six billion kilometres from Earth, turned round and took a photograph of our planet. In that photograph the whole Earth is a point of light smaller than a single pixel, suspended in a beam of sunlight. The astronomer Carl Sagan called it the “Pale Blue Dot”.

Brothers and sisters, that “I” we quarrel over, get hurt over, lie awake all night over — in that photograph it doesn’t even take up one pixel. Yet here is the most wonderful thing about the Bible: the God who made the entire universe cares for the people on that tiny dot of light, and even gave up his own Son for them.

So Paul says, “while we don’t look at the things which are seen, but at the things which are not seen. For the things which are seen are temporal, but the things which are not seen are eternal” (2 Corinthians 4:18). The 321 vision describes this as a shift of perspective: from the human perspective to God’s, from the earthly to the heavenly, from the temporary to the eternal, from the worldly to the godly. Once the perspective shifts, the “self” that had us so tightly bound suddenly looks very small.

The lesson ends this section beautifully: selflessness is not a rejection of who we are; it is letting Christ live in me. It is not giving up on ourselves, but being filled by God. The less we fix our eyes on ourselves, the more we reflect the glory of Christ.

John the Baptist summed up this road in a single short sentence: “He must increase, but I must decrease” (John 3:30). Notice: not “I must disappear”, but “I must decrease” — I step back to the place where I ought to stand, so that he can stand where he ought to stand. That is returning to our originally intended position: let man be man and let God be God.

sections.heading: 5. Integrating the 321 Vision: The Selfless Life and God’s System
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, 321 is not a set of slogans; it is a road home. Today’s lesson strings the whole core of 321 together.

First, the Three Foundations. One: Jesus is my role model — he “emptied himself” (Philippians 2:7). He is the only completely selfless human being, the living map for our return to the original pattern. Two: the Bible is my standard — Eve’s fall, in the end, was a change of standard: she swapped God’s word for her own judgement. If today we don’t hand the standard back to the Bible, we will replay that scene from Eden. Three: the Holy Spirit is my guide — no one can break free of “self” by their own effort, just as a hand can’t grasp itself and a knife can’t whittle its own handle. Only the Holy Spirit can do in us what we cannot do.

Next, the Two Core Values. First, let Jesus be King. Brothers and sisters, a heart has room for only one throne. Either I sit on it or he does. Eve’s problem wasn’t that she wanted good things; it was that she wanted to sit in that chair. Second, let Jesus receive all the glory. Paul says, “Whether therefore you eat, or drink, or whatever you do, do all to the glory of God” (1 Corinthians 10:31). When the glory goes back to God, our hearts are lightened; if the glory stays on us, sooner or later it will crush us.

Then the Goal: establish God’s system. The Garden of Eden was the first expression of God’s system — God reigning as King, humanity as steward, all things in their proper place. The moment “self” came in, that system collapsed. Today God is re-establishing that system on earth — and that is the church. And what will one day be completely fulfilled is what the Lord’s Prayer says: “Let your Kingdom come. Let your will be done on earth as it is in heaven” (Matthew 6:10).

321 speaks of the old self and the new self. Paul says, “that you put away, as concerning your former way of life, the old man that grows corrupt after the lusts of deceit, and that you be renewed in the spirit of your mind, and put on the new man, who in the likeness of God has been created in righteousness and holiness of truth” (Ephesians 4:22–24). Look at that last phrase — the new self is “in the likeness of God … created”. Brothers and sisters, do you hear it? The new self is the human being of Genesis chapter 1, restored. The old self is self-centred; the new self is selfless. The gospel doesn’t patch up the old self; it puts on the new.

And again: “knowing this, that our old man was crucified with him, that the body of sin might be done away with, so that we would no longer be in bondage to sin” (Romans 6:6). The way to deal with the old self is not to improve it but to crucify it with Christ.

321 says: humility overcomes pride; selflessness overcomes Satan. Why can selflessness overcome Satan? Because every attack of Satan needs a point of leverage, and that point of leverage is our “self”. His way of dealing with you is first to make you care about yourself — care about face, about winning and losing, about whether it’s fair. When there is no “self” in a person left to be trodden on, the enemy has nowhere to get a grip. As the lesson’s gentle reminder says: what Satan fears most is not how hard you try, but your willingness to be selfless. He can make use of your effort; he can’t make use of your cross.

321 speaks of fivefold change: mindset, life, daily living, relationships and ministry. Change the mindset and you change the life; change the life and you change daily living. In today’s lesson the first step is a change of mindset — from “my problem is my circumstances, other people, bad luck” to “my problem is ‘self’”. Once that mindset turns, life begins to turn; once life turns, daily living follows; once daily living turns, relationships are restored; and once relationships are restored, ministry has roots.

Paul says, “Don’t be conformed to this world, but be transformed by the renewing of your mind, so that you may prove what is the good, well-pleasing, and perfect will of God” (Romans 12:2). Everything begins with “the renewing of your mind”.

321 speaks of the priority of relationships: first with God, then with ourselves, then with others, and last with things. Many people live their whole lives in a whirl precisely because they walk this order backwards — busy with things first, then coping with people, occasionally dealing with themselves, and thinking of God last of all. Get the order wrong, and people fall apart.
