321 says: rely on the heart and the Holy Spirit, not on the brain and ourselves; rely on the brain and you worry, rely on the heart and you rejoice. Scripture says, “Keep your heart with all diligence, for out of it is the wellspring of life” (Proverbs 4:23).

For practical training, today’s lesson is especially suited to 920. What is 920? Everyone we have a relationship with is our “2”. When we practise living out the selfless “0” in front of them, we bear the fruit of the Spirit in all nine of its expressions — “But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith, gentleness, and self-control” (Galatians 5:22–23). Brothers and sisters, look carefully: not one of these nine is borne for ourselves; every one of them can only be borne within relationships. A person shut up alone in a room can’t practise patience; a person alone with themselves can’t practise gentleness. God has put that hardest-to-get-along-with person beside you not to wear you down, but to bear fruit in you.

Then come the 235 relationships. A selfless person doesn’t walk alone. We become a “2” with others who are likewise selfless, spiritual companions who support one another; then we build “3” — spiritual parents and spiritual children — passing life on; and finally we become a “5” — a fivefold-ministry team of spiritual comrades working hand in hand. One person alone can go fast; only a band of selfless people can go far.

Finally, the Path of Serving: Spirit, Understanding, Life, Service, God. The Holy Spirit is my guide (Spirit), the Bible is my standard (Understanding), Jesus is my role model (Life), let Jesus be King (Service), let Jesus receive all the glory (God). Brothers and sisters, every step of this road is another goodbye said to “self”.

sections.heading: 6. Putting It into Practice: Going Deeper with the Eight Stages of Changing Our Mindset
sections.html:
The lesson gives us three very concrete practices:

First, ask yourself every day: “Are the decisions I make today meant to satisfy myself, or to glorify God?”

Second, when you feel hurt or offended, practise asking: “Are my feelings in charge here, or is Jesus in charge within me?”

Third, list the three things you have been most “stubbornly attached” to lately, and pray for the Lord to help you let them go and let Jesus reign.

Next, we’ll use 321’s eight stages of changing our mindset to take these three practices deeper and make them solid.

Stage one, Information. This morning you have already received the information: “self” is the root of our fall. Copy out three verses by hand — Genesis 1:27, Genesis 3:5 and Philippians 1:21. Words you have copied by hand are the ones that come to live in your heart.

Stage two, Revelation. Information stays in the head; revelation reaches the heart. Ask the Holy Spirit to shine his light with a simple prayer: “Search me, God, and know my heart. Try me, and know my thoughts. See if there is any wicked way in me, and lead me in the everlasting way” (Psalm 139:23–24). Don’t ask God to point out other people’s faults; ask him to point out my “self”.

Stage three, Conviction. Conviction isn’t just agreeing; it’s surrendering. Take a sheet of paper and write one sentence: “I admit that ‘self’ is the root of all my problems.” Write it, then sign and date it. Nodding is easy; signing is a decision.

Stage four, Implementation. This is where the lesson’s three practices touch the ground.

Practice one lands in the morning: tomorrow, the first thing you do when you open your eyes is not to look at your phone but to ask yourself that question — are the decisions I make today meant to satisfy myself, or to glorify God? Write it on a sticky note and put it by your bed or next to the mirror.

Practice two lands in the moment of conflict: when that remark stings you or that look wounds you, don’t respond yet. Pause in your heart for three seconds and ask: are my feelings in charge here, or is Jesus in charge within me? Brothers and sisters, three seconds is often the distance between heaven and hell.

Practice three lands this week: actually take a pen and list the three things you are most stubbornly attached to — perhaps a position, a word of vindication, or an insistence that the other person must apologise first. List them, and bring them one by one before the Lord in prayer: Lord, I put this into your hands; you be King.

Stage five, Evaluation. Give yourself three minutes each night before you sleep to look back quietly: how many times today did I put myself at the centre? What was I caring about in that moment? There’s no need to berate yourself; just be honest.

Stage six, Correction. Evaluation without correction is merely regret. The quickest form of correction is an apology. If someone was hurt by your “self” today, go and say sorry to them. Brothers and sisters, one sincere apology proves you’ve really let go better than ten prayer meetings.

Stage seven, Repetition. These eight stages aren’t done once and finished; we walk them round and round. In a study published in the European Journal of Social Psychology in 2010, the psychologist Phillippa Lally and her colleagues found that forming a new habit takes on average about sixty-six days, with wide individual differences, from eighteen days to more than two hundred. Brothers and sisters, change doesn’t come from one moment of being moved; it comes from repeating, again and again. “Self” is a lifelong lesson, and denying of self is a daily one — in the Lord Jesus’ own words in Luke 9:23, as the Chinese Union Version renders them, we are to take up our cross “daily” and follow him.

Stage eight, Multiplication. What you have received, pass on to one person. This week, find one of your “2”s — your spouse, a child, a colleague, a brother or sister in your small group — and share one sentence from today’s lesson with them. Multiplication is the final and truest test of any practice; only what can be passed on has truly been received.

sections.heading: 7. Closing and Call: No Longer Seeing Myself, Seeing Only Jesus
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, we have come to the end of today’s lesson — and to a new beginning.

“Self” makes people fall; selflessness brings revival. When we no longer see ourselves but see only Jesus, the life of heaven will flow out from within us once again.

Let’s look back once more over the road: in the beginning, human beings were selfless, full of God’s image. Satan used a lie to make humanity see itself, and humanity fell from selflessness into the self-centred life; from then on sin, suffering, strife and death spread on and on. Then the Son of God came. He “emptied himself” and walked the completely opposite road, retracing step by step at Golgotha the wrong turn taken in Eden. Now he invites us: follow me — come home.

Listen to the lesson’s gentle reminder: what Satan fears most is not how hard you try, but your willingness to be selfless. A heart that has laid itself down is a channel through which God’s mighty power flows.

Brothers and sisters, God has never been short of capable people; what God is short of is “empty” people. A pipe doesn’t need to be wide, only clear; glass doesn’t need to be thick, only transparent; a cup doesn’t need to be beautiful, only empty.

So this morning, let’s make a decision together: let Jesus be King, and let Jesus receive all the glory.

Let him reign as King in your home — not your opinions, but him. Let him reign as King in your emotions — not your feelings, but him. Let him reign as King in your plans, in your service, in your wallet, in your diary.

Let us return to the original pattern — living not for ourselves but only for Christ, so that his glory is fully displayed in us.

The Lord Jesus said, “I am the vine. You are the branches. He who remains in me and I in him bears much fruit, for apart from me you can do nothing” (John 15:5). The branch doesn’t need to fight for glory on the vine’s behalf; the branch only needs to stay connected.

May each of us today be that clear window, so that people can see through us the Lord of glory.

keyVerses: “God created man in his own image. In God’s image he created him; male and female he created them.” (Genesis 1:27)
“For to me to live is Christ, and to die is gain.” (Philippians 1:21)
practices: Ask yourself every day: “Are the decisions I make today meant to satisfy myself, or to glorify God?”
When you feel hurt or offended, practise asking: “Are my feelings in charge here, or is Jesus in charge within me?”
List the three things you have been most “stubbornly attached” to lately, and pray for the Lord to help you let them go and let Jesus reign.
prayer: Dear Lord Jesus, we thank you. In the beginning you made us in your own image and gave us dignity and authority; it was we ourselves who reached out to grab a place that never belonged to us.

Lord, I confess that “self” is the root of all my problems. Forgive me for the times I have fixed my eyes on myself, relied on myself and insisted on my own way. Forgive me for making “my feelings, my views, my rights” my standard, and for hurting those around me at home, at church and at work for the sake of my own face.
Lord, remove the blind spot from before my eyes, so that I can see my own “self”; and remove that “self” from before my eyes, so that I see only you.
From today, I am willing to lay down “self” and let you reign within me, so that I may live out your image again and recover the glory of your original creation.
Holy Spirit, remind me every day: “I” no longer live, but Christ lives in me. Make me an empty vessel, filled by you; a clear window through which people can see you.
May you reign as King; may you receive all the glory. In the holy name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen.
discussion: Discussion 1: Genesis 3:5 says, “For God knows that in the day you eat it, your eyes will be opened, and you will be like God, knowing good and evil.” Eve already bore God’s image — so why was she still drawn by the temptation to “be like God”? What in your life recently has shown you that you too want to “decide good and evil for yourself”?

Discussion 2: Philippians 1:21 says, “For to me to live is Christ, and to die is gain.” For you, which area is hardest to hand over right now — the hardest in which to let Jesus be King? This week, what concrete action will you take to say “I don’t know you” to the “self” in that area?
l062.title: “Self” Is the Root of Our Fall
l062.subtitle: The Road Home from the Self-Centred Life to Selflessness
l062.partTitle: Unit 5 · The Road to Revival — Selflessness

sections.heading: Introduction: Who Sits at the Centre of Your Life?
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, good morning. Early this morning I’d like to begin with a piece of the history of astronomy.

In AD 1543 the Polish astronomer Copernicus, lying on his deathbed, received a freshly printed copy of his book On the Revolutions of the Heavenly Spheres. The book said just one thing: the earth is not the centre of the universe; the earth goes round the sun. At the time it sounded close to absurd. People looked up at the sky and plainly saw the sun rise in the east and set in the west — how could it be the earth that was moving? Yet once humanity accepted that shift, astronomy for the first time could calculate accurately, see clearly and go far.

Brothers and sisters, have you noticed? What Copernicus did was not to remove the earth, nor to destroy it. He simply put the earth back in the place where it had always belonged. The earth is still the earth; it just no longer pretends to be the centre.

That is exactly the lesson we are going to learn together today, and it is the very heart of the 321 vision — “selflessness”.

“Selflessness” is not losing yourself. It is not the extinction of your personality. It is not turning into someone with no thoughts and no feelings. “Selflessness” is letting Jesus replace “me” as the centre of my life. The earth was not destroyed; it simply no longer sits on the throne at the centre. In the same way, I as a person am not destroyed; it is just that “I” no longer reign as king — I let Jesus be King.

Inside every one of us is a deeply rooted “earth-centred universe”. Its language is easy to recognise, because it has only three phrases: I want, I feel, I think. Something happens, and our first reaction is, “I feel he shouldn’t treat me like this.” A decision has to be made, and our first criterion is, “What do I want?” Our days go round and round inside those three phrases — for thirty years, for fifty years — and we still end up back where we started.

Modern brain science offers a piece of corroborating evidence. In 2001 Marcus Raichle, a neuroscientist at Washington University in the United States, proposed what he called the “default mode network”: when a person is not engaged in any particular task and the mind is idle, one group of regions in the brain actually becomes more active — and the chief content of that activity is thinking about “self”. In other words, the human brain’s screensaver is “me”. Science cannot stand above the Bible, but it confirms from the side what Scripture said long ago: unless a person is renewed, his default centre is himself.

That is why Paul’s declaration in Galatians 2:20 is so staggering. Brothers and sisters, notice this: Paul is not boasting about his own spiritual attainment. He is bearing witness to an exchange of life, a relocation of the centre — from “me” at the centre to “Jesus” at the centre.

This is the life of “selflessness”. And this is the heart of revival.

This morning I want to ask you to carry three questions with you, and not to put them down all day.

The first question: this thing I am doing today — is it so that people will see me, or see Jesus?

The second question: this decision I am making today — am I relying on my own cleverness, or on the guidance of the Holy Spirit?

The third question: this outcome I am pursuing today — is it to satisfy myself, or to please the Lord?

These three questions are the three key points of this lesson, and they are the threefold shift of a “selfless” life: a shift of goal, a shift of means, and a shift of centre of gravity. May the Holy Spirit himself today invite us down from the throne at the centre, and let Jesus take his seat there.

sections.heading: Scripture Background: A Letter Written in the Heat of Battle
sections.html:
Galatians was written by the apostle Paul. Most evangelical scholars believe it is the earliest of Paul’s letters, written around AD 48–49, that is, around the time of the Jerusalem Council (Acts 15). It was addressed to the churches of Galatia that Paul had planted on his first missionary journey, including Pisidian Antioch, Iconium, Lystra and Derbe (Acts 13–14).

Why did Paul write this letter? Because a group of teachers known as the “Judaizers” had followed in his footsteps, telling these Gentile believers: believing in Jesus isn’t enough; you must be circumcised and keep the law of Moses before you are truly saved. It sounded “more rigorous, more devout”. In fact it was putting people back on the track of “relying on self”. For the essence of legalism has never been godliness; it is “the self-centred life” — a person trying to win himself a standing by his own deeds, his own credentials, his own performance.

The theme verse comes in Galatians 2:20, and its context is crucial. Galatians 2:11–14 records the famous “Antioch incident”. The apostle Peter had been eating at the same table as the Gentile believers, but when the men from James arrived — “For before some people came from James, he ate with the Gentiles. But when they came, he drew back and separated himself, fearing those who were of the circumcision” (Galatians 2:12). And what did Paul do? “But when Peter came to Antioch, I resisted him to his face, because he stood condemned” (Galatians 2:11).

Brothers and sisters, see this clearly: Peter drew back not because he couldn’t work out the theology, but because he was “afraid”. Afraid of what? Afraid of what people would think, afraid for his own image, afraid of losing face in front of his own people. That is “the self-centred life” — while “I” still sit at the centre, even an apostle will play the hypocrite.

From that incident Paul goes on all the way to the heart of justification by faith, and reaches the summit in 2:19–20: “For I, through the law, died to the law, that I might live to God. I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me.”

There are three words in the original here worth looking at closely.

First, “I have been crucified with Christ” — in the Greek, συνεσταύρωμαι (synestaurōmai), in the perfect tense and the passive voice. The perfect tense means something completed in the past whose effect continues right up to the present. The passive voice means I did not climb up onto the cross myself; God put me there. So “crucified with Christ” is not a goal I must strive to reach; it is an accomplished fact, and all I need to do is stand on it by faith day by day.

Second, “no longer I” — in the Greek, οὐκέτι ἐγώ (ouketi egō), literally “no longer that I”. “ἐγώ” is the root of the English word ego. Paul says it plainly: the “I” who used to reign has stepped down from the throne.

Third, the word closest of all to “selflessness” appears in Philippians 2:7: “emptied himself” — in the Greek, ἐκένωσεν (ekenōsen), from the verb κενόω, meaning “to empty out”. The Lord Jesus emptied himself and took the form of a servant. Brothers and sisters, notice this: after the Lord Jesus emptied himself, he did not become nothing. On the contrary, he became Lord of all: “God also highly exalted him, and gave to him the name which is above every name” (Philippians 2:9).

This is what the 321 vision wants us to see: selflessness is not having nothing; it is entering into the infinite and living out the infinite. “I” no longer live, but Christ lives in me.

The setting in which Paul wrote this letter was a battle over “who will be King”. And that battle is still going on today in the heart of every one of us.

sections.heading: 1. A Shift of Goal: No Longer Living for Myself, but Letting People See Jesus
sections.html:
The first step of “selflessness” is to change the goal we live for.

1. The Example the Lord Jesus Set

Every day the Lord Jesus lived on earth, his aim was not to make people know him, but to make them know the Father. Once Philip said to him, “Lord, show us the Father.” How did the Lord answer?

Jesus said to him, “Have I been with you such a long time, and do you not know me, Philip? He who has seen me has seen the Father. How do you say, ‘Show us the Father?’ (John 14:9)

This is one of the most wonderful pieces of self-testimony in the whole Bible. The Lord Jesus did not say, “You must get to know me properly.” He said, “If you have seen me, you have seen the Father.” His whole existence was a transparent window; what people saw through him was the Father.

He also said, “For I have come down from heaven, not to do my own will, but the will of him who sent me.” (John 6:38)

The word “will” here is θέλημα (thelēma) in the Greek, meaning intention, purpose, desire. It is not that the Lord Jesus had no will of his own. In the garden of Gethsemane he said, “Father, if you are willing, remove this cup from me” (Luke 22:42). But straight after that he said, “Nevertheless, not my will, but yours, be done.” That is “selflessness” — not having no will, but placing your own will beneath the Father’s will.

That is why the Lord could say, “He who speaks from himself seeks his own glory, but he who seeks the glory of him who sent him is true.” (John 7:18) The line between true and false runs right here.

2. Scripture Interpreting Scripture: Let Your Light Shine Before People, and Give the Glory to the Father

Someone may ask: does that mean we shouldn’t do anything at all — just go and hide? No. The Lord put it in perfect balance:

Even so, let your light shine before men; that they may see your good works, and glorify your Father who is in heaven. (Matthew 5:16)

Look at how this verse is built: the deeds are to be seen, but the glory is to go to the Father. The Lord did not tell us to hide our light; he told us to pass the glory on. True “selflessness” is not refusing to shine; it is shining and then not letting the credit stay with you.

Paul put this goal as clearly as it can be put: “For we don’t preach ourselves, but Christ Jesus as Lord, and ourselves as your servants for Jesus’ sake.” (2 Corinthians 4:5)

3. An Illustration from Life: Why the Moon Can Light Up the Night

Brothers and sisters, think about the moon.

The moon does not give off any light of its own. Astronomers have measured it: the moon’s surface reflects only about twelve per cent of the light that falls on it, which means nearly eighty-eight per cent of the sunlight striking it is absorbed. The lunar surface is actually quite dark — about as dark as old asphalt. And yet this grey, dull ball can light up an entire wilderness at night.

Why? Because it faces the sun, and it never claims that the light is its own.

What’s more interesting still: when is the moon at its least bright? When it squeezes in between the sun and the earth, wanting to stand right at the front — that’s called a solar eclipse. At that moment it blocks the light, and the sky goes dark. When are we least able to let people see Jesus? Precisely when we push in front of Jesus because we want to be seen.

True revival is this: when people see you, they see Jesus.

4. Supporting Evidence from Psychology: The Spotlight Effect

Why do we long so much to be seen? To a large extent, we have been taken hostage by an illusion.

In 2000 the Cornell University psychologists Thomas Gilovich, Victoria Medvec and Kenneth Savitsky published a series of experiments and proposed what they called the “spotlight effect”. They asked college students to put on a deeply embarrassing T-shirt and walk into a classroom full of people, and then to estimate what proportion of those present had noticed. On average the students guessed about half; when the people in the room were actually asked, only about a quarter had really noticed.

The researchers’ conclusion: we consistently overestimate how much attention others pay to us. We live as though there were a spotlight above our heads, when in fact that light is switched on only inside our own hearts.

The twentieth-century Christian apologist C. S. Lewis is commonly credited with saying that humility is not thinking less of yourself, but thinking of yourself less. Scholars still debate where the saying comes from, but the insight agrees with Scripture. John the Baptist put it most beautifully of all: “He must increase, but I must decrease.” (John 3:30)

5. Applying the 321 Vision: Jesus Is the Focal Point

The first of the 321 vision’s foundations is “Jesus is my role model”. As the Lord Jesus lived, so I live. His goal was to let people see the Father; my goal is to let people see him.

321 also keeps reminding us: Jesus is the focal point — not ourselves, not other people, not our circumstances. Focus on yourself, and you live in comparison and inferiority; focus on other people, and you live in criticism and complaint; focus on your circumstances, and you live in anxiety and fear. Only when Jesus is the focal point are we secure.

This is also a change of perspective: from man’s to God’s, from the earthly to the heavenly, from the temporary to the eternal, from the worldly to the godly. Man’s perspective asks, “If I do this, what will people think of me?” God’s perspective asks, “If I do this, will it let people see Jesus?”

A life like that will shine with heavenly light in the most ordinary of days. When people see our humility, gentleness, forgiveness and love, they will be drawn — not because we are good, but because we bear the likeness of Jesus.

sections.heading: 2. A Shift of Means: No Longer Relying on Myself, but Wholly Relying on Jesus
sections.html:
Once the goal has shifted, the means must shift with it. For if the goal is Jesus but the method is still “me”, the road still leads nowhere.

1. Part of Your Heart, or All of It?

The Bible says:

Trust in Yahweh with all your heart, and don’t lean on your own understanding. In all your ways acknowledge him, and he will make your paths straight. (Proverbs 3:5–6)

There are a few Hebrew words here worth pausing over.

“With all your heart” is בְּכָל־לִבְּךָ (bekol-libbekha) in the original — literally “with the whole of your heart”. Not a portion of your heart handed over to God, but the entire heart.

“Trust” is בָּטַח (batach) in the original, and the picture is vivid: it means “to lean your whole weight upon”, like someone lying full-length on a bed. Not steadying yourself with a hand, but resting your whole weight on it.

“Understanding” is בִּינָה (binah) in the original, meaning discernment, comprehension. God did not say, “Have no understanding.” He said, “Don’t lean on your own understanding.” You may use your head; just don’t rest your whole life on your head.

2. Scripture Interpreting Scripture: Even the Lord Jesus Did Not Rely on Himself

The Lord Jesus said:

Most certainly, I tell you, the Son can do nothing of himself, but what he sees the Father doing. For whatever things he does, these the Son also does likewise. (John 5:19)

Brothers and sisters, what astonishing words. The one speaking them is the Son of God, the Lord who created all things. If even he, in his days on earth, chose not to act on his own, how much more should we?

The Bible has a heartbreaking example of this. Joshua 9 records how the Gibeonites put on worn-out clothes and carried mouldy bread to deceive the Israelites, claiming they had come from a distant land. How were the Israelites taken in? The Bible explains it in a single sentence: “The men sampled their provisions, and didn’t ask counsel from Yahweh’s mouth.” (Joshua 9:14)

Notice: it isn’t that they didn’t check. They did — they looked at the clothes, touched the bread, listened to the story. They used every ounce of their own cleverness; they just didn’t ask God. And the result was a mistaken treaty that stayed with Israel for hundreds of years.

3. A Scientific Illustration: Why People Can’t Walk in a Straight Line

In 2009 Jan Souman and his colleagues at the Max Planck Institute for Biological Cybernetics in Germany published a study in the journal Current Biology. They had volunteers walk through a forest and the Sahara Desert, recording their routes by GPS. They found that as long as the sun or the moon was in the sky as a point of reference, people could walk more or less in a straight line; but once clouds covered the sun, or there was no moon at night, people began to walk in circles without realising it — sometimes even crossing ground they had just covered — and were completely unaware of it.

Brothers and sisters, what a portrait of us. Without an outside point of reference, a person who goes by his own sense of direction is bound to walk in circles while believing he is moving forward. Some people’s predicament ten years ago is exactly the same ten years on. It isn’t that they haven’t tried hard; it’s that they have only one point of reference — themselves.

In 1999 David Dunning and Justin Kruger of Cornell University published research describing what later came to be called the “Dunning–Kruger effect”: the less competent people are in a given area, the more likely they are to overestimate themselves, because what they lack is precisely the competence needed to see their own shortcomings. Our biggest blind spot is not knowing we have blind spots.

That is why Proverbs says, “There is a way which seems right to a man, but in the end it leads to death.” (Proverbs 14:12) The trouble with that road is not that it looks evil, but that it “seems right to a man”.

4. The Fruit of Reliance: Strong in Weakness

When we rely on ourselves, anxiety and failure are bound to follow; but when we choose to rely on the Lord, we find strength in weakness and a way out of every predicament.

Yahweh says: “Cursed is the man who trusts in man, relies on strength of flesh, and whose heart departs from Yahweh.” (Jeremiah 17:5)

“Blessed is the man who trusts in Yahweh, and whose confidence is in Yahweh. For he will be as a tree planted by the waters, who spreads out its roots by the river, and will not fear when heat comes, but its leaf will be green, and will not be concerned in the year of drought. It won’t cease from yielding fruit.” (Jeremiah 17:7–8)

Brothers and sisters, notice: the tree planted by the waters is not spared the heat, nor does it escape the drought. The heat still comes; the drought still happens. The difference is this — its roots are not at the surface; its roots are in the water.

Paul learned this lesson. The Lord said to him, “My grace is sufficient for you, for my power is made perfect in weakness.” And Paul answered, “Most gladly therefore I will rather glory in my weaknesses, that the power of Christ may rest on me.” (2 Corinthians 12:9)

So a life like this is no longer “I can” but “the Lord can”; no longer “I decide” but “the Lord leads”. Every act of surrender and reliance is a practice of “selflessness”.

5. Applying the 321 Vision: Rely on the Heart and the Holy Spirit, Not on the Brain and Ourselves

The second and third foundations of 321 are “the Bible is my standard” and “the Holy Spirit is my guide”. Relying on the Lord doesn’t mean wandering about by feelings; it means running on two clear rails: the Bible is the objective standard, the Holy Spirit is the subjective guide, and the two never conflict, because the Bible itself was inspired by the Holy Spirit.

321 has a reminder that is very plain yet cuts to the heart: rely on the heart and the Holy Spirit, not on the brain and ourselves; rely on the heart and you’ll be glad, rely on the brain and you’ll be troubled. The wellspring of life flows from the heart. Turning something over and over until you can’t sleep at midnight is usually relying on the brain and ourselves; bringing it before the Lord and handing it over, until your heart grows quiet — that is relying on the heart and the Holy Spirit.

This also brings about the fivefold change: mindset, life, daily living, relationships and ministry. Change the mindset and you change the life; change the life and you change daily living. Once our mindset about reliance changes, the whole line of our life changes with it.

Not by might, nor by power, but by my Spirit. (Zechariah 4:6)

sections.heading: 3. A Shift of Centre: No Longer Seeking My Own Benefit, but Pleasing Jesus
sections.html:
“Selflessness” is not only humility in behaviour; it is a transformation of motive. Behaviour can be faked; motive cannot.

1. The Watershed of Motive

So long as “satisfying myself” remains our starting point, our lives will still be held captive by Satan, even when what we do is good; but when we turn to seeking “to please the Lord”, we are set free from the dominion of sin.

Paul says:

Therefore also we make it our aim, whether at home or absent, to be well pleasing to him. (2 Corinthians 5:9)

“We make it our aim” is φιλοτιμέομαι (philotimeomai) in the original. Literally it means “to hold honour dear”, “to be ambitious”; in the Greco-Roman world it was a word full of drive. Paul does not tell us to abolish ambition; he redirects it: the one great ambition of my whole life is to please the Lord.

“Well pleasing” is εὐάρεστος (euarestos) in the original, meaning “acceptable, wholly satisfying”.

So a truly selfless person does not ask, “Is this of any benefit to me?” but, “Will this make the Lord’s heart glad?”

2. Scripture Interpreting Scripture: The Love of Christ Constrains Us

Where does this change of motive come from? Not from gritting our teeth and holding on; it is love that drives it.

For the love of Christ constrains us; because we judge thus, that one died for all, therefore all died. He died for all, that those who live should no longer live to themselves, but to him who for their sakes died and rose again. (2 Corinthians 5:14–15)

“Constrains” is συνέχω (synechō) in the original, carrying the sense of “gripping tightly, hemming in, pressing on”, the way riverbanks hold the water in so that it can only rush in one direction. The love of Christ does not gently encourage us; it grips us tightly, so that our whole life can flow in only one direction.

Paul was also very honest about the state of things in his day: “For they all seek their own, not the things of Jesus Christ.” (Philippians 2:21) And he asked himself, “Or am I striving to please men? For if I were still pleasing men, I wouldn’t be a servant of Christ.” (Galatians 1:10)

And there is a path to pleasing God: “Without faith it is impossible to be well pleasing to him, for he who comes to God must believe that he exists, and that he is a rewarder of those who seek him.” (Hebrews 11:6) Enoch was such a man: “Enoch walked with God, and he was not found, for God took him” (Genesis 5:24).

The highest example is still the Lord himself. By the Jordan the Father bore witness to him: “This is my beloved Son, with whom I am well pleased.” (Matthew 3:17) And the Lord said, “He who sent me is with me. The Father hasn’t left me alone, for I always do the things that are pleasing to him.” (John 8:29)

3. An Illustration from Life: A Tale of Two Lakes

Israel has two famous bodies of water, both fed by the same river Jordan.

In the north is the Sea of Galilee. The Jordan flows in from the north and flows out again to the south. Water comes in and goes out, so the water is alive: fish abound, the shores are green, and most of the Lord Jesus’ ministry took place there.

In the south is the Dead Sea. The Jordan flows in and never flows out again, because there is no outlet; the water can leave only by evaporation, and the minerals left behind build up year after year, until the Dead Sea’s salinity reaches around thirty per cent — roughly ten times that of ordinary seawater. The result? No fish can live there, no water plants can grow, and nothing living can make its home in it.

Brothers and sisters, the same source of water, the same sunshine — why is one a sea of life and the other a sea of death? There is only one difference: one is willing to give out, and the other keeps everything for itself.

A life lived only for yourself looks like “storing up”, but in reality it is “turning to salt”.

4. Supporting Evidence from Psychology: Spending Money on Others

In 2008 Elizabeth Dunn and Lara Aknin of the University of British Columbia and Michael Norton of Harvard Business School published a study in the journal Science. In the morning they gave participants a sum of money and randomly assigned half of them to spend it on themselves and the other half to spend it on someone else; that evening they measured how happy they were. The group that had spent the money on others was clearly happier.

Of course, the Bible is the highest standard and psychology can only play a supporting role; but this finding at least tells us that human beings were made to “flow out”, not to “pile up”. The Lord said it long ago: “It is more blessed to give than to receive.” (Acts 20:35)

The twentieth-century missionary Jim Elliot wrote in his journal in 1949: “He is no fool who gives what he cannot keep to gain what he cannot lose.” Six years later he was martyred while taking the gospel to the Auca people of Ecuador. He was just twenty-eight.

5. Applying the 321 Vision: Let Jesus Be King, Let Jesus Receive the Glory

This is precisely the Two Core Values of 321: let Jesus be King; let Jesus receive all the glory.

To let Jesus reign as King is to stop asking, in every decision, “What do I want?” and to ask instead, “What does the King want?” To let Jesus receive all the glory is, after every success, not to keep the credit in your own hands but to pass it straight up to him.

Paul says, “But we have this treasure in clay vessels, that the exceeding greatness of the power may be of God, and not from ourselves.” (2 Corinthians 4:7) The moment a clay vessel starts drawing attention to how finely made it is, people can no longer see the treasure inside.

Life is no longer about amassing wealth, chasing a name and guarding power for ourselves, but simply about glorifying him. A life like this sets us free from “the bondage of gain and loss” and brings us into the free life of “overcoming in all things”.

Whether therefore you eat, or drink, or whatever you do, do all to the glory of God. (1 Corinthians 10:31)

sections.heading: 4. Integrating the 321 Vision: Selflessness Is Returning to Our Originally Intended Position
sections.html:
Having walked through the three shifts, let’s spread out the whole picture of 321 once more and take another look.

1. The Three Foundations, the Two Core Values, the Goal

The Three Foundations are: Jesus is my role model, the Bible is my standard, the Holy Spirit is my guide. The three key points of this lesson fit exactly onto these three foundations: the shift of goal, because Jesus is my role model; the shift of means, because the Bible is my standard and the Holy Spirit is my guide; and the shift of centre, so that Jesus may be satisfied.

The Two Core Values are: let Jesus be King, let Jesus receive all the glory. These are exactly the two sides of “selflessness”. I step down, he steps up; I am hidden, he is magnified. Paul says, “as always, now also Christ will be magnified in my body.” (Philippians 1:20)

The Goal is: establish God’s system. Whatever is built with “me” at the centre is a human system; only what is built with Jesus at the centre is God’s system. The same family, the same church, can be God’s system or a human system; the only difference is who sits at the centre.

2. The Old Self Is “Self-Centred”, the New Self Is “Selfless”

“The self-centred life” is the root of humanity’s fall. The words the serpent spoke to the woman are words we must remember all our lives: “For God knows that in the day you eat it, your eyes will be opened, and you will be like God, knowing good and evil.” (Genesis 3:5) Satan did not tell people to go and worship idols. He simply told them to be “like God” — you can be your own god; you can define good and evil for yourself.

Trace it further back, to the words of Satan’s own fall, where he says “I will” five times: “You said in your heart, ‘I will ascend into heaven! I will exalt my throne above the stars of God! I will sit on the mountain of assembly, in the far north! I will ascend above the heights of the clouds! I will make myself like the Most High!’” (Isaiah 14:13–14)

So 321 puts it with great precision: pride is leaving our originally intended position, seizing rights and wanting to take God’s place; humility is laying down our rights and returning to our originally intended position — let man be man and let God be God.

And the promise of Scripture is certain: “God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble.” (James 4:6)

And so humility overcomes pride, and selflessness overcomes Satan. Pride provokes pride, and both sides lose; humility draws out humility, and both sides win. Why does a quarrel between husband and wife keep getting bigger? Because one side’s pride provokes the other’s. How does peace in a family begin? Very often, because one person humbles himself first.

3. Selflessness Is Not Having Nothing; It Is Entering the Infinite

Many people are frightened the moment they hear “selflessness”: won’t there be nothing left of me? Brothers and sisters, it is exactly the opposite.

Put a drop of water on a table and in a few hours it has dried up; put the same drop into the ocean and it lasts as long as the ocean does. Selflessness is not the water vanishing; it is the water entering the infinite.

The Lord Jesus said, “For whoever desires to save his life will lose it, and whoever will lose his life for my sake will find it.” (Matthew 16:25) He also said, “Most certainly I tell you, unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains by itself alone. But if it dies, it bears much fruit.” (John 12:24)

If a grain of wheat insists on keeping itself, its end is to remain for ever just one grain.

4. Life First, Then Relationships, Then Ministry

The 321 vision says: life first, then relationships, then ministry. People matter more than tasks; relationships matter more than things. The priority of relationships is: first with God, then with ourselves, then with others, and last of all with things.

The self-centred person has the order exactly reversed: things first, then people, and only then God. So he is very busy, very tired, very accomplished — and very lonely. The selfless person first puts his relationship with God right; when the life is right, the relationships come right; when the relationships are right, the ministry has life in it.

Here 321 gives us two concrete practices.

The first is the 920 practice. Everyone we are in a relationship with is our “2”; facing that “2”, I practise living out “0” — the selfless life — bearing the fruit of the Spirit in all nine of its expressions: “But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith, gentleness, and self-control.” (Galatians 5:22–23) Fruit is not squeezed out; it grows from a branch that stays joined to the vine.

The second is the 235 relationships. Become a “2”, a spiritual companion, with someone who is selfless; build the “3”, spiritual parents and spiritual children; and then become the “5”, a fivefold-ministry team of spiritual comrades. All three tiers of relationship rest on “selflessness”: two self-centred people will never become companions, only rivals; self-centred spiritual parents will control their children rather than bring them to maturity.

5. The Path of Serving and the Change of Perspective

321 draws the Path of Serving as five steps: Spirit, Understanding, Life, Service, God. Spirit is the guidance of the Holy Spirit; Understanding is the standard of the Bible; Life is living out the life with Jesus as our role model; Service is letting Jesus be King; God is letting Jesus receive all the glory. None of these five steps can be skipped. Much of today’s weariness comes from people jumping straight from “Spirit” to “Service”.

And what holds all of this up is a change of perspective: from man’s to God’s; from the earthly to the heavenly; from the temporary to the eternal; from the worldly to the godly.

Brothers and sisters, the aim of all this is to establish God’s system and to fulfil the Lord’s Prayer — your kingdom come, your will be done on earth as it is in heaven — pressing on into the end time revival, and walking alongside every person until they become an overcomer.

sections.heading: 5. Putting It into Practice: Turning Mindset into Daily Living
sections.html:
The lesson gives us three very practical exercises. Let’s pair them with 321’s “eight stages of changing our mindset” — Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication — and go deeper into them one by one.

Practice One: Ask yourself every day — is this so that people will see me, or see Jesus?

Information: first put the truth into your head. Today, copy John 14:9 and Matthew 5:16 onto a small card and put it where you’ll see it.

Revelation: ask the Holy Spirit to carry these words from your head into your heart. Pray: Lord, please show me which thing in my schedule today is really about getting people to see me.

Conviction: when the Holy Spirit points it out, don’t argue. Admit it: Lord, you are right. Conviction is a decision, not a feeling.

Implementation: today, choose at least one thing where you deliberately pass the credit on. When someone praises you, say: thank the Lord. When someone sees the result, point out the co-worker nobody noticed.

Evaluation and Correction: before bed tonight, spend three minutes looking back. At what moment today did I push myself in front of Jesus? Don’t condemn yourself; just correct: next time I meet the same situation, what will I do differently?

Repetition: keep it up for forty days in a row. A change of mindset doesn’t come from being moved once; it comes from repetition.

Multiplication: find a brother or sister, share this practice with them, and invite them to do it with you. Those who have been won are to go and win others — this is multiplication in 321.

Practice Two: When facing a choice, first lay down your own judgement and ask the Lord in prayer what he wants you to do

Information: remember Joshua 9:14 — the Israelites “didn’t ask counsel from Yahweh’s mouth” — and remember Proverbs 3:5–6 too.

Revelation: ask the Lord to show you whether there is an area of your life where you “habitually decide for yourself”: money, your children’s education, or the way you speak.

Conviction: admit that my cleverness is limited, and that my blind spots are the very things I can’t see myself.

Implementation: this week, for every important decision, pray for three minutes before deciding, without exception. It needn’t be long, but it must come before the decision, not after it.

Evaluation and Correction: look back over the week. Which decision did you make first and only pray about afterwards? How did it turn out? Turn the order of “act first, pray afterwards” the other way round, into “pray first, then act”.

Repetition: put prayer into your diary, so that it becomes a fixed habit rather than an occasional inspiration.

Multiplication: take the lead at home. When husband and wife disagree, pray together first and then talk it through; you’ll find that a discussion that has been prayed over carries half the heat.

Practice Three: Name one thing in which you still cling to satisfying yourself, and ask the Holy Spirit to help you turn it into pleasing the Lord

Information: read 2 Corinthians 5:9 and 5:14–15, and grasp the weight of the phrase “we make it our aim”.

Revelation: grow quiet and let the Holy Spirit search you. “Search me, God, and know my heart. Try me, and know my thoughts. See if there is any wicked way in me, and lead me in the everlasting way.” (Psalm 139:23–24)

Conviction: write that one thing down specifically — a position you won’t let go of, a relationship you won’t forgive, a sum of money you won’t release your grip on. Writing it down is the beginning of conviction.

Implementation: hand this thing over in concrete terms. If it’s a relationship, take the first step yourself; if it’s authority, genuinely hand one task over to someone else.

Evaluation and Correction: once you have handed it over, does your heart feel lighter, or full of regret? If you’re still clutching it, hand it over again. Selflessness is not an operation completed once; it is taking up the cross every day. “If anyone desires to come after me, let him deny himself, take up his cross, and follow me.” (Luke 9:23)

Repetition: go back over this list once a month.

Multiplication: when you have truly experienced release, go and tell someone who is still in bondage. Your freedom will become their hope.

sections.heading: 6. A Gentle Reminder: Selflessness Is Not Disappearing, but Being Renewed
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, before we close, there is one very important reminder.

“Selflessness” is not disappearing; it is being renewed. When you lay down “me”, Jesus appears; when you stop being in control, God’s power goes to work.

Paul says, “Don’t be conformed to this world, but be transformed by the renewing of your mind, so that you may prove what is the good, well-pleasing, and perfect will of God.” (Romans 12:2) “Be transformed” is μεταμορφόω (metamorphoō) in the original — the very kind of change by which a caterpillar becomes a butterfly. The caterpillar is not destroyed; it is renewed into another way of existing.

So once you are “selfless”, you will not end up with no personality, no gifts, no likes and dislikes. On the contrary, the Holy Spirit will prune your character into something more beautiful, and your life will be more real, more free and more powerful than before. For “we all, with unveiled face seeing the glory of the Lord as in a mirror, are transformed into the same image from glory to glory, even as from the Lord, the Spirit” (2 Corinthians 3:18).

sections.heading: 7. Closing and Call: Not Passively Letting Go, but Actively Turning Round
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, let us say it once more: “selflessness” is not passively letting go; it is actively turning round.

Letting go sounds like loss; turning round is the truth of the matter. Copernicus did not destroy the earth; he simply turned the earth towards the sun. When we no longer live for ourselves but for Jesus, we return to God’s original intention — living out his image and displaying his glory.

Think about it: the sun accounts for more than ninety-nine per cent of the total mass of the solar system, and the earth is insignificant beside it. Yet the earth has not lost its worth because of that; it is precisely because it keeps to its place, going round the sun, that there are seasons, day and night, and life. The earth’s worth does not lie in whether it is the centre, but in whether it is in the right place.

Brothers and sisters, are you in the right place today?

Letting Jesus be King is not throwing you out; it is bringing you home. Letting Jesus receive all the glory is not making you small; it is letting you be lit up by eternal light.

This morning I want to issue a call to you: from this moment on, let Jesus take his seat again on the throne of your life. In your home, let Jesus be King; in your work, let Jesus be King; in your money, your time, your emotions and your words, let Jesus be King. Every time “I want, I feel, I think” pops up, ask just one question: Lord, what is your will?

May we learn this lesson day by day, so that “no longer I, but Jesus” becomes the reality of our lives.

I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me. (Galatians 2:20)

keyVerses: I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me. That life which I now live in the flesh, I live by faith in the Son of God, who loved me, and gave himself up for me. (Galatians 2:20)
For I have come down from heaven, not to do my own will, but the will of him who sent me. (John 6:38)
He died for all, that those who live should no longer live to themselves, but to him who for their sakes died and rose again. (2 Corinthians 5:15)
declarations: Lord, I am willing to learn “no longer I, but you living in me”. Teach me no longer to fix my attention on my own interests, feelings and opinions, but to fix my eyes on you alone. May my life let people see Jesus, may your heart be satisfied, and may your glory be lifted high.
practices: Ask yourself daily: is this so people see me, or see Jesus?
Facing a choice, lay down your own judgement and ask the Lord in prayer what he wants you to do
Name one thing you still cling to for your own satisfaction, and ask the Holy Spirit to help you turn it into pleasing the Lord
prayer: Dear Lord Jesus, we bow down before you.

Lord, we confess that the “I” inside us is far too big. Our thoughts, our plans and our emotions keep revolving around ourselves; we want to be seen, we want to be affirmed, we want to do things our own way. Please forgive us.

Thank you, Lord Jesus. Though you existed in the form of God, you emptied yourself and took the form of a servant; you humbled yourself and became obedient to the point of death, even the death of the cross. You set us the example of “selflessness”, and you paid the price of “selflessness” for us.

Lord, today I am willing to be crucified with you. Please invite me down from the throne at the centre, and take your seat there. Holy Spirit, remind me every day: my goal is to let people see Jesus, my way is to rely wholly on Jesus, and my centre is to please Jesus.
Make my home God’s system, and make my service for your glory alone. May every person I meet see you because they have seen me.
In the holy name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen.
May the Lord bless you and keep you; may the Lord make his face shine on you and be gracious to you; may the Lord lift up his face toward you and give you peace.
discussion: The Lord Jesus said, “For I have come down from heaven, not to do my own will, but the will of him who sent me.” (John 6:38) In your recent life, what is one thing in which you quite clearly “did your own will”? If you could do it again, what would the choice that lets Jesus be King look like?

Paul says, “Therefore also we make it our aim, whether at home or absent, to be well pleasing to him.” (2 Corinthians 5:9) Share with one another: what is one thing in which you are still clinging to “satisfying yourself”? How are you willing to turn it into “pleasing the Lord”? Pray for one another.
l063.title: The Selfless Life
l063.subtitle: No Longer I, but Jesus
l063.partTitle: Unit 5 · The Road to Revival — Selflessness

sections.heading: Introduction: Who Is in the Pilot’s Seat of Your Life?
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, good morning. Today we are going to reflect together on a lesson that looks simple yet takes a lifetime to learn — “selflessness”.

Let me begin with a rule from the world of aviation. In the cockpit of a passenger airliner, when control passes between the captain and the first officer, there is a set of call-outs that must never be left vague. The one handing the aircraft over says, “Your aircraft.” The one taking it replies, “My aircraft.” The one handing over confirms once more: “Your aircraft.” Only when those three lines have been spoken do his hands leave the controls. Why go to so much trouble? Because high in the air, the most dangerous situation is not that nobody is flying the plane, but that two people both think they are flying it — or that two people both think the other one is. When authority is unclear, disaster has already begun.

Brothers and sisters, our lives are an aircraft too. The spiritual predicament of many Christians is not that they don’t know Jesus, but that they have never clearly handed over the controls. With our lips we sing, “I will follow you,” but our hands still grip the yoke tightly. In the meeting we say, “Lord, you are King,” but back at the office, back at home, back in front of our bank account, the one reigning as king is still ourselves. And so our lives keep flying in a state of “two people fighting over the controls” — now high, now low, now hot, now cold, and utterly exhausted.

“Selflessness” is not an abstract spiritual idea; it is a way of living that has to be practised every day. It is not merely a wish in our prayers but a choice in our lives — in every thought, decision and action, laying down “my sovereignty” and letting Jesus truly reign. Revival does not begin with outward enthusiasm; it begins with inward surrender. When a person is willing to lay himself down and let the Lord have first place, the kingdom of God comes in his life.

Today’s message comes down to one sentence: hand over the controls and say, “Lord, it’s your aircraft.” You will be saying that sentence for the rest of your life — and every time you hand the controls over, the kingdom of God moves one step further forward.

sections.heading: Scripture Background: Two Passages, One Kingship
sections.html:
This lesson has two theme passages, one from the Gospel of John and one from the Gospel of Matthew; one is a man’s testimony, the other is the Lord’s teaching. Taken together, they give us the whole picture of “selflessness”.

Church history is unanimous that the author of the Gospel of John is John, the disciple whom the Lord loved. He wrote it in Ephesus in Asia Minor around AD 80–90, for a wide readership — Jews as well as Gentiles of the Greek world. John states his purpose in John 20:31: “but these are written, that you may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and that believing you may have life in his name.” The backbone of the whole book is the exalting of Christ’s glory.

The scene in John 3:22–30 is an awkward case of “ministry competition”. Jesus’ disciples were baptising in the Judean countryside, and John the Baptist was also baptising at Aenon near Salim. John’s disciples came running to him with a complaint: “Rabbi, he who was with you beyond the Jordan, to whom you have testified, behold, he baptizes, and everyone is coming to him.” (John 3:26) That sentence is full of alarm — “everyone is coming to him”: our numbers are draining away, our influence is shrinking. It’s an anxiety every leader, every parent and every co-worker understands.

At exactly that moment John the Baptist spoke the words that have shaken every generation since. And before he said them, he laid down three sentences as groundwork. First: “A man can receive nothing unless it has been given him from heaven.” (John 3:27) Second: “You yourselves testify that I said, ‘I am not the Christ,’ but, ‘I have been sent before him.’” (John 3:28) Third: “He who has the bride is the bridegroom; but the friend of the bridegroom, who stands and hears him, rejoices greatly because of the bridegroom’s voice. This, my joy, therefore is made full.” (John 3:29) Only then came the summing-up: “He must increase, but I must decrease.” (John 3:30)

The original language deserves attention. “Increase” is the Greek αὐξάνω (auxanō), meaning “to grow, to increase, to become larger”; “decrease” is ἐλαττόω (elattoō), meaning “to lessen, to become smaller, to be lowered”. In the original both verbs are in the present tense, indicating an ongoing process — not a one-off stepping aside, but a lifetime of continually giving way, a daily, continual becoming smaller. More importantly, both verbs carry the force of “must”: this was not a fate John grudgingly accepted, but an order he willingly embraced.

The Gospel of Matthew, by contrast, was written for Jewish readers. Matthew had been a tax collector before he was called to be an apostle. He completed the book around AD 50–70, and it quotes the Old Testament again and again to prove that Jesus is the Messiah King the Old Testament promised. The Lord’s Prayer in Matthew 6 sits right at the centre of the Sermon on the Mount, and of its six petitions the first three are all about God — your name, your kingdom, your will — and only the last three are about us — our food, our forgiveness, our temptation. The order itself is a sermon: God first, then me.

“Your Kingdom come” — “kingdom” is the Greek βασιλεία (basileia). The emphasis of the word is not territory but “kingship, rule, reign”. So this line of the Lord’s Prayer means, “May your kingship come and be at work here.” And “will” is θέλημα (thelēma), meaning “desire, intention, what has been decreed”. In other words, the heart of the Lord’s Prayer is a handover of sovereignty: not my name, but your name; not my kingdom, but your kingdom; not my will, but your will.

Brothers and sisters, do you see it? What the prophet in the wilderness lived out over a lifetime is exactly what the Lord Jesus teaches us to pray every day. John says, “I must decrease”; the Lord teaches us to ask, “Your Kingdom come” — two sides of the same thing. Today, let us receive this lesson under three headings.

sections.heading: 1. The Core Definition of “Selflessness”: Laying Down Our Own Sovereignty and Letting Jesus Reign
sections.html:
“Selflessness” is not just an emotional humility; it is a transfer of authority. When we say, “Lord, may your will be done,” it means I no longer insist on my own ideas but am willing to let Jesus be King.

Please notice the distinction: emotional humility is a feeling; a transfer of authority is a decision. A person can be moved to tears in a meeting and feel very small, and then, as soon as the meeting ends, go straight back to his own throne. That is emotion, not selflessness. True selflessness is handing over “the final say” to the Lord in concrete matters.

The Lord Jesus himself is our role model on this road. On that night in Gethsemane he said, “Father, if you are willing, remove this cup from me. Nevertheless, not my will, but yours, be done.” (Luke 22:42) Look at the turning word — “nevertheless”. The Lord did not pretend he wasn’t in anguish; he honestly said, “remove this cup”. But after speaking his own will, he added one word: “nevertheless”. Brothers and sisters, the practice of “selflessness” very often takes place inside that “nevertheless”. You can have your ideas, you can have your struggles, you can pray honestly; but you must learn to add one sentence after every idea: “Nevertheless, not my will, but yours, be done.”

So it was with Paul too. He says, “I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me. That life which I now live in the flesh, I live by faith in the Son of God, who loved me, and gave himself up for me.” (Galatians 2:20) “No longer I, but Christ” — this is not self-annihilation but a change of sovereignty. Paul is still Paul; his abilities, his learning, his passion are all still there. What has changed is who sits on the throne.

The first command the Lord Jesus gave to those who follow him is about exactly this: “If anyone desires to come after me, let him deny himself, and take up his cross, and follow me.” (Matthew 16:24) “Deny” is the Greek ἀπαρνέομαι (aparneomai), meaning “to disown completely, to refuse to acknowledge”. Interestingly, the same word appears again a few chapters later, when the Lord says to Peter, “tonight, before the rooster crows, you will deny me three times.” (Matthew 26:34) When Peter “denied” the Lord, this is the word used. So this is what the Lord means: just as you once disowned me, so now you must disown yourself. When “self” pops up and says, “On this one, you should listen to me,” you need to be able to say to it, “I don’t know you.”

The life of “selflessness” can be measured by one question: “Whose hands hold the sovereignty over this matter?”

First, do I let my own reasoning be in charge, or the Lord’s word? Second, do I let my emotions control my decisions, or the Holy Spirit guide my actions? Third, do I rely on my experience to judge, or do I seek the Lord’s heart? The Bible puts it very clearly: “Trust in Yahweh with all your heart, and don’t lean on your own understanding. In all your ways acknowledge him, and he will make your paths straight.” (Proverbs 3:5–6)

There is a misunderstanding to avoid here: true “selflessness” is not losing your mind but bringing your mind into submission to Christ; not abandoning judgement but letting the Holy Spirit direct your judgement. God has never wanted us to become people without brains. What he wants is a renewed mind: “Don’t be conformed to this world, but be transformed by the renewing of your mind, so that you may prove what is the good, well-pleasing, and perfect will of God.” (Romans 12:2) To “prove” takes thinking — only that thinking has been renewed and has submitted.

Psychology has a fascinating finding that helps us see through the self-deception of “self”. In 1975 the Harvard psychologist Ellen Langer published her famous study of the “illusion of control” in the Journal of Personality and Social Psychology. She had participants take part in a lottery: one group was handed tickets at random, while the other could “pick their own”. The result? Those who had chosen their own tickets wanted a markedly higher price to sell them back — even though both groups had exactly the same chance of winning. As soon as people feel “I chose it myself”, they overestimate how much control they have over the outcome.

Brothers and sisters, we often cling tightly to sovereignty not because we can really control things, but because holding on feels safer. The book of James saw through this long ago: “Come now, you who say, ‘Today or tomorrow let’s go into this city, and spend a year there, trade, and make a profit.’ Whereas you don’t know what your life will be like tomorrow. For what is your life? For you are a vapor that appears for a little time, and then vanishes away. For you ought to say, ‘If the Lord wills, we will both live, and do this or that.’” (James 4:13–15) It turns out that what we’ve been gripping was never the control column at all — only a stick we hold to comfort ourselves.

From the perspective of 321, this is exactly the watershed between “the old self, self-centred, and the new self, selfless”. The self-centred life is the root of humanity’s fall; pride is the root of every problem. Satan’s fall began with five “I will”s: “You said in your heart, ‘I will ascend into heaven! I will exalt my throne above the stars of God! I will sit on the mountain of assembly, in the far north! I will ascend above the heights of the clouds! I will make myself like the Most High!’” (Isaiah 14:13–14) Pride is leaving our originally intended position, seizing rights and wanting to take God’s place; humility is laying down our rights and returning to our originally intended position — let man be man and let God be God. That is why we say: humility overcomes pride, and selflessness overcomes Satan.

And the “less” in “selflessness” is not zero, not emptiness, not nothing. Selflessness is entering the infinite and living out the infinite; “I” no longer live, but Christ lives in me. Only when a cup has been emptied can it hold something new; only when nothing blocks a pipe can living water flow through it. Selflessness doesn’t shrink you down to zero; it connects you to the Infinite One.

sections.heading: 2. The Role Model of “Selflessness”: The Life Testimony of John the Baptist
sections.html:
The life of John the Baptist is the finest portrait of “selflessness”. When the crowds began to leave him to follow Jesus, he was not jealous, he did not compare, he did not feel a sense of loss; on the contrary, he said joyfully, “He must increase, but I must decrease.” (John 3:30)

To feel the weight of those words, we first need to know just how “popular” John the Baptist was at the time. The Bible records: “Then people from Jerusalem, all of Judea, and all the region around the Jordan went out to him. They were baptized by him in the Jordan, confessing their sins.” (Matthew 3:5–6) Even King Herod feared him; even the priests and Levites came down from Jerusalem specially to ask him, “Who are you?” (John 1:19) He was the most influential spiritual leader in the whole land of Israel at the time. And then, at the very height of his influence, he pointed the crowds with his own hand towards another: “Behold, the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world!” (John 1:29)

How could he do it? On the strength of the three sentences he had spoken earlier.

The first: “A man can receive nothing unless it has been given him from heaven.” (John 3:27) This is the eye of grace. A person who is convinced that everything he has was received will not cling to it as private property. Paul says, “For who makes you different? And what do you have that you didn’t receive? But if you did receive it, why do you boast as if you had not received it?” (1 Corinthians 4:7) The reason we find it so hard to let go is that we wrongly think it is “mine”.

The second: “I am not the Christ,” but, “I have been sent before him.” (John 3:28) This is the eye of our originally intended position. John knew clearly who he was, and knew clearly who he was not. The greatest confusion in the spiritual life is being unclear about our originally intended position — putting ourselves in God’s place, or putting someone else in God’s place.

The third: “He who has the bride is the bridegroom; but the friend of the bridegroom, who stands and hears him, rejoices greatly because of the bridegroom’s voice. This, my joy, therefore is made full.” (John 3:29) This is the eye of order. In Jewish wedding custom, “the friend of the bridegroom” played an important part in the wedding: he took charge of all the preparations, the arrangements and the escorting of the bride, rushing about for days on end. But on the wedding night, his job was to stand outside the door, hear the joyful voice of the bridegroom within, and then go home content. He never got one thing wrong: the bride was not his. Brothers and sisters, this is something every servant of God must learn: the flock is not mine, the children are not mine, the ministry is not mine, the fruit is not mine — the bride belongs to the bridegroom.

His focus was not on how many people he could attract, but on fulfilling what God had entrusted to him — preparing the way for Jesus. This is what “selflessness” really looks like: first, not measuring worth by results, but counting it an honour to make Jesus complete; second, not seeking to be seen, but seeking for Jesus to be seen; third, not fearing being replaced, because he knew he was only preparing the road for the Lord.

Speaking of “not seeking to be seen”, psychology has a very apt finding. In 2000 Thomas Gilovich of Cornell University and his colleagues described the “spotlight effect” in the Journal of Personality and Social Psychology. They had participants put on an embarrassing T-shirt and walk into a room, then asked them to guess how many people had noticed. The participants generally assumed about half would notice; in fact only about a quarter remembered. It turns out that the spotlight we fear all our lives is mostly one we have trained on ourselves.

Brothers and sisters, so much of our anxiety, comparison and rivalry comes from living under a spotlight that doesn’t even exist. And John the Baptist’s freedom lay precisely in this: he had long since turned the spotlight round and trained it on the bridegroom. When you no longer need to be seen, you never again need to fear being replaced.

Management studies have made a similar observation. In Good to Great, published in 2001, Jim Collins studied eleven companies that had leapt from mediocrity to excellence, and found that their chief executives all had what he called “Level 5 Leadership”: a blend of personal humility and professional will. He observed that these leaders “look in the mirror” to take responsibility and “look out of the window” to give credit to others. A leader who truly achieves great things is often the one who least needs to be seen. If that is true even in the world, how much more in the kingdom of God?

The Lord Jesus’ verdict on John the Baptist was: “Most certainly I tell you, among those who are born of women there has not arisen anyone greater than John the Baptizer.” (Matthew 11:11) Brothers and sisters, this is God’s arithmetic: the one most willing to become small is the greatest in God’s eyes.

A life like this is a life that has laid down its sovereignty completely. When John the Baptist chose to “step back behind the scenes”, Jesus’ ministry was lifted high; when he chose “not to fight for a place for himself”, God’s will was brought to completion in him.

C. S. Lewis has a penetrating passage in Mere Christianity which says, in essence, that a proud man is always looking down on people and things; and as long as you are looking down, you can never see the One who is above you. The reason John could see the beauty of Christ was precisely that all his life he was looking up.

In 321 terms, this is “Jesus is the focal point — not ourselves, not other people, not our circumstances”. John’s disciples fixed their focus on someone else — “everyone is coming to him”; John fixed his focus on Jesus — “He must increase.” The same event, a different focus, and a completely different ending: focus on people, and comparison and jealousy are born; focus on the Lord, and joy and contentment are born. This is also the Two Core Values in practice: let Jesus be King; let Jesus receive all the glory.

sections.heading: 3. The Practice of “Selflessness”: Prayer and Action That Transfer Sovereignty
sections.html:
The Lord’s Prayer says: “Let your Kingdom come. Let your will be done on earth as it is in heaven.” (Matthew 6:10) The heart of this prayer is “laying myself down and letting the Lord reign”.

We should take note of the order of the Lord’s Prayer. When the Lord taught his disciples to pray, he said: “Our Father in heaven, may your name be kept holy. Let your Kingdom come. Let your will be done on earth as it is in heaven.” (Matthew 6:9–10) First “your name”, then “your Kingdom”, then “your will” — and only after that does it come to “our daily bread”. Brothers and sisters, if from the very first line our prayer is, “Lord, please give me …”, it shows that we are still sitting on the throne and simply treating God as a supplier. The Lord’s Prayer is a daily coronation: every time we pray it, we place the crown on the Lord’s head again.

The coming of God’s kingdom is not only an end-time hope; it is a discipline of daily living. Every time I choose to obey the Lord rather than myself, God’s kingdom expands a little further in me.

First, when I am willing to forgive someone who has wronged me, Jesus reigns in that relationship. Forgiveness is hard because it means giving up the right to “get justice”. The Lord says, “For if you forgive men their trespasses, your heavenly Father will also forgive you.” (Matthew 6:14) When you hand the right to judge back to God, God’s kingdom has come into that relationship.

Second, when I lay down my habit of wanting to control my family, Jesus is King in my home. Much of the pain in many families is not because there is no love, but because the love is mixed with control. Paul says, “subjecting yourselves to one another in the fear of Christ.” (Ephesians 5:21) “Subjecting yourselves to one another” — the moment those words walk through the door, the home gains one King and loses two kings.

Third, when in my service I don’t fight for credit or a name but only want the Lord to be glorified, God’s will is carried out in the church. The Lord says, “It shall not be so among you, but whoever desires to become great among you shall be your servant. Whoever desires to be first among you shall be your bondservant.” (Matthew 20:26–27)

God’s kingdom will not come into a heart that still insists on its own sovereignty; only a “selfless” heart can carry the glory of God’s kingdom.

The Old Testament has a startling contrast. King Nebuchadnezzar, walking on the roof of the royal palace of Babylon, said, “Is not this great Babylon, which I have built for the royal dwelling place, by the might of my power and for the glory of my majesty?” (Daniel 4:30) While the words were still in his mouth, the kingdom departed from him; he was driven away from people, ate grass like an ox, and seven times passed over him. When at last he lifted his eyes to heaven and his reason returned, he spoke entirely different words: “Now I, Nebuchadnezzar, praise and extol and honor the King of heaven; for all his works are truth, and his ways justice; and those who walk in pride he is able to abase.” (Daniel 4:37) Brothers and sisters, the same man, the same mouth — one time it’s “I built”, the other time it’s “his works”. Between “I” and “he” lay seven seasons in the wilderness. May we not need to go through such a wilderness; may we step down from the throne ourselves, today.

Scripture declares this spiritual law again and again: “God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble.” (James 4:6; 1 Peter 5:5) Peter goes on: “Humble yourselves therefore under the mighty hand of God, that he may exalt you in due time.” (1 Peter 5:6) Notice that “humble yourselves” is an active verb — not waiting for circumstances to press you down, but stepping down yourself. This is the direction in which grace flows: grace is like water; it always flows to the lowest place. If you build yourself into a high platform, grace has no choice but to flow around you.

So will laying down our sovereignty make life lose its direction and its fruitfulness? Quite the opposite. There is a wonderful design in nature called “apoptosis” — programmed cell death — a concept formally proposed in 1972 by John Kerr and his colleagues. The cells in the human body, following their instructions, bring themselves to an orderly end at the proper time so that the whole body stays healthy. The webbing between an unborn baby’s fingers can separate into five nimble fingers precisely because those cells “deny themselves” on time. Conversely, when cells refuse to die and insist on expanding without limit, that is called cancer.

Brothers and sisters, how true this picture is: in the body of Christ, whatever insists on expanding itself becomes a source of disease; whatever is willing to deny itself in due time brings health and beauty to the whole. The Lord says, “unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains by itself alone. But if it dies, it bears much fruit.” (John 12:24)

This is exactly what 321 means by “life first, then relationships, then ministry”. Many people have the order reversed: they charge into ministry first, patch up relationships next, and think about life last of all — and so the bigger the ministry gets, the emptier the life and the more broken the relationships. The Lord’s order is this: first let Jesus be King in our life; then there will be forgiveness and submission in our relationships, and power and glory in our ministry. People matter more than tasks; relationships matter more than things. And relationships have an order too: first with God, then with ourselves, then with others, and last of all with things. If this morning you hand your sovereignty over to the Lord, your relationship “with God” is set right — and only then, for the rest of the day, can the other relationships be set right.

sections.heading: Integrating the 321 Vision: Selflessness Is the Ticket into God’s Kingdom
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, when we place today’s message within the framework of 321, it becomes clearer still.

The Three Foundations: Jesus is my role model — in Gethsemane he said, “not my will”, the highest demonstration of selflessness; the Bible is my standard — it isn’t right because I feel it is right; what the Lord’s word says is what counts; the Holy Spirit is my guide — not relying on our own cleverness, but relying on the heart and the Holy Spirit. The Two Core Values: let Jesus be King, let Jesus receive all the glory. The Goal: establish God’s system. Brothers and sisters, look: the three key points of this lesson are exactly a concrete unfolding of the Three Foundations, the Two Core Values and the Goal. The core definition of selflessness is letting the Bible be our standard and the Holy Spirit our guide; the role model of selflessness is letting Jesus be our role model; the practice of selflessness is letting Jesus be King and letting Jesus receive the glory, so that God’s kingdom — that is, God’s system — comes on earth.

The fivefold change shows that selflessness is a road with an order to it: change the mindset and you change the life; change the life and you change daily living; change daily living and you change relationships; change relationships and you change ministry. Today what we ask for first is the first of the five — mindset. When your mindset shifts from “this is my life” to “this is the Lord’s life”, everything begins to be different.

The change of perspective is the other side of selflessness. From man’s perspective to God’s: John’s disciples saw “everyone has left”; John saw “the Lord has been lifted up”. From the earthly to the heavenly: earth’s arithmetic says whoever has the most people wins; heaven’s arithmetic says whoever is willing to become small is great.
