From the temporary to the eternal: influence will pass, applause will pass, but only the one who does God’s will remains for ever. From the worldly to the godly: the worldly wants to grab hold; the godly is willing to let go. The Bible says, “If then you were raised together with Christ, seek the things that are above, where Christ is, seated on the right hand of God. Set your mind on the things that are above, not on the things that are on the earth.” (Colossians 3:1–2)

The 920 practice puts selflessness to work in our relationships every single day. Everyone we are in a relationship with is our “2”; in front of every “2”, we practise living out “0” — the selfless life — and the result is the fruit of the Spirit in all nine of its expressions: “But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith, gentleness, and self-control.” (Galatians 5:22–23) Brothers and sisters, notice: not one of these nine graces can grow in the soil of “the self-centred life”. A self-centred person cannot have true patience, because patience is precisely laying down your own rights; a self-centred person cannot have true gentleness, because gentleness is precisely having strength and not using it. Every difficult person you meet today is not an obstacle to you, but a lesson God has given you for practising selflessness.

The 235 relationships, for their part, are the fruit of a selfless life. Only when we are selfless within can we become a “2” with another selfless person — a genuine spiritual companion, transparent with each other and praying for each other; only then can we build the “3” — spiritual parents and spiritual children, willing to pass on all we have and rejoicing when our children surpass us; and only then can we finally become the “5” — a fivefold-ministry team of spiritual comrades, of one heart in advancing the gospel. Brothers and sisters, think about it: whom do spiritual parents most resemble? John the Baptist. Because what spiritual parents do all their lives is point their children to Christ and then step back, gladly, into the background.

And the direction of all this is the Path of Serving: Spirit — the Holy Spirit is my guide; Understanding — the Bible is my standard; Life — Jesus is my role model; Service — let Jesus be King; God — let Jesus receive all the glory. From the inside out, from self to the Lord — this is the whole journey of selflessness.

sections.heading: Putting It into Practice: The Eight Stages from Information to Multiplication
sections.html:
The lesson gives us three exercises, and we will deepen them with “the eight stages of changing our mindset” — Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication.

Practice One: Pray every morning, “Lord, today the sovereignty is yours, not mine.”

Information: first let the truth in. Today you have already heard two passages — John 3:30 and Matthew 6:10. Copy them onto a piece of paper and stick it by your bed or next to the mirror. Revelation: ask the Holy Spirit to make these words not just knowledge but illumination. You might pray, “Lord, please show me what there was yesterday that I did not hand over to you.” Conviction: you must truly believe that handing it to the Lord is safer and better than keeping it in your own hands. Implementation: starting tomorrow morning, the first words when you open your eyes are that prayer — no more than ten seconds, but said out loud. Evaluation: before bed, spend two minutes looking back: at what moment today did I grab the controls back? Correction: not self-reproach, but handing them back at once — “Lord, I’m sorry, I took charge of this myself again; now I’m giving it back to you.” Repetition: keep practising for forty days in a row, until it becomes a habit. Multiplication: find a brother or sister, pass this practice on to them, and remind each other.

Practice Two: Before making a major decision, stop and ask, “Is this from me, or from the Lord?”

Information: learn the standard for discerning. Whatever does not agree with the Bible is certainly not from the Lord; whatever comes from the lust of the flesh, the lust of the eyes and the pride of life is certainly not from the Lord: “For all that is in the world, the lust of the flesh, the lust of the eyes, and the pride of life, isn’t the Father’s, but is the world’s.” (1 John 2:16) Revelation: be still in prayer and let the Holy Spirit shine on your motives. David’s prayer is worth learning every day: “Search me, God, and know my heart. Try me, and know my thoughts. See if there is any wicked way in me, and lead me in the everlasting way.” (Psalm 139:23–24) Conviction: believe that “to obey is better than sacrifice” — “Samuel said, ‘Has Yahweh as great delight in burnt offerings and sacrifices, as in obeying Yahweh’s voice? Behold, to obey is better than sacrifice, and to listen than the fat of rams.’” (1 Samuel 15:22) Implementation: set yourself a rule — any decision above a certain sum of money, beyond a certain length of time, or affecting your family must be prayed over for a night before it is made. Evaluation: look back at three major decisions from the past six months. Which of them came from me? How did it turn out? Correction: if a decision came from self and went astray, ask the Lord’s forgiveness, and adjust wherever it can still be adjusted. Repetition: make “ask the Lord first, then decide” a fixed procedure in your family meetings. Multiplication: teach this principle to your children or to the members of your small group.

Practice Three: List three areas (such as time, money, relationships) where you most easily “take charge yourself”, and learn to hand the sovereignty over to Jesus.

A pastor named Robert Boyd Munger wrote a widely circulated little booklet, My Heart — Christ’s Home. He describes a man who invites Jesus to live in the house of his heart and hands it over room by room: the study, the dining room, the living room, the workshop; until one day the Lord notices a smell and, pointing to a small locked cupboard at the end of the hall, asks, “What’s in there?” It held the things he couldn’t bear to give up. Brothers and sisters, every one of us has a small locked cupboard like that in our heart.

Information: list three areas honestly. Don’t write spiritual platitudes; write their real names — my diary, my savings, my relationship with so-and-so. Revelation: ask the Lord to show you what that “locked cupboard” really is. Conviction: believe that the Lord is the most trustworthy manager of all: “Commit your way to Yahweh. Trust also in him, and he will do this.” (Psalm 37:5) Implementation: hand them over one area at a time. You might write a simple “handover document” — date, area, signature — declaring to the Lord that from today the sovereignty over this belongs to him. Evaluation: check once a week whether you have quietly taken anything back in these three areas. Correction: if you have taken it back, hand it over again; don’t let it go more than a week. Repetition: after three months, list three new areas. Multiplication: share in your small group how God has worked since you handed over the sovereignty, so that others gain the faith to hand theirs over too.

A Gentle Reminder

Laying down sovereignty is not losing control; it is handing control to the most trustworthy Lord. When you let Jesus be King, his wisdom and peace will guide you forward.

Brothers and sisters, remember: what you hand over is not handed to fate, not handed to luck, and not handed to people; it is handed to the Lord who laid down his life for you and loves you to the end. There is no captain in the world who knows better than he does how to bring you safely home.

sections.heading: Closing and Call: The Threshold of Revival
sections.html:
“Selflessness” is the threshold of revival. When we are willing to let Jesus reign, individuals, families, churches and indeed the whole kingdom will experience the works of God. Revival does not depend on how hard we try, but on how fully we surrender. Lay yourself down and let the Lord reign — this is the only road to the glory of God’s kingdom.

Brothers and sisters, what is a threshold? A threshold is the line you must step over before you can go in. You can stand outside the door for a long time; you can sing, attend meetings and serve outside the door for many years; but as long as you haven’t stepped over that threshold, you cannot enter the room. “Selflessness” is that threshold.

Augustine says in The City of God that two cities have been formed by two loves: the love of self, even to the contempt of God, formed the earthly city; the love of God, even to the contempt of self, formed the heavenly city. Brothers and sisters, which city are you building today?

Every true revival in history has begun not with a new method but with a broken heart. It is commonly said that as a young man D. L. Moody heard a sentence that stirred him deeply: “The world has yet to see what God will do with a man fully consecrated to him.” Moody said, “I will be that man.” Brothers and sisters, this morning, are you willing to be that person?

Let’s go back to that flight-deck call-out. Today the Lord is asking in your ear, “Is it your aircraft, or mine?” May we all be able to answer clearly and out loud: “Lord, it’s your aircraft.”

Let Jesus be King; let Jesus receive all the glory. May he increase; may I decrease. Amen.

keyVerses: “He must increase, but I must decrease.” (John 3:30)
“Let your Kingdom come. Let your will be done on earth as it is in heaven.” (Matthew 6:10)
declarations: Lord, I am willing to lay down my own sovereignty and no longer make decisions by myself. Reign in every area of my life. May your kingdom come, and may your will be done in me as it is in heaven.
practices: Pray every morning: “Lord, today the sovereignty is yours, not mine.”
Before a major decision, stop and ask: “Is this from me, or from the Lord?”
List three areas (such as time, money, relationships) where you most easily “take charge yourself”, and learn to hand the sovereignty over to Jesus
prayer: Dear Lord Jesus, we thank you. You are the King worthy of all glory, yet for our sake you emptied yourself, took the form of a servant, and became obedient to the point of death, even the death of the cross.

Lord, forgive us. With our lips we call you Lord, yet our hands still grip our own sovereignty tightly; in our meetings we surrender, yet in our daily living we still reign as king. Wash away our pride and our self with your precious blood.

Lord, this morning I hand the controls over to you. My time is yours, my money is yours, my family is yours, my service is yours, my future is yours. May your kingdom come in my thoughts and intentions, and may your will be done in my daily living as it is in heaven.

Holy Spirit, remind me every day: whenever “self” climbs back onto the throne, let me step down at once. Make me like John the Baptist, finding my joy in your increase and my contentment in your name being lifted high.
In the holy name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen.
discussion: John 3:27 says, “John answered, ‘A man can receive nothing unless it has been given him from heaven.’” In your life right now, what one thing (a gift, a position, a relationship, an achievement) are you most likely to mistake for “mine”? If you truly believed it had been given from heaven, how would you treat it differently?

Matthew 6:10 says, “Let your Kingdom come. Let your will be done on earth as it is in heaven.” Name one specific area (time, money, family, work, service) whose sovereignty you will hand over to the Lord this week. How do you plan to hand it over? Ask the members of your small group to pray for you, and review it together at your next meeting.
l064.title: Let Go of Sovereignty, Let Jesus Reign
l064.subtitle: Practising the Selfless Life (Part 1)
l064.partTitle: Unit 5 · The Road to Revival — Selflessness

sections.heading: 1. Introduction: Who Sits in the Middle Seat?
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, good morning.

Let me begin with a scene that has played out in a great many churches.

A planning meeting. On the table lies a proposal for an event. One brother says, “I’ve worked in marketing for ten years — this will definitely work.” A sister says, “But that isn’t the tradition of our church.” A deacon clears his throat: “I started this ministry. I know it best.” An hour and a half goes by: three minutes of prayer, eighty-seven minutes of discussion. When the meeting breaks up, the proposal has passed — but two people go home wounded.

Nobody in that meeting committed an obvious sin. Nobody lied; nobody was greedy for money. Every one of them was speaking “for the good of the church.” But the seat in the middle of that table was empty. Jesus was not sitting there.

Brothers and sisters, this is the problem we have to face today. Spiritual things can still be done by fleshly methods. In the last lesson we came to understand the teaching of “selflessness.” Today we take a step further: “selflessness” is not merely a spiritual theory; it is an intensely practical discipline of the life of faith.

In every act of service and every decision, we must learn to let go of our own sovereignty and let Jesus reign.

If we still insist on “I can,” “I know,” “I decide,” then even when we are doing spiritual things, we are still operating in “self.” And the result? The result is only a human kingdom being built; it cannot display the glory of God. But when we are willing to submit in humility and confess that “the Lord is the commander,” we will experience God’s wonderful leading and victory.

There is an episode from history that captures our difficulty very well. In AD 1543 the Polish astronomer Nicolaus Copernicus published On the Revolutions of the Heavenly Spheres. Before that, humanity had believed for fourteen hundred years that the earth was the centre of the universe, and that the sun, the moon and all the stars revolved around us. What Copernicus proposed was really just a simple correction — the centre is not the earth; the centre is the sun.

Mathematically, the correction was not complicated, yet it took humanity nearly a hundred and fifty years truly to accept it. Why was it so hard? Because admitting “I am not the centre” has never been a mathematical problem. It is a problem of the heart.

The “self” in the church is just such a belated Copernican revolution. With our lips we confess that Jesus is Lord, but on the working diagram of our service, the seat at the centre is very often still occupied by us. Today’s lesson is about giving the seat at the centre back to the Lord who is worthy of it.

sections.heading: 2. Scripture Background: The Setting of Two Passages
sections.html:
This lesson has two key passages, one in the Old Testament and one in the New. More than fourteen hundred years apart, they are saying the same thing.

The first is Joshua 5:13–15.

The book of Joshua records Israel’s entry into Canaan; Jewish tradition holds that it came mainly from Joshua’s own hand. The story is set forty years after the exodus. Moses has died, and a new generation of Israelites has just crossed the Jordan.

Notice the order of chapter 5: first they are circumcised at Gilgal, then they keep the Passover, and then the manna stops falling (Joshua 5:2–12). Before the first battle is fought, what God deals with first is not military matters but identity and worship. Life comes first; the battle comes after.

It is at exactly this moment that Joshua meets that man.

“When Joshua was by Jericho, he lifted up his eyes and looked, and behold, a man stood in front of him with his sword drawn in his hand. Joshua went to him and said to him, ‘Are you for us, or for our enemies?’” (Joshua 5:13)

It is the most natural question for a commander to ask: whose side are you on? But the answer is unexpected: “No.”

Brothers and sisters, this is the weightiest “No” in the whole Bible. What he means is: you’re asking the wrong question. I have not come to take sides; I have come to take command. Then he declares who he is — in Hebrew sar-tsevaʾ-YHWH, literally “commander of Yahweh’s army.” Sar means a commander, one who holds authority.

Evangelical commentators through the ages have mostly held that this was an Old Testament appearance of Christ, because he accepts Joshua’s worship, whereas angels in Scripture never accept worship (see Revelation 19:10). His next command confirms it: “Take off your sandals, for the place on which you stand is holy.” (Joshua 5:15)

You have heard those words before. Forty years earlier, Moses heard exactly the same words before the burning bush at Horeb: “Don’t come close. Take off your sandals, for the place you are standing on is holy ground.” (Exodus 3:5)

Two generations, two leaders, the same God, the same demand: first take off your sandals, then lead the troops.

The second passage is Matthew 16:18.

The Gospel of Matthew was written by the apostle Matthew, a former tax collector. Most scholars date it to the 60s or 70s AD, and it was addressed mainly to believers of Jewish background. It is worth noting that the word “church” appears in only one of the four Gospels — Matthew — and only twice (Matthew 16:18; 18:17).

This conversation took place at Caesarea Philippi. That is no ordinary place. It lies on the southern slopes of Mount Hermon; originally called Panion, it was a major centre for the worship of the god Pan. In the cliff face there is a huge cave that the locals believed was the entrance to the underworld, and they called it “the gates of Hades.” The city took its name from the tetrarch Herod Philip.

Pagan altars beside them, Roman power over their heads, “the gates of Hades” right before their eyes — here Jesus asks his disciples, “Who do you say that I am?” Peter answers, “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God.” (Matthew 16:16)

Then the Lord speaks the words that shook history: “On this rock I will build my assembly” — that is, my church.

The verb in the original, oikodomēsō, is future tense, active voice, first person singular — the subject is perfectly clear: “I.” And “my church” — the possessive is perfectly clear too: “mine.”

The word ekklēsia is made up of ek (out) and kaleō (to call). It originally meant the assembly of citizens called together in a city-state. So the very first word defines the church: the church is not a club that gathers itself; it is a people called out. And the one who calls is not us. It is the Lord.

Finally, what comes immediately after these words? “From that time, Jesus began to show his disciples that he must go to Jerusalem … and be killed, and the third day be raised up.” (Matthew 16:21)

Brothers and sisters, please keep this order in your heart: the Lord first says, “I will build my church,” and immediately afterwards he says, “I must be killed.” His way of building the church is not power. It is the cross.

And Peter’s reaction on the spot? He takes Jesus aside and remonstrates with him: “Far be it from you, Lord!” We all remember the Lord’s reply: “Get behind me, Satan!” (Matthew 16:23)

The same Peter — praised one minute, rebuked the next. What made the difference? The difference was this: the first time, he spoke what God had revealed; the second time, he spoke what he himself had calculated.

That is the theme of our whole lesson today: a person can be in the church, doing the most spiritual things, saying the finest words, and yet be an instrument of Satan — simply because the subject of the sentence is “I.”

sections.heading: 3. Who Is Leading? — The Selfless View of Leadership
sections.html:
Israel’s exodus from Egypt and entry into Canaan were the two greatest spiritual journeys in history.

If someone asks, “Who led the Israelites out of Egypt?” we answer, “Moses.” If someone asks, “Who led them into Canaan?” we say, “Joshua.”

On an exam paper, both answers would get the marks. But brothers and sisters, if we could ask Moses himself, or Joshua himself, they would both give the same reply: “God led Israel!”

That rod was never Moses’ from the first day

Let’s look at Moses first.

Moses was already eighty when he met God at Horeb. His first reaction was not eagerness but retreat: “Who am I, that I should go to Pharaoh, and that I should bring the children of Israel out of Egypt?” (Exodus 3:11) God did not praise his abilities. He said only, “Certainly I will be with you.” (Exodus 3:12)

Then comes one of the most crucial conversations in Scripture:

“Yahweh said to him, ‘What is that in your hand?’ He said, ‘A rod.’” (Exodus 4:2)

It was a shepherd’s staff. Eighty years of life — forty in the palace, forty in the wilderness — now all condensed into a piece of wood in his hand. And that rod was exactly what God wanted.

So God told him to throw the rod on the ground, and then told him to reach out and take hold of it (see Exodus 4:3–4). Brothers and sisters, that throwing down and picking up was a transfer of ownership. When it went down, it was still “Moses’ rod.” When it was picked up again, Scripture changed what it called it.

“Moses took his wife and his sons, and set them on a donkey, and he returned to the land of Egypt. Moses took God’s rod in his hand.” (Exodus 4:20)

God’s rod. Not Moses’ rod — God’s rod.

From that moment on, every time the rod was raised, it was not Moses displaying his power; it was God acting. The rod stretched over the Nile, and the water turned to blood; the rod stretched over the Red Sea, and the sea parted. And on the day of the battle with Amalek, Moses himself put it even more plainly: “Tomorrow I will stand on the top of the hill with God’s rod in my hand.” (Exodus 17:9)

Brothers and sisters, here is a detail we often miss: from beginning to end, that rod was in Moses’ hand — but its name had changed. God did not confiscate his rod. God changed who owned it.

That is “selflessness.” Selflessness is not throwing things away; it is not burying our gifts. Selflessness is this: the same hands, the same rod, with a different name hanging on it. Your expertise is still there; your experience is still there. But the name tag no longer says “mine.” It says “God’s.”

That is why what Moses cried out at the Red Sea was, “Yahweh will fight for you, and you shall be still.” (Exodus 14:14) The greatest skill of a truly selfless leader is not shouting loudly but knowing when to keep quiet and let God speak.

No wonder Scripture gives Moses this verdict: “Now the man Moses was very humble, more than all the men who were on the surface of the earth.” (Numbers 12:3)

That one “No” took over the command of the whole war

Now look at Joshua.

Joshua was about to fight his first hard battle — Jericho. It was a fortress city with strong walls, and Israel had no siege engines. At a moment like that, any general wants to know one thing above all: who is on my side?

So he asks, “Are you for us, or for our enemies?” (Joshua 5:13)

The one holding the drawn sword replies, “No; but I have come now as commander of Yahweh’s army.” (Joshua 5:14)

Brothers and sisters, listen carefully to that sentence. He did not say, “I am here to help you.” He said, “No.” Because the question itself was wrong.

We often think: I have my plan, and then I pray and ask God to help my plan. But God is never anyone’s deputy. God does not come to join our team; God comes to take over the whole battlefield.

The real question is not “Is God on my side?” but “Am I on God’s side?”

Joshua understood. His response was not to argue but to fall on his face to the earth and worship, saying, “What does my lord say to his servant?” (Joshua 5:14) In that moment, command of Israel’s army was formally handed over.

And the order in the next verse is even more remarkable: before the battle, take off your sandals (see Joshua 5:15).

Brothers and sisters, what a strange military order! Isn’t the thing a man going into battle needs most his boots? But God says: before you put on your army boots, let me know that you understand how to take off your sandals.

In chapter 6 God’s battle plan comes out, and it is in the perfect tense: “Yahweh said to Joshua, ‘Behold, I have given Jericho into your hand, with its king and the mighty men of valor.’” (Joshua 6:2)

Notice — “I have given.” The battle has not yet been fought, and the outcome is already settled. The orders that follow are to march around the city, blow the trumpets and shout: that is not tactics; that is worship. Because it was never Joshua’s battle in the first place. It was Yahweh’s battle; every victory was accomplished by God’s plan and God’s hand.

That is “selfless” leadership: not fighting over who plays the lead, only making sure that “God is in control”

In Good to Great (published in 2001), the management scholar Jim Collins sifted through 1,435 companies and found eleven that had truly leapt from “good” to “great.” He had expected to find a group of dazzling star CEOs. He found the very opposite: these leaders were almost all low-key, even shy. Collins called them “Level 5 leaders” — combining extreme personal humility with intense professional will.

Collins also observed what he called “the window and the mirror.” When things went well, these leaders looked out of the window and gave the credit to colleagues and to good luck; when things went badly, they looked in the mirror and took the responsibility on themselves. Mediocre leaders do exactly the reverse — they look in the mirror when they succeed and out of the window when they fail.

Brothers and sisters, if that is true even of a business, how much more of the church of Christ? But we must go one level deeper: when Collins’s leaders look out of the window, they see colleagues and luck; when a selfless spiritual leader looks out of the window, he sees the Commander standing in the middle of the battlefield.

Leadership in the church should be like this too. The point is not “Who is leading?” but “Is God leading?”

Sometimes we misdiagnose the church’s problem, thinking what it lacks is a gifted leader. But Scripture says, “Unless Yahweh builds the house, they who build it labor in vain. Unless Yahweh watches over the city, the watchman guards it in vain.” (Psalm 127:1)

The prophet Zechariah gave the same warning long ago: “‘Not by might, nor by power, but by my Spirit,’ says Yahweh of Armies.” (Zechariah 4:6)

When we stop exalting leaders and exalt God’s will instead, the church can be united, and the church can move forward.

Applying the 321 vision: Jesus is the focal point, not ourselves

Brothers and sisters, this is precisely the first of the 321 vision’s Three Foundations: Jesus is my role model.

Moses’ rod changed its name; Joshua’s army changed its commander. Neither of them went from “I can’t” to “I can.” They went from “mine” to “God’s.”

321 says: the focus is on Jesus — not on ourselves, not on others, not on our circumstances. If the focus is on ourselves, we ask, “Am I doing well enough?” If the focus is on others, we ask, “What gives him the right?” If the focus is on our circumstances, we ask, “Why is this so hard?” None of those three questions will bring victory.

Only when we move our focus onto Jesus do we ask the right question: “What does my lord say to his servant?”

321 also says: pride is leaving our originally intended position and seizing rights, wanting to take the place of God; humility is laying down our rights and returning to our originally intended position — let man be man and let God be God.

That is exactly what Joshua did outside Jericho. He stepped down from the commander’s seat and returned to his originally intended position as a servant; and the true Commander stepped into the place that was his all along. Once the positions were right, the walls came down.

Brothers and sisters, remember this: it is not our position that gives us power. It is our originally intended position that gives us power.

sections.heading: 4. Who Is Building? — The Selfless View of Ministry
sections.html:
Jesus said it with perfect clarity: “On this rock I will build my assembly.” (Matthew 16:18)

Brothers and sisters, it is only a handful of words, yet it settles three things once and for all:

Not “You will build my church,”

nor “I will build your church,”

but “I will build my church.”

He is the subject, he is the object, and the possessive is his as well. From start to finish, there is no share in it for us.

Then what are we? We are the living stones being built, the members of his body. Paul puts it in the strongest terms: Christ “is the head of the body, the assembly … that in all things he might have the preeminence” (Colossians 1:18).

There is only one head. The tragedy of a church is often not that it lacks members, but that it has a few extra heads.

This sentence exposes the greatest temptation in church service — “self.”

In ministry we often fall into four wrong mindsets. Brothers and sisters, follow along with me and hold yourselves up to each one like a mirror.

The first: “We will build our church” — the Babel church

This is the easiest one to recognise. We are the subject, and we are the object too.

Scripture recorded the prototype of this mindset long ago: “They said, ‘Come, let’s build ourselves a city, and a tower whose top reaches to the sky, and let’s make a name for ourselves, lest we be scattered abroad on the surface of the whole earth.’” (Genesis 11:4)

The purpose of the tower of Babel was to make people know “our name.” So the first thing God did was not to tear down the tower but to confuse their language — a group of people who will not unite for God’s name will sooner or later split over their own.

The second: “We will build Jesus’ church” — taking the place of God

This one is harder to recognise, because it looks so very spiritual. We are still the subject, but the object has become Jesus.

But brothers and sisters, notice: this is in fact “taking the place of God” — accomplishing God’s work by human methods, and the result is full of pressure and reliance on the flesh.

Scripture has a most heartbreaking example. God promised Abram descendants as many as the stars of heaven; ten years went by, and Sarai still had not conceived, so she gave her maidservant Hagar to her husband (see Genesis 16:2). Look closely: they did not abandon God’s promise. They simply used their own method to fulfil God’s promise. The goal was right; the method was their own. The result was Ishmael, and strife in the household from then on.

There is an even more sobering example. David brought the ark back to Jerusalem on a new cart, not on the shoulders of the Levites. “Uzzah reached for God’s ark, and took hold of it; for the cattle stumbled. Yahweh’s anger burned against Uzzah; and God struck him there for his error” (2 Samuel 6:6–7).

Where did Uzzah go wrong? His motive was good — he couldn’t bear to see the ark of God fall to the ground. But he forgot one thing: the ark of God has never needed a human hand to hold it up. When we reach out to “steady” God, what we really believe in our hearts is: without me, God can’t hold it together.

This is the deepest root of the disease of “taking the place of God” — not ungodliness, but unbelief.

Psychology has studied this tendency to overrate ourselves very thoroughly. A 1981 survey by the Swedish psychologist Ola Svenson found that eighty-eight per cent of the American drivers surveyed believed they drove more safely than the median driver — which, statistically, is of course impossible.

Doing God’s work by human methods has three classic symptoms: very busy, very tired, very little prayer. Because whatever I can carry, I don’t need to ask for; and whatever I don’t need to ask for, the Holy Spirit doesn’t need to come for.

The third: “Jesus will build our church” — using God

In the third mindset, the subject has become Jesus, but the object is still us. This is “using God”: hoping God will bless our plans and make us successful, while in substance “self” is still on the throne.

We have all heard this kind of prayer — we have probably all prayed it: “Lord, please bless our plan, open the way, and make this a success.” Notice the structure of that prayer: the plan is mine, the success is what I want, and God is the one called in to put his stamp on it.

Scripture has a scene that plays this mindset out to the full. The Israelites were defeated by the Philistines at Aphek, and the elders said, “Let’s get the ark of Yahweh’s covenant out of Shiloh and bring it to us, that it may come among us and save us out of the hand of our enemies.” (1 Samuel 4:3)

They did not repent. They did not ask, “Why is God not with us?” They did just one thing — they fetched the ark. The ark was treated as a lucky charm, and God was treated as a piece of tactical equipment.

The result? Thirty thousand Israelite foot soldiers were killed, the ark was captured, and Eli’s two sons died on the same day (see 1 Samuel 4:10–11).

God will not be used. God can be trusted, God can be worshipped, God can be obeyed — but God will never be used. God himself drew the line clearly long ago: “I am Yahweh. That is my name. I will not give my glory to another, nor my praise to engraved images.” (Isaiah 42:8)

Brothers and sisters, if we invite God into our own plans, wanting his power but not his sovereignty, then what we worship is not really God. It is an idol called “success.”

The fourth: “Jesus will build Jesus’ church” — the selfless church

This is the “selfless” church: its focus has returned entirely to the Lord’s will, letting Jesus himself accomplish his own work.

Jesus is the subject; Jesus is the object. Where are we? We are in his hands, as vessels for his use; at his feet, as servants who obey.

Brothers and sisters, will service like this become passive? Not at all. Look at how the Lord himself lived.

“Jesus therefore answered them, ‘Most certainly, I tell you, the Son can do nothing of himself, but what he sees the Father doing. For whatever things he does, these the Son also does likewise.’” (John 5:19)

Brothers and sisters, the Son of God says he “can do nothing of himself.” The most powerful one in the whole universe lived a life that relied on himself not at all. It is not that he did nothing; it is that whatever he saw the Father doing, that is what he did.

That is not passivity; that is the highest form of initiative. Because every single thing he did hit the Father’s will exactly, and not an ounce of strength was wasted.

Paul applies this principle to service in the church: “I planted. Apollos watered. But God gave the increase. So then neither he who plants is anything, nor he who waters, but God who gives the increase.” (1 Corinthians 3:6–7)

Neither he who plants is anything, nor he who waters. Brothers and sisters, this does not belittle us; it sets us free. When I know that the growth is not my responsibility, I don’t have to be anxious about the outcome, and I can do my part faithfully, simply and joyfully.

That is why Paul declares, “being confident of this very thing, that he who began a good work in you will complete it until the day of Jesus Christ.” (Philippians 1:6) He is the one who begins the work, and he is the one who finishes it — and yet he still writes our names on the list of his fellow workers (see 1 Corinthians 3:9).

Wherever “we” is the subject, “self” is present

Brothers and sisters, let’s set the four mindsets side by side:

The first: we build ours — making a name for ourselves.

The second: we build Jesus’ — taking the place of God.

The third: Jesus builds ours — using God.

The fourth: Jesus builds Jesus’ — letting God be God.

In the first three, “we” is hidden in either the subject or the object. Only in the fourth is it completely absent.

Wherever “we” is the subject, “self” is present. Only when “we” step down completely can Jesus truly reign as King.

The true church is not an institution built by human effort, but the body that Christ himself raises up; our duty is not to “replace” him but to “obey” him.

So the psalmist’s prayer should become the daily prayer of everyone who serves: “Not to us, Yahweh, not to us, but to your name give glory, for your loving kindness, and for your truth’s sake.” (Psalm 115:1)

Notice that the psalmist says “not to us” twice.

Why twice? Because we so easily forget once.

sections.heading: 5. Selfless Service: Letting Jesus Accomplish God’s Will Through Us
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, by this point some of you may be getting nervous: “So should I do nothing at all? Won’t the church just grind to a halt?”

No.

“Selfless” service is not passively letting go; it is actively entrusting.

The difference between the two is huge. Passively letting go is washing your hands of it — spiritual laziness dressed up in the clothes of humility. Actively entrusting is handing over the steering wheel and then sitting in the passenger seat, fully attentive and ready for orders at any moment.

When in our service we no longer compete over who leads or who gets known, but seek God’s will with one heart, Jesus is able to accomplish the Father’s plan through us.

John the Baptist: the one who handed the bride to the bridegroom

Scripture gives us a most beautiful example in John the Baptist.

His situation was actually rather awkward. John’s disciples came to him with a complaint, and there was a sour note in their voice: everyone used to come to you, and now they’re all going to Jesus (see John 3:26). If it were us, we’d probably say, “That’s fine, I don’t mind” — and then go home and lie awake all night.

But John’s answer came from another world.

First he spoke a foundational word: “John answered, ‘A man can receive nothing unless it has been given him from heaven.’” (John 3:27)

Brothers and sisters, that one sentence pulls envy up by the roots. What I have was given from heaven; what he has was given from heaven too. If it is all a gift, what right do I have to envy? And what right do I have to boast?

Then he used the picture of a wedding: “He who has the bride is the bridegroom; but the friend of the bridegroom, who stands and hears him, rejoices greatly because of the bridegroom’s voice. This, my joy, therefore is made full.” (John 3:29)

At a Jewish wedding, “the friend of the bridegroom” held a real office, responsible for all the preparations, the arrangements and escorting the bride. He would be busy for months, yet on the wedding day he stood to one side. The bride was not his; she was the bridegroom’s. His greatest joy was to hear the bridegroom’s voice.

Brothers and sisters, this is where every servant of God stands: we are the best man, not the bridegroom. The church is the bride of Christ, not ours. We bustle about in front and behind, and in the end we must step aside and watch the Lord receive his bride — and then our joy is made full.

So he spoke those words that will last for ever: “He must increase, but I must decrease.” (John 3:30)

The original deserves a closer look. “Increase” is auxanō, the word for a plant growing, gradually getting bigger; “decrease” is elattoō, meaning to become smaller, to be reduced. And more crucially, “decrease” here is in the passive voice — not “I make myself small,” but “I am made less.”

What does that mean? It means John did not become small by putting himself down. He simply stood there and let Jesus grow; and as Jesus grew, he naturally became smaller by comparison.

Brothers and sisters, someone who tries to be humble by “pushing himself down” will sooner or later wear out — and his heart will still be full of himself, just a miserable version of himself. True selflessness is not straining to think little of ourselves; it is seeing Jesus high enough. When he is truly lifted up, we naturally step back into the place where we belong — and we step back gladly.

How did the Lord Jesus assess this man who was willing to become small? He said that among those born of women, none has risen greater than John the Baptist (see Matthew 11:11). The one who is willing to be least, the Lord calls great. That is the arithmetic of the kingdom of heaven.

When we are willing to step down, Jesus is lifted up; when we are willing to be made less, God’s kingdom is enlarged.

The source of “selflessness” is Christ emptying himself

In fact, what John did was simply to follow the example of the one he pointed to.

“Have this in your mind, which was also in Christ Jesus, who, existing in the form of God, didn’t consider equality with God a thing to be grasped, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of men. And being found in human form, he humbled himself, becoming obedient to the point of death, yes, the death of the cross.” (Philippians 2:5–8)

“Emptied himself” is ekenōsen in the original, from the root kenoō, meaning “to pour out, to empty.” He did not lose his divinity; he laid down the rights and glory he could have enjoyed.

Brothers and sisters, notice how this passage begins: “Have this in your mind, which was also in Christ Jesus.” Paul did not write this towering passage on Christ for the sake of theological debate; he wrote it to deal with the quarrels in the Philippian church (see Philippians 2:2–4). The loftiest Christology was written to solve the most practical relational problems.

The ultimate basis of selflessness is not whether we try hard enough; it is that the Lord has already walked this road ahead of us. And the end of that road is exaltation — he went down to the lowest place, and God raised him to the highest (see Philippians 2:9).

The Lord also put this law in the form of a grain of wheat: unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains alone; but if it dies, it bears much fruit (see John 12:24). Selflessness is not loss; selflessness is multiplication.

A church like this will be full of unity, joy and power

When the focus is not on “what people do” but on “how the Lord works,” three things appear in the church.

The first is unity.

When the early church in Jerusalem dealt with the dispute over whether Gentiles had to be circumcised, their resolution used a remarkable phrase: “For it seemed good to the Holy Spirit, and to us, to lay no greater burden on you” (Acts 15:28).

“The Holy Spirit, and to us” — not “We have voted it through; please, Holy Spirit, endorse it.” This was the first major council in the history of the church, and their way of resolving the dispute was to go together to the one who is the true Commander.

In 1999 the Harvard Business School scholar Amy Edmondson introduced the idea of “psychological safety” — whether people on a team dare to speak the truth at the risk of being criticised. From 2012, Google’s “Project Aristotle” analysed a hundred and eighty of its own teams and found that the leading factor in team effectiveness was not how clever the members were, but psychological safety.

Brothers and sisters, think about it: on a team where everyone has to prove themselves, will there be psychological safety? Of course not, because everyone is on the defensive. But on a team where everyone is selfless, saying the wrong thing isn’t frightening, because nobody needs to save face; having your idea overruled isn’t frightening either, because what we were looking for was never “my way” in the first place, but “the Lord’s heart.”

Selflessness is the most practical soil for unity.

The second is joy.

People who compete are never happy, because there is always someone to compare themselves with. But the selfless can say, like John the Baptist, “This, my joy, therefore is made full.” (John 3:29) The Lord also said, “One who is the greater among you, let him become as the younger, and one who is governing, as one who serves.” (Luke 22:26)

The third is power.

“I am the vine. You are the branches. He who remains in me and I in him bears much fruit, for apart from me you can do nothing.” (John 15:5)

The branch doesn’t have to worry on the vine’s behalf. The branch needs only one thing — to stay connected.

Paul condensed this experience into the greatest self-introduction a Christian has ever written: “I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me. That life which I now live in the flesh, I live by faith in the Son of God, who loved me, and gave himself up for me.” (Galatians 2:20)

Brothers and sisters, listen carefully to the structure of that sentence: “It is no longer I who live” — that is selflessness; “but Christ lives in me” — that is the infinite.

Selflessness is not having nothing; it is entering into the infinite — the fullness and victory of Jesus — and living it out.

Brothers and sisters, in AD 1727 at Herrnhut in Germany, a group of refugee believers who had nearly split apart through rivalry signed a covenant of brotherly love under the leadership of Count Zinzendorf. As they took Communion together, the Holy Spirit was poured out powerfully. That village of fewer than three hundred people then began a round-the-clock prayer relay that lasted more than a hundred years, and sent out missionaries wave after wave. When “we” step back, the Lord steps forward.

sections.heading: 6. Integrating the 321 Vision
sections.html:
The Three Foundations, the Two Core Values, the Goal

Jesus is my role model — he said, “The Son can do nothing of himself.” (John 5:19) If even the Son of God did not act on his own, what right have we to act on our own?

The Bible is my standard — God’s first command to Joshua was not a military deployment but this: “This book of the law shall not depart from your mouth, but you shall meditate on it day and night.” (Joshua 1:8) The method is not something I think up; it is something God has written down.

The Holy Spirit is my guide — the concluding sentence of the Jerusalem council was “It seemed good to the Holy Spirit, and to us” (Acts 15:28), not “It seemed good to us; please, Holy Spirit, agree.”

The Two Core Values are the very title of this lesson. Let Jesus be King — he said, “I will build my church,” so let’s not snatch his verb. Let Jesus receive all the glory — “Not to us, Yahweh, not to us” (Psalm 115:1).

The Goal is to establish God’s system. Brothers and sisters, the tower of Babel was a system too. A human system and God’s system look very alike from the outside; they differ in only one place: whose name is written at the top.

The old self is self-centred; the new self is selfless

The self-centred life is the root of humanity’s fall, and pride is the root of the problem.

Scripture records the prototype of pride in Isaiah: “You said in your heart, ‘I will ascend into heaven! I will exalt my throne above the stars of God! … I will make myself like the Most High!’” (Isaiah 14:13–14)

One “I will” after another. From the first fall in heaven to that little flicker of resentment in our hearts this morning, the recipe is exactly the same.

That is why Scripture says, “Pride goes before destruction, and an arrogant spirit before a fall.” (Proverbs 16:18) And again: “God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble.” (James 4:6)

Notice the word “resists.” For a proud servant of God, the greatest obstacle is not Satan. It is God himself.

Humility overcomes pride; selflessness overcomes Satan. Satan is most skilled at dealing with the self-centred, because that is the very road by which he fell. But against the selfless, Satan has no weapon at all — how do you bribe someone who doesn’t want glory? How do you threaten someone who has already been crucified with Christ?

Pride provokes pride; humility inspires humility

Why did someone leave that planning meeting wounded? Because pride is contagious. One person brings out “I’ve worked in marketing for ten years,” and another simply has to produce “I started this ministry.” Pride provokes pride, and both sides lose.

On the other hand, humility is contagious too. All it takes is one person to say first, “I’m sorry, I was too hasty just now. Shall we pray first?” and the whole atmosphere changes at once. Humility inspires humility, and both sides win.

Life first, then relationships, then ministry

321 says: people matter more than tasks; relationships matter more than things.

Think back to the order of Joshua chapter 5: circumcision, the Passover, the manna ceasing — and only then Jericho. God dealt first with identity (life), then with worship (relationships), and only last with the battle (ministry). Yet we often walk it backwards: we charge ahead with ministry, deal with relationships only when the ministry runs into trouble, and remember life only when the relationships have broken down.

The priority of relationships is: first with God, then with ourselves, then with others, and last with things. First pray; then admit that our own motives are not pure; then submit to one another and listen to one another. Talk about methods after that, and you will be able to reach agreement.

And the fivefold change is: mindset, life, daily living, relationships, ministry. Change the mindset and you change the life; change the life and you change daily living. The first step of today’s lesson is a change of mindset — exchanging “we will build our church” for “Jesus will build Jesus’ church.” Once the mindset changes, the other four will follow of their own accord.

A shift of perspective

From the human to the divine: no longer asking “Who is leading?” but “Is God leading?”

From the earthly to the heavenly: no longer looking only at the figures in the report, but at the register in heaven.

From the temporary to the eternal: no longer asking “Was this event a success?” but “Will this stand on the day of Jesus Christ?”

From the worldly to the godly: no longer leading the church by the world’s logic of power, but by the logic of the cross — right after the Lord said, “I will build my church,” he said he must be killed (see Matthew 16:21).

Brothers and sisters, remember too: rely on the heart and the Holy Spirit, not on the brain and ourselves. Rely on the brain and you worry; rely on the heart and you rejoice. “Keep your heart with all diligence, for out of it is the wellspring of life.” (Proverbs 4:23)

The 920 practice and the 235 relationships

The 920 practice is this: everyone we are in relationship with is our “2”; before them we practise living out a selfless (0) life and bearing the fruit of the Spirit in all nine (9) of its expressions.

“But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith, gentleness, and self-control.” (Galatians 5:22–23)

Notice: not one of these nine is a “power”; every one of them can be seen only in relationships. The person across the meeting table who disagrees with you is the “2” God has given you; whether you are patient or impatient with them — that is your report card.

The 235 relationships are these: become a “2,” a spiritual companion, with someone who is selfless; build “3,” spiritual parents and spiritual children; and go on to become a “5,” a fivefold-ministry team of spiritual comrades.

“He gave some to be apostles; and some, prophets; and some, evangelists; and some, shepherds and teachers; for the perfecting of the saints, to the work of serving, to the building up of the body of Christ” (Ephesians 4:11–12). Look at the purpose in this passage: not each showing off their own abilities, but “the work of serving”; not building our church, but “the building up of the body of Christ.”

sections.heading: 7. Putting It into Practice
sections.html:
The lesson gives us three practices. We will use the eight stages of changing our mindset — Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication — to drive each one deep, one at a time.

Practice 1: Before every meeting and every decision, pray first

The content of the prayer: “Lord, be Lord here. Let your will be done, not ours.”

Information: Remember today’s truth — “On this rock I will build my assembly” (Matthew 16:18). The subject is the Lord, not me.

Revelation: Ask the Holy Spirit to shine his light and remind you of the last time you skipped prayer and went straight into a meeting — and how that matter turned out.

Conviction: Say to God in your heart, “I truly believe you love this church more than I do.” Conviction is not admitting it with your mouth; it is surrendering in your heart.

Implementation: From this week on, before any discussion involving more than two people, pray for one minute before anyone speaks. Just one minute — but it must not be skipped.

Evaluation: At the end of each week, look back: how many times did you do it, and how many times did you forget? On the occasions you forgot, what was your heart in such a hurry about?

Correction: If you find that after praying you still go ahead and do things your own way, change the prayer into thirty seconds of silence — listen first, then speak.

Repetition: Keep this practice up for six weeks in a row. A change of mindset doesn’t come from excitement; it comes from repetition.

Multiplication: Find a co-worker to do it with you, and check in with each other once a week.

The Lord Jesus set the example in the garden of Gethsemane: “My Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass away from me; nevertheless, not what I desire, but what you desire.” (Matthew 26:39) Selflessness does not mean you’re not allowed to have ideas. Selflessness means that once you have them, you still say “nevertheless.”

Practice 2: In service, learn to step back, and ask yourself, “Does the glory for this go to the Lord, or to me?”

Information: Remember the verse — “Not to us, Yahweh, not to us.” (Psalm 115:1)

Revelation: Ask the Lord to show you the one area of service you are least willing to hand over. That one is usually the room where “self” lives most comfortably.

Conviction: Admit one fact — the Lord could get that thing done perfectly well without you; that he still chooses to use you is grace, not necessity.

Implementation: This month, take the area of service you handle most easily, bring someone else in to do it with you, give them the front of the stage, and step to the back to hand them the tools.

Evaluation: When they do it less well than you would, what is your first thought? That is your real spiritual health report.

Correction: If you find you can’t help stepping in and taking over, agree with yourself beforehand next time: “This time I won’t lift a hand. I’ll only pray.”

Repetition: Every quarter, hand over at least one area of service and raise up one person.

Multiplication: Ask the person you raised up to raise up someone else in the same way next quarter. That is the “3” of spiritual parents and spiritual children.

Practice 3: When the team disagrees, first lay down the argument, seek God’s heart, and let the Lord have the last word

Information: Remember the order in Acts 15:28 — “It seemed good to the Holy Spirit, and to us.”

Revelation: Ask the Lord to let you see whether what you insisted on last time was really God’s heart or your own face. Those two often wear the same clothes.

Conviction: If the Lord really wants something done, he has ten thousand ways to do it; if the Lord does not want it done, winning the argument won’t help.

Implementation: The next time a disagreement reaches deadlock, take the initiative and say three things: “Let’s stop for a moment.” “Let’s pray together.” “I’d like to hear your concerns.”

Evaluation: After the argument is over, is your relationship with the other person better? If the matter is resolved but the relationship is broken, that is not victory.

Correction: If you find that what you were really fighting for was control, go and tell them, “I was too insistent last time.” One apology is worth more than ten explanations.

Repetition: Make “pray first, discuss next, decide last” the team’s standard procedure.

Multiplication: Teach this procedure to the small group, the family and the team you serve, so that a culture of selflessness keeps spreading.

A Gentle Reminder

God does not work together with “self”; he is with those who are “selfless.”

When you let go of “I want,” God begins the work of “he wants.”

sections.heading: 8. Closing and Call
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, let us come back to the words we started with.

The heart of “selflessness” is “letting God be God.”

It sounds simple, but living it is the lesson of a lifetime. Because letting God be God means that I am not God; letting Jesus be King means that I step down.

Moses, Joshua, Peter and Paul — all four of them knew this deeply.

Moses knew it, which is why from the very first day that rod was called “God’s rod.”

Joshua knew it, which is why outside Jericho he fell down in worship and said, “What does my lord say to his servant?” (Joshua 5:14)

Peter knew it. When the lame man at the Beautiful Gate got up and walked, and the crowd came running in amazement, Peter’s first words were: “You men of Israel … why do you fasten your eyes on us, as though by our own power or godliness we had made him walk?” (Acts 3:12) The man once rebuked by the Lord at Caesarea Philippi now instinctively turned the crowd’s eyes away from himself.

Later, writing to the elders, he went deeper still: “Shepherd the flock of God which is among you … not as lording it over those entrusted to you, but making yourselves examples to the flock.” (1 Peter 5:2–3) Notice — it is “the flock of God,” not “your flock.”

Paul knew it too. He said, “For we don’t preach ourselves, but Christ Jesus as Lord.” (2 Corinthians 4:5) Looking back on a lifetime of labour, he said only this: “yet not I, but the grace of God which was with me.” (1 Corinthians 15:10)

Brothers and sisters, look at what these four have in common: the true leader is not the person standing at the front, but the Lord who reigns behind the scenes.

The people at the front change. Moses died, and Joshua took over; Joshua died, and the judges took over. But the Commander who stood outside Jericho has never changed. He still stands in the midst of our church today, and he still asks us the same question: are you willing to hand over command?

So this morning I want to issue three calls.

First, hand over your rod. What is in your hand? Your expertise, your experience, your connections, your time. This morning, throw it down before the Lord, and then take it up again from his hand. When it goes down it is “my rod”; when it is taken up again, it is “God’s rod.”

Second, give up your seat. At the next meeting, let prayer speak before discussion; in the next argument, let Scripture speak before opinion.

Third, give the glory back. When things succeed, you know it wasn’t you; when things fail, you know the Lord hasn’t left. From now on, stop saying “We did this,” and say, “The Lord did this.”

When we learn to let Jesus build his church and lead his people, his kingdom will surely come, and his glory will fill the whole earth.

“Let your Kingdom come. Let your will be done on earth as it is in heaven.” (Matthew 6:10)

Brothers and sisters, the first half of this prayer is “your Kingdom,” not “my kingdom.” The moment the Lord’s Prayer opens its mouth, it invites us down from the throne.

Let Jesus be King. Let Jesus receive all the glory.

keyVerses: “I also tell you that you are Peter, and on this rock I will build my assembly, and the gates of Hades will not prevail against it.” (Matthew 16:18)
“He said, ‘No; but I have come now as commander of Yahweh’s army.’ Joshua fell on his face to the earth, and worshiped, and asked him, ‘What does my lord say to his servant?’” (Joshua 5:14)
declarations: Brothers and sisters, please declare with me:
Lord, I am willing to let go of my sovereignty and acknowledge that you alone are the head of the church.
Lead, build and reign yourself, so that our service comes not from ourselves but from you.
Let your kingdom come; let your will be done on earth as it is in heaven.
practices: Before every meeting and decision, pray first
In service, learn to step back and ask yourself
prayer: Dear Lord Jesus,
We thank you, because you said, “On this rock I will build my assembly.” The church is yours, not ours; the will is yours, not ours; the glory is yours, and not ours either.
Lord, we confess that in our hearts we often still sit in the middle seat. We wrap our own wishes in spiritual words and use your name to push our own plans. Please forgive us.

Speak to us as you spoke to Joshua; let us fall down before you, take off the sandals from our feet, and say, “What does my lord say to his servant?” Holy Spirit, help us to pray first before every meeting, and to step back first in every act of service.
Lord, may you increase, and may we decrease. May your name be lifted high, and may our names be forgotten. Lead us yourself, build yourself, reign yourself.
Let your kingdom come; let your will be done on earth as it is in heaven.
In the holy name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen.
discussion: Matthew 16:18 says, “On this rock I will build my assembly.” In your present service, which mindset are you closest to — “we build ours,” “we build Jesus’,” “Jesus builds ours,” or “Jesus builds Jesus’”? Give one specific example to back it up.

John 3:30 says, “He must increase, but I must decrease.” Share a time when you willingly stepped back and gave your place to someone else: what did you honestly feel at the time? And afterwards, what did you see God do?
l065.title: Let Jesus Build His Church
l065.subtitle: A Selfless View of Leadership and Ministry — Let Go of Our Own Sovereignty, Let Jesus Reign (Part 2)
l065.partTitle: Unit 5 · The Road to Revival — Selflessness

sections.heading: Introduction: The Secret of a Grain of Wheat
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, good morning. Today we begin with a grain of wheat.

A grain of wheat lies in the palm of a farmer’s hand — golden, plump, whole and flawless. It can be stored in a granary for three years, five years, ten years, and it will not spoil. Grains preserved for thousands of years have been found in the pyramids of Egypt, their husks still intact. Yet however long and however well it is kept, it remains just a grain of wheat — a single, solitary grain.

Unless the farmer sows it in the soil. Once it falls into the ground, the seed coat swells with water and bursts, the endosperm inside is broken down and used up, and that once-perfect form disappears completely. From a human point of view, that is called “ruined.” But a few days later, a tender shoot pushes up through the split seed coat and out of the soil; a few months later, a stalk of wheat sways in the wind, bearing dozens of times as many grains.

The Lord Jesus used this very picture to speak of himself — and of us: “Most certainly I tell you, unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains by itself alone. But if it dies, it bears much fruit.” (John 12:24)

Brothers and sisters, there is an order here that we often get backwards. We tend to think we must first reach the state of “selflessness” before we can talk about “denying of self”; that we must first reach a spiritual height before we can let go of ourselves. And so “selflessness” becomes a distant mountain that belongs only to Moses, to Paul, to the saints in the biographies — and has nothing to do with me, someone who frets every day over the daily grind, the children’s homework and my performance review at work.

But the order in Scripture is exactly the opposite. It is not that we first have “selflessness” and then “deny ourselves”; it is that as we “deny ourselves” every day, “selflessness” naturally flows out. The wheat does not first grow into an ear and then fall into the ground; it falls into the ground, and only then grows into an ear.

The introduction to this lesson puts it beautifully: “selflessness” is not an unattainable ideal, nor a state that only saints can reach; it is a pattern of life that every Christian can live out. It does not depend on human effort but on the grace of Jesus. Jesus’ death broke the dominion of sin, and his resurrection gives us new life, so that we are able to choose: “it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me.” When we choose every day to “deny ourselves,” the life of “selflessness” will naturally flow out and become the reality of our daily living.

I want to ask you three questions, brothers and sisters. Keep them in your heart as you listen to the whole lesson:

First, have you ever gritted your teeth and “tried hard to be selfless,” only to end up more tired, more defeated, and more aware of yourself?

Second, do you think “denying of self” means losing out, being taken advantage of, trampling yourself underfoot?

Third, do you feel that “self” is too strong — so strong that you’ve given up the fight and just want to keep the peace?

If even one of these three questions has struck home, then today’s lesson is one God has prepared for you. Because today we are going to see together: selflessness is not achieved by effort but received by grace; denying of self is the only road to selflessness; and the strength to keep on denying ourselves lies not in our willpower but in the grace of Jesus.

sections.heading: Scripture Background: Three Scenes Beneath the Cross
sections.html:
To truly understand “denying of self” and “selflessness,” we must first go back to three scenes in Scripture. These three scenes correspond exactly to the three key points of this lesson.

The first scene: the mountain road at Caesarea Philippi (Matthew 16)

The Gospel of Matthew was written by the apostle Matthew for Jews, and is generally thought to have been written between AD 50 and 70. It quotes the Old Testament again and again, to prove to Matthew’s fellow Jews that Jesus of Nazareth is the Messiah promised in the Old Testament, the Son of David, the King of kings.

Matthew 16 is the turning point of the whole book. The place is Caesarea Philippi — a frontier town north of Galilee, built by Herod Philip. The town had a shrine to the Greek god Pan, the cliff face was carved full of niches for idols, and there was a white marble temple dedicated to the Roman emperor. In other words, it was a place “crowded with gods, where the emperor called himself god.” It was in just such a place that Jesus asked his disciples, “But who do you say that I am?” And Peter answered, “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God.” (Matthew 16:15–16)

Immediately after this confession, Jesus did two things. First, for the first time he spoke plainly of how he “must go to Jerusalem and suffer many things from the elders, chief priests, and scribes, and be killed, and the third day be raised up” (see Matthew 16:21). Second, when Peter took hold of him and remonstrated, “Far be it from you, Lord!” Jesus rebuked him: “Get behind me, Satan! You are a stumbling block to me, for you are not setting your mind on the things of God, but on the things of men.” (Matthew 16:23)

Notice how closely one follows the other: Peter has only just been praised, and in the blink of an eye he is rebuked. Why? Because he put the things of men above the things of God. And the Lord Jesus’ very next words are our theme verse today: “If anyone desires to come after me, let him deny himself, and take up his cross, and follow me.” (Matthew 16:24)

So the original setting of “denying of self” was not a monastery or a fasting chamber, but a fork in the road: “Will I set my mind on the things of God, or on the things of men?” To deny ourselves is, at that fork in the road, to yield “my thinking” to “God’s thinking.”

The second scene: the controversy in the churches of Galatia (Galatians 2)

Galatians was written by the apostle Paul and is generally thought to be one of his earliest letters, written around AD 48–55, to the Gentile churches in the region of Galatia in Asia Minor. A group of Judaizers had slipped into the church, insisting that Gentile believers had to be circumcised and keep the law in order to be saved. Paul fought to the end for the gospel truth of “justification by faith.”

Galatians 2:20 is the deepest sentence in that whole controversy. Paul did not write it at a retreat; he wrote it amid the gunsmoke of a battle for the truth: “I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me.”

“I have been crucified with Christ” — in Greek this verb is in the perfect tense (συνεσταύρωμαι), meaning a fact that has been completed and whose effect continues to this day. Not “I am trying hard to nail myself up there,” but “I have already been nailed there; it is an accomplished fact.” This is exactly the foundation of the first key point of this lesson.

The third scene: the arena of Corinth and the inner battlefield of Romans

First Corinthians was written around AD 55, Paul’s letter to a church rich in gifts but riddled with problems. Near the city of Corinth, the Isthmian Games were held every two years, second only to the Olympic Games. Paul uses running and boxing as illustrations: “but I beat my body and bring it into submission, lest by any means, after I have preached to others, I myself should be rejected.” (1 Corinthians 9:27)

Romans was written around AD 57 and is the most theologically complete of Paul’s letters. Chapter 7 describes a most real inner war: “For desire is present with me, but I don’t find it doing that which is good.” (Romans 7:18) All the way to that cry of anguish: “What a wretched man I am! Who will deliver me out of the body of this death?” (Romans 7:24)

Brothers and sisters, keep these three scenes in mind: the fork on the mountain road, the declaration amid the gunsmoke, and the battlefields of the arena and the heart. Today’s three key points unfold from these three scenes.

sections.heading: 1. Selflessness Is Not Achieved by Effort but Received by Grace
sections.html:
We often think of “selflessness” as a spiritual discipline that can only be achieved through perseverance and struggle — as if the spiritual life were a steep slope, and whoever has the strongest willpower climbs the highest. But Scripture tells us plainly:

“Therefore if anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation. The old things have passed away. Behold, all things have become new.” (2 Corinthians 5:17)

Notice that Paul did not say, “If anyone tries hard enough, he gradually becomes a new creation.” He said, “If anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation.” This is an identity already established, not a reward still to be won.

Key word: new creation

“New creation” in Greek is καινὴ κτίσις (kainē ktisis). The word for “new” is not νέος (new in time, fresh off the production line) but καινός (new in kind, never seen before). The word for “creation,” κτίσις, is often used in the New Testament for God’s work of creating (for example, “the creation” in Romans 8:19).

In other words, being born again is not a renovation of the old self, a refurbishment of the old self, a self-improvement of the old self; it is an entirely new creation by God. It is not the result of human effort but the work of God’s grace. Just as the light in Genesis 1 did not come from the darkness trying hard to grow brighter; God said, “Let there be light,” and there was light.

The death and resurrection of Jesus: the two cornerstones of selflessness

This lesson points out two things, every word of them the heart of the gospel:

First, Jesus’ death dealt with the root of “self” — sin and the sinful nature. “Knowing this, that our old man was crucified with him, that the body of sin might be done away with, so that we would no longer be in bondage to sin.” (Romans 6:6) The “old man” is the old self — the self-centred “me,” the “me” inherited from Adam, with myself at the centre. It has not been locked up; it has been put to death.

Second, Jesus’ resurrection gives us his life — the selfless life. “Thus consider yourselves also to be dead to sin, but alive to God in Christ Jesus our Lord.” (Romans 6:11) “Consider” — the Greek λογίζεσθε — is an accounting term, meaning “reckon the books this way.” God has already declared it so; all we have to do is reckon accordingly, believe accordingly and live accordingly.

So “selflessness” is not something we produce; it is something Jesus lives out within us. When we are willing to submit to him and let him reign, his life naturally shows itself. Paul gave the most honest testimony to this: “But by the grace of God I am what I am. His grace which was given to me was not futile, but I worked more than all of them; yet not I, but the grace of God which was with me.” (1 Corinthians 15:10)

Listen to the structure of that sentence: “I worked more than all of them” — he gave everything he had; “yet not I, but the grace of God which was with me” — but he was not the source of the strength. He gave everything, but not by relying on himself. That is the difference — as wide as heaven and earth — between effort within grace and effort relying on the flesh.

Psychology confirms it: willpower runs out, grace does not

In a study published in 1998 in the Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, the American psychologist Roy F. Baumeister and his colleagues proposed the concept of “ego depletion”: self-control is like a muscle, a limited resource; a person who has suppressed a desire in one task is more likely to lose control in the next. In their experiment, participants who were told to resist chocolate chip cookies and eat only radishes then gave up sooner than the control group when working on an unsolvable puzzle.

It should be said that researchers have since debated the size of this effect quite a lot, and replication results have been mixed. But there is one experience every one of us can confirm: in the morning you resolve to be patient today, and you hold on until three in the afternoon — then one remark, and it all falls apart. The harder you push “self” down, the louder “self” gets.

Why? Because suppression just locks “self” in the basement. It hasn’t died; it is only waiting. But the gospel says that “self” has not been locked up — it has already been crucified with Christ. We are not guarding a living prisoner; we are acknowledging a fact of death. The difference between the two is the difference between religion and the gospel — and the difference between weariness and rest.

Moses and Joshua: two witnesses to selflessness

This lesson mentions Moses and Joshua, both of them witnesses to “selflessness.”

For his first forty years, Moses was a prince in the Egyptian palace. He “was instructed in all the wisdom of the Egyptians. He was mighty in his words and works.” (Acts 7:22) At forty he killed an Egyptian in a fit of temper, thinking he could deliver his people — and ended up fleeing into the wilderness for forty years. When God called him at eighty, his first words were: “Who am I, that I should go to Pharaoh, and that I should bring the children of Israel out of Egypt?” (Exodus 3:11)

Brothers and sisters, Moses at forty said, “I can.” Moses at eighty said, “Who am I?” God took forty years to grind a self-centred prince down into a selfless servant. In the end, Scripture’s verdict on him was: “Now the man Moses was very humble, more than all the men who were on the surface of the earth.” (Numbers 12:3) And his deepest prayer was: “If your presence doesn’t go with me, don’t carry us up from here.” (Exodus 33:15) — without God’s presence, he would rather not go at all. That is selflessness.

Joshua was the same. He was a seasoned military leader, yet the victory at Jericho came not from battering rams but from marching around the city and shouting. Before entering Canaan, he met a man with a drawn sword in his hand and asked, “Are you for us, or for our enemies?” The man replied, “No; but I have come now as commander of Yahweh’s army.” And Joshua fell on his face to the earth and worshipped (see Joshua 5:13–14).

Listen carefully to that answer. Joshua was asking, “Which side are you on?” and the answer was, “I am not on your side; I am the commander.” The real question was never “Is God on my side?” but “Am I on God’s side?” Joshua understood, and so he fell down and worshipped. In that moment the commander became a servant. That is selflessness.

sections.heading: Applying the 321 Vision
sections.html:
The first of the Three Foundations says: Jesus is my role model. The source of selflessness is not our resolve but Jesus himself. He, “existing in the form of God, didn’t consider equality with God a thing to be grasped, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant” (Philippians 2:6–7). “Emptied himself” is ἐκένωσεν in the original, meaning “to pour oneself out.” He emptied himself first, so that we would have something to receive.

321 says: the old self is self-centred; the new self is selfless. The self-centred life is the root of humanity’s fall, and pride is the root of the problem. And selflessness is not having nothing; it is entering into the infinite and living out the infinite — “I” no longer live, but Christ lives in me. Brothers and sisters, hold on to this: selflessness is not reducing yourself to zero; it is letting the infinite Lord come and dwell in the vessel that has been emptied to zero. An empty cup is not a loss; only an empty cup can be filled with living water.

So the conclusion of the first key point is clear: stop asking, “How can I become selfless?” and start asking, “Am I willing to let Jesus be King?” The first question puts the focus on ourselves, and the more we ask it, the more tired we get; the second puts the focus on Jesus, and the more we ask it, the stronger we become. Jesus is the focal point — not ourselves, not others, not our circumstances. That is what 321 reminds us again and again.

sections.heading: 2. Denying of Self Is the Only Road to Selflessness
sections.html:
Jesus said, “If anyone desires to come after me, let him deny himself, and take up his cross, and follow me.” (Matthew 16:24)

Brothers and sisters, notice a reminder in this lesson: this is not a suggestion; it is a condition. The Lord did not say, “If anyone desires to come after me, it would be best for him to deny himself.” He said, “let him deny himself.” When Luke records the same saying, the Chinese Union Version — like most English versions — has one word more: “let him deny himself, take up his cross daily, and follow me” (Luke 9:23). Daily — that one word turns the cross from a ceremony into an everyday thing.

Key word: deny oneself

“Deny himself” in Greek is ἀπαρνησάσθω ἑαυτόν, from the verb ἀπαρνέομαι, meaning “to deny, to disown, to draw a clear line against.” The same word appears once more in Matthew, and it cuts to the heart: when Jesus said to Peter, “you will deny me three times” (Matthew 26:34), this was the very word he used.

Brothers and sisters, what a sobering contrast. When Peter denied the Lord, he treated the Lord as a stranger; when the Lord asks us to deny ourselves, he is asking us to treat “self” as a stranger. Every day, you and I choose between the two: either “self” is denied, or the Lord is denied. There is no third way.

So “denying of self” is not “giving up certain things”; it is “disowning a certain person” — the self that keeps wanting to sit on the throne. People can offer up a great many things and still not deny themselves; because if what we give up is not the throne, whatever else we give up is mere decoration.

Denying of self makes room for Jesus

This lesson puts it precisely: “denying of self” is the starting point for entering into “selflessness.” When we are willing to give up our own opinions, feelings, face and rights, we make room for Jesus, so that he can live out his life within us.
