Imagine a tiny house, so crammed with furniture that you have to turn sideways just to walk through. Now an honoured guest is coming to live there. What do you do? You don’t build an extension; you first move the old furniture out. Denying of self is moving out the furniture; selflessness is when the guest has moved in and the whole house is filled with his presence.

You don’t first need to learn “how to make the house feel like the guest is there”; you only need to make room, and his presence follows naturally. In the same way, we don’t first need to learn “how to be selfless”; we only need to make room today and let Jesus be King.

Denying of self is not painful asceticism but a willing choice

This is a precious line in the lesson, and it is the very mindset many of us most need renewed.

Denying of self is not gritting your teeth, not punishing yourself, not putting on a long face so that everyone knows how hard done by you are. If we give something up while keeping a ledger, that isn’t denying of self — that’s investing. True denying of self is willing, and it carries joy, because we know what we are giving up, and we know what we are gaining.

The American missionary Jim Elliot wrote a line in his journal on 28 October 1949 that is still quoted today: “He is no fool who gives what he cannot keep to gain that which he cannot lose.” Six years later, while taking the gospel to the Waodani (then called the Auca) in Ecuador, he was speared to death at just twenty-eight. He gave up the years he could not keep and gained the glory he could not lose.

The German theologian Dietrich Bonhoeffer wrote in The Cost of Discipleship in 1937: “When Christ calls a man, he bids him come and die.” That is not tragedy; it is glory. Because the one who calls us to die died first himself — and has already risen.

Where denying of self happens: the moment the thought arises

This lesson points to a very practical place to practise: every time we become aware that “self” is in charge — wanting to control, wanting to argue, wanting to prove ourselves, wanting to protect ourselves — that is the moment to practise “denying of self.”

Brothers and sisters, write these four verbs on your heart: wanting to control, wanting to argue, wanting to prove, wanting to protect ourselves. These four verbs are the four faces of “self.”

Wanting to control is “I want to be in charge”; wanting to argue is “I want to win”; wanting to prove is “I want to be seen”; wanting to protect myself is “I don’t trust God to protect me.” These four faces show up every day in our homes, our offices and our group chats.

A sister once told me that the fiercest row she ever had with her husband started over whether the spoons in the kitchen drawer should lie sideways or lengthways. Afterwards even she thought it was absurd. But she said something very perceptive: “Actually, we weren’t fighting about the spoons. We were fighting about who gets the final say.” Brothers and sisters, eight or nine out of ten conflicts in our lives aren’t about the spoons. They’re about who gets the final say.

321 puts it penetratingly: pride is leaving our originally intended position and seizing rights, wanting to take the place of God; humility is laying down our rights and returning to our originally intended position — let man be man and let God be God. Pride provokes pride, and both sides lose; humility inspires humility, and both sides win. In that moment, if one person is willing to deny themselves first, the fire goes out; if both people insist on winning, both will lose.

The Lord himself walked this road

Denying of self is not a road God asks us to walk but will not walk himself. That night in the garden of Gethsemane: “My Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass away from me; nevertheless, not what I desire, but what you desire.” (Matthew 26:39)

Notice that the Lord Jesus did not pretend it wasn’t bitter. He said, “let this cup pass away from me” — real humanity, real struggle. But straight away he said, “nevertheless, not what I desire, but what you desire.” Denying of self is not having no feelings; denying of self is having feelings and obeying anyway.

Brothers and sisters, if today you find denying yourself hard, a struggle, your heart weeping inside, I want to tell you: this doesn’t mean you’re unspiritual. It means you are walking the road the Lord walked. The one whose sweat fell to the ground like great drops of blood understands your struggle at this moment completely.

Psychology confirms it: only willing choices go the distance

Self-Determination Theory, put forward by the American psychologists Edward L. Deci and Richard M. Ryan (first proposed in 1985 and set out systematically in the journal American Psychologist in 2000), shows that when a behaviour comes from autonomy rather than outside pressure, people’s persistence, quality of performance and well-being are all significantly higher. Compliance under compulsion tends to be short-lived; only voluntary commitment lasts.

This fits Scripture exactly. When Paul urged believers to give, he said: “Let each man give according as he has determined in his heart, not grudgingly or under compulsion, for God loves a cheerful giver.” (2 Corinthians 9:7) God has never wanted a cross carried under duress. What he wants is a willing heart.

Another study is helpful too. Phillippa Lally’s team at University College London, in a study published in 2010 in the European Journal of Social Psychology, found that it takes an average of sixty-six days for a new habit to become automatic, with individual differences ranging from eighteen to two hundred and fifty-four days. Brothers and sisters, listen to that number — sixty-six days on average. Deny yourself for three days and it is a struggle; deny yourself for sixty-six days and it starts to become like breathing. That is exactly what this lesson says: denying of self is not a one-off but a daily practice; not an emotional impulse but an ongoing decision.

sections.heading: Applying the 321 Vision
sections.html:
The fivefold change of 321 is: mindset, life, daily living, relationships, ministry. Change the mindset and you change the life; change the life and you change daily living. The first step in denying ourselves is always the renewal of our mindset: from “I want to win” to “I want to let Jesus win”; from the human perspective to God’s perspective, from the earthly to the heavenly, from the temporary to the eternal, from the worldly to the godly.

And the 920 practice is the most concrete arena for denying of self. Everyone we are in relationship with is our “2”; as we practise living out a selfless (0) life before each “2,” the nine graces of the fruit of the Spirit — love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith, gentleness and self-control (Galatians 5:22–23) — grow naturally.

Brothers and sisters, fruit is never squeezed out by force. Have you ever seen an apple tree grit its teeth to produce apples? Never. Fruit is the natural overflow of life. The Lord Jesus said, “I am the vine. You are the branches. He who remains in me and I in him bears much fruit, for apart from me you can do nothing.” (John 15:5) Denying of self is the branch no longer setting up on its own; selflessness is the sap flowing through freely.

sections.heading: 3. Keep On Denying Self by Grace, and Overcome the Power of Self
sections.html:
We all know that “self” is hard to deal with. That isn’t the complaint of a spiritual failure; it is the apostle Paul’s own confession:

“What a wretched man I am! Who will deliver me out of the body of this death?” (Romans 7:24)

Brothers and sisters, take great comfort today: the Paul who wrote a chapter as glorious as Romans 8 also wrote a cry as anguished as Romans 7. The spiritual giants are not people without struggles; they are people who know where to cry out.

Thank the Lord, the answer comes straight away: “I thank God through Jesus Christ, our Lord!” (Romans 7:25)

Notice the direction of this way out. Paul did not say, “Thank God, I finally figured it out,” nor, “Thank God, my willpower is strong enough.” He said, “through Jesus Christ, our Lord.” The secret of overcoming “self” lies not in suppressing ourselves but in relying on the grace of Jesus.

From chapter 7 to chapter 8: the law and the Spirit

The main character of Romans 7 is “I.” Someone has counted that in this short passage the word “I” appears dozens of times, yet the Holy Spirit is almost nowhere to be seen. But the moment we reach chapter 8, the Holy Spirit becomes the main character: “For the law of the Spirit of life in Christ Jesus made me free from the law of sin and of death.” (Romans 8:2)

There is an important spiritual principle here: one law can only be overcome by a higher law. Gravity makes a sheet of paper fall to the ground, but when it is shaped into the wing of an aeroplane, a higher law — aerodynamics — makes it fly. Gravity has not been abolished; it has simply been surpassed.

The law of “self” works the same way. The more you press it down with “Don’t! Don’t!”, the harder it springs back. But when “the law of the Spirit of life” is at work, you find that you naturally no longer want to fight for the last word. That is why Paul says, “walk by the Spirit, and you won’t fulfill the lust of the flesh.” (Galatians 5:16) — not “try hard not to fulfil it,” but “walk by the Spirit, and you won’t.”

Key word: beat my body

Paul says, “but I beat my body and bring it into submission, lest by any means, after I have preached to others, I myself should be rejected.” (1 Corinthians 9:27)

The Greek for “beat” is ὑπωπιάζω, literally “to strike under the eye” — a term from the boxing ring, meaning to hit an opponent until his eye socket is black and blue. Paul uses the picture his Corinthian readers knew best: the boxing ring of the Isthmian Games.

But brothers and sisters, don’t misunderstand: this is not self-punishment by willpower. The same Paul, in the same letter, says: “yet not I, but the grace of God which was with me.” (1 Corinthians 15:10) The reason he could step into the ring every day was that he knew deeply a fact already accomplished: “Those who belong to Christ have crucified the flesh with its passions and lusts.” (Galatians 5:24)

Put these two verses side by side: Galatians 5:24 says the old self “has been” crucified; 1 Corinthians 9:27 says Paul beats his body “every day.” “Has been” is the fact of our position; “every day” is the practice of our experience. The position is given by grace; the experience is drawn on by faith. Without “has been,” “every day” is mere asceticism; without “every day,” “has been” is mere knowledge.

This lesson puts it well: the old self has already been crucified with Christ, and therefore he chose every day to “deny himself” and let the Holy Spirit be in control. Listen carefully to that “therefore” — not denying ourselves “in order to be crucified,” but denying ourselves “because we have already been crucified.” The first is the logic of religion; the second is the logic of the gospel.

Denying of self is not losing your personality

This point is very important, and this lesson stresses it: “denying of self” does not make us lose our personality; it renews our life so that we become more and more like Christ.

Look at the people in Scripture. After the Lord renewed Peter, he was still the same blunt, impulsive Peter — only that drive no longer charged after his own face; it charged onto the platform at Pentecost. After the Lord renewed Paul, he was still the same Paul, rigorous in logic and strong in will — only that strength no longer persecuted the church; it suffered for the church. John in his youth was a “Son of Thunder,” wanting to call fire down from heaven to burn up a Samaritan village (see Mark 3:17; Luke 9:54); in old age he became “the apostle of love.” God did not take his fire away; God rekindled his fire on the altar.

Brothers and sisters, denying of self does not turn you into someone else; it turns you back into the person God always meant to make. C. S. Lewis says in Mere Christianity: “Give up yourself, and you will find your real self.” What is given up is the “me” twisted by sin; what is found is the “me” created in the image of God.

Science confirms it: repeated choices reshape the brain

In The Organization of Behavior (1949), the Canadian psychologist Donald O. Hebb put forward a famous principle, often summed up since as “neurons that fire together wire together.” What modern neuroscience calls “neuroplasticity” builds on exactly this: the brain’s neural connections are strengthened by repeated use and weakened by long disuse.

That gives us great encouragement. The first time you choose not to answer back, it will feel very strange, like cutting a new path through dense forest. By the tenth time, the path already shows a trace. By the hundredth time, the path has become a highway — and it is the old path that is overgrown with weeds.

Of course, brothers and sisters, we must be clear: neuroplasticity only describes how the body God made works; it can never replace the work of the Holy Spirit. Habits can change behaviour; only the Holy Spirit can change a life. But this shows one thing — the brain God made was designed from the start for “repeated obedience.” “Repetition” among the eight stages is not a cliché; it is a law of God’s creation.

The less we fight for ourselves, the more the Lord fights for us

This lesson’s “Gentle Reminder” is the pearl of the whole lesson: “denying of self” is not passive retreat but actively letting Jesus reign. The less we fight for ourselves, the more the Lord fights for us; the less we try to prove ourselves, the more the Lord displays his glory.

This is the consistent principle of Scripture. When Moses faced the attack of Korah’s faction, Scripture says he “fell on his face” (see Numbers 16:4); he did not defend himself, and God defended him. When David was hunted by Saul, twice he had the chance to strike, and both times he said, “Yahweh forbid that I should stretch out my hand against Yahweh’s anointed” (1 Samuel 26:11) — and God himself opened the way for him. Before the council, the Lord Jesus “stayed quiet, and answered nothing” (Mark 14:61) — and on the third day God himself raised him from the dead.

The South African pastor Andrew Murray wrote in his book Humility in 1895 that humility is the soil in which every virtue takes root. Brothers and sisters, without the soil of humility, all our gifts, talents and service are just cut flowers in a vase — lovely to look at, but without roots, they won’t last three days.

sections.heading: Applying the 321 Vision
sections.html:
The 321 Path of Serving is: Spirit (the Holy Spirit is my guide), Understanding (the Bible is my standard), Life (Jesus is my role model), Service (let Jesus be King), God (let Jesus receive all the glory). The starting point of this path is exactly the answer of the third key point — not relying on our own brains or our own strength, but on the Holy Spirit.

321 reminds us: rely on the heart and the Holy Spirit, not on the brain and ourselves; rely on the heart and you rejoice, rely on the brain and you worry. Because “out of it is the wellspring of life” (Proverbs 4:23). When we use our brains to calculate, “Will I lose out if I give this up?” we start to worry; when we use our hearts to trust, “The Lord will surely vindicate me,” we find joy.

And the 235 relationships are the most practical protection for keeping on denying ourselves. One person denying themselves alone can easily give way; but when two selfless people become each other’s “2,” spiritual companions who remind each other and pray for each other, they walk steadily. Going further, building “3,” spiritual parents and spiritual children, passes the life of denying of self on; and finally, becoming a “5,” a fivefold-ministry team of spiritual comrades, we establish God’s system together.

Brothers and sisters, remember 321’s order: life first, then relationships, then ministry. People matter more than tasks; relationships matter more than things. The priority of relationships is: first with God, then with ourselves, then with others, and last with things. If we get the order upside down — charging into ministry first and talking about life later — we will feed the very “self” that ought to be denied with the achievements of our ministry. That is the most dangerous failure of all, and the hardest to detect.

sections.heading: 4. Integrating the 321 Vision: From Denying of Self to Establishing God’s System
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, when we place today’s three key points into the whole picture of 321, we see a clear road.

The Three Foundations: denying of self is not a lonely fight

Jesus is my role model. He does not ask us to walk a road he has not walked. The road of Philippians 2 is this: he emptied himself, was made in the likeness of men, humbled himself, became obedient to the point of death, yes, the death of the cross — and then God raised him to the highest place. First down, then up; first give up, then gain — that is an order in the universe that cannot be changed.

The Bible is my standard. How do we know what should be given up and what should not? Not by feelings, not by the look on someone else’s face, not by a passing impulse, but by Scripture. Some things should be given up — my opinions, my face, my rights; some things must never be given up — the truth, holiness, the responsibilities God has entrusted to us. Denying of self never means failing to tell right from wrong, still less tolerating sin. The standard for discernment is the Bible alone.

The Holy Spirit is my guide. Without the Holy Spirit, denying of self becomes a moral performance; with the Holy Spirit, it becomes the overflow of life. In that very moment the Holy Spirit will gently remind you, “Don’t say that.” The one who obeys in that moment gains freedom.

The Two Core Values and the Goal

Let Jesus be King — this is the very centre of this lesson. The third practice in this lesson asks exactly the right question: “Am I in charge here, or is Jesus?” Brothers and sisters, this question can be used to test every decision we make in a day.

Let Jesus receive all the glory — the less we try to prove ourselves, the more the Lord displays his glory. Glory is like water: it only flows downhill. Wherever there is a hollow of humility, it fills up with glory.

Establish God’s system — this is the Goal. We deny ourselves not in order to be lonely good people, but so that God can build his house, his kingdom, his army among a people who are selfless. A stone that insists on keeping its sharp edges cannot be laid into a wall with other stones. A system is built from stones that are willing to be dressed and shaped.

The old self is self-centred; the new self is selfless

321 says again and again: the self-centred life is the root of humanity’s fall, and pride is the root of the problem. The serpent’s temptation in Eden was “you will be like God, knowing good and evil” (Genesis 3:5); the fall of the morning star was “I will make myself like the Most High!” (Isaiah 14:14). From heaven to Eden, sin’s recipe comes down to one word: self.

Therefore humility overcomes pride, and selflessness overcomes Satan. This is not a slogan; it is the tactic of spiritual warfare. Satan’s favourite lines of attack are your self-esteem, your sense of grievance, your “What am I, then?” When someone has already denied themselves, Satan can find no foothold — just as the Lord Jesus said: “for the prince of the world comes, and he has nothing in me.” (John 14:30)

Brothers and sisters, think about that. Satan had “nothing” in the Lord — not a single handle he could grab and pull on. The more we deny ourselves, the fewer handles the enemy has to grab. That is the most effective spiritual protection there is.

And selflessness is not having nothing; it is entering into the infinite and living out the infinite. What you give up is a small “me”; what you gain is the infinite Lord. That is not a loss; it is the best bargain in human history.

The fivefold change and the shift of perspective

The fivefold change of 321 is: mindset, life, daily living, relationships, ministry. In today’s lesson, the most important is the first — mindset.

Exchange the old mindsets: from “selflessness is a state for saints” to “selflessness is the pattern of life for every Christian”; from “denying of self means losing out” to “denying of self means gaining freedom”; from “I must overcome self by willpower” to “I must let Jesus reign by grace.”

When the mindset changes, the life changes; when the life changes, daily living changes; when daily living changes, relationships change; when relationships change, ministry changes. This is the order 321 has witnessed over twenty years, and the road countless brothers and sisters have walked themselves.

At the same time, our perspective must shift in four ways: from the human perspective to God’s — no longer asking “What do others think of me?” but only “How does God see this?”; from the earthly to the heavenly — “Set your mind on the things that are above, not on the things that are on the earth” (Colossians 3:2); from the temporary to the eternal — will today’s quarrel still matter in ten years? In a hundred? From the worldly to the godly — not using the world’s methods to fight for the world’s things.

920 and 235

The 920 practice: everyone we are in relationship with is our “2.” Your spouse is your 2, your children are your 2, and that colleague who opposes you at every meeting is your 2 as well. As we practise living out a selfless (0) life before each “2,” the nine graces of the fruit of the Spirit grow.

Notice the order: it is not that we first have the fruit and then become selfless; we first become selfless, and then the fruit comes. Zero is the soil of the fruit.

The 235 relationships: become a “2,” a spiritual companion, with someone who is selfless, and walk the road of denying of self together; build “3,” spiritual parents and spiritual children, and pass this life on; become a “5,” a fivefold-ministry team of spiritual comrades, and fight for the Lord together. Brothers and sisters, walk the road of denying of self alone and it gets cold; walk it with others and it grows warm.

sections.heading: 5. Practice for Daily Living
sections.html:
This lesson gives us three very concrete practices. We will deepen them one by one following 321’s eight stages of changing our mindset — Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication.

Practice 1: Pray every day, “Lord, help me choose to deny myself today, and let your will be done in me”

Information: First put the truth into your head. Today you have learned: denying of self is not a condition but a response to grace; selflessness is not cultivated by us but lived out by Jesus.

Revelation: Ask the Holy Spirit to turn this teaching into your own seeing. You could pray like this: “Lord, let me see with my own eyes that I have been crucified with Christ.” Teaching is given by others; seeing is given by the Holy Spirit.

Conviction: Move from “I know” to “I believe, and I am willing.” Conviction is the moment you hand over sovereignty.

Implementation: Put this prayer at the very start of your day. Try praying it as soon as you open your eyes, before your feet touch the floor. Because whoever takes possession of the beginning of your day shapes the rest of it.

Evaluation: In the evening, spend three minutes looking back: at what moment today did I snatch the throne back? Not to condemn yourself, but to see the truth.

Correction: Don’t say vaguely, “I’ll do better tomorrow.” Say specifically, “Tomorrow morning, when I take the children to school, I won’t use that tone of voice again.”

Repetition: Remember that number? Sixty-six days on average. Set yourself a practice period of at least sixty-six days.

Multiplication: Find a spiritual companion and do this sixty-six-day practice together, checking in on each other and reminding each other. “Two are better than one, because they have a good reward for their labor.” (Ecclesiastes 4:9)

Practice 2: When opinions differ, learn to listen quietly for the Lord’s voice, and don’t rush to argue

Information: Scripture says, “let every man be swift to hear, slow to speak, and slow to anger” (James 1:19). Those few seconds between “swift to hear” and “slow to speak” are the battlefield of denying of self.

Revelation: Ask the Lord to show you what you are really trying to protect in the moment you rush to argue. Usually it isn’t the truth; it’s your pride.

Conviction: Believe this — not arguing does not mean admitting defeat; the vindication God gives you is more complete than any you could win for yourself.

Implementation: Make a rule — when you feel the heat rising inside, first count to three silently and pray silently, “Lord, you are King.” Three seconds is often the distance between heaven and hell.

Evaluation: This week, how many times did I manage to stay quiet? How many times did I lose ground? On the occasions I lost ground, what was the common trigger?

Correction: Identify your trigger — being misunderstood? Being interrupted? Being compared? For that particular trigger, write down in advance a sentence you will say, such as: “I need to think about what you’ve said. Let’s talk again in a little while.”

Repetition: Start practising in your safest relationships, then gradually extend it to the most difficult ones.

Multiplication: When your family ask you, “Why have you changed lately?” — that is the door to the gospel opening. Don’t miss it.

Practice 3: When facing a challenge, first ask, “Am I in charge here, or is Jesus?” and choose to obey the Lord

Information: Recognise the four faces of “self” — wanting to control, wanting to argue, wanting to prove, wanting to protect ourselves.

Revelation: Ask the Lord to place this question in your heart in every moment. It is a prayer the Holy Spirit is only too glad to answer.

Conviction: Truly believe that Jesus being King is better than me being in charge. Because he loves the people I love more than I do, and he knows better than I do what is best for me.

Implementation: Write this question on a small card and stick it where you’ll see it most — beside your computer screen, next to the steering wheel, on the kitchen cupboard door.

Evaluation: Each week, pick one specific incident and write three lines: Was I in charge then? What did it cost me? If I had let Jesus be in charge, how would it have ended?

Correction: Hand over your most stubborn area. Everyone has a drawer marked “Don’t touch” — it might be money, it might be your children’s future, it might be a particular wounded relationship. Open that drawer today.

Repetition: Once a day, one thing at a time. Don’t try to hand over everything at once — you won’t manage it.

Multiplication: Share your failures and your victories in your small group. Your failures will give others courage; your victories will give others hope.

sections.heading: 6. Closing and Call
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, the closing words of this lesson are beautiful: “selflessness” is not a faraway dream but a daily choice; “denying of self” is not a painful bondage but the starting point of freedom. When we keep on “denying ourselves” and let Jesus reign, his life will naturally flow out, and the world will surely see Christ because of us.

Let us gather up today’s three key points once more:

First, selflessness is not achieved by effort but received by grace. You don’t have to keep struggling up the mountain, because the cross has already accomplished it.

Second, denying of self is the only road to selflessness. There is no shortcut, but there is grace; you don’t have to be perfect, only take today’s step.

Third, keep on denying self by grace, and overcome the power of self. Not by suppression, but by walking by the Spirit; not by self-punishment, but by letting the King take his throne.

Let’s go back to that grain of wheat from early this morning. Brothers and sisters, when that grain fell into the ground, there was no thunder in the sky, and the earth did not shake. No one took a photo; no one applauded. The soil simply covered it quietly. Denying of self is often just like that — it happens where no one sees: in a retort left unspoken, in a door not slammed, in a little extra done in silence.

But God sees. And a few months later, at harvest time, everyone sees.

So this morning I want to give you a threefold call.

The first call: let Jesus be King. Not your consultant, not your emergency fire brigade — your King. King means that what he says goes.

The second call: starting today, don’t try to get there all at once; just take one step a day. There is one thing today that you already know the Lord wants you to let go of. That one. Don’t put it off until tomorrow.

The third call: let Jesus receive all the glory. When one day people ask you “Why?” because of your gentleness, your patience, your refusal to fight, please don’t leave them with “I’m just good-natured by birth.” Please say, “It isn’t me. It is Christ who lives in me.”

“For to me to live is Christ, and to die is gain.” (Philippians 1:21) Brothers and sisters, may these words be the epitaph of every one of us — and, even more, our daily living today.

keyVerses: “Then Jesus said to his disciples, ‘If anyone desires to come after me, let him deny himself, and take up his cross, and follow me.’” (Matthew 16:24)

“I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me. That life which I now live in the flesh, I live by faith in the Son of God, who loved me, and gave himself up for me.” (Galatians 2:20)
declarations: This lesson’s declaration of faith — brothers and sisters, please declare it aloud once every day:

Lord, thank you for your grace, which sets me free from the dominion of “self.” Please help me choose every day to deny myself — not my will, but only yours. May my life become a testimony to your glory, living out the reality of “no longer I, but Christ.”
practices: Pray every day, “Lord, help me choose to deny myself today, and let your will be done in me”
When opinions differ, learn to listen quietly for the Lord’s voice, and don’t rush to argue
When facing a challenge, first ask, “Am I in charge here, or is Jesus?” and choose to obey the Lord
prayer: Dear Lord Jesus,

We come before you this morning confessing how stubborn the “self” within us is. It wants to control, it wants to argue, it wants to prove itself, it wants to protect itself. Many times we have tried in our own strength to overcome it, and time after time we have failed, grown weary and lost heart.

Lord, today you have let us see that our old self has already been crucified with you. This is not a project we must complete; it is a salvation you have already accomplished. Thank you for your death, which broke the dominion of sin; thank you for your resurrection, which gave us new life.

Help us, from today on, to choose every day to deny ourselves. When opinions differ, give us quietness; when we are misunderstood, give us the freedom not to defend ourselves; when we could take control, give us the courage to let go. Holy Spirit, gently remind us in every moment: “Am I in charge here, or is Jesus?”

Lord, be King in our homes, King in our workplaces, King in our church, King in every one of our thoughts. May our lives bear the fruit of the Spirit; may we stand together with our spiritual companions; and may everything we do bring glory to you.
In the holy name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen.
discussion: Question 1: “I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me.” (Galatians 2:20) Have you ever tried to “reach selflessness by effort”? What did that experience bring you? Now that you have heard today that “selflessness is received by grace, not achieved by effort,” how specifically has your mindset been renewed?

Question 2: “If anyone desires to come after me, let him deny himself, take up his cross daily, and follow me.” (Luke 9:23, as the Chinese Union Version reads) In your present relationships, which face does “self” wear most often — wanting to control, wanting to argue, wanting to prove, or wanting to protect yourself? Describe one specific situation, and agree with your small group on a sixty-six-day practice of denying of self, praying for one another and reviewing together.
l066.title: Hold to Denying of Self, and Selflessness Comes Naturally
l066.subtitle: Selflessness Is Not Achieved by Self-Cultivation; It Is Jesus Living Out His Life in Me
l066.partTitle: Unit 5 · The Road to Revival — Selflessness

sections.heading: Introduction: Why Is That One Breath So Hard to Let Go?
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, peace be with you this morning. Today we’re going to reflect together on a lesson that is very short to say and takes a lifetime to learn. It comes down to three words: denying of self.

Let me begin with a scene many of us have lived through. A lift is packed with people. Just as the doors start to close — beep — the overload alarm goes off. The lift falls silent. Everyone looks at everyone else, and nobody moves. Each person has a perfectly reasonable reason in their heart: I’m in a hurry; I got in first; I’ve been waiting ages. The alarm keeps sounding, the doors keep failing to close, and everyone is stuck there. Until one person speaks up: “I’ll take the next one.” The moment he steps out, the doors close and the lift moves.

Brothers and sisters, that little scene is a picture of life. So many relationships are stuck, so many families are stuck, so much church ministry is stuck — not because nobody is capable, but because nobody is willing to step out first. Everyone stays inside, the alarm keeps sounding, and the doors never close.

Here is a scene closer to home. A husband and wife go three days in cold silence over one sentence. In truth, both of them badly want to make up. But both of them have the same sentence in their hearts: “Why should I be the one to speak first?” That “Why should it be me?” is exactly what we have to deal with today. It isn’t that we don’t know how to love. It’s that we can’t bear to let go of that one breath of pride.

That is why the first thing Jesus said to his disciples was not “You must try harder,” nor “You must give more,” but “let him deny himself.” Denying of self is the first step in following Jesus, and it is a lifelong lesson.

In the 321 vision we often say that the old self is self-centred and the new self is selfless. The self-centred life is the root of humanity’s fall; pride is the root of every problem. And denying of self is the very door that leads from the self-centred life into selflessness. The door is narrow, but it opens into a place of vast breadth.

When many people hear the words “denying of self,” their first reaction is fear. Does denying of self mean repressing myself? Does it mean always being hard done by? Does it mean being left with nothing? The lesson’s introduction puts it very clearly: many people think denying of self means pain, passivity and loss, but in fact it is exactly the opposite — denying of self is where true freedom begins.

Why is it where freedom begins? Because as long as a person is still fighting for himself, he will always be in chains. One remark from someone else can colour his whole day; one look can keep him awake all night. His emotions hang in other people’s hands; his worth hangs on other people’s lips. That isn’t freedom; that’s forced labour. On the other hand, a person who is willing to deny himself no longer needs to win, so no one can make him lose; he no longer needs to prove himself, so no one can condemn him. His heart rests secure in God’s hand.

On 28 October 1949, a twenty-two-year-old American named Jim Elliot wrote in his journal a sentence that would later travel the world: “He is no fool who gives what he cannot keep to gain what he cannot lose.” Seven years later, on 8 January 1956, he and four other young missionaries, Nate Saint among them, were speared to death on the banks of the Curaray River in Ecuador by the very Waodani people they had gone to reach with the gospel. They had pistols with them, yet they had agreed beforehand: we will never fire on them. Because, they said, we are ready to meet the Lord; they are not.

That day the world said: what a waste. But this is how the story went on. Jim’s wife, Elisabeth Elliot, and Nate’s sister, Rachel Saint, took a child with them and went back to that tribe. They lived among the people who had killed those dearest to them and taught them to read the Bible. Years later, several of the men who had thrown the spears were baptised and came to the Lord, and one of them later baptised Nate’s son. A grain of wheat fell into the earth and died, and it bore much fruit.

Brothers and sisters, that is denying of self. Denying of self is not loss. Denying of self is placing one grain of wheat in God’s hand and letting him turn it into a whole field.

In today’s lesson we will take the three key points of the lesson text one step at a time. First, denying of self means laying ourselves down and obeying Jesus. Second, denying of self means breathing our last — refusing to fight for that one breath for ourselves. Third, denying of self brings glory to God and good to others.

sections.heading: Scripture Background: In a City of Idols, He Spoke of the Cross
sections.html: First let’s set out the background of our theme verse clearly, because once we understand the background, the force of these words will be completely different.

sections.heading: 1. Author, Audience and Date
sections.html:
The Gospel of Matthew was written by the apostle Matthew, also called Levi, who had been a tax collector in Capernaum (Matthew 9:9). He had been the kind of man who would sell out his own people for money — a man who knew better than anyone how to “hold on to himself.” The Lord called him, and he left everything and followed. That the Lord’s teaching “let him deny himself” should be recorded by the man who was best at grasping is itself a testimony to grace.

Matthew’s Gospel is generally thought to have been written somewhere between the 50s and the 70s AD, mainly for Jewish believers. That is why it quotes the Old Testament so heavily and says again and again, “This was to fulfil what was spoken by the prophet.” The church at that time was facing persecution; following Jesus came at a cost. For first-century readers, “take up his cross” was not a figure of speech. It was a bloody picture they might see any day beside a Roman road.

sections.heading: 2. The Place: Caesarea Philippi
sections.html:
Matthew 16, where our theme verse is found, takes place in a very particular location — Caesarea Philippi. The city lay on the southern slopes of Mount Hermon at the source of the Jordan. It had been enlarged by Herod Philip, and it was a centre of Gentile idol worship: there was a shrine to the Greek god Pan, and a temple built in honour of Caesar. It was a place filled with “man wants to be God,” a place where power, fame and achievement were exalted to the very limit.

It was in that very place that Jesus asked his disciples, “But who do you say that I am?” Peter answered, “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God.” (Matthew 16:15-16) Then the Bible says: “From that time, Jesus began to show his disciples that he must go to Jerusalem and suffer many things from the elders, chief priests, and scribes, and be killed, and the third day be raised up.” (Matthew 16:21)

Brothers and sisters, notice the order here. First they recognise that he is King; then he explains that the road the King must walk is the cross. Knowing who Jesus is and being willing to walk the way of Jesus are two sides of the same thing.

sections.heading: 3. What Came Before: The Sternest of Rebukes
sections.html:
What happens next is the key to the whole passage. “Peter took him aside, and began to rebuke him, saying, ‘Far be it from you, Lord! This will never be done to you.’ But he turned, and said to Peter, ‘Get behind me, Satan! You are a stumbling block to me, for you are not setting your mind on the things of God, but on the things of men.’” (Matthew 16:22-23)

Peter, who had only just been praised — “flesh and blood has not revealed this to you” — is called “Satan” in the very next breath. Why so severe? Jesus himself gives the reason: “for you are not setting your mind on the things of God, but on the things of men.”

The word for “setting your mind on” is the Greek φρονέω (phroneō), meaning “to think on, to be intent on, to fix the mind somewhere.” The same root appears in Philippians 2:5: “Have this in your mind, which was also in Christ Jesus.” It appears again in Colossians 3:2: “Set your mind on the things that are above, not on the things that are on the earth.” So what Jesus rebuked in Peter was not a bad motive — his motive was excellent; it came from love. What Jesus rebuked was that his point of view was wrong. He was standing on a human point of view, an earthly point of view, a temporary point of view, a worldly point of view, and making decisions for God from there.

This is exactly what 321 calls the first of the changes: a change of mindset. From the human to the divine; from the earthly to the heavenly; from the temporary to the eternal; from the worldly to the godly. If the mindset doesn’t change, even the one who loves the Lord most can become a stone that trips the Lord. Once the mindset changes, the life changes, daily living changes, relationships change and ministry changes.

sections.heading: 4. The Passage Itself: The Lord’s Call to Everyone
sections.html:
Straight after that rebuke, the Lord speaks our theme verse for today: “Then Jesus said to his disciples, ‘If anyone desires to come after me, let him deny himself, and take up his cross, and follow me. For whoever desires to save his life will lose it, and whoever will lose his life for my sake will find it.’” (Matthew 16:24-25)

When Luke records the same teaching, the Chinese Union Version has one extra word: “He said to all, ‘If anyone desires to come after me, let him deny himself, take up his cross, and follow me’” (Luke 9:23) — and where we read “take up his cross,” the Chinese Union Version, like most modern translations, reads “take up his cross daily.” That word “daily” matters a great deal. Denying of self is not a one-off decision, not one moving meeting. It is a practice in every morning, every conversation, every choice.

Brothers and sisters, this is the road we are to walk today. In a city that exalted itself, the Lord spoke of the cross. In a generation that exalts itself, the Lord calls us to deny ourselves.

sections.heading: Key Point 1: Denying of Self Means Laying Ourselves Down and Obeying Jesus
sections.html: The lesson text says: denying of self is not denying that the self exists; it is being willing to lay down “our own sovereignty” and let Jesus be Lord. This sentence is very important, so let’s take it a phrase at a time.

sections.heading: 1. The Original Language: Saying “I Don’t Know Him” to the Self-Centred Me
sections.html:
The Greek for “deny himself” is ἀπαρνέομαι ἑαυτόν (aparneomai heauton), literally “to disown oneself, to refuse to acknowledge oneself.” In the Gospels this same verb appears in a scene we all know well: “Jesus said to him, ‘Most certainly I tell you that tonight, before the rooster crows, you will deny me three times.’” (Matthew 26:34) When Peter three times “denied” the Lord, this is the very word used.

Brothers and sisters, the contrast is startling. In the courtyard, Peter pointed at Jesus and said, “I don’t know the man.” And the Lord says to us: point at that self-centred old self of yours and say, “I don’t know the man.”

So denying of self is not wiping out the existence of the self. It isn’t erasing the uniqueness God created in you. It isn’t turning us into people with no opinions, no feelings and no personality. Denying of self is changing bosses — changing who sits on the throne. Before, I sat on the throne of my heart; now I let Jesus sit there. Before, I asked of everything, “What do I want?” Now I ask of everything, “What does the Lord want?” This is the first of the Two Core Values in 321: let Jesus be King.

321 puts it very plainly: pride is leaving our originally intended position, seizing rights and wanting to take God’s place; humility is laying down our rights, returning to our originally intended position, and letting man be man and letting God be God. Denying of self is returning to our originally intended position. When a creature returns to the place of a creature, that isn’t humiliation; it is the greatest security there is. A planet that leaves its orbit hasn’t found freedom; it is heading for destruction.

sections.heading: 2. The Role Model: Surrender in the Garden of Gethsemane
sections.html:
The lesson text says that Jesus’ prayer in the Garden of Gethsemane is the supreme model of denying of self. Let’s read the verse through in full: “He went forward a little, fell on his face, and prayed, saying, ‘My Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass away from me; nevertheless, not what I desire, but what you desire.’” (Matthew 26:39)

The name “Gethsemane” comes from Aramaic and means “place of the oil press.” The Mount of Olives was covered with olive trees, and in the garden stood a stone olive press. For an olive to yield its oil, there is only one way: it must be pressed. The first pressing yields the finest oil; only when it is pressed again, harder, does the oil run out completely.

Brothers and sisters, it is no coincidence that the Lord prayed in “the place of the oil press.” Luke records: “Being in agony he prayed more earnestly. His sweat became like great drops of blood falling down on the ground.” (Luke 22:44) His denying of self was not numb, not unfeeling, not easy. He truly hurt, he truly struggled, he truly said, “let this cup pass away from me.”

That gives us enormous comfort: someone who is denying himself can tell God honestly how he feels. Denying of self does not mean pretending it doesn’t hurt. The Lord didn’t say, “I don’t care.” What the Lord said was, “nevertheless, not what I desire, but what you desire.” The key word in denying of self is that “nevertheless.”

Here I need to point out something in particular. Psychology draws a very important distinction. Professor James J. Gross of Stanford University put forward his “process model of emotion regulation” in 1998. In a study he published with Oliver P. John in 2003 in the Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, they found that people who habitually use “cognitive reappraisal” — that is, reinterpreting what an event means — experience more positive emotion, have better relationships and report greater well-being; while people who habitually use “expressive suppression” — that is, forcing their emotions down and putting on a face that says nothing is wrong — experience more negative emotion and less closeness with others.

Brothers and sisters, hear this clearly: suppression is not reappraisal, and repression is not denying of self. Swallowing the bitterness, smiling on the outside while hating on the inside — that isn’t denying of self; that’s slow poisoning. True denying of self turns the whole meaning of the situation around — not “I’m biting my tongue,” but “I know this cup is the one the Father has given me.” In Gethsemane the Lord did not repress anything; he saw afresh that this cup was the Father’s cup. That is why John records him saying to Peter: “The cup which the Father has given me, shall I not surely drink it?” (John 18:11)

This is exactly what 321 says: rely on the heart and the Holy Spirit, not on the brain and ourselves; rely on the brain and you worry, rely on the heart and you rejoice. Repression is the brain gritting its teeth; reappraisal is the heart looking up to God. Out of the heart is the wellspring of life.

sections.heading: 3. Letting Go Is Not Losing: The Mathematics of a Grain of Wheat
sections.html:
The lesson text says that people are often afraid to let go, because we think “letting go” means “losing.” The Lord answered that fear with a grain of wheat: “Most certainly I tell you, unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains by itself alone. But if it dies, it bears much fruit.” (John 12:24)

Let’s do some sums here. Plant a single grain of wheat and it will send up tillers and put out ears; under normal conditions each ear yields roughly thirty to fifty grains. In other words, that one grain that “died” brings a return many times over. But the grain that “refuses to die” is still a single grain after one year, still a single grain after two, and in the end it goes mouldy in the barn and is eaten by weevils. It can’t even save itself.

Brothers and sisters, this is the Lord’s mathematics. The world’s arithmetic is addition: what you hold on to is what you have. God’s arithmetic is multiplication: what you hand over is what he accomplishes. The only thing the grain of wheat loses is its hard husk; what it gains is a whole field of wheat.

So the Lord goes on: “He who loves his life will lose it. He who hates his life in this world will keep it to eternal life.” (John 12:25) The word for “life” here is the Greek ψυχή (psychē), meaning a person’s soul, a person’s self-life. The Lord does not mean we should loathe ourselves or despise ourselves. He means: don’t clutch that self-centred life to your chest like a treasure. The tighter you hold on to yourself, the more you lose yourself; the more willing you are to let go for the Lord, the more you gain true life.

Here’s a picture from everyday life. There’s a kind of monkey trap made from a jar with a narrow neck and peanuts inside. The monkey reaches in and grabs the peanuts, and with its hand balled into a fist it can’t pull it out. If only it would let go, it could run off at any moment. But it can’t bear to give up that handful of peanuts, so it stays stuck there until the hunter comes. Brothers and sisters, what holds us captive is very often not the jar; it’s the hand we keep clenched.

sections.heading: 4. Applying the 321 Vision: The Fivefold Change Begins Here
sections.html:
321 says the fivefold change is mindset, life, daily living, relationships and ministry. Change the mindset and you change the life; change the life and you change daily living. Denying of self is exactly the first place where a change of mindset lands: I am no longer my own master; Jesus is my King.

This is also the real practice of the Three Foundations. Jesus is my role model — as he prayed in Gethsemane, so I learn to pray. The Bible is my standard — not according to my feelings, but according to the Lord’s word. The Holy Spirit is my guide — “if by the Spirit you put to death the deeds of the body, you will live” (Romans 8:13). Denying of self has never been about gritting our teeth on willpower; it is by the Spirit.

Paul describes this life more penetratingly than anyone: “I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me. That life which I now live in the flesh, I live by faith in the Son of God, who loved me, and gave himself up for me.” (Galatians 2:20)

Brothers and sisters, notice how the verse ends: “who loved me, and gave himself up for me.” Our denying of self is always a response to his. I didn’t give myself up first; he did. It isn’t that I love enough; it’s that he loved first. Selflessness is not having nothing; it is entering into the fullness and victory of Jesus and living out that fullness. “I” no longer live, but Christ lives in me.

sections.heading: Key Point 2: Denying of Self Means Breathing Our Last — Not Fighting for That One Breath
sections.html: The lesson text says: the cross is the actual place where denying of self happens; it is the place where a person “breathes his last.” That is superbly put, and we need to look at it carefully.

sections.heading: 1. “His Breath Was Cut Off”: A Phrase from the Chinese Union Version
sections.html:
In Chinese we have a common saying: “fighting for one breath.” It means refusing to swallow an insult, fighting to vindicate yourself. How many quarrels in a lifetime, how many fallings-out, how many friends turned enemies — trace them to the root, and they weren’t about money, and they weren’t about principle. They were about that one breath. We can’t swallow that breath, so the words come out; once the words come out, the relationship breaks.

And when the Bible records the Lord’s final moments on the cross, the Chinese Union Version uses a phrase that means, literally, “his breath was cut off”: “Jesus, crying with a loud voice, said, ‘Father, into your hands I commit my spirit!’ Having said this, he breathed his last.” (Luke 23:46)

“He breathed his last” is the Greek ἐξέπνευσεν (exepneusen), which literally means “he breathed out.” The Lord actively breathed his breath out; it was not snatched from him. He himself had said: “No one takes it away from me, but I lay it down by myself. I have power to lay it down, and I have power to take it again.” (John 10:18)

Brothers and sisters, there is a beautiful lesson here. All their lives people are “fighting for one breath,” but on the cross the Lord “let his breath be cut off.” We draw our breath in hard to puff ourselves up; he breathed all of his out, to give his life to us.

sections.heading: 2. No Opening His Mouth, No Answering Back, No Self-Defence
sections.html:
The lesson text says: on the cross Jesus did not fight for that one breath for himself. He was betrayed, reviled, flogged and crucified, yet he did not open his mouth, did not answer back, did not defend himself, because he knew the Father would vindicate him. This is exactly what the prophet had foretold seven hundred years earlier:

“He was oppressed, yet when he was afflicted he didn’t open his mouth. As a lamb that is led to the slaughter, and as a sheep that before its shearers is silent, so he didn’t open his mouth.” (Isaiah 53:7)

Peter saw that scene with his own eyes. As a young man he was the one quickest to “fight for that breath” on the Lord’s behalf: in Gethsemane he drew his sword and cut off Malchus’s ear. Many years later, the old apostle wrote:

“When he was cursed, he didn’t curse back. When he suffered, he didn’t threaten, but committed himself to him who judges righteously.” (1 Peter 2:23)

Notice the words “committed himself.” The Lord’s silence was not powerlessness, not repression, not giving up on himself. It was a definite act of entrusting: I hand this matter over to the one who judges righteously. Brothers and sisters, not defending myself isn’t because I have nothing to say. It’s because I have a Father who speaks far better than I do.

The Lord Jesus even prayed for those who crucified him: “Father, forgive them, for they don’t know what they are doing.” (Luke 23:34) That is not weakness. That is the greatest power in the universe.

sections.heading: 3. Turning the Left Cheek Is Not Cowardice but Strength
sections.html:
The Lord’s teaching is consistent: “whoever strikes you on your right cheek, turn to him the other also.” (Matthew 5:39)

To hear these words properly, we have to set them in their culture. In Jewish society the right hand was the hand you did things with. For a right-handed man to strike you on the “right cheek,” he would most likely use the back of his hand — an insulting slap, meant not to injure you but to humiliate you, to make you know your place was beneath his. And “turning the other also” amounts to standing there and saying to him: you can humiliate me, but you cannot decide who I am.

The lesson text has it right: this is not cowardice but a display of strength, because only love can overcome hatred, and only denying of self can bring fighting to an end. Paul says: “Don’t be overcome by evil, but overcome evil with good.” (Romans 12:21)

Let me use a rather interesting comparison here — audio feedback. Any brother or sister who has ever run the sound desk at church knows this. When the microphone gets too close to the speaker, the sound from the speaker is picked up by the microphone, amplified, played out again, picked up again — and you get that piercing shriek nobody in the hall can stand. Where does that shriek come from? From two sides amplifying each other.

Brothers and sisters, quarrels between people work just like that: you get loud, I get louder; you say one thing, I say two. This is what 321 says: pride provokes pride, and both sides lose; humility draws out humility, and both sides win. There’s only one way to stop that piercing shriek — one side turns the volume down. The one who turns the volume down isn’t the loser. He’s the one who rescues the whole room.

The Bible said it long ago: “A gentle answer turns away wrath, but a harsh word stirs up anger.” (Proverbs 15:1)

sections.heading: 4. What Science Says: The Breath You Won’t Let Go Hurts You First
sections.html:
There’s a frequently cited study worth our reflection. Charlotte vanOyen Witvliet of Hope College in the United States and her colleagues published research in the journal Psychological Science in 2001. They asked participants to recall someone who had genuinely hurt them, and to enter in turn an “unforgiving” frame of mind (rehearsing the hurt, imagining revenge) and a “forgiving” one (trying to empathise, wishing the other person well), while their physiological responses were measured. They found that in the unforgiving frame of mind, participants’ blood pressure, heart rate and the electrical activity of the frowning muscle in the brow all rose markedly, and their negative emotions were stronger; in the forgiving frame of mind, all these measures were lower.

Brothers and sisters, this study reminds us of a piece of spiritual common sense. We think that by fighting for that one breath we are punishing the other person, but it is our own blood pressure that goes up and our own brow that tightens. The person you hate is sleeping soundly tonight; you’re the one lying awake.

So denying of self isn’t only for other people’s good; it is also God’s mercy towards us. Nothing God commands us is ever meant to rob us. All of it is meant to protect us.

sections.heading: 5. After the Last Breath: God’s Breath Comes In
sections.html:
The lesson’s “A Gentle Reminder” contains a very precious sentence: when you are willing to “breathe your last,” God’s breath can enter you and give you the power to love, to forgive, to endure and to overcome. That sentence has deep biblical roots.

The Bible describes how humanity began: “Yahweh God formed man from the dust of the ground, and breathed into his nostrils the breath of life; and man became a living soul.” (Genesis 2:7) Human life is something God breathed in.

And after the Lord rose from the dead, what was the first thing he did for his disciples? “When he had said this, he breathed on them, and said to them, ‘Receive the Holy Spirit!’” (John 20:22)

There’s a beautiful link in the original languages here. The word the Septuagint uses for “breathed” in Genesis 2:7 and the word used when the Lord breathed on his disciples in John 20:22 are one and the same: ἐνεφύσησεν (enephysēsen). With the first breath, man became a living soul; with the second, man became a new self filled with the Holy Spirit.

Brothers and sisters, here is the order: first the cross, where “he breathed his last”; then, after the resurrection, “Receive the Holy Spirit!” First the breath goes out; then the breath comes in. If we are stuffed full of our own one breath, there is no room for the Holy Spirit. A balloon blown up tight can’t take in any new air; to take in the new, you first have to let out the old.

This is the heart of 321: selflessness overcomes Satan. What Satan fears most is not the gifted person but the person with no “self.” Because then he has nothing to grab hold of. The Lord said: “the prince of the world comes, and he has nothing in me.” (John 14:30)

sections.heading: 6. Applying the 321 Vision: 920 as a Training Ground
sections.html:
321 has a very concrete practice called “920”: every person we have a relationship with is our “2”; before each of our “2”s we practise living a selfless (0) life and bearing the fruit of the Spirit in all nine (9) of its expressions.

“But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith, gentleness, and self-control. Against such things there is no law.” (Galatians 5:22-23)

Brothers and sisters, notice: of those nine graces, at least five — patience, kindness, goodness, gentleness and self-control — can only be borne when someone is getting on your nerves. If nobody provokes you, where would you need patience? If nobody misunderstands you, where would you need gentleness?

So the “2” who gives you the hardest time is not your enemy; that person is the training ground God has prepared for you. The colleague who always takes the credit, the elder who shoots you down the moment they open their mouth, the family member you can never get through to — they are all a cross the Lord has given you, so that every day you have the chance to let that one breath go, and his life can flow out from within you.

This is what 321 means by life first, then relationships, then ministry. People matter more than tasks; relationships matter more than things. If you win the argument over a “task” but lose a “person,” then on the books of God’s kingdom you’ve made a loss.

sections.heading: Key Point 3: Denying of Self Brings Glory to God and Good to Others
sections.html: The lesson text says: history teaches us that when people fight for power and advantage for themselves, the church falls into darkness; when people are willing to deny themselves, God’s glory comes down. Revival has never been brought about by forcefulness or control; it begins with humility and denying of self.

sections.heading: 1. The Witness of Church History: From Strife to Revival
sections.html:
This is a law that shows up again and again in church history. Whenever a church spends its energy fighting over status, over who’s in charge, over whose name goes first, the pulpit may still be splendid and the meetings may still be lively, but the glory has quietly departed.

Let me tell you a true story. In the early eighteenth century, a band of refugees who had fled Moravia took shelter with Count Nikolaus Ludwig von Zinzendorf in Germany and built a village on his estate called Herrnhut, “the Lord’s watch.” At first the community was anything but beautiful. People from different backgrounds quarrelled over doctrine, over rules and over leadership, and they very nearly split apart.

The turning point came in 1727. They made a covenant to be of one heart and mind, and began to confess their sins, to forgive one another and to lay down what they insisted on. On 13 August that year, during a communion service, the Holy Spirit was poured out powerfully, and the whole community was renewed. From then on they kept up prayer in shifts, around the clock; according to the records of the Moravian Brethren, that prayer went on for more than a hundred years. In 1732 they sent out their first missionaries, to the island of St Thomas in the West Indies. Their watchword was: may the Lamb that was slain receive the reward of his suffering.

Brothers and sisters, see this order clearly: first came the confession and forgiveness of denying of self, then the outpouring of the Holy Spirit; first the letting go, then the revival. Revival has never come out of arguing. It begins on our knees.

The Bible gives us an example from much earlier. As Stephen was being stoned to death, “He kneeled down, and cried with a loud voice, ‘Lord, don’t hold this sin against them!’ When he had said this, he fell asleep.” (Acts 7:60) The young man standing by, guarding the coats and approving in his heart, was named Saul. Augustine, the church father, is commonly said to have remarked that if Stephen had not prayed, the church would never have had Paul. In this world people who deny themselves look as if they’ve been knocked out of the race; in God’s kingdom they are the ones sowing seed.

sections.heading: 2. A Life of Denying Self Is in No Hurry to Defend Itself
sections.html:
The lesson text says: a life of denying self is no longer in a hurry to defend itself, no longer chasing people’s praise, but lets God himself speak and God himself make things plain.

Why are we in such a hurry to defend ourselves? Because we’re afraid of being misunderstood, afraid our image will suffer, afraid of coming off worse. But the Bible says: “Don’t seek revenge yourselves, beloved, but give place to God’s wrath. For it is written, ‘Vengeance belongs to me; I will repay, says the Lord.’” (Romans 12:19)

In the Psalms, David gives us a very practical exercise: “Commit your way to Yahweh. Trust also in him, and he will do this: he will make your righteousness shine out like light, and your justice as the noon day sun.” (Psalm 37:5-6)

Brothers and sisters, notice the promise here: he will make your righteousness shine out like light. Light has one particular quality — light doesn’t need to argue. Light only has to shine, and the darkness retreats. The busier you are defending yourself, the less clearly people see the truth; the more quietly you hand the matter to God, the more room God has to bring the truth to light.

Here’s an everyday comparison. Anyone with experience knows that if you get an oil stain on your clothes and scrub at it hard on the spot, you only spread the oil further and damage the fibres more. The right way is to leave it to soak and let the solvent do its work. Many wounds in relationships are the same. Trying hard to “get it all straightened out” right then often makes things worse the more you talk. Be quiet first, pray first, hand sovereignty over to God first, talk again in a few days — and very often the thing dissolves.

This is exactly the first practice in the lesson: when someone misunderstands or criticises you, don’t rush to explain yourself; first pray quietly and hand sovereignty over to God.

sections.heading: 3. Denying of Self Brings Good to Others: The Power of the Giver
sections.html:
Denying of self doesn’t only bring glory to God; it truly does others good. The lesson text says: a life like this can move people, heal people and even turn the hearts of enemies towards God.

The Lord himself taught his disciples this way: “It shall not be so among you, but whoever desires to become great among you shall be your servant. Whoever desires to be first among you shall be your bondservant, even as the Son of Man came not to be served, but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many.” (Matthew 20:26-28)

Adam Grant, a professor at the Wharton School of the University of Pennsylvania, in his 2013 book Give and Take, divides people into three types: “givers,” “takers” and “matchers.” He observed something intriguing. At the bottom of the success rankings, many are givers, because they are easily worn out; yet at the very top, givers are likewise in the majority. In other words, in the long run, those willing to give often go furthest and have the deepest influence.

Brothers and sisters, this is only a human observation; it isn’t yet the ledger of eternity. But even the world’s research has seen it: those who grasp can’t hold on; those who give end up gaining. How much more in the kingdom of God!

Our Lord all the more so. In his final week on earth, troubled in heart, he said: “Now my soul is troubled. What shall I say? ‘Father, save me from this time?’ But I came to this time for this cause. Father, glorify your name!” (John 12:27-28) He did not ask to be rescued; he asked that the Father’s name be glorified. This is the second of the Two Core Values in 321: let Jesus receive all the glory.

John the Baptist was that kind of man too. When his disciples told him that everyone was going after Jesus, he said: “He must increase, but I must decrease.” (John 3:30) Brothers and sisters, that one sentence is a lesson every servant of God must spend a lifetime learning. Our success is not that our name is remembered; it is that the name of Jesus is seen.

sections.heading: 4. True Victory Is Letting God Be Lord
sections.html:
The lesson text says: true victory is not fighting to the very end, but laying the argument down and letting God be Lord. When we choose to deny ourselves, we open a road for God’s glory.

The Bible says: “God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble.” (James 4:6) This verse deserves our holy fear. God doesn’t simply ignore the proud; he “resists” them. The proud person’s problem isn’t that there’s too little grace; it’s that God himself is standing in his way. Peter says too: “Humble yourselves therefore under the mighty hand of God, that he may exalt you in due time.” (1 Peter 5:6)

Those three words, “in due time,” are the deepest rest of the person who denies himself. We don’t have to arrange our own promotion, pave our own way or grab our own place. We only have to bow quietly low under God’s mighty hand, and when the time comes, he himself will lift us up.

This is what 321 calls the Goal: establish God’s system. Man’s system is a pyramid you climb; whoever is strongest ends up on top. God’s system serves downwards: the Lord Jesus is at the very bottom, holding everyone up. People who deny themselves are establishing God’s system on earth, one block at a time.

sections.heading: Integrating the 321 Vision: Denying of Self Is the Doorway to the Selfless Life
sections.html: Having come this far, let’s set out the 321 vision once more, so that today’s message stands more firmly in our lives.

sections.heading: 1. The Three Foundations: Denying of Self Is Not Something We Achieve by Effort
sections.html:
Jesus is my role model. In Gethsemane he said, “not what I desire, but what you desire” (Matthew 26:39); on the cross “he breathed his last” (Luke 23:46). We don’t have to imagine out of thin air what denying of self looks like; we have a living role model.

The Bible is my standard. When my heart has a hundred reasons to defend myself, the Bible says: “Vengeance belongs to me; I will repay.” (Romans 12:19) The standard is above; feelings are beneath. It isn’t right because I feel it’s right; it’s what the Lord’s word says.

The Holy Spirit is my guide. If denying of self depends on my own willpower, it won’t last three days. Paul says: “if by the Spirit you put to death the deeds of the body, you will live.” (Romans 8:13) Denying of self is the work the Holy Spirit does within us; we only need to obey and not stand in his way.

sections.heading: 2. The Two Core Values and the Goal
sections.html:
Let Jesus be King — denying of self is giving up the throne. There is only one throne in the human heart: either I sit on it, or he does. Denying of self isn’t driving me out; it’s inviting him to take his seat.

Let Jesus receive all the glory — people who deny themselves don’t steal the limelight. “He must increase, but I must decrease.” (John 3:30) God says: “I will not give my glory to another.” (Isaiah 42:8) Only one is worthy of glory.

Establish God’s system — when a group of people willing to deny themselves come together, that is God’s system; when a group of people who all want to be head come together, all you get is a human battlefield.

sections.heading: 3. The Self-Centred Life and Selflessness
sections.html:
321 says: the old self is self-centred; the new self is selfless. The self-centred life is the root of humanity’s fall. The temptation in the Garden of Eden was: “you will be like God, knowing good and evil.” (Genesis 3:5) From that day on, man left his originally intended position and wanted to take God’s place.

But selflessness is not having nothing; it is entering into the fullness and victory of Jesus and living out that fullness. “I” no longer live, but Christ lives in me (Galatians 2:20). Put a drop of water in the palm of your hand and it soon dries up; put a drop of water into the sea and it takes on the vastness of the sea. Denying of self is putting that drop of water into the sea.

Humility overcomes pride; selflessness overcomes Satan. Satan can’t get a grip on someone with no “self,” because every bait he uses hangs on the “self”: face, status, fairness, reputation. When someone has truly denied himself, Satan’s hook has nowhere to catch.

sections.heading: 4. The Fivefold Change and the Priority of Relationships
sections.html:
The fivefold change is: mindset, life, daily living, relationships and ministry. In today’s lesson, the mindset we need to change is this: denying of self is not losing but gaining; not passive but the most active thing there is; not being pushed around but being set free.

Once the mindset changes, the life changes; once the life changes, daily living changes — that grumble in the morning traffic jam, that answering back at the dinner table, that counter-attack in the group chat will all be different. When daily living changes, relationships change; when relationships change, ministry finally bears real fruit.

The order must never be reversed: life first, then relationships, then ministry. The priority of relationships is likewise: first with God, then with ourselves, then with others, and last with things. Many people serve until they are utterly drained precisely because they put things first and squeeze God to the very end.

sections.heading: 5. 920 and 235
sections.html:
The 920 practice: every person we have a relationship with is our “2”; before them we live out a selfless (0) life and bear the fruit of the Spirit in all nine (9) of its expressions. When you get home today, who is your first “2”? Perhaps it’s the very person who most easily makes you want to “fight for that one breath.”

The 235 relationships: become a “2” — a spiritual companion — with someone who is selfless; build “3” — spiritual parents and spiritual children; become “5” — a fivefold-ministry team of spiritual comrades. Brothers and sisters, remember: don’t practise the lesson of denying of self alone. Find a spiritual companion, remind each other, pray for each other, and you’ll go a long way.

The Path of Serving is walked the same way: Spirit (the Holy Spirit is my guide), Understanding (the Bible is my standard), Life (Jesus is my role model), Service (let Jesus be King), God (let Jesus receive all the glory). Denying of self is the posture of every step along that path.

sections.heading: Putting It into Practice: Walking the Eight Stages of Changing Our Mindset into Daily Living
sections.html:
The lesson text gives us three very practical exercises. Let’s use 321’s eight stages of changing our mindset — Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication — to put them into practice one by one.

Practice 1: When you are misunderstood, don’t rush to explain yourself; first pray quietly and hand sovereignty over to God

Information: Copy out today’s verse — “When he was cursed, he didn’t curse back. When he suffered, he didn’t threaten, but committed himself to him who judges righteously.” (1 Peter 2:23)

Revelation: Ask the Holy Spirit to shine his light, so you can see what you are really afraid of when you rush to defend yourself — is it being misunderstood, or is it your image suffering?

Conviction: Acknowledge from your heart that God will vindicate me, far better than I could vindicate myself.

Implementation: Set yourself a concrete rule — when you’re misunderstood, pray for ten minutes before you respond; when emotions are running high, don’t type, don’t reply to messages, don’t make phone calls.

Evaluation: In the quiet of the evening, ask yourself: did I keep to those ten minutes today? When I didn’t, which sentence set me alight?

Correction: Write that “flashpoint” down and ask the Lord to deal with its root — usually the root isn’t in the other person; it’s in my pride.

Repetition: Once isn’t enough. Practise it over and over until it becomes the instinct of your life.

Multiplication: Share your experience with your spiritual companion or small group, and bring one person along to practise with you.

Practice 2: Ask yourself every day: what is one thing today where I can lay down a little of my “self” for Jesus?

Information: Remember the Lord’s words — “If anyone desires to come after me, let him deny himself, take up his cross, and follow me.” (Luke 9:23) The key, as the Chinese Union Version renders it, is “daily.”

Revelation: Ask the Lord to point out one specific thing; don’t stay vague. It might be a habit, a pet phrase, or a topic on which you simply have to win.

Conviction: Believe that laying down this little bit won’t leave you short of anything; on the contrary, you’ll gain something more.

Implementation: Every morning after your devotion, write one sentence: “Today, for Jesus, I will lay down …” Then come back and look at it again in the evening.

Evaluation and Correction: At the end of the week, look back over the seven days’ entries and see in which area the Lord has spoken to you most often. That is the work he wants to do in you this year.

Repetition and Multiplication: Keep it up for thirty days, then invite a brother or sister to do thirty days with you.

Practice 3: When you face unfairness, remember Jesus’ example: don’t fight for that one breath, and let God’s glory be revealed

Information: Memorise this verse — “Commit your way to Yahweh. Trust also in him, and he will do this.” (Psalm 37:5)

Revelation: When unfairness comes, first ask one question: Lord, what do you want me to see in this?

Conviction: True victory is not fighting to the very end, but laying the argument down and letting God be Lord.

Implementation: Prepare a “last-breath prayer,” and when a quarrel starts heating up, say it silently: “Lord, I hand this breath over to you. Fill me with your Spirit.”

Evaluation, Correction, Repetition: After every quarrel, honestly go back over it — was I reappraising, or only suppressing? If it was only suppressing, bring it before the Lord and entrust it to him afresh, until you are truly released inside.

Multiplication: When God really does vindicate you and really does bring the truth to light, tell that testimony, so that more people will dare to deny themselves.

A Gentle Reminder: The Last Breath Is Not the End but the Beginning

The lesson’s gentle reminder says: denying of self is not a mark of failure but the way to victory. When you are willing to “breathe your last,” God’s breath can enter you and give you the power to love, to forgive, to endure and to overcome.

Brothers and sisters, keep this in your heart: what you let go of is your own one breath; what you receive is the breath of God. That exchange is always worth it.

In The Cost of Discipleship, Dietrich Bonhoeffer wrote a sentence that shook the church: when Christ calls a man, he bids him come and die. On 9 April 1945 he was executed at Flossenbürg concentration camp, aged just thirty-nine. His death did not make him disappear; instead it carried his message around the world. Because if a grain of wheat dies, it bears much fruit.

sections.heading: Closing and Call: Walking the Way of the Cross
sections.html:
The lesson’s closing word says: denying of self is the way of the cross, the calling of a Christian’s whole life. Jesus’ denying of self accomplished salvation; our denying of self accomplishes a testimony.
