Brothers and sisters, this morning the Lord isn’t asking us to do anything great. He asks only one question: that one breath — are you willing to let it go?

Perhaps it’s the “Why should I be the one to apologise first?” you hold against your spouse. Perhaps it’s the “You’ve never understood me” you hold against your parents. Perhaps it’s the “Who does he think he is?” you hold against a co-worker at church. Today the Lord says gently: my child, give it to me. I’ll take care of it.

Denying of self isn’t meant to turn you into someone without a voice; it’s meant to make you someone who carries the voice of Jesus. Denying of self isn’t telling you to disappear; it’s letting Christ be magnified in you.

The Bible says: “looking to Jesus, the author and perfecter of faith, who for the joy that was set before him endured the cross, despising its shame, and has sat down at the right hand of the throne of God.” (Hebrews 12:2) The Lord himself has walked this road, and he knows where it leads — to the throne, to glory.

So let Jesus be King. In your heart, in your home, in your service, let him sit on the throne. And let Jesus receive all the glory — not that my name is remembered, but that his name is seen.

When we learn to lay down our own will and seek only his, the world will see Jesus in our lives — the Lord who truly denied himself for love.

keyVerses: “Then Jesus said to his disciples, ‘If anyone desires to come after me, let him deny himself, and take up his cross, and follow me. For whoever desires to save his life will lose it, and whoever will lose his life for my sake will find it.’” (Matthew 16:24-25)
declarations: Lord, I want to learn from your example and not fight for that one breath for myself. May I lay myself down and obey your will in every choice, so that your glory is seen through my life.
practices: Ask yourself every day
prayer: Dear Heavenly Father, we thank you. Thank you for sending your beloved Son, Jesus Christ, to walk the way of the cross for us. He could have fought for himself, yet he chose not to open his mouth; he had all authority, yet he willingly laid down his life. Lord, your denying of self accomplished our salvation.

Lord Jesus, please forgive us. So often we say with our lips that you are King, while in our hearts we still sit on our own throne. So often, for the sake of one breath, we have wounded those closest to us, and wounded ourselves too. Wash us in your precious blood, and let your cross deal with the self-centred life within us.

Holy Spirit, come and fill us. As we become willing to let our own breath be cut off, breathe your breath into us, and give us the power to love, the power to forgive, the power to endure and the power to overcome.

Lord, help us from this day on to take up our cross daily and follow you: to be quiet in every misunderstanding, to entrust ourselves to you in every unfairness, and in every relationship to live out a selfless life and bear the fruit of the Spirit.

May our families, our fellowship and our church, through our denying of self, become living stones in establishing God’s system. Reign as King among us, and may all the glory be yours. In the holy name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen.
discussion: “When he was cursed, he didn’t curse back. When he suffered, he didn’t threaten, but committed himself to him who judges righteously.” (1 Peter 2:23) Please share: is there something recently that made you badly want to fight for that one breath for yourself? If you were to entrust this matter “to him who judges righteously,” what specifically would you need to lay down?

“Most certainly I tell you, unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains by itself alone. But if it dies, it bears much fruit.” (John 12:24) Please share: in your family, workplace or church, in what specific matter is the Holy Spirit reminding you to be that grain of wheat that “falls into the earth”? How do you plan to act on it this week?
l067.title: Denying of Self
l067.subtitle: Not Fighting to Save Face, but Letting Jesus Be King
l067.partTitle: Unit 5 · The Road to Revival — Selflessness

l068.intro:
I. Introduction: One Man Steps Out of the Line

Brothers and sisters, peace be with you this morning. Today we come together to lesson sixty-eight of 321 Morning Devotion — “For Jesus, for Others, Not for Self.” Before we turn to the lesson text, I’d like you to come and stand with me in a real moment of history.

Late July 1941, Auschwitz concentration camp in Poland. A prisoner had escaped. Under the Nazis’ rules, ten men from the same block had to be locked in an underground starvation bunker and left to starve to death, as a collective reprisal. The names were called one by one. When one of the men selected, Franciszek Gajowniczek, heard his number, he could not hold back his cry: “My wife! My children!”

The air froze. At that very moment a frail figure stepped out of the line — a forty-seven-year-old Catholic priest named Maximilian Kolbe. He calmly told the officer, “I want to take this man’s place.” The exchange was approved. Kolbe was pushed into the starvation bunker, where he sang hymns and prayed with the others. He held on for two whole weeks, and on 14 August 1941 he was killed with an injection of carbolic acid. And Gajowniczek, the man whose place he took, survived the war and lived until 1995. In the years that followed, he returned to Auschwitz year after year to tell people how, on that day, one man had stepped out of the line for him.

Brothers and sisters, have you noticed? What shakes us about this story is not that there is death in it — there was death in the camp every day. It’s that there is a choice in it that was “not for self.” In a place where everyone only wanted to survive, one man chose not to live for himself.

The world we live in today is exactly the opposite. Two loud slogans float in the air of this world: “As long as I’m happy” and “Be true to yourself.” They sound kindly, as if they’re protecting a weary modern person. But brothers and sisters, if someone really makes “as long as I’m happy” the highest rule of life, he will discover something terrible: that “I” is never satisfied. The more you feed it, the hungrier it gets; the more you indulge it, the louder it shouts.

In the first book of his Confessions, Augustine wrote a sentence that has been passed down for sixteen hundred years: “You have made us for yourself, and our heart is restless until it rests in you.” The human heart was made for God, so it can’t be filled by anything smaller than God — including “myself.”

That is why Jesus gives us an invitation that runs in the completely opposite direction. He says, “If anyone desires to come after me, let him deny himself, and take up his cross, and follow me.” (Matthew 16:24) This lesson calls that road “For Jesus, for Others, Not for Self.”

Please note: this is not repressing yourself, not self-punishment, nor some self-negation born of feeling worthless. Denying of self isn’t meant to make you someone without a voice; it is finding a higher, more glorious direction for your life. Paul says: “even as I also please all men in all things, not seeking my own profit, but the profit of the many, that they may be saved.” (1 Corinthians 10:33) Here is what denying of self truly looks like: letting every choice we make become a testimony that blesses others and glorifies Jesus. In today’s lesson we’ll look at one principle — “For Jesus, for Others, Not for Self” — and two ways of practising it: “living it for you to see” and “dying for you to see.”

II. Scripture Background: A Letter to a Troubled Church

To really grasp the weight of our theme verses, we need to know the situation in which Paul wrote these lines.

sections.heading: 1. Author, Date and Recipients
sections.html: The author of 1 Corinthians is the apostle Paul. Going by the clues in the letter itself, he wrote it during his stay in Ephesus on his third missionary journey: “But I will stay at Ephesus until Pentecost” (1 Corinthians 16:8). The date is roughly AD 54 to 55. The letter was addressed to the church at Corinth, which he himself had planted on his second missionary journey (Acts 18).

sections.heading: 2. Historical and Cultural Setting
sections.html:
Corinth was then the capital of the province of Achaia. It commanded the isthmus between the Peloponnese and the Greek mainland, with a seaport on each side, east and west, and it was a hub of the Mediterranean world. Merchant ships, sailors and travellers streamed through; wealth poured in, idols stood everywhere, and morals were corrupt. Classical Greek even coined a verb — “to live like a Corinthian” — to describe debauched behaviour.

So Paul’s letter is almost a “list of problems”: factions and quarrels, sexual immorality, believers taking each other to court, marriage difficulties, food sacrificed to idols, disorder in worship, rivalry over spiritual gifts, even some who didn’t believe in the resurrection. A church newly born out of the mire, still spattered all over with mud. Brothers and sisters, that is actually good news — because it means God’s word isn’t spoken only to perfect people.

sections.heading: 3. The Context: An Argument about “Rights”
sections.html:
Our theme verse isn’t a maxim that floated down out of nowhere. It is the conclusion of a discussion three chapters long. 1 Corinthians 8 to 10 deals with “food sacrificed to idols.” Much of the meat sold in the market at the time came from temple sacrifices, and social banquets were often held in rooms attached to the temples. A “knowledgeable” party in the church argued that an idol is nothing, so there’s no harm in eating. Theologically, what they said wasn’t wrong.

But Paul reminded them: “Knowledge puffs up, but love builds up.” (1 Corinthians 8:1) And again: “But be careful that by no means does this liberty of yours become a stumbling block to the weak.” (1 Corinthians 8:9)

Then in chapter 9 Paul lays himself open as an example. He plainly had the right to make his living by the gospel, the right to be supported, yet he says: “Nevertheless we didn’t use this right, but we bear all things, that we may cause no hindrance to the Good News of Christ.” (1 Corinthians 9:12) He even says: “For though I was free from all, I brought myself under bondage to all, that I might gain the more.” (1 Corinthians 9:19)

By the end of chapter 10, Paul gathers the whole discussion into one principle: “‘All things are lawful for me,’ but not all things are profitable. ‘All things are lawful for me,’ but not all things build up. Let no one seek his own, but each one his neighbor’s good.” (1 Corinthians 10:23-24) Our theme verse follows immediately, and the discussion closes at 11:1: “Be imitators of me, even as I also am of Christ.”

Brothers and sisters, keep this context in mind: our theme verse is the conclusion of a “dispute over rights.” It doesn’t mean “you have no rights.” It means “those who have rights willingly lay them down for the sake of others.” That is exactly the pattern of Jesus.

sections.heading: 4. The Setting of 1 John 3:16
sections.html:
Our other theme verse comes from 1 John. This letter is generally thought to have been written by the apostle John in his old age in Ephesus, around AD 85 to 95, to the churches of the province of Asia. Early Gnostic ideas were already sprouting in the church at the time: they despised the body, denied that Christ had truly come in the flesh, and turned “love” into something that existed only in words and ideas.

So John pulls love back to the most concrete place. He first gives Cain as the negative example, then says: “By this we know love, because he laid down his life for us. And we ought to lay down our lives for the brothers.” (1 John 3:16) Then at once he brings it down to the most practical everyday level: “But whoever has the world’s goods and sees his brother in need, then closes his heart of compassion against him, how does God’s love remain in him?” (1 John 3:17)

Love that never lands in action is only noise. Denying of self that never lands in the day we’re living today is only a slogan.

III. Key Point 1: The Rule for Living — For Jesus, for Others, Not for Self

“Whether therefore you eat, or drink, or whatever you do, do all to the glory of God.” (1 Corinthians 10:31)

The world lives with “me” at the centre, but Christians should live with “Jesus” at the centre. Everyone has a centre they live around — the needle in the heart that really points the way when we make decisions. When we shift our focus from “What do I want?” to “What does the Lord want?”, life begins to change.

Paul uses an extremely down-to-earth example here: “eat, or drink.” He didn’t say “whether you preach or pray”; he talked about eating and drinking. Brothers and sisters, what grace this is — God doesn’t only want those two hours of your Sunday; he wants your whole day. Glorifying God isn’t a religious activity; it’s a direction for daily living.

sections.heading: 1. “For Jesus” — First Ask: Does This Glorify the Lord?
sections.html:
“Glory” in New Testament Greek is doxa; the corresponding Old Testament Hebrew word is kabod, whose root means “heavy,” “weighty.” So the plainest meaning of “glorifying God” is this: letting God carry real weight in my life. Not putting God in the gaps in my diary, but putting him at the centre of the scales.

A picture often comes to mind: an orchestra tuning up before it goes on stage. Whether violin, flute or double bass, every instrument has to tune to the same reference pitch — the international standard A above middle C vibrates 440 times a second, a standard adopted at an international conference in 1939 and still in use today. Why must there be a shared reference pitch? Because if every instrument tuned to whatever note sounded good to it, the result wouldn’t be freedom; it would be noise.

Brothers and sisters, “for Jesus” is the tuning of our lives. This is exactly what the 321 vision calls the Two Core Values: let Jesus be King, and let Jesus receive all the glory; and it is the first of the Three Foundations: Jesus is my role model. When everyone in a family, a small group or a church tunes themselves to Jesus as the reference pitch, harmony comes naturally — not because people compromise with each other, but because they all face the same Lord.

So in everything you do, first ask one question: “Does this glorify the Lord?” Ask it before you hit the reply button; ask it before you say the thing you’re itching to say; ask it before you fight for a position in a meeting. That one question is handing the throne back to Jesus.

sections.heading: 2. “For Others” — Then Ask: Will This Build Others Up?
sections.html:
“Let no one seek his own, but each one his neighbor’s good.” (1 Corinthians 10:24)

A little later in the same passage Paul speaks of seeking “the profit of the many” (10:33); the word for “profit” there is made up in Greek of “together” and “bring” — meaning “a benefit brought about together.” The word itself tells us that true profit is never one person winning alone. In Philippians he says too: “each of you not just looking to his own things, but each of you also to the things of others.” (Philippians 2:4) Notice that he didn’t say “don’t look to your own things”; he said “not just.” Christian faith never denies people’s legitimate needs. It simply refuses to let “me” be the only audience.

Even social-science research bears witness to this principle. In 2008 three researchers — Dunn, Aknin and Norton — published a study in the journal Science. They gave participants an unexpected sum of money and randomly assigned one group to spend it on themselves and the other to spend it on someone else. When their happiness was measured that evening, the group who had spent the money on others was clearly happier. And the Harvard Study of Adult Development has followed the same group of people since 1938, for more than eighty years. Its current director, Robert Waldinger, sums it up: what best predicts a person’s health and happiness in later life is not wealth, not fame, but good relationships.

Brothers and sisters, this is just what the 321 vision keeps saying: people matter more than tasks, relationships matter more than things; life first, then relationships, then ministry. When God made us, he wrote “for others” into our blueprint.

sections.heading: 3. “Not for Self” — Learning to Lay Down Self-Interest and Stop Putting Me at the Centre
sections.html:
“He died for all, that those who live should no longer live to themselves, but to him who for their sakes died and rose again.” (2 Corinthians 5:15)

This verse states the heartbeat of the whole lesson: no longer living for ourselves.

The 321 vision often says: the old self is self-centred; the new self is selfless. The self-centred life is the root of humanity’s fall; pride is the root of every problem. Let’s go back to the Garden of Eden and hear what the serpent said to the woman: “for God knows that in the day you eat it, your eyes will be opened, and you will be like God, knowing good and evil.” (Genesis 3:5) At the heart of the temptation was not a piece of fruit but a position: you don’t have to be under God; you can be God yourself.

Isaiah 14 records the “I will” in the heart of the fallen one: “I will ascend above the heights of the clouds! I will make myself like the Most High!” (Isaiah 14:14) The formula of pride hasn’t changed from ancient times until now: leaving our originally intended position, seizing rights and wanting to take God’s place. Humility is just the opposite: laying down our rights and returning to our originally intended position — letting man be man and letting God be God.

In Mere Christianity, C. S. Lewis makes a razor-sharp observation: pride is essentially competitive. It gets no pleasure out of having something, only out of having more of it than the next person. So pride always needs an opponent. That is why, when two proud people meet, it’s like two goats meeting head-on on a single-plank bridge — neither will back down, and in the end both fall into the water. The 321 vision puts it vividly: pride provokes pride, and both sides lose; humility draws out humility, and both sides win.

So the Bible says: “Pride goes before destruction, and an arrogant spirit before a fall.” (Proverbs 16:18) And: “God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble.” (James 4:6) Hear this clearly: it isn’t just that God dislikes the proud; God “resists” the proud. What the proud run into isn’t mere setbacks; they run into the hand of God.

sections.heading: 4. It Looks Like Losing Out, but It Is Spiritual Victory
sections.html:
Living like this looks like losing out. If you don’t fight, someone else takes your position; if you don’t argue, someone else ruins your reputation; if you give way, the benefits land in someone else’s hands. In human eyes, the books show nothing but losses. But remember the shift of perspective the 321 vision speaks of: from the human to the divine, from the earthly to the heavenly, from the temporary to the eternal, from the worldly to the godly. Change the frame of reference, and the plus and minus signs on the very same thing are reversed.

Because every choice that is “not for self” is a testimony that “Jesus is Lord.” Your not fighting says: my position was given by God, not grabbed by me. Your not arguing says: the one who vindicates me is the Lord, not my mouth. Your giving way says: my provision is in heaven, not on this table.

And the deepest reason of all is this: it was on the very road of “not for self” that Jesus accomplished salvation.

“Have this in your mind, which was also in Christ Jesus, who, existing in the form of God, didn’t consider equality with God a thing to be grasped, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of men. And being found in human form, he humbled himself, becoming obedient to the point of death, yes, the death of the cross.” (Philippians 2:5-8)

The Greek word for “emptied himself” means “to pour out until empty.” He did not lose his divinity; he emptied himself of his rights. The one in the whole universe with the greatest claim to live “for himself” chose to live completely “not for himself.” That’s why the Lord himself said: “For the Son of Man also came not to be served, but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many.” (Mark 10:45) Brothers and sisters, the one we follow is a King who emptied himself.

IV. Key Point 2: The First Practice, “Living It for You to See” — A Life That Bears Witness to Denying of Self

“Even so, let your light shine before men; that they may see your good works, and glorify your Father who is in heaven.” (Matthew 5:16)

“For Jesus, for Others, Not for Self” is not something we just say; it is something we practise with our lives. So the lesson text puts forward the first way of practising it, called “living it for you to see.”

sections.heading: 1. The Trap of “It’s for Your Own Good”
sections.html:
Sometimes we say, “It’s for your own good.” Those few words are the declaration of love heard most often in Chinese families — and the most damaging sentence of all. Because it wraps a demand up as a gift and calls control by the name of love.

In the heart of the one who says it, two things are usually mixed together: half is genuine tenderness, and half is pride and the urge to control — I see more clearly than you do, so you should do as I say. When the other person doesn’t comply, we get angry; and the real reason for our anger isn’t that they’ve suffered a loss, it’s that I wasn’t obeyed. Brothers and sisters, that is what the self-centred life looks like when it hides inside love.

So the lesson text puts it very precisely: truly being “for your good” doesn’t mean demanding that others change; it means starting by changing myself.

The 321 vision speaks of a fivefold change: mindset, life, daily living, relationships and ministry. Notice the order — it moves from the inside outwards, and the starting point is always “me,” not “you.” We often want to do it backwards: change the relationship first, so we set about correcting the other person; change the ministry first, so we set about adjusting the structures. The result is that everyone is changing everyone else, nobody is changing themselves, and the more we repair the relationships, the worse they get.

sections.heading: 2. Living It for You to See: Letting People See Jesus in My Life
sections.html:
So “living it for you to see” means letting others see in our lives the pattern of Jesus — see a person who doesn’t live for himself.

Peter says: “For you were called to this, because Christ also suffered for us, leaving you an example, that you should follow his steps.” (1 Peter 2:21) The word “example” here originally referred in Greek to the copybook a schoolchild placed underneath the page when learning to write: the teacher wrote the letters out first, and the child traced them stroke by stroke. Jesus has already written out the lesson of “not for self”; we are the ones tracing over it. And as we trace, the people around us are watching our exercise books.

Psychological research confirms this spiritual principle too. In 1961 Albert Bandura of Stanford University conducted the famous Bobo doll experiment. Children watched an adult hit and kick an inflatable doll, and were then left alone with the doll; the children who had seen the aggressive behaviour clearly imitated what they had watched. From this Bandura developed social learning theory, which holds that people learn by “observation.”

In other words, children don’t grow up according to what you say; they grow up according to how you live. Co-workers aren’t persuaded by your arguments; they’re moved by your example. That is why God didn’t only give the law but sent his Son to become flesh — God knew that people need to see.

sections.heading: 3. Three Places to “Live It for You to See”
sections.html:
First, in the family: not fighting for the last word, but choosing quiet and forgiveness — that is “living it for you to see.”

In decades of research into how married couples interact, John Gottman of the University of Washington has shown that the strongest predictor of a marriage breaking down is not how often a couple argues but the presence of “contempt” in their interactions — the eye-rolling, the sneering, the belittling of the other. He calls criticism, contempt, defensiveness and stonewalling the “four horsemen” of marriage. Brothers and sisters, have you noticed? What drives us to “fight for the last word” is very often contempt: I want to prove you’re beneath me.

So at home, “living it for you to see” usually isn’t doing something great; it’s saying one sentence less — the sentence that was already on the tip of your tongue, packed with destructive power and entirely reasonable, and you swallowed it back. Scripture says love “is not provoked, takes no account of evil.” (1 Corinthians 13:5) When one person stops keeping accounts, the air in the home changes.

Second, in serving at church: being willing to help others flourish and gladly taking a behind-the-scenes role — that is “living it for you to see.”

Ephesians says that God gave the fivefold ministry “for the perfecting of the saints, to the work of serving, to the building up of the body of Christ” (Ephesians 4:12). The goal of ministry has never been to build ourselves up, but to build up the body.

The Bible has a very beautiful example: Andrew. John’s Gospel records that the first thing he did after meeting the Lord was to find his own brother Simon: “He brought him to Jesus.” (John 1:42) At the feeding of the five thousand, it was Andrew who brought to Jesus the boy who had five barley loaves and two fish (John 6:8-9). When some Greeks wanted to see Jesus, it was again Philip who told Andrew, and Andrew who went with Philip to tell Jesus (John 12:22). Brothers and sisters, Andrew’s place all his life was standing just beside someone else’s shadow, bringing people to the Lord. He never wrote a single letter, yet he brought to the Lord Peter, who wrote two.

The most precious service in a church often has no spotlight on it: the one who arrives early to unlock the doors, the one who straightens the chairs after everyone leaves, the one who quietly prays for the speaker, the one who gives the opportunity to a young person and goes to sit in the congregation. However magnificent the pipe organ, someone has to work the bellows behind it.

Third, at work: not fighting for your own advantage, but being willing to treat others fairly — that is “living it for you to see.”

The workplace is often thought to be the last place you could practise denying of self. But Adam Grant of the Wharton School, having gathered a great deal of organisational research in his book Give and Take, shows that in many fields “givers” do often turn up at the very bottom of the performance rankings, because they are easily worn out; yet at the very top, the people who appear most often are givers too — because over time trust accumulates, and people will go through fire and water for someone who has genuinely helped them.

Of course, we don’t refrain from fighting for ourselves in order to climb higher later; if that were the reason, we’d be right back to “for self.” We do it because our Boss is in heaven: “And whatever you do, work heartily, as for the Lord, and not for men.” (Colossians 3:23)

sections.heading: 4. A Life of Denying Self Is Contagious
sections.html:
When we live this way, others are moved, reminded, even transformed. Because a life of denying self is contagious — not because we are especially cultivated, but because the life of Jesus is living within us. Paul says it with absolute certainty: “I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me. That life which I now live in the flesh, I live by faith in the Son of God, who loved me, and gave himself up for me.” (Galatians 2:20)

The 321 vision says: selflessness is not having nothing; it is entering into the fullness and victory of Jesus and living out that fullness. “I” no longer live, but Christ lives in me. Brothers and sisters, what a comfort this is — denying of self doesn’t reduce you to zero; it connects you to the infinite. A drop of water in the palm of your hand soon dries up; put it into the sea and it will never run dry.

Let me give another example close to home for us. On 9 March 1872 a twenty-seven-year-old Canadian, George Leslie Mackay, arrived in Tamsui, Taiwan. He didn’t speak the local language, so he learned it from the herd boys out among the rice paddies. Knowing that many people suffered from toothache, he pulled teeth and preached Jesus at the same time; according to his journals and biographies, he extracted more than twenty thousand teeth in his lifetime. He married a Taiwanese woman, Tiun Chhang-bêng, and in the end he was buried in Tamsui. His motto is generally said to have been: “Rather burn out than rust out.” The gospel came into that land not only through arguments, but through a band of people who “lived it for others to see.”

In 321 practice, this is “920”: every person we have a relationship with is our “2”; before each “2” we practise living a selfless life — that “0” — so that the nine graces of the fruit of the Spirit grow from us: “But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith, gentleness, and self-control.” (Galatians 5:22-23) Fruit is never for the tree to eat itself; the fruit you bear is for the “2” beside you to eat.

V. Key Point 3: The Second Practice, “Dying for You to See” — Denying of Self as Love at Its Fullest

“By this we know love, because he laid down his life for us. And we ought to lay down our lives for the brothers.” (1 John 3:16)

sections.heading: 1. A Clarification First: Not a Threat, but Laying Down Your Life
sections.html:
In Chinese, the phrase “I’ll die for you to see” is often misused, so we must make this clear from the outset: “dying for you to see” is not threatening someone with death. Some people, when they’ve been hurt in a relationship, use self-harm, hunger strikes, even threats to kill themselves, to force the other person to give in. Brothers and sisters, that is not denying of self; that is blowing the “self” up to its very largest — using the most extreme means to make the whole world revolve around me. Once denying of self becomes a weapon, it is no longer denying of self.

What this lesson means by “dying for you to see” is the expression of a love that holds nothing back: “I am willing to pay the price for you, so that you may benefit.”

The Lord Jesus said: “No one takes it away from me, but I lay it down by myself. I have power to lay it down, and I have power to take it again. I received this commandment from my Father.” (John 10:18) The “laid down his life” of 1 John 3:16 uses the Greek verb for “to lay down.” Listen to that word — lay down. Denying of self isn’t having something snatched from us; it’s me laying it down myself. It isn’t the helplessness of being backed into a corner; it is an active choice made standing in freedom.

sections.heading: 2. This “Death” Is Mostly Not a Physical Death
sections.html:
This “death” is not necessarily physical death; it means laying down our attachment to self, our pride, our face and our rights.

Paul says: “I die daily.” (1 Corinthians 15:31) Daily — so this is something ordinary and everyday. The cross isn’t a one-off event; it’s something to be taken up again every morning. Jesus said: “If anyone desires to come after me, let him deny himself, take up his cross, and follow me.” (Luke 9:23) — and there the Chinese Union Version, like most modern translations, reads “take up his cross daily.”

“Deny himself” is a very strong word in Greek, meaning “to disown utterly, to flatly refuse to acknowledge.” Interestingly, it is the very same word used of Peter when he three times “denied the Lord.” Brothers and sisters, this gives us a very deep reminder. Peter once denied the Lord to save himself; what the Lord asks of us is to deny ourselves for the Lord’s sake. The same action, in completely opposite directions. Whom will you deny today?

sections.heading: 3. Three Places to “Die for You to See”
sections.html:
First, when you are willing to lay down who’s right and who’s wrong for the sake of reconciliation in your family — that is “dying for you to see.”

The hardest thing to let go of in a family isn’t money; it’s “I’m right.” Trace the cracks in so many families to their root, and they come down to one sentence: “I’m not in the wrong — why should I be the one to speak first?” Brothers and sisters, here’s a question worth taking home with you today: do you want to win the argument, or win the person?

When Paul rebuked the brothers for suing one another, he said something very weighty: “Therefore it is already altogether a defect in you, that you have lawsuits one with another. Why not rather be wronged? Why not rather be defrauded?” (1 Corinthians 6:7) In God’s kingdom, the one willing to lose out isn’t the loser; he’s the one who has gone a step ahead.

Second, when you are willing not to insist on your own opinion for the sake of the church’s unity — that is “dying for you to see.”

“being eager to keep the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace.” (Ephesians 4:3) The words “being eager” — the Chinese Union Version has “make every effort” — tell us that unity doesn’t happen by itself; someone has to pay a price for it.

The Jerusalem Council in Acts 15 is a beautiful demonstration. There was fierce debate at the time over whether Gentile believers should be circumcised. In the end the council wrote to the Gentile churches asking them to exercise restraint in a few matters, so that brothers from a Jewish background would not stumble. Look — both sides laid something down: the Jewish believers laid down the demands of legalism, and the Gentile believers laid down part of their freedom. Unity has never been one side swallowing the other; it’s both sides taking a step closer to the cross in the middle.

“See how good and how pleasant it is for brothers to live together in unity!” (Psalm 133:1) Brothers and sisters, beauty like this has a price.

Third, when you are willing to sacrifice your own convenience and comfort for someone else’s growth — that is “dying for you to see.”

In 1853 the twenty-one-year-old Hudson Taylor set out from England for China. Most Western missionaries then lived in the treaty ports, wore Western clothes and spoke English. But Hudson Taylor did something many of his colleagues could not accept: he put on a Chinese gown and jacket, grew a queue, and went into the interior. What he gave up was comfort and respectability; what he gained was an open door. He once said something that has been widely quoted: if he had a thousand pounds, China could have every penny; if he had a thousand lives, he would not keep back one from China.

Helping others grow comes at a cost. Training a newcomer is ten times slower than doing it yourself; letting a young person preach is far riskier than giving a safe sermon yourself; walking alongside a struggling brother may mean late nights, being misunderstood and starting over again and again. Brothers and sisters, these are all little deaths. Yet this is exactly how spiritual parents are born.

sections.heading: 4. The Law of the Grain of Wheat
sections.html:
The Lord himself stated this principle as a law: “Most certainly I tell you, unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains by itself alone. But if it dies, it bears much fruit.” (John 12:24)

Botanically, this sentence is remarkably precise. A seed buried in the soil must first absorb water and swell, and its hard seed coat must split open; then the nutrients stored in its seed leaf are used up little by little, feeding the shoot as it pushes upwards and the root as it drives downwards. By the time the seedling breaks the surface and begins to photosynthesise for itself, the once-plump seed leaf has shrivelled and dried and finally falls away. That grain of wheat really has died — and precisely because it died, one wheat plant can bear dozens of new grains. God wrote this law into the soil, and he wrote it onto the cross: refuse to die, and there is only one grain; be willing to die, and there is much fruit.

One study echoes this from another angle. In 2003, Stephanie Brown and colleagues at the University of Michigan published a longitudinal study in the journal Psychological Science. They followed more than four hundred older married couples for five years and found that those who regularly gave practical help and support to others had a markedly lower risk of death, while simply “receiving help” had no such effect. Doesn’t this bear out the words of the Lord Jesus? “It is more blessed to give than to receive.” (Acts 20:35)

Church history gives us two sayings worth taking to heart today. On 28 October 1949 a twenty-two-year-old young man wrote in his journal: he is no fool who gives what he cannot keep to gain what he cannot lose. His name was Jim Elliot. On 8 January 1956 he and four companions were speared to death on the banks of the Curaray River in Ecuador by the very tribe they had gone to reach with the gospel. The world called it a waste. Yet a few years later his wife Elisabeth took their little daughter and went to live among that tribe, and later many of the men who had done the killing were baptised and came to the Lord. Those five lives were exchanged for the salvation of a whole people.

The other saying comes from Dietrich Bonhoeffer. In The Cost of Discipleship, published in 1937, he wrote: when Christ calls a man, he bids him come and die. On 9 April 1945 he was executed at Flossenbürg concentration camp, aged just thirty-nine.

Brothers and sisters, this is exactly what Jesus’ love is like: “By this we know love, because he laid down his life for us.” (1 John 3:16) His “death” gives us “life”; his denying of self accomplished salvation. And when we are willing, in one small thing after another, to “die for others to see,” we are living out the love of Christ.

Paul puts this mystery most beautifully: “So then death works in us, but life in you.” (2 Corinthians 4:12) Brothers and sisters, the “death” at work in you will become “life” in someone else. That is the glory of “dying for you to see.”

VI. Integrating the 321 Vision: The Road Home

Brothers and sisters, set this lesson within the whole picture of the 321 vision and you’ll see that it is in fact the heart of all of 321.

sections.heading: 1. The Three Foundations
sections.html:
Jesus is my role model — the ground of “for Jesus.” Though he existed in the form of God, he emptied himself (Philippians 2:6-7), leaving us an example, that we should follow his steps.

The Bible is my standard — the measure of “for others.” How do I know what “my neighbour’s good” is? Not according to my feelings, but according to God’s word.

The Holy Spirit is my guide — the power for “not for self.” “For as many as are led by the Spirit of God, these are children of God.” (Romans 8:14) Brothers and sisters, if you deny yourself in your own strength, you’ll end up exhausted and bitter; if you deny yourself by the Holy Spirit, you’ll end up bearing the fruit of the Spirit in all nine of its expressions.

sections.heading: 2. The Two Core Values and the Goal
sections.html:
Let Jesus be King means handing the decision-making authority of our lives back to him. The prayer in Gethsemane is the deepest demonstration: “Father, if you are willing, remove this cup from me. Nevertheless, not my will, but yours, be done.” (Luke 22:42)

Let Jesus receive all the glory means passing every round of applause on to the Lord. John the Baptist’s “He must increase, but I must decrease” (John 3:30) is the finest translation of “not for self” there is.

Establish God’s system is the ultimate aim of “for others.” We aren’t building a kingdom with me at the centre; we are working towards “the building up of the body of Christ” (Ephesians 4:12), fulfilling the longing of the Lord’s Prayer: “Let your Kingdom come. Let your will be done on earth as it is in heaven.” (Matthew 6:10)

sections.heading: 3. From the Self-Centred Life to Selflessness, from Pride to Humility
sections.html:
The old self is self-centred; the new self is selfless. The self-centred person is measuring all day long: Was I noticed? Was I treated unfairly? Was I thanked? Measuring like that will measure a person until they’re dried up.

Selflessness isn’t erasing yourself; it is setting yourself in the right place: letting man be man and letting God be God. Humility overcomes pride; selflessness overcomes Satan. Because every attack of Satan plugs into our “self”; when that socket is gone, his cable has nowhere to plug in.

The Lord himself said: “Take my yoke upon you, and learn from me, for I am gentle and humble in heart; and you will find rest for your souls.” (Matthew 11:29) Notice the Lord’s logic — the result of humility is not being hard done by; it’s rest.

sections.heading: 4. The Fivefold Change and the Right Order
sections.html:
The fivefold change is: mindset, life, daily living, relationships and ministry. The first thing to change today is the mindset — exchanging “as long as I’m happy” for “for Jesus, for others, not for self.” Change the mindset and you change the life; change the life and you change daily living.

So the 321 vision says: life first, then relationships, then ministry. People matter more than tasks; relationships matter more than things. Relationships have their order too: first with God, then with ourselves, then with others, and last with things. Brothers and sisters, a great deal of weariness in ministry comes from getting the order upside down — we rush to get things done, go back afterwards to patch up relationships, and only at the very end remember God.

sections.heading: 5. Four Shifts of Perspective
sections.html: From the human to the divine: no longer asking “What do people think of me?” but “How does God see this?” From the earthly to the heavenly: “Set your mind on the things that are above, not on the things that are on the earth.” (Colossians 3:2) From the temporary to the eternal: the step you give way today, no one will remember in fifty years — but the person you helped flourish in that step may remember it for ever. From the worldly to the godly: the world’s arithmetic is “I win, you lose”; the arithmetic of God’s kingdom is “I let go, you live.”

sections.heading: 6. 920 and 235: Living Out Denying of Self in Relationships
sections.html:
The 920 practice tells us: every person we have a relationship with is our “2” — your spouse is a 2, your children are a 2, your colleagues are a 2, and the person you find hardest to get along with is a 2 as well. Before every 2 we practise the selfless 0, so that the nine graces of the fruit of the Spirit grow from us.

The 235 relationships tell us: become a “2” — a spiritual companion — with someone who is selfless; go on to build “3” — spiritual parents and spiritual children; and finally become “5” — a fivefold-ministry team of spiritual comrades. Brothers and sisters, do you see it? “Living it for you to see” builds the 2; “dying for you to see” gives birth to the 3; and the final fruit of “for Jesus” is the 5 — an army that isn’t living for itself.

And here is a word for any brother or sister whose heart is weary today: rely on the heart and the Holy Spirit, not on the brain and ourselves; rely on the heart and you rejoice, rely on the brain and you worry. “Keep your heart with all diligence, for out of it is the wellspring of life.” (Proverbs 4:23)

VII. Putting It into Practice: Living the Principle Out as Days

The lesson text gives us three exercises. Let’s use the eight stages of changing our mindset — Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication — to take them deeper.

Practice 1: Before you do anything each day, ask three questions

Before you do anything each day, ask: “Am I doing this for Jesus? For others? Or for myself?” I suggest writing these three questions on a small card and keeping it in your phone case, on your desk, or on the kitchen cupboard door. Don’t wait for the big things to ask them; the smaller the matter, the more you should ask — ask before you reply to a message, ask before deciding who does the washing-up, ask before choosing where to sit.

Practice 2: Say “It’s for your own good” less, and show love in action more

With family or co-workers, say “It’s for your own good” less, and show love in action more. This week, please try an experiment: replace the “It’s for your own good” you were about to say with one concrete action. If you want to remind your child to go to bed early, first put your own phone down. If you want to urge your spouse to get angry less, first pour them a glass of water. If you want to change a co-worker’s attitude, first take a little of their burden onto your own shoulders. “My little children, let’s not love in word only, or with the tongue only, but in deed and truth.” (1 John 3:18)

Practice 3: Write down one thing where you are willing to “die for others to see”

Write down one thing where you are willing to “die for others to see” — laying down your own ideas so that someone else can flourish. Make it specific enough to write down. Is it that phone call you keep putting off? The serving role you’ve never been willing to hand over? The apology you’ve been waiting three years to make? Write it down, set a date, and then go and do it.

Taking These Three Practices Deeper through the Eight Stages

Stage one, Information. Today you have received the theme verses, their background and the three key points. Information is the starting point, but information doesn’t change people automatically; many people have heard thousands of sermons without changing, precisely because they got stuck at this stage.

Stage two, Revelation. Ask the Holy Spirit to turn information into revelation — not “So that’s what the Bible says,” but “So God is speaking to me.” Be still for one minute: the face that suddenly comes to mind is today’s assignment.

Stage three, Conviction. The most common resistance in our hearts is: “But he was in the wrong first.” “But I’ve already given way so many times.” Conviction is saying to the Lord: Lord, I agree that you are right; I will no longer defend myself.

Stage four, Implementation. Do one thing today; don’t wait until you’ve thought it all through. Denying of self has never been something you do once you feel sure; it’s something you understand once you’ve obeyed.

Stage five, Evaluation. Before bed, take three minutes to look back: at which moment today was I “for Jesus”? At which moment did I quietly slip back into “for self”? Evaluation isn’t condemning yourself; it’s looking in the mirror.

Stage six, Correction. If you’ve hurt someone, go and apologise; if your motive was impure, confess it before the Lord; if your method was wrong, find another way and love once more.

Stage seven, Repetition. Denying of self is a muscle, not a flash of inspiration; it runs on practice, not on feelings. Give yourself at least forty days of asking those three questions every day.

Stage eight, Multiplication. When change begins to show in you, take someone along: teach this lesson to your “2” and walk the forty days with them. Unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains by itself alone; life only truly comes alive when it is passed on.

VIII. Closing and Call: Two Roads, One King

The lesson text closes with a gentle reminder: the road of “for self” is broad, but it leads to emptiness; the road of “for Jesus, for others” is narrow, but it leads to life.

The Lord Jesus said it long ago: “Enter in by the narrow gate; for wide is the gate and broad is the way that leads to destruction, and many are those who enter in by it. How narrow is the gate, and restricted is the way that leads to life! Few are those who find it.” (Matthew 7:13-14)

Brothers and sisters, the narrow gate is narrow not because God is stingy, but because that gate only has room for one person — there’s no room for you and your “self” to go through together. Anyone with too much luggage has to put the luggage down first.

So denying of self is not losing yourself; it’s letting Jesus be seen more clearly in you. The cleaner a window is, the less people notice the glass, and the more they see the light outside.

“For Jesus, for Others, Not for Self” is the truest practice of denying of self. When we are willing to “live it for others to see,” and even to “die for others to see,” the love of Jesus will be revealed through us. A life like this is a life that glorifies God, builds others up and is truly free.

Yes, truly free. Because only when a person no longer needs to prove himself, no longer needs to beat others, no longer needs everyone’s approval, is he the freest person in the world. “For to me to live is Christ, and to die is gain.” (Philippians 1:21)

So this morning I want to issue a call to you: let Jesus be King — starting with the first decision you make today, hand the throne back to him; let Jesus receive all the glory — starting with the first word of praise you receive today, pass the applause on to him.

Brothers and sisters, may we all, our whole lives long, be like the man who stepped out of the line — so that when someone needs a person to take their place, a voice in our hearts says: “Lord, I am willing.”

keyVerses: “Whether therefore you eat, or drink, or whatever you do, do all to the glory of God. Give no occasion for stumbling, whether to Jews, or to Greeks, or to the assembly of God; even as I also please all men in all things, not seeking my own profit, but the profit of the many, that they may be saved.” (1 Corinthians 10:31-33)
“By this we know love, because he laid down his life for us. And we ought to lay down our lives for the brothers.” (1 John 3:16)
declarations: Lord, today I choose to live “for you, for others, not for myself.” Give me the strength to show your love in every small thing, to live a life of denying self, and to be a blessing to others.
practices: Before you do anything each day, ask three questions
Say “It’s for your own good” less, and show love in action more
Write down one thing where you are willing to “die for others to see”
prayer: Dear Lord Jesus, we thank you. Though you existed in the form of God, for our sake you emptied yourself, took the form of a servant, and walked a road that was wholly not for yourself, all the way to the cross. Lord, so often we speak of love with our lips while caring only for ourselves in our hearts; so often we say “It’s for your own good” when really we want others to listen to us. Please forgive us.

Lord, let your Holy Spirit begin working within us today: change our mindset and transform our lives. Make us willing to “live it for others to see” — not fighting for the last word at home, gladly serving behind the scenes at church, treating others fairly at work; and make us willing to “die for others to see” — laying down who’s right for the sake of reconciliation, laying down our own opinions for the sake of unity, laying down our convenience and comfort for the sake of others’ growth.
May every “2” around us see you in us. May every choice we make let you be King; may every bit of glory go to you. In the holy name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen.
discussion: “Let no one seek his own, but each one his neighbor’s good.” (1 Corinthians 10:24) This week, in your family, workplace or ministry, what is one thing you had been doing “for yourself” that you are now willing to change to “for Jesus, for others”? Please name that specific thing, and share how you plan to go about it.

“By this we know love, because he laid down his life for us. And we ought to lay down our lives for the brothers.” (1 John 3:16) In your current relationships, is there something where you have kept insisting “I’m right,” and reconciliation has stalled because of it? Are you willing to “die for them to see” in this one matter? What is holding you back?
l068.title: For Jesus, for Others, Not for Self (Part 1)
l068.subtitle: Principles and Practice for a Life of Denying of Self
l068.partTitle: Unit 5 · The Road to Revival — Selflessness

sections.heading: Introduction: An Order Hidden in the English Word for Joy
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, good morning. This morning I’d like to begin by asking you to look at a very small yet very deep word — JOY.

JOY is, of course, simply the English word for joy. Someone took its three letters apart and found a spiritual order in them: J is for Jesus; O is for Others; Y is for Yourself. Jesus first, others second, yourself last. This is not a play on words; it is the arrangement of the kingdom of heaven. When a person’s life is set in this order, joy comes without being invited; when the order is turned upside down — yourself first, others second, Jesus last — that person may own the whole world and still be empty inside.

I often think of an elderly sister who served in her church for more than thirty years. She cooked, washed dishes, mopped floors, gave people lifts and visited the sick — all the kinds of work nobody applauds. One year she fell seriously ill and spent forty days in hospital. In those forty days the door of her ward was hardly ever still. People came to see her in wave after wave, bringing soup, bringing flowers, bringing prayers. In the end a nurse couldn’t help asking her, “Auntie, are you somebody important?” She smiled and said, “I’m not anybody important. I’m just someone who gave herself away.”

Brothers and sisters, that is today’s theme. In the last lesson we looked at the truth of living “for Jesus, for others, not for ourselves.” In this lesson we want to bring that truth down to earth, down into daily living. Because denying of self is not just a doctrine; it is a way of life.

Jesus never only “taught us.” He “lived it out before our eyes,” and he “died it out before our eyes.” His living was a service of love — every day, every hand stretched out, every time he turned towards someone. His dying was an offering of love — offered once, effective for ever. When we follow him and choose to live “for Jesus, for others, not for ourselves,” our lives are transformed, our relationships are healed and our surroundings are filled with joy.

Today’s message has three key points. First, Jesus lived it out before us — laying down his own rights for the needs of others. Second, Jesus died it out before us — willingly laying down his life so that others might have life. Third, denying of self brings joy — this is the spiritual principle of JOY.

In the 321 vision we often say that of the Three Foundations, the first is “Jesus is my role model.” A role model is not a portrait hanging on the wall; a role model is a set of footprints you can step into. Today, step by step, let’s walk in Jesus’ footprints.

sections.heading: Scripture Background: A Lord About to Depart, and the Last Testament He Left His Disciples
sections.html:
To understand today’s main passage, we first have to stand in that room.

John chapter 15 records words Jesus spoke after the Last Supper. John 13:1 puts it like this: “Now before the feast of the Passover, Jesus, knowing that his time had come that he would depart from this world to the Father, having loved his own who were in the world, he loved them to the end.” Chapters 13 to 17 are usually called the “Upper Room Discourse” or the “Farewell Discourse.” They are the last words Jesus spoke to the eleven disciples on the night he was betrayed, closing with the high-priestly prayer of chapter 17.

The book was written by the apostle John, the one who calls himself “the disciple whom Jesus loved.” According to the consistent testimony of church history — including Irenaeus in the second century — John lived in Ephesus in his old age and wrote this Gospel around the AD 80s to 90s. By then most of the first generation of apostles had been martyred, and the church faced persecution from the Jewish synagogue as well as the infiltration of early Gnostic ideas. John’s purpose in writing is very clear: “but these are written, that you may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and that believing you may have life in his name.” (John 20:31)

Notice the setting. The one speaking is a Lord who, in a few hours, will be arrested, flogged and crucified. Those listening are a band of disciples who are about to scatter and run, one of whom will even deny his Lord three times. At a moment like that, Jesus talks not about his own fear but about his disciples’ joy. He says, “that my joy may remain in you, and that your joy may be made full.” (John 15:11)

Brothers and sisters, that alone is enough to make us bow our heads. Someone who, at the very moment of greatest pain, still cares about the joy of others — that is what “not for ourselves” means.

What comes before this in chapter 15 is the parable “I am the true vine” (verses 1–8): unless the branch remains in the vine, it cannot bear fruit by itself. Then verses 9–11 speak of “remain in my love,” and verses 12–13 take that love to its furthest point: “This is my commandment, that you love one another, even as I have loved you. Greater love has no one than this, that someone lay down his life for his friends.” (John 15:12–13)

So what comes before “joy” is “connection,” and what comes after “joy” is “laying down one’s life.” True joy sits between “union with the Lord” and “denying ourselves for others.” Apart from those two, everything people chase is mere emotion, not joy.

Today we’ll also look at two other passages. One is in Mark chapter 6, a slice of Jesus “living it out before us.” Mark is generally held to be the earliest Gospel, written around the AD 60s; its author, Mark (John Mark), recorded the testimony Peter preached and wrote it for the believers in Rome. Mark’s Jesus is a “servant” — always moving, always working, always serving — and the key verse of the whole book is Mark 10:45. The other passage is in John chapter 10, the Good Shepherd discourse, Jesus’ declaration that he would “die it out before us.”

A Lord who lived it out before us, a Lord who died it out before us, and who in the end left us “joy made full.” That is today’s road map.

sections.heading: Key Point 1: Jesus “Lived It Out Before Us” — Laying Down His Own Rights for the Needs of Others
1. The Text: A Weary Lord, a Compassionate Heart
sections.html:
Every day Jesus lived on earth, he was showing us the pattern of denying of self. Mark chapter 6 records a very real scene:

“The apostles gathered themselves together to Jesus, and they told him all things, whatever they had done, and whatever they had taught. He said to them, ‘You come apart into a deserted place, and rest awhile.’ For there were many coming and going, and they had no leisure so much as to eat. They went away in the boat to a deserted place by themselves. They saw them going, and many recognized him and ran there on foot from all the cities. They arrived before them and came together to him. Jesus came out, saw a great multitude, and he had compassion on them, because they were like sheep without a shepherd, and he began to teach them many things.” (Mark 6:30–34)

Brothers and sisters, look closely at these verses. The disciples had just come back from their mission, so worn out they didn’t even have time to eat. Jesus himself was wearier still — he had just heard the terrible news that John the Baptist had been beheaded. He proposed going to a deserted place to rest awhile; that was a perfectly reasonable right. He got into the boat, finally made it to the other shore, and what happened? The shore was already thick with people.

If it had been us, a sentence would most likely have bubbled up inside: “Can’t a person even get some rest?” But Scripture says that Jesus “saw a great multitude, and he had compassion on them.”

sections.heading: 2. The Original Language: A Love That Churns from the Depths
sections.html:
The word for “compassion” here is the Greek σπλαγχνίζομαι (splanchnizomai), whose root is σπλάγχνα, meaning “the inward parts, the bowels.” The Jews believed that the deepest emotions lived in a person’s inner organs. So this word is not polite sympathy, not standing at a distance and saying, “What a pity.” It means that a person’s whole insides are churned up and wrung. Chinese expressions such as “heart and bowels torn to pieces” or “moved with tender mercy” come closest to it.

In the New Testament this verb is used almost exclusively of Jesus, or of figures who stand for God in the parables Jesus told — like the prodigal son’s father, who “was moved with compassion” (Luke 15:20), or the good Samaritan, who “was moved with compassion” (Luke 10:33).

In other words, Jesus’ service didn’t come out of a schedule; it came out of his very insides. It came not from duty but from love; not because he “ought to” but because he “couldn’t bear not to.”

Duty can hold you up for a while; only love can hold you up for a lifetime. Much service dries up because it flows from “ought to” rather than from “can’t bear not to.” Service that comes from “ought to” turns into resentment over time; service that comes from “can’t bear not to” grows sweeter over time.

There’s another phrase worth savouring slowly: “they were like sheep without a shepherd.” This was not something new Jesus coined; it was a heavy lament from the Old Testament. As Moses was about to die, he asked God for a leader “that the congregation of Yahweh may not be as sheep which have no shepherd.” (Numbers 27:17) The prophet Micaiah saw a vision: “I saw all Israel scattered on the mountains, as sheep that have no shepherd.” (1 Kings 22:17) Ezekiel chapter 34 rebukes Israel’s shepherds even more severely: “You eat the fat. You clothe yourself with the wool. You kill the fatlings, but you don’t feed the sheep.” (Ezekiel 34:3)

So when Jesus says “like sheep without a shepherd,” he is announcing that the true Shepherd Ezekiel prophesied has come. Ezekiel 34:15 says, “I myself will be the shepherd of my sheep, and I will cause them to lie down,” says the Lord Yahweh. That day on the shore of Galilee, the prophecy was fulfilled — the true Shepherd stepped out of the boat, saw the flock, and walked towards them.

sections.heading: 3. Scripture Interpreting Scripture: Laying Down His Rights and Taking the Form of a Servant
sections.html:
What did Jesus lay down? His “rights.” He had the right to rest, the right to be served, the right to say, “No consultations today.” But he laid them down.

Paul puts this most clearly: “Have this in your mind, which was also in Christ Jesus, who, existing in the form of God, didn’t consider equality with God a thing to be grasped, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of men. And being found in human form, he humbled himself, becoming obedient to the point of death, yes, the death of the cross.” (Philippians 2:5–8)

The Greek for “emptied himself” is κενόω (kenoō), meaning “to empty out.” Jesus did not lose his divine nature; rather, he laid down his right to use the privileges of that divinity. He could have called on more than twelve legions of angels, yet he chose to be crucified; he could have had quiet in the wilderness, yet he chose to teach.

Mark 10:45 is the key to the whole book: “For the Son of Man also came not to be served, but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many.” He is the Lord, yet he carries the basin of water; he is the Teacher, yet he washes the disciples’ feet. John 13:14–15 says, “If I then, the Lord and the Teacher, have washed your feet, you also ought to wash one another’s feet. For I have given you an example, that you should also do as I have done to you.”

Brothers and sisters, please remember: true denying of self is not repressing yourself; it is an expression of love — compassion flowing from the heart of God. Repression locks your emotions away; love throws your life open. Repression builds up resentment; love bears fruit.

sections.heading: 4. Illustration: Giving Away Your Rights as a Gift
sections.html:
There’s a picture that captures this vividly. Someone once said that life is like holding a handful of sand. Open your hand, and the sand stays in your palm; clench your fist, and it runs out between your fingers. Our rights are the same: the tighter we grip them, the faster we lose them; the more willing we are to open our hands, the more we’re actually able to hold.

In daily living, this comes down to three very practical little things:

First, when you’re willing to listen instead of rushing to defend yourself, you’re living out the gentleness of Jesus. Most of us don’t lack the ability to talk; we lack the ability to stop talking. James 1:19 says, “So, then, my beloved brothers, let every man be swift to hear, slow to speak, and slow to anger.”

Second, when you’re willing to help without seeking anything in return, you’re living out the servanthood of Jesus. Only help that expects nothing back can be called grace; the moment you start keeping accounts, it becomes a transaction.

Third, when you’re willing to give way rather than argue, you’re living out the peace of Jesus. Romans 12:18 says, “If it is possible, as much as it is up to you, be at peace with all men.”

“Living it out before others” isn’t about proving how good you are; it’s about letting people see how real Jesus is.

sections.heading: 5. Supporting Evidence from Science and Psychology: People Who Give Live Better
sections.html:
There is a frequently cited study in psychology. In 2003, Stephanie L. Brown of the University of Michigan and her colleagues published a paper in the journal Psychological Science titled “Providing Social Support May Be More Beneficial Than Receiving It.” The research team followed 423 older married couples in the Detroit area for five years. They found that, after controlling for health, age, finances and other variables, the people who regularly “gave help” had a significantly lower risk of dying, whereas simply “receiving help” had no such effect.

Brothers and sisters, this doesn’t mean we are saved by doing good; salvation is entirely God’s grace. But from another angle this research confirms the words of Scripture: human beings were made to live by “giving themselves away.” A heart that beats only for itself doesn’t actually live long.

Speaking of hearts, here’s a beautiful fact. The human heart beats about a hundred thousand times a day and never takes a day off in a whole lifetime, sending blood to every cell in the body. And the heart itself? It is supplied by just a few thin coronary arteries. It gives away the most and keeps the least for itself. God has written the truth of denying of self inside our very chests.

sections.heading: 6. Applying the 321 Vision: From the Self-Centred Life to Selflessness
sections.html:
In the 321 vision we say that the mark of the old self is the self-centred life, and the mark of the new self is selflessness. The self-centred life is the root of humanity’s fall; pride is the root of every problem. Pride is leaving our originally intended position, seizing rights and wanting to take God’s place; humility is laying down our rights and returning to our originally intended position — let man be man and let God be God.

What did Jesus do on the shore of Galilee? He laid down his “right to rest” and returned to his “position as Shepherd.” That is selflessness.

Selflessness is not having nothing; it is entering into the infinite and living out the infinite. Galatians 2:20 says, “I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me.” What you lay down is your limited self; what you gain is the limitless Christ.

And remember the 321 order: life first, then relationships, then ministry. Jesus first had a life connected to the Father, then a relationship of compassion with the flock, and only last a ministry of teaching. Turn the order around, and ministry will crush life, and service will turn into a performance.

sections.heading: Key Point 2: Jesus “Died It Out Before Us” — Willingly Laying Down His Life So That Others Might Have Life
1. The Text: No One Takes My Life from Me
sections.html:
Jesus knew that to save the lost sheep of the world it would take not only teaching the truth but paying the price of his life. So in the Good Shepherd discourse he said:

“I am the good shepherd. The good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep.” (John 10:11)

“Therefore the Father loves me, because I lay down my life, that I may take it again. No one takes it away from me, but I lay it down by myself. I have power to lay it down, and I have power to take it again. I received this commandment from my Father.” (John 10:17–18)

Brothers and sisters, listen carefully to this sentence: “No one takes it away from me, but I lay it down by myself.” The cross was not an accident, not a slip, not a victory for Roman soldiers. The cross was the deliberate choice of the Son of God.

sections.heading: 2. The Original Language: Laying Down Life, and Authority
sections.html:
The Greek for “lay down his life” is τίθημι τὴν ψυχήν (tithēmi tēn psychēn), literally “to lay down one’s soul, one’s life.” The verb τίθημι means “to lay down, to set out, to place.” Jesus did not have his life snatched away by others; he laid it down himself, step by step.

The word translated “power” is the Greek ἐξουσία (exousia), meaning lawful authority and freedom. Jesus said, “I have power to lay it down, and I have power to take it again.” Only someone who truly has authority is in a position to lay it down; when someone without authority lets go, that is called helplessness. So denying of self is not the weak resigning themselves to fate; it is the choice of the one who has the power.

These words reveal what true denying of self is — not forced but voluntary; not grudging but born of love.

sections.heading: 3. Scripture Interpreting Scripture: The Logic of a Grain of Wheat
sections.html:
Jesus’ death was not a defeat but a glorious victory. His “death” bought our “life”; his denying of self accomplished our redemption.

He explained it himself with a picture any farmer understands: “Most certainly I tell you, unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains by itself alone. But if it dies, it bears much fruit.” (John 12:24)

A grain of wheat has two choices: stay in the barn and keep itself intact, or fall into the ground and lose itself. Stay in the barn, and it will be a single grain for ever; fall into the ground, and it becomes a whole field of wheat. The arithmetic of God’s kingdom is the exact opposite of the world’s: the world says “keeping is having”; God says “giving is gaining.”

The Old Testament foreshadowed this long ago. On the night of the Passover, the lamb was slain and its blood was smeared on the doorframe, and death passed over that household (Exodus chapter 12). The lamb had to die so that the firstborn would not. Isaiah chapter 53 paints this suffering Servant in the fullest colours: “Surely he has borne our sickness and carried our suffering … But he was pierced for our transgressions. He was crushed for our iniquities. The punishment that brought our peace was on him; and by his wounds we are healed.” (Isaiah 53:4–5) Notice the “we” and the “he” here — this is a complete exchange: he suffers, we receive; he dies, we live.

Paul says, “But God commends his own love toward us, in that while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.” (Romans 5:8) John says, “By this we know love, because he laid down his life for us. And we ought to lay down our lives for the brothers.” (1 John 3:16) Peter says, “For you were called to this, because Christ also suffered for us, leaving you an example, that you should follow his steps.” (1 Peter 2:21)

So “dying it out before you” is not passive surrender but active self-offering — being willing to lay ourselves down for the good of others. When, in our relationships, we choose “I die so that you may live,” the love of Jesus is at work in us.

sections.heading: 4. Illustration: Marriage, Family, Co-Workers
sections.html:
The easiest place to test this truth is at home.

In marriage, when a husband is willing to “die it out before his wife” — to lay down his pride and apologise first — the marriage is healed. So many couples, when they quarrel, aren’t really fighting over right and wrong; they’re fighting over face. Whoever bows first looks like Jesus first.

When a wife is willing to “die it out before her husband” — to lay down her complaints and choose forgiveness — the family has joy. Complaining is taking yesterday’s bill out every day and settling it all over again; forgiveness is tearing up the bill and saying, “I’ve paid this one.”

When co-workers are willing to “die it out before one another” — not competing for name, not competing for credit — the church will be united. Philippians 2:3–4 says, “doing nothing through rivalry or through conceit, but in humility, each counting others better than himself; each of you not just looking to his own things, but each of you also to the things of others.”

sections.heading: 5. Supporting Evidence from Psychology: Findings from the Marriage Lab
sections.html:
From the 1970s onwards, the University of Washington psychologist John Gottman observed couples’ interactions in his famous “Love Lab.” In research he published with Robert Levenson in 1992, he showed that by observing a couple’s conflict conversation for a period of time, one could predict with considerable accuracy whether the marriage would head towards breakdown.

Gottman identified four of the most destructive patterns of interaction, which he called the “Four Horsemen of the Apocalypse”: criticism, contempt, defensiveness and stonewalling (the cold shoulder). The most damaging of them is “contempt.” He also found that healthy marriages are not marriages without conflict, but marriages in which the couple know how to make “repair attempts” in the middle of conflict — an apology, a joke, a reaching out. In his 1994 research Gottman also proposed that in stable marriages the ratio of positive to negative interactions is roughly five to one.

Brothers and sisters, have you noticed? What psychology calls a “repair attempt,” Scripture spoke of long ago: it’s called “first be reconciled.” Matthew 5:24 says, “leave your gift there before the altar, and go your way. First be reconciled to your brother, and then come and offer your gift.” Science can only tell us that it “works”; Scripture tells us “why” — because the cross is the repair attempt God reached out to make with us.

sections.heading: 6. Applying the 321 Vision: Humility Sparks Humility, and Everyone Wins
sections.html:
The 321 vision says: humility overcomes pride; selflessness overcomes Satan. And it says: pride provokes pride, and both sides lose; humility sparks humility, and both sides win.

Why do quarrels at home keep escalating? Because pride is contagious. You raise your voice by one decibel, I raise mine by two; you drag up one old grievance, I drag up two. In the end both sides are hurt and there is no winner.

So how does it stop? Someone has to die first. Not the relationship dying — the “self” dying. When one person chooses “I die so that you may live,” that downward spiral is broken, and humility begins to spark humility.

What Satan fears most is not our gifts but our selflessness. His own downfall began with “I will” — Isaiah 14:13–14 records his five “I will”s: “I will ascend into heaven! I will exalt my throne above the stars of God! … I will make myself like the Most High!” But the Lord Jesus took the opposite road: he “emptied himself,” he “humbled himself,” he became “obedient.” That’s why James 4:6 says, “God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble.”

Brothers and sisters, if you want to overcome Satan, you don’t need to argue with him; you only need to go lower than he will. He will not bow his head, but you will; that is your victory.

sections.heading: Key Point 3: Denying of Self Brings Joy — the Spiritual Principle of JOY
1. The Text: That Your Joy May Be Made Full
sections.html:
When we take “for Jesus, for others, not for ourselves” as the conviction of our lives, we enter into the secret of joy. True joy lies not in what we gain but in what we are able to give away.

Jesus said, “Even as the Father has loved me, I also have loved you. Remain in my love. If you keep my commandments, you will remain in my love; even as I have kept my Father’s commandments, and remain in his love. I have spoken these things to you, that my joy may remain in you, and that your joy may be made full.” (John 15:9–11)

Notice three key phrases: remain, my joy, made full.

The Greek for “remain” is μένω (menō), meaning “to settle down, to stay, to continue on.” In the short space of the first eleven verses of John 15, this word appears ten times or more. It isn’t an occasional visit; it’s living there for good and never moving out. The branch doesn’t have to strain to bear fruit; the branch only has to stay on the vine. Jesus said, “apart from me you can do nothing.” (John 15:5)

Brothers and sisters, this sentence makes clear where the power for denying of self comes from. Denying of self doesn’t come from your willpower; it comes from connection. A branch that has been cut off, however hard it tries, cannot produce a single grape.

sections.heading: 2. The Original Language: Joy and Grace Share a Root
sections.html:
The Greek for “joy” is χαρά (chara), and “grace” is χάρις (charis); the two words share the same root. This tells us that joy is a product of grace, not a product of effort. You can’t “squeeze out” joy; you can only “receive” it.

The Greek for “made full” is πληρόω (plēroō), meaning “filled to overflowing.” Jesus uses it with the sense of completion — not filled for the moment, but continually full.

Notice too that Jesus says “my joy,” not “your joy.” What he wants to put inside us is his own share of joy. And what kind of joy is that? Hebrews 12:2 tells us: “who for the joy that was set before him endured the cross, despising its shame, and has sat down at the right hand of the throne of God.”

So Jesus’ joy is a joy that passes through the cross. Joy, then, has nothing to do with comfort; joy has everything to do with denying of self.

sections.heading: 3. Scripture Interpreting Scripture: It Is More Blessed to Give Than to Receive
sections.html:
When Paul said farewell to the Ephesian elders at Miletus, he told them, “In all things I gave you an example, that so laboring you ought to help the weak, and to remember the words of the Lord Jesus, that he himself said, ‘It is more blessed to give than to receive.’” (Acts 20:35)

Interestingly, this saying, “It is more blessed to give than to receive,” is not found in any of the four Gospels, yet Paul solemnly marks it as “the words of the Lord Jesus.” This shows how much weight the saying carried among the Lord’s teachings passed down by word of mouth in the early church.

The Old Testament said the same long before. Nehemiah 8:10: “the joy of Yahweh is your strength.” Notice the order: it isn’t that we have joy once we have strength; it’s that joy brings strength. Psalm 16:11: “You will show me the path of life. In your presence is fullness of joy. In your right hand there are pleasures forever more.” Where is fullness of joy found?
