In God’s presence, not in our circumstances.

There is another person in the New Testament who lived this secret out: John the Baptist. When his disciples came running to complain that “all are coming to him,” John answered, “He who has the bride is the bridegroom; but the friend of the bridegroom, who stands and hears him, rejoices greatly because of the bridegroom’s voice. This, my joy, therefore is made full.” (John 3:29) And then came those famous words: “He must increase, but I must decrease.” (John 3:30)

Brothers and sisters, look closely: John’s joy was not made full when he was lifted up; it was made full when he stepped back. This completely overturns the world’s logic. The world says, “I’m happy when I’m seen.” John says, “When he is seen, I am satisfied.”

Paul wrote Philippians from prison, and the whole letter is about joy: “Rejoice in the Lord always! Again I will say, ‘Rejoice!’” (Philippians 4:4) A man in prison telling free people to rejoice proves that joy is not a thermometer of our circumstances but a spring deep within our life.

sections.heading: 4. Illustration: The Sea of Galilee and the Dead Sea
sections.html:
In Israel, one and the same river, the Jordan, feeds two lakes.

In the north is the Sea of Galilee. The river flows in, and it also flows out. So the lake has fish, its shores have grass, and villages surround it; most of Jesus’ ministry took place there.

In the south is the Dead Sea. The river flows in, but it cannot flow out. Water only comes in and never leaves; the blazing sun evaporates it and the salt grows more and more concentrated — the Dead Sea’s salinity reaches about 34 per cent, roughly ten times that of ordinary seawater. As a result, fish cannot live there and grass cannot grow, and so it is called the “Dead Sea.”

Brothers and sisters, the two lakes share the same source; the only difference between them is one thing — whether or not they have an “outlet.”

People are the same. Some people let grace come in and flow out again, and their lives have fish and grass. Others let grace come in and only keep collecting it inside, and their lives grow saltier and saltier, more and more bitter. Someone who refuses to give will sooner or later become a dead sea.

sections.heading: 5. Supporting Evidence from Science and Psychology: Spending Money on Others
sections.html:
In 2008, Michael I. Norton of Harvard University, together with Elizabeth W. Dunn and Lara B. Aknin, then at the University of British Columbia, published a study in the journal Science titled “Spending Money on Others Promotes Happiness.” They ran several experiments. In one of them, participants were each given a small sum of money (five or twenty dollars); half were told to spend it on themselves, and half were told to spend it on someone else or give it away. When their happiness was measured that evening, the group who had spent the money on others was clearly happier — and the amount of money made no difference.

In addition, Harvard’s Study of Adult Development, begun in 1938, has followed several hundred men for more than eighty years, making it one of the longest studies of human happiness ever undertaken. Its fourth director, Robert Waldinger, summed up the study by saying that what keeps people healthy and happy is not wealth, not fame, but good relationships.

Brothers and sisters, science has taken eighty years of detours to prove what Scripture said from the very beginning — human beings were made for love. But science can only measure “happiness”; it can’t measure “joy.” Happiness depends on circumstances; joy depends on Jesus.

sections.heading: 6. Testimonies from Well-Known Christians
sections.html:
The missionary Jim Elliot is generally held to have written this sentence in his journal on 28 October 1949: “He is no fool who gives what he cannot keep to gain what he cannot lose.” Six years later, in January 1956, he and four companions were martyred in Ecuador while trying to reach the Auca (Waorani) people with the gospel; the oldest of them was barely over thirty, and Jim himself was only twenty-eight. The world called it a waste, but later his wife, Elisabeth Elliot, went in among that tribe, the gospel took root there, and the very men who had killed them became disciples of the Lord.

At the opening of his Confessions, the Church Father Augustine wrote, “You have made us for yourself, and our heart is restless until it rests in you.” That sentence goes straight to the heart of the matter: the restlessness of the human heart comes from getting the order wrong. Those who put themselves at the centre will never find rest; those who put Jesus at the centre can rest at any moment.

sections.heading: 7. The Order of JOY
sections.html:
When husband and wife deny themselves for each other, the home is filled with joy; when co-workers deny themselves for one another, the church overflows with joy; when brothers and sisters deny themselves for one another, the community is filled with love.

Denying of self looks like loss, but in fact it is entering into the true source of joy.

JOY — Jesus, Others, Yourself. Notice that this order doesn’t delete “yourself”; it simply puts “yourself” in third place. The Christian faith has never asked people to destroy themselves; it asks them to put themselves back in their proper place. When Jesus is first and others are second, you’ll find that “you” are actually the one best cared for — because a God who knows how to look after you far better than you do is looking after you on your behalf.

sections.heading: Integrating the 321 Vision: A Road Home
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, let’s walk today’s message through the framework of 321.

The Three Foundations. Jesus is my role model — he lived it out before us and died it out before us. The Bible is my standard — we don’t define denying of self by our feelings, but by Scripture. The Holy Spirit is my guide — denying of self doesn’t come from gritting our teeth; it comes from the Holy Spirit. Galatians 5:22–23 says, “But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith, gentleness, and self-control.” Notice that joy is a “fruit,” not a “product.” Fruit is grown; products are manufactured.

The Two Core Values. Let Jesus be King — move yourself off the throne and let him sit on it. Let Jesus receive all the glory — we don’t deny ourselves so that people will praise us for being loving, but so that people will see how real Jesus is. John the Baptist put it best: “He must increase, but I must decrease.” (John 3:30)

The Goal: establish God’s system — a system made up of selfless people, a system of “I die so that you may live,” a system of washing one another’s feet. This is exactly what the Lord’s Prayer asks for: “Let your Kingdom come. Let your will be done on earth as it is in heaven.” (Matthew 6:10)

The fivefold change: mindset, life, daily living, relationships, ministry. In today’s lesson, the first thing to change is our mindset — from “denying of self is a loss” to “denying of self is a gain.” Change the mindset and you change the life; change the life and you change daily living; change daily living and you change relationships; change relationships and you change ministry. The order can’t be skipped.

A shift in perspective: from man’s perspective to God’s perspective; from an earthly perspective to a heavenly one; from a temporary perspective to an eternal one; from a worldly perspective to a godly one. From man’s perspective, that grain of wheat died; from God’s perspective, that grain of wheat became a whole field.

The priority of relationships: first with God, then with ourselves, then with others, and last of all with things. People matter more than tasks; relationships matter more than possessions. Many people find denying of self terribly hard because they’ve skipped the “first with God.” Those who haven’t drawn love from God have nothing to give but reluctance, not love.

The 920 practice: everyone connected with us is our “2.” Who is your “2” today? Your spouse at home, your child in a rebellious phase, a difficult colleague, that brother you’d rather avoid. Practise living a selfless (0) life, and on that person bear the fruit of the Spirit in all nine (9) of its expressions. You don’t need to feel it first; you only need to choose it first.

The 235 relationships: with a selfless person, become a “2” — spiritual companions who can speak the truth to each other; build a “3” — spiritual parents and spiritual children, passing life on; become a “5” — a fivefold-ministry team of spiritual comrades, building up the body of the Lord together. Denying of self isn’t one person silently swallowing everything; denying of self is being seen, supported and passed on within relationships.

Then there is the Path of Serving: Spirit, Understanding, Life, Service, God. First let the Holy Spirit lead; then let Scripture open our understanding; then live out the life of Jesus; only then do we enter into service; and finally we give all the glory to God.

Brothers and sisters, 321 has never been a slogan. It is a road home.

sections.heading: Putting It into Practice: Walking the Truth into Daily Living Through the Eight Stages of Changing Our Mindset
sections.html:
The lesson gives us three practices. Let’s deepen them using the 321 “eight stages of changing our mindset” — Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication.

Practice One: A Prayer Every Morning

“Lord, today let me live for you, act for others, and not for myself.”

Information: you have heard today’s word — Jesus lived it out before us and died it out before us.

Revelation: ask the Holy Spirit to carry this sentence from your head into your heart, and to let you “see” it in one particular face.

Conviction: truly believe that “giving away is more blessed than holding on,” rather than merely thinking it sounds beautiful.

Implementation: make this prayer the very first thing you say when you open your eyes tomorrow morning. Don’t wait until you’re in a good mood to pray; prayer will bring the mood with it.

Evaluation: in the evening, ask yourself whether this prayer influenced any single decision you made today.

Correction: if it didn’t, move the prayer earlier — before you look at your phone.

Repetition: keep it up for forty days in a row. Forty is not a superstitious number; it’s a stretch of time long enough for a new habit to take root.

Multiplication: find a brother or sister and invite them to do these forty days of practice with you.

Practice Two: Take Practical Action — Give Someone Your Time or Care, Expecting Nothing in Return

Information: it is more blessed to give than to receive (Acts 20:35).

Revelation: let God name one particular person and lay them on your heart — not “everyone,” but “that one person.”

Conviction: believe that God remembers every bit of time you give. Matthew 10:42 says, “Whoever gives one of these little ones just a cup of cold water to drink in the name of a disciple, most certainly I tell you he will in no way lose his reward.”

Implementation: this week, do one concrete thing — a phone call, a meal, a lift, an hour of keeping someone company. Set a time and put it in your calendar.

Evaluation: while I was doing it, was I hoping for something in return? Was I hoping to be noticed?

Correction: if you find your motives are mixed, don’t condemn yourself; simply offer it up again. Even our motives for giving need to be cleansed — that is grace, not failure.

Repetition: at least once a week, for a whole season.

Multiplication: bring your small group or your family along to do it with you, so that this moves from an individual action to a shared culture.

Practice Three: An Evening Review — Did I Live Out the Order of JOY Today?

Jesus, Others, Yourself.

Information: the order of joy is Jesus first, others second, yourself third.

Revelation: let the Holy Spirit shine a light on what your real order was today. Much of the time our order is Y-O-J, and we still think we’re very spiritual.

Conviction: believe that once the order changes, everything changes.

Implementation: three minutes before bed, write three lines — What did I do for Jesus today? What did I do for others? Was I tied up by myself?

Evaluation: look back once a week and see your own patterns.

Correction: for the weakest link, add one small action tomorrow.

Repetition: let this review become a bedtime habit, as natural as brushing your teeth.

Multiplication: take the entry you’re most thankful for in your review notes and share it with your small group, so it becomes a blessing to others.

A Reminder

Living “for myself” brings only passing happiness; living “for Jesus and for others” is what brings eternal joy.

Happiness needs conditions; joy needs only Jesus. Happiness peaks at the moment you receive and slides downhill from there; joy begins at the moment you give and keeps increasing from there.

A Declaration of Faith

Let us declare together:

Lord, I want to learn from your example — to live for others and to die for others.

Help me choose every day to live “for you, for others, not for myself,”

so that my life is filled with your love and overflows with your joy.

sections.heading: Closing and Call: Let Jesus Be Seen
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, living “for Jesus, for others, not for ourselves” is a road of denying of self, but it is also a road full of glory and joy.

This road isn’t easy. It asks us not to defend ourselves when we’re misunderstood, to apologise first when we’re in the right, to keep reaching out when we ought to be resting. But please remember: every choice to deny yourself is a moment when Jesus is seen.

When you hand the credit to someone else at the office, someone sees Jesus.

When you’re the first at home to say “I’m sorry,” someone sees Jesus.

When you quietly stack the chairs and wash the cups at church, someone in heaven sees Jesus.

When we keep living like this, joy is no longer a feeling but the fruit of a life. Feelings change with the weather; fruit grows as life grows.

True joy will always belong to those who are willing to deny themselves for love.

So this morning I want to issue you a call: please move yourself off the throne and let Jesus be King. Not just King on Sundays, but King over your calendar, King over your wallet, King over your words, King over your grievances.

Paul says, “He died for all, that those who live should no longer live to themselves, but to him who for their sakes died and rose again.” (2 Corinthians 5:15)

Brothers and sisters, he has already died for you; today, will you live for him?

May all the glory go to the Lord Jesus Christ, who lived for us and died for us.

keyVerses: “If you keep my commandments, you will remain in my love; even as I have kept my Father’s commandments, and remain in his love. I have spoken these things to you, that my joy may remain in you, and that your joy may be made full.” (John 15:10–11)
declarations: Let us declare together:
Lord, I want to learn from your example — to live for others and to die for others.
Help me choose every day to live “for you, for others, not for myself,”
so that my life is filled with your love and overflows with your joy.
practices: A prayer every morning
Take practical action — give someone your time or care, expecting nothing in return
An evening review: did I live out the order of JOY today?
prayer: Dear Lord Jesus,
We thank you. You lived it out before us, so that we know what love looks like; you died it out before us, so that we know how far love can go.

Lord, forgive us. So often we put ourselves first, others second and you last. We serve in your name while in our hearts we are fighting for ourselves. Wash us in your precious blood, and nail the self-centred old self to the cross.

Give us a selfless heart. Let us be willing to bow first at home, to forgive first in our relationships, and to step back first in our service. Holy Spirit, work within us, so that denying of self is no longer a teeth-gritting effort but an outpouring of love.

Lord, put your joy in our hearts, so that our joy may be made full. Let our lives be like the Sea of Galilee — water flowing in and out, full of fish and grass; not like the Dead Sea, taking in and never giving out, growing ever more bitter.
Reign as King in our homes, reign as King in our fellowship, reign as King in every one of our twenty-four hours. May all glory, praise and honour be yours.
In the holy name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen.
discussion: Mark 6:31–34: Jesus had intended to “rest awhile,” but when he saw the flock he laid down his right to rest. Share: this week, what is one thing that “you have a right to enjoy but could lay down for someone”? What is the biggest obstacle to laying it down?

John 15:11: “I have spoken these things to you, that my joy may remain in you, and that your joy may be made full.” Share: in what experience of denying yourself have you tasted true joy? What did God show you at the time?
l069.title: For Jesus, for Others, Not for Self
l069.subtitle: A Life of Denying of Self, the Secret of Joy
l069.partTitle: Unit 5 · The Road to Revival — Selflessness

sections.heading: 1. Introduction: What You Fear Losing Is Not God but Yourself
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, good morning. This morning I want to begin with a very honest question: when you first heard the word “selflessness,” what was your real reaction inside?

I’ve met a good many brothers and sisters whose first reaction was almost identical: “Selflessness? Then won’t I have nothing left at all? Will I even be me any more?” One sister, very capable in her career, said to me, “Pastor, I can give my time, I can give my money, I can get up early to pray, I can go out and share the gospel. But when you tell me to lay down my ‘self,’ I start trembling inside. Because that’s the only thing I have left.”

Those words are very real, and they cut deep. What we fear is often not losing God but losing ourselves. We’re willing to give God everything except “me.” We’re willing to let Jesus be our Saviour, our friend, our helper, but not quite so willing to let him be King. Because letting him be King means that I am no longer king.

But brothers and sisters, this morning I want to tell you with great confidence: in spiritual truth, selflessness has never been loss but gain; not emptiness but abundance; not being weakened but being filled. Because when “self” is no longer in charge, Jesus can be King; when my limited life steps back, his limitless life comes in.

Let me use a picture. When someone goes diving, they carry an oxygen tank on their back. The air in the tank is limited; it usually lasts only forty to sixty minutes. You can breathe very sparingly, very carefully, very economically, but however hard you try, the air in the tank will eventually run out. That is the self-centred life — all your strength is confined to that one little tank.

But if there is a hose bringing air down from the surface in an endless supply, the situation is completely different. You no longer have to calculate how much is left, because the supply no longer comes from the tank on your back but from the boundless atmosphere above. That is the selfless life — you haven’t run out of air; you’ve been connected to the whole sky.

That is exactly Paul’s testimony: “I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me.” (Galatians 2:20) Notice that Paul doesn’t say “I have disappeared.” He says “it is no longer I who live.” He was still alive — still preaching, still writing letters, still sitting in prison, still being stoned — but the source of his life had been changed. The tank had been swapped for the hose; the limited had been swapped for the limitless.

This is the lesson we are entering together today: selflessness — entering into the fullness and victory of Jesus.

sections.heading: 2. Scripture Background: Three Passages, Three Scenes
sections.html:
To understand a verse, you first have to step into the scene where it was spoken. Today’s three main passages come from three very different scenes, which nonetheless confirm one another.

(1) Galatians 2:20: The Dispute at the Table in Antioch

Galatians is a letter of the apostle Paul. On the “South Galatian” view, it may well be Paul’s earliest letter, written around AD 48–49, close to the time of the Jerusalem Council (Acts chapter 15). It was addressed to the churches of Galatia that Paul had planted on his first missionary journey, including Pisidian Antioch, Iconium, Lystra and Derbe.

At that time a group of “Judaizers” had appeared in the church. They followed in Paul’s footsteps and told the Gentile believers: believing in Jesus isn’t enough on its own; you must also be circumcised and keep the law of Moses before you are truly saved. This was a battle over the very survival of the gospel.

Galatians 2:20 is not a devotional maxim Paul wrote in his study. It comes right after a very heated account. Paul has just described how he opposed Cephas (Peter) to his face in Antioch — because Peter had been eating with the Gentile believers, but as soon as men came from James, he drew back and separated himself from the Gentiles out of fear of the circumcision party (Galatians 2:11–14).

Why did Peter shrink back? Not because he couldn’t work out the theology, but because of “self.” Because he cared what others thought, because he was afraid of losing his standing among the Jewish believers. Paul says, “he drew back and separated himself, fearing those who were of the circumcision.” (Galatians 2:12)

So Paul goes straight on to speak of justification by faith (Galatians 2:15–21), and concludes with verse 20: the real issue is not whether the law is enough, but whether “I” am still there. If “I” am still sitting on the throne, then circumcision, the law, spiritual gifts — they are all just tools I use to shore myself up. Only when “I” have been crucified with Christ does the gospel truly become the gospel.

Brothers and sisters, remember this: Galatians 2:20 is a declaration of selflessness born out of a failure of the self-centred life.

(2) John 10:10: The Good Shepherd Discourse

The setting of John chapter 10 is Jesus’ Good Shepherd discourse in Jerusalem. From the context, these words follow straight on from chapter 9, the healing of the man born blind — the man who was healed and confessed Jesus, and as a result was thrown out of the synagogue by the Pharisees (John 9:34).

The Lord said, “The thief only comes to steal, kill, and destroy. I came that they may have life, and may have it abundantly.” (John 10:10)

The contrast here is very sharp. What the false shepherd does is “steal, kill, and destroy” — three verbs that build on one another: first he takes what is yours, then he takes your life, and finally he tears down the whole ecosystem. What the good shepherd does is to give the sheep “life, and … abundantly.”

The Greek word for “abundantly” is περισσόν (perisson), meaning “beyond what is needed, surplus, more than enough.” God’s abundance is never just enough; it overflows.

(3) Philippians 4:13: Contentment in Prison

Philippians is a letter Paul wrote from prison, generally thought to date from around AD 61–62, during his first imprisonment in Rome. The church in Philippi had sent Epaphroditus to bring Paul a gift, and Paul wrote to thank them, taking the opportunity to urge them to be of one mind.

Philippians 4:13 is not a motivational slogan to stick on the wall of a gym. Its context runs like this: “Not that I speak because of lack, for I have learned in whatever state I am, to be content in it. I know how to be humbled, and I also know how to abound. In everything and in all things I have learned the secret both to be filled and to be hungry, both to abound and to be in need. I can do all things through Christ, who strengthens me.” (Philippians 4:11–13)

The Greek for “learned the secret” is μεμύημαι (memyēmai), originally a technical term in the ancient mystery religions for “being initiated into the mysteries, receiving enlightenment.” Paul is saying that the lesson of how to abound and how to be humbled is something you are led into step by step, trained in by a master, not something that drops on you overnight.

And “strengthens me” is the Greek ἐνδυναμοῦντι (endynamounti), whose root is δύναμις (dynamis, power), with ἐν (in, within) placed in front. So the heart of the sentence is: the Lord who pours power into me from within. Not someone giving me a push from outside, but power welling up from inside.

Brothers and sisters, three scenes, three situations: one a conflict inside the church, one the loneliness of being thrown out of the synagogue, one the poverty of prison. And all three passages point to the same answer — not I, but he.

sections.heading: 3. The First Key Point: Selflessness Takes Us from the Limited into the Limitless
sections.html:
1. Every limitation we have comes from that “self”

Brothers and sisters, please think quietly for a moment: what is the greatest obstacle in your life? Is it your circumstances? Other people? The times we live in?

The lesson puts it very sharply: every limitation a person has comes from “self” — our own reasoning, our own feelings, our own experience, our own calculations.

Your vision is only as wide as your reasoning; your emotions are only as steady as your feelings; your courage is only as deep as your experience; your sense of security is only as great as your calculations are accurate. The trouble is that not one of these four is limitless. And so —

Where there is the self-centred life, there is fear, because I can’t see tomorrow;

Where there is the self-centred life, there is lack, because my pockets are only so deep;

Where there is the self-centred life, there is comparison, because I have to know where I rank;

Where there is the self-centred life, there is anxiety, because everything depends on me holding it up.

In his 2004 book The Curse of the Self, the Duke University psychologist Mark R. Leary points out that the uniquely human capacity for self-reflection, though it has given us civilisation and the ability to plan, has also become the source of much suffering — we grow anxious about things that haven’t happened yet, we are wounded by other people’s opinions, and we replay our own mistakes in our heads over and over. His observation simply confirms, from the angle of psychology, what Scripture said long ago: the root of the problem is not outside but inside; not in our circumstances but in “self.”

Another line of research is also worth noting. In 2004 the psychologists Jennifer Crocker and Lora E. Park published “The Costly Pursuit of Self-Esteem” in Psychological Bulletin. They showed that when people make their self-worth contingent on some condition (such as appearance, achievement or other people’s approval), the pursuit of self-esteem itself brings anxiety, damaged relationships and a drain on self-regulation. In other words, the harder we fight to protect the “self,” the more fragile the “self” becomes.

Brothers and sisters, this is exactly what the 321 vision says: the self-centred life is the root of humanity’s fall; pride is the root of our problems. Pride is leaving our originally intended position, seizing rights and wanting to take God’s place; humility is laying down our rights and returning to our originally intended position — let man be man and let God be God.

2. But when we are selfless, we are connected to the limitless

But thank the Lord, the story doesn’t end there. When we choose selflessness and let Jesus live in us, our lives are joined to the limitless God.

Jesus said, “I am the vine. You are the branches. He who remains in me and I in him bears much fruit, for apart from me you can do nothing.” (John 15:5)

Notice the Lord’s words: not “apart from me you can do less,” but “apart from me you can do nothing.” The branch’s problem is never that it doesn’t try hard enough; it’s whether or not it is connected. Take a broken-off branch and tie fruit onto it, and in three days all you’ll have is rotten mush.

Jesus’ life is an “abundant” life. He said, “I came that they may have life, and may have it abundantly.” (John 10:10) That means he wants not only to keep us alive, but to make us live fulfilled, free and strong.

Paul’s prayer for the Ephesian church points the same way: “and to know Christ’s love which surpasses knowledge, that you may be filled with all the fullness of God. Now to him who is able to do exceedingly abundantly above all that we ask or think, according to the power that works in us.” (Ephesians 3:19–20)

“Above all that we ask or think” — brothers and sisters, hear this clearly: God’s plan is not capped by your imagination; your imagination is only the floor of God’s plan.

3. Four contrasts: from the self-centred life to selflessness

The lesson lists four very precious contrasts. Let’s confirm each one from Scripture:

First, the self-centred “we” are afraid, but the selfless “we” have peace. John says, “There is no fear in love; but perfect love casts out fear, because fear has punishment. He who fears is not made perfect in love.” (1 John 4:18) Fear isn’t driven out by willpower; it’s crowded out by love.

Second, the self-centred “we” are weak, but the selfless “we” are strong. The Lord said to Paul, “My grace is sufficient for you, for my power is made perfect in weakness.” And so Paul said, “Most gladly therefore I will rather glory in my weaknesses, that the power of Christ may rest on me.” (2 Corinthians 12:9) What wonderful logic this is — weakness is no longer an ugly thing to hide, but the doorway to grace.

Third, the self-centred “we” are in want, but the selfless “we” are provided for. Paul says, “My God will supply every need of yours according to his riches in glory in Christ Jesus.” (Philippians 4:19) David says, “Yahweh is my shepherd: I shall lack nothing.” (Psalm 23:1) The Hebrew root behind “lack” is חָסֵר (chaser), meaning to be short of, to be insufficient. David means that as long as Yahweh is the shepherd, the books will always balance.

Fourth, the self-centred “we” fail, but the selfless “we” overcome through him. Paul says, “No, in all these things, we are more than conquerors through him who loved us.” (Romans 8:37) The Greek for “more than conquerors” is ὑπερνικῶμεν (hypernikōmen), which takes “to conquer” (νικάω) and adds “over and beyond” (ὑπέρ) — not a narrow win but a resounding one, a victory with something left over.

4. Stop relying on methods; start relying on the Holy Spirit

The lesson puts it well: true selflessness means ceasing to rely on our own methods and relying entirely on the guidance of the Holy Spirit.

There’s a saying in Chinese martial arts: “no set moves defeats set moves” — every set move has its opening; only having no set moves is true freedom. This fits the spiritual life remarkably well. When we cling to a fixed set of methods, we are limited by those methods; but when we are selfless, we no longer respond to our circumstances by our own logic. We are led by the Holy Spirit and live out wonderful breakthroughs.

What does Scripture say? “Not by might, nor by power, but by my Spirit,” says Yahweh of Armies (Zechariah 4:6). Zerubbabel was facing the ruins of a temple on which work had stopped for sixteen years. God didn’t give him more might and more ability; God gave him “my Spirit.”

Solomon also said, “Trust in Yahweh with all your heart, and don’t lean on your own understanding. In all your ways acknowledge him, and he will make your paths straight.” (Proverbs 3:5–6) The Hebrew for “trust” is בָּטַח (batach), whose basic meaning is “to lean your whole weight on something with ease,” like someone lying full length on a bed, no longer holding themselves up.

5. Applying 321: Jesus is the focal point; our perspective shifts from man’s to God’s

Brothers and sisters, of the Three Foundations in the 321 vision, the third is “the Holy Spirit is my guide.” This key point is exactly the practice of that foundation.

When we run into difficulty, if our first reaction is “What am I going to do?” that is the self-centred life; if it is “Lord, how do you see this?” that is selflessness.

When we weigh something up, if we use a human, earthly, temporary, worldly perspective, that is the self-centred life; if we shift to God’s perspective — heavenly, eternal, godly — that is selflessness.

321 says: Jesus is the focal point — not ourselves, not other people, not our circumstances. It also says: rely on the heart and the Holy Spirit, not on the brain and ourselves; rely on the brain and you’ll be troubled, rely on the heart and you’ll be glad. Because “out of it is the wellspring of life” (Proverbs 4:23).

A limited tank connected to the limitless sky. That is the first key point.

sections.heading: 4. The Second Key Point: Selflessness Lets the Life of Jesus Replace Our Life
sections.html:
1. Selflessness is not becoming a blank; it is letting Jesus become everything

The lesson puts it very precisely: selflessness doesn’t turn us into a blank; it lets Jesus become our everything.

This has to be made clear, because many people misunderstand it. The selflessness the Christian faith speaks of is not the “emptiness and extinction” of Eastern philosophy; it is not dissolving the self into nothingness. The 321 vision puts it well: selflessness is not having nothing; it is entering into the infinite and living out the infinite; “I” no longer live, but Christ lives in me.

This is the mystery of selflessness: his life is the source of our life; his wisdom is the fountain of our wisdom; his power is the strength by which we overcome.

2. From “emptying himself” to “denying himself”: two key words in the original

To understand this “replacing,” we need to know two key words.

The first is “emptied himself.” Paul says, “Have this in your mind, which was also in Christ Jesus, who, existing in the form of God, didn’t consider equality with God a thing to be grasped, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of men. And being found in human form, he humbled himself, becoming obedient to the point of death, yes, the death of the cross.” (Philippians 2:5–8)

The Greek for “emptied himself” is ἐκένωσεν (ekenōsen), from the verb κενόω (kenoō), meaning “to empty out.” Notice that what the Lord Jesus emptied out was not his divine nature — he existed in the form of God, and that never changed. What he emptied out was his right to use his authority, his entitlement to be served. This was the most thorough act of selflessness in the universe.

Brothers and sisters, the 321 vision says: pride is leaving our originally intended position, seizing rights and wanting to take God’s place; humility is laying down our rights and returning to our originally intended position. In Isaiah 14:13–14 Satan says “I will” five times: “I will ascend into heaven! I will exalt my throne above the stars of God! I will sit on the mountain of assembly, in the far north! I will ascend above the heights of the clouds! I will make myself like the Most High!” But in the Garden of Gethsemane the Lord Jesus said only one thing: “Nevertheless, not my will, but yours, be done.” (Luke 22:42)

One says “I will” five times; the other says “not my will” once. The first fell from heaven; the second was lifted up from the earth. This is the great watershed of the whole Bible.

The second key word is “deny himself.” The Lord said, “If anyone desires to come after me, let him deny himself, and take up his cross, and follow me.” (Matthew 16:24)

The Greek for “deny himself” is ἀπαρνέομαι (aparneomai), meaning “to deny, to disown, to cut off all connection.” Interestingly, this is the very same verb the Lord used when he foretold that Peter would “deny” him three times (Matthew 26:34).

In other words, Peter once said to people, “I don’t know this Jesus”; and what the Lord Jesus wants us to learn is that one day we will be able to say to the old self, “I don’t know you. You are no longer my master.” This is not self-abuse; it is a transfer of sovereignty.

3. The picture of the glove: no longer straining to be like him, but letting him live out himself

Let me use a simple picture. A glove lies on the table. It has five fingers, it’s perfectly shaped, and the material may even be expensive. But it can’t pick up a glass of water, can’t write a word, can’t hug anyone. Why? Because there is no hand inside it.

Now slip a hand inside. The same glove can suddenly play the piano, do a day’s work, lift up someone who has fallen. Nothing about the glove has changed; what has changed is that there’s a hand inside.

Brothers and sisters, this is what the lesson means: then we are no longer merely “trying hard to become people like Jesus,” but “letting Jesus live out himself within us.”

The difference between these two is far greater than we imagine. The first is “imitation”; the second is “indwelling.” In the first, I supply the effort; in the second, he does. The first is called religion; the second is called the gospel.

Paul speaks of “Christ in you, the hope of glory” (Colossians 1:27). And he says, “But by the grace of God I am what I am. His grace which was given to me was not futile, but I worked more than all of them; yet not I, but the grace of God which was with me.” (1 Corinthians 15:10)

Paul worked harder than all the apostles — he gave it everything; he was never passive. But he immediately adds, “yet not I.” That is the most beautiful posture of a selfless person: giving everything, yet claiming no credit.

4. His attributes made visible in us

The lesson lists three things. Let’s look at them one by one:

First, his love enables us to love the unlovable. The Lord said, “But love your enemies, and do good, and lend, expecting nothing back.” (Luke 6:35) In our own strength this is a mission impossible; but Paul says, “But God commends his own love toward us, in that while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.” (Romans 5:8) We can love the unlovable because we ourselves were loved in just that way.

Second, his wisdom enables us to see a way out in hard places. James says, “But if any of you lacks wisdom, let him ask of God, who gives to all liberally and without reproach, and it will be given to him.” (James 1:5) Notice the phrase “without reproach” — God won’t scold you for being foolish just because you’ve come asking for wisdom.

Third, his faith enables us to keep believing in the face of the impossible. When Abraham was about a hundred years old, Scripture says that “looking to the promise of God, he didn’t waver through unbelief, but grew strong through faith, giving glory to God, and being fully assured that what he had promised, he was also able to perform” (Romans 4:20–21).

5. Supporting evidence from psychology and science

In his 2001 book Good to Great, the management writer Jim Collins described what he called “Level 5 Leadership”: the leaders who took their companies to sustained excellence had in common not dazzling charisma but “extreme personal humility” combined with “intense professional will.” He found that these leaders credited others and good fortune for success and took the blame themselves for failure. Collins’s research is management science, not theology; but it confirms from another angle that truly lasting fruitfulness comes from selflessness, not from self-exalting.

Here’s another scientific fact: an adult’s heart beats on average about a hundred thousand times a day. When you woke up this morning, you didn’t issue an order for your heart to start beating; when you fell asleep last night, your heart didn’t stop work either. The most vital operations of our life have never been kept going by our willpower.

6. Applying 321: the old self is self-centred, the new self is selfless; life first, then relationships, then ministry

The lesson concludes: a life like this no longer relies on the flesh but on the Holy Spirit.

The 321 vision describes this change as “the old self is self-centred; the new self is selfless.” Paul says, “Therefore if anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation. The old things have passed away. Behold, all things have become new.” (2 Corinthians 5:17)

And 321 is very clear about the order of this change: the fivefold change — mindset, life, daily living, relationships, ministry. First the mindset changes, then the life changes; once the life has changed, daily living changes; once daily living has changed, relationships will change; once relationships have changed, ministry bears real fruit.

That’s why we often say: life first, then relationships, then ministry. People matter more than tasks; relationships matter more than possessions. Many brothers and sisters throw themselves into ministry yet are dried up in their life, because the order has been reversed — trying to do selfless ministry with a self-centred life, and in the end everyone gets hurt.

Brothers and sisters, today don’t rush to do more things. First let Jesus live a little more within you.

sections.heading: 5. The Third Key Point: The Victory and Freedom That Selflessness Brings
sections.html:
1. The key is not “I can do all things” but “through him”

Brothers and sisters, Philippians 4:13 is probably one of the most quoted — and most misused — verses in the Bible.

Paul says, “I can do all things through Christ, who strengthens me.” (Philippians 4:13)

The lesson goes straight to the heart of it: the key to this sentence is “through him.”

Many people read this verse as “I can do all things.” Once the weight of the sentence shifts onto “I,” the verse turns from gospel into self-motivation, from comfort into a burden. Because someone who believes “I can do all things” has nothing left but self-blame when they fail.

If we rely on ourselves, we can do nothing; but if we rely on him, we can do all things. This sentence has two sides: it is both a limitation and a release. The limitation is that without him I am nothing; the release is that with him nothing is impossible.

Notice too that Paul wrote this sentence while he was in prison. The context makes it very clear: “I know how to be humbled, and I also know how to abound. In everything and in all things I have learned the secret both to be filled and to be hungry, both to abound and to be in need.” (Philippians 4:12)

Brothers and sisters, please hear one thing: Paul says he learned how “to abound” — which means that abounding is also a lesson that has to be learned, and perhaps an even harder one than being humbled. Because when we’re brought low, we know to cling to God; when we abound, we often think what we’re clinging to is ourselves.

2. Victory is not conquering our circumstances but overcoming the “I” that wants control

The lesson offers an extremely important definition: victory is not conquering our circumstances but overcoming the “self” — the “I” that wants to control, to prove itself, to take charge.

The world says victory is pushing the other person down and getting the result in your hands; Scripture says victory is the “I” on the throne giving way to Jesus.

The Lord Jesus himself is the best illustration. He said, “I have told you these things, that in me you may have peace. In the world you have trouble; but cheer up! I have overcome the world.” (John 16:33)

Brothers and sisters, notice when the Lord said this. It was the night of the Passover. In a few hours Judas would come to betray him, the disciples would scatter and run, Peter would deny him three times, and he would be nailed to the cross. Judging by the circumstances, everything was collapsing. But the Lord said, “I have overcome the world.”

The Lord’s victory came not from changing his circumstances but from never once leaving the Father’s will in the midst of them. That is the victory of selflessness.

I often use a picture: the thermometer and the thermostat. A thermometer can only reflect its surroundings — when the room is cold, it drops; when the room is hot, it rises. It is always passive. A thermostat is different. It has a set point inside it; it doesn’t swing with its surroundings but instead changes them.

Brothers and sisters, are you a thermometer today, or a thermostat? The self-centred person is a thermometer: one remark from someone else sets the temperature of their whole day. The selfless person is a thermostat, because the set point inside them is not their own emotions but Christ.

The Austrian psychiatrist Viktor Frankl survived the concentration camps, and in Man’s Search for Meaning, first published in 1946, he set down a profound observation: everything can be taken from a person but one thing — the freedom to choose one’s attitude in any given set of circumstances. That is the truth a psychiatrist saw in the most extreme conditions. And Scripture tells us something deeper still: the source of that freedom is not in the human will but in Christ.

3. From the bondage of anxiety into the freedom of faith

The lesson says: selflessness means we are no longer bound by weakness but enter into the freedom of faith; no longer anxious about outcomes, but enjoying the peace of walking with Jesus.

The Lord said, “If you remain in my word, then you are truly my disciples. You will know the truth, and the truth will make you free.” And he said, “If therefore the Son makes you free, you will be free indeed.” (John 8:31–32, 36)

The world thinks freedom is “doing whatever I want”; Scripture says freedom is “finally no longer being ruled by ‘me.’” Someone who must win, must be right, must be seen, is actually the least free person in the world — because their peace is locked inside other people’s reactions.

Paul gives us a very concrete path: “In nothing be anxious, but in everything, by prayer and petition with thanksgiving, let your requests be made known to God. And the peace of God, which surpasses all understanding, will guard your hearts and your thoughts in Christ Jesus.” (Philippians 4:6–7)

Notice the order: prayer, petition, and then thanksgiving. The thanksgiving comes before the answer arrives. Research published in 2003 in the Journal of Personality and Social Psychology by the psychologists Robert A. Emmons and Michael E. McCullough showed that participants assigned to write down things they were grateful for each week reported clearly higher well-being, and more optimism about the coming week, than control groups who wrote about everyday events or hassles.

Gratitude has power because it shifts the focus from “what I lack” to “what he has given.” That is selflessness in miniature.

4. Our circumstances may not have changed, but inside we have already overcome

The lesson has a sentence worth copying onto the flyleaf of your Bible: when we let Jesus reign, our circumstances may not have changed, but inside we have already overcome.

Brothers and sisters, what a great comfort this is. Perhaps you’ve been praying about that matter for three years and nothing has changed; perhaps you’ve shed many tears over that family member and they are still the same. But if, in the process, you are no longer the one who has to control how it ends, you have already overcome.

Paul begged the Lord three times about a thorn in his flesh. The Lord did not take it away, but said only, “My grace is sufficient for you, for my power is made perfect in weakness.” (2 Corinthians 12:9) And Paul said, “Therefore I take pleasure in weaknesses, in injuries, in necessities, in persecutions, and in distresses, for Christ’s sake. For when I am weak, then am I strong.” (2 Corinthians 12:10)

The thorn was still there, but Paul had overcome.

Isaiah says, “but those who wait for Yahweh will renew their strength. They will mount up with wings like eagles. They will run, and not be weary. They will walk, and not faint.” (Isaiah 40:31) An eagle can circle high in the sky for hours without flapping its wings — not by the power of its own muscles but by rising thermals of warm air. All it does is spread its wings and stop struggling.

Brothers and sisters, this morning perhaps this is the very word the Lord wants to say to you: stop struggling, and spread your wings.

5. Applying 321: let Jesus be King, and become an overcomer

The Two Core Values of the 321 vision are: let Jesus be King; let Jesus receive all the glory.

The third key point is about exactly the first core value — let Jesus be King. And the other side of “let Jesus be King” is “I am no longer king.” A kingdom cannot have two kings. Every time we say, “Lord, you have the final say,” it is a coronation; every time we say, “No, I’m going to decide this one myself,” it is a coup.

The aim of 321 is to walk alongside every person until they become an overcomer. And the mark of an overcomer is not having no difficulties; it is still letting Jesus be King in the middle of them.

sections.heading: 6. Integrating the 321 Vision: From the Self-Centred Old Self to the Selfless New Self
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, let’s set today’s three key points within the whole picture of 321.

1. The Three Foundations, the Two Core Values, the Goal

The Three Foundations are: Jesus is my role model; the Bible is my standard; the Holy Spirit is my guide.

All three foundations are present in today’s lesson. Jesus “emptying himself” in Philippians chapter 2 is our role model for selflessness; the truth Paul declares in Galatians 2:20 is our standard; and “ceasing to rely on our own methods and relying entirely on the guidance of the Holy Spirit” is the Holy Spirit being our guide.

The Two Core Values are: let Jesus be King; let Jesus receive all the glory. Selflessness is not the goal; letting Jesus be King is the goal. We lay ourselves down not to become empty of everything, but so that the One who is worthy may sit on the throne. Paul says, “Whether therefore you eat, or drink, or whatever you do, do all to the glory of God.” (1 Corinthians 10:31)

The Goal is: establish God’s system. When one person is selfless, he is an overcomer; when a group of people are selfless, they become God’s system. The Lord’s Prayer says, “Let your Kingdom come. Let your will be done on earth as it is in heaven.” (Matthew 6:10) God’s kingdom is not a place; it is the territory where he has the final say.

2. Humility overcomes pride; selflessness overcomes Satan

Scripture says, “Pride goes before destruction, and an arrogant spirit before a fall.” (Proverbs 16:18)

And it says, “But he gives more grace. Therefore it says, ‘God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble.’ Be subject therefore to God. Resist the devil, and he will flee from you.” (James 4:6–7)

Brothers and sisters, look carefully at the order in this passage: first “be subject to God,” and only then can you “resist the devil.” Submitting to God is selflessness; resisting the devil is overcoming. 321 puts it exactly: humility overcomes pride; selflessness overcomes Satan.

Satan’s very nature is pride. He attacks us with pride, and he can only gain a foothold in us through pride. Satan can find no place to get a grip on a truly selfless person, because every bait he uses hangs on the hook of “self” — being seen, being affirmed, being proved right, being compensated. When the “self” is gone, so is the hook.

In Genesis 3:5 the serpent said to Eve, “for God knows that in the day you eat it, your eyes will be opened, and you will be like God, knowing good and evil.” He has only ever sold one product: you can be your own god. The Lord Jesus offers the opposite: “Take my yoke upon you, and learn from me, for I am gentle and humble in heart; and you will find rest for your souls.” (Matthew 11:29)

321 also says: pride provokes pride, and both sides lose; humility sparks humility, and both sides win. It’s true in the family, it’s true in the workplace, and it’s true in the church. When a hard word meets a hard word, the fire flares up; when a soft word meets a hard word, the fire goes out.

3. The fivefold change and the priority of relationships

321 speaks of the fivefold change — mindset, life, daily living, relationships, ministry. Change the mindset and you change the life; change the life and you change daily living.

Paul says, “Don’t be conformed to this world, but be transformed by the renewing of your mind, so that you may prove what is the good, well-pleasing, and perfect will of God.” (Romans 12:2) “Transformed by the renewing of your mind” is a change of mindset, and the result of that transformation is being able to “prove” God’s will.

The priority of relationships is: first with God, then with ourselves, then with others, and last of all with things. Today’s three key points fall precisely on the first two levels — our relationship with God (selflessness connects us to the limitless) and our relationship with ourselves (selflessness enables us to overcome the “I” that wants control). When these two levels are right, our relationships with people and with things will follow.

The shift in perspective is: from man’s to God’s, from earthly to heavenly, from temporary to eternal, from worldly to godly. Paul says, “Set your mind on the things that are above, not on the things that are on the earth.” (Colossians 3:2) And he says, “while we don’t look at the things which are seen, but at the things which are not seen. For the things which are seen are temporal, but the things which are not seen are eternal.” (2 Corinthians 4:18)

4. The 920 practice: living out the “0” before every “2”

The 920 practice in 321 means this: everyone connected with us is our “2”; before them we practise living a selfless (0) life and bearing the fruit of the Spirit in all nine (9) of its expressions.

Paul says, “But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith, gentleness, and self-control. Against such things there is no law.” (Galatians 5:22–23)

Brothers and sisters, notice: what’s spoken of here is “fruit,” not a “product.” Products are manufactured; fruit is grown. You can’t squeeze out patience by effort; you can only stay joined to the vine and let patience grow.

And not one of these nine graces grows in a vacuum. Love has to grow in front of people who are hard to love; patience has to grow in front of people who provoke you; gentleness has to grow in front of people who tread on you. That’s why God has placed your “2” beside you — your spouse, your children, your colleagues, the members of your group — precisely so that you have somewhere to grow fruit.

This morning, when the “2” who troubles you most comes to mind, don’t ask God to take them away; ask God to let your “0” be lived out in front of them.

5. The 235 relationships: only selfless people can walk together

The 235 relationships in 321 mean this: with a selfless person, become a “2” — spiritual companions; build a “3” — the legacy of spiritual parents and spiritual children; and finally become a “5” — a fivefold-ministry team of spiritual comrades.

Ecclesiastes says, “Two are better than one, because they have a good reward for their labor. For if they fall, the one will lift up his fellow; but woe to him who is alone when he falls, and doesn’t have another to lift him up.” And it says, “a threefold cord is not quickly broken.” (Ecclesiastes 4:9–10, 12)

Paul says, “He gave some to be apostles; and some, prophets; and some, evangelists; and some, shepherds and teachers; for the perfecting of the saints, to the work of serving, to the building up of the body of Christ.” (Ephesians 4:11–12)

Brothers and sisters, why is selflessness the precondition for relationships? Because when two self-centred people are together, there will always be rivalry; when one is self-centred and one is selfless, there is forbearance; only when two selfless people are together is there walking together.

6. The Path of Serving: Spirit, Understanding, Life, Service, God

321 sketches the whole road in five words: Spirit, Understanding, Life, Service, God. Today’s lesson begins with “Spirit” — being guided by the Holy Spirit; passes through “Understanding” — taking the Bible as our standard; enters “Life” — letting the life of Jesus replace our life; moves on to “Service” — letting Jesus be King; and finally returns to “God” — letting Jesus receive all the glory. This is not a five-stage course; it is a road to be walked afresh every single day.

sections.heading: 7. Practice for Daily Living: Walking the Truth into Footsteps
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, if truth stays only in our heads, it is merely information; truth has to be walked out in footsteps before it becomes life. The lesson gives us three very concrete practices. Let’s take them one at a time, and deepen them using the 321 “eight stages of changing our mindset” — Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication.

Practice One: A Declaration Every Morning

The lesson says: every morning, declare, “Lord, today I am willing to lay myself down and let you live in me.”

Why in the morning? Because the first thought of the day often sets the direction of the whole day. The psalmist says, “Be still, and know that I am God.” (Psalm 46:10) The original word behind “be still” carries the sense of “let go, release your grip” — only when we first let go do we recognise that he is God.

Please say this declaration out loud. Not just thinking it in your heart, but speaking it with your mouth. Because selflessness is not an emotion; it is a decision — and decisions need to be declared.

How to do it: write this sentence on your phone’s lock screen, or stick it on the bathroom mirror. Say it once while you brush your teeth, and once more before you go out. Thirty days without a break.

Practice Two: When Difficulty Comes, Stop and Ask the Lord First

The lesson says: when facing difficulties, don’t rush to use your own methods. Stop first and ask, “Jesus, how do you see this? What do you want me to do?”

Brothers and sisters, our problem usually isn’t that we react too slowly but that we react too fast. A message that makes us angry — we’ve replied within thirty seconds. A tricky situation — we’ve worked out three plans before we’ve even prayed.

Proverbs says, “Trust in Yahweh with all your heart, and don’t lean on your own understanding. In all your ways acknowledge him, and he will make your paths straight.” (Proverbs 3:5–6) “In all your ways” — including that message, including that phone call, including that decision.

How to do it: set yourself a rule — “ninety seconds first.” Whenever something makes your heart race, be still for ninety seconds first and ask these two questions in your heart: “Jesus, how do you see this? What do you want me to do?” Ninety seconds won’t ruin anything, and they often save the day.

Practice Three: In Anxiety and Weakness, Speak Out Your Dependence

The lesson says: in every moment of anxiety or weakness, learn to say, “I don’t rely on myself; I rely on Jesus.”

Paul says, “In the same way, the Spirit also helps our weaknesses, for we don’t know how to pray as we ought. But the Spirit himself makes intercession for us with groanings which can’t be uttered.” (Romans 8:26) So at the very moment we can least find words, the Holy Spirit is speaking for us.

And he says, “For God didn’t give us a spirit of fear, but of power, love, and self-control.” (2 Timothy 1:7)

How to do it: prepare a small card that says, “I don’t rely on myself; I rely on Jesus,” and keep it in your wallet or pocket. Every time anxiety rises up, take the card out and read it once. Anxiety is not the enemy; anxiety is the alarm bell reminding you that it’s time to change what you are leaning on.

Deepening These Three Practices Through the Eight Stages of Changing Our Mindset

Stage one, Information. This morning you have already received it: selflessness is not loss but gain; the limited connected to the limitless. That is information. But information can’t save anyone; information only lays the materials out on the table.

Stage two, Revelation. Ask the Holy Spirit to drive this truth from your head into your heart. Revelation is that “Oh — he’s talking about me” moment. Ask specifically: “Lord, show me the ‘self’ that is still reigning as king within me. Where is it hiding?”

Stage three, Conviction. Seeing it isn’t enough; you need to say, wholeheartedly convinced, “Lord, you are right, and I am wrong.” Conviction is the surrender of the will, not the stirring of the emotions.

Stage four, Implementation. Starting tomorrow morning, do those three practices. Don’t wait until you’re ready — no one is ever ready.

Stage five, Evaluation. Each evening spend three minutes looking back: how many times today did “self” climb back onto the throne? In what kind of situation? Who set it off?

Stage six, Correction. Turn evaluation into adjustment. If you find you always explode when you’re contradicted, then you know that what your “self” cares about most is being affirmed, and you can ask the Lord to deal with you on exactly that point.

Stage seven, Repetition. Brothers and sisters, selflessness is not a one-time operation; it is daily breathing. Paul says, “I die daily.” (1 Corinthians 15:31) Only through repetition does it become instinct.

Stage eight, Multiplication. Once you’ve walked it through, go and walk alongside someone else. Find a spiritual companion and do these thirty days of practice together, reporting to each other and praying for each other. That is the “2” in the 235 relationships.

sections.heading: 8. A Gentle Reminder
sections.html:
The lesson’s gentle reminder is only one sentence, yet it is like a key: the self-centred “you” is limited; the selfless “you,” because you have Jesus, faces nothing impossible.

Brothers and sisters, please say that sentence over to yourself three times. Every “impossible” in your life today only holds true once you add the words “on my own.” Take those words away, and the sentence is rewritten.

sections.heading: 9. Closing and Call: When I Decrease, Jesus Increases
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, we’re nearly at the end. The lesson’s closing words are beautiful: selflessness is not disappearing but being renewed; not being weakened but being filled with Jesus. When “I” decrease, Jesus increases; when “I” am still, his power is at work.

This is exactly the testimony of John the Baptist. When his disciples came running to tell him, “all are coming to him,” John answered, “He must increase, but I must decrease.” (John 3:30)

Notice that John was not a failure forced off the stage. When he said this, he was full of joy — he said he was the friend of the bridegroom, who rejoices greatly when he hears the bridegroom’s voice (John 3:29). That is the heart of a selfless person: not grudgingly giving up his place, but gladly giving it up.

Brothers and sisters, this morning the Lord may have just one question to ask you: in your life, who is on the throne?

If “self” is on the throne, you are responsible for solving every problem, responsible for producing all the strength, responsible for keeping up every appearance. No wonder you’re tired.

If Jesus is on the throne, he is responsible for the supply, he is responsible for opening the way, he is the one who receives the glory. And you need only be a branch joined to the vine.

The Lord promises, “He who overcomes, I will give to him to sit down with me on my throne, as I also overcame, and sat down with my Father on his throne.” (Revelation 3:21) Brothers and sisters, we give up our own throne, and the Lord invites us to sit on his. What a wonderful exchange!

So let us learn every day to lay down “self,” to enter into the fullness and victory of Jesus, and to live a glorious life that no longer relies on ourselves but depends on the Lord alone.

Let Jesus be King; let Jesus receive all the glory. That is our call this morning.

“looking to Jesus, the author and perfecter of faith” (Hebrews 12:2). “being confident of this very thing, that he who began a good work in you will complete it until the day of Jesus Christ.” (Philippians 1:6)

keyVerses: “I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me. That life which I now live in the flesh, I live by faith in the Son of God, who loved me, and gave himself up for me.” (Galatians 2:20)
“The thief only comes to steal, kill, and destroy. I came that they may have life, and may have it abundantly.” (John 10:10)
“I can do all things through Christ, who strengthens me.” (Philippians 4:13)
declarations: Lord Jesus, thank you for giving me a selfless life.
I am willing to lay down my own limits and let your limitlessness fill me.
From today on, it is no longer I who live, but you who live in me.
practices: A declaration every morning
When difficulty comes, stop and ask the Lord first
In anxiety and weakness, speak out your dependence
prayer: Dear Lord Jesus,

We thank you for shining the light of your word on us this morning. You have shown us that the limits on our whole lives lie not in our circumstances, not in other people, but in that “self” that refuses to come down from the throne.

Lord, we confess that we often say with our lips that you are King, yet in our hearts we are still in charge; we often ask you to give us power, yet refuse to hand over our sovereignty. Have mercy on us.
Crucify us together with you, so that we can truly say: it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me.
Lord, fill our limitations with your limitlessness. Give us peace when we are afraid, strength when we are weak, supply when we are in want, and victory when we fail.

Holy Spirit, be our guide, so that we stop relying on our own methods. Let your word be our standard, so that we live not by feelings but by truth. Jesus, be our role model, so that we learn your gentleness and humility.

Help us, from today on, to live a selfless life before every person you place in our path, and to bear the fruit of the Spirit. Make us people who bring humility and bring blessing — at home, at work and in the church.
Let your Kingdom come; let your will be done on earth as it is in heaven.
In the holy name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen.
discussion: “I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me.” (Galatians 2:20) In your life right now, is there one specific area that you say you’ve handed over to the Lord but in fact are still gripping tightly in your own hands? How are you willing to hand it over this week?

“I can do all things through Christ, who strengthens me.” (Philippians 4:13) Think back to a recent time when you “used your own methods first and only thought of praying later.” If that time you had stopped first and asked the Lord, “How do you see this?”, how might the outcome have been different? Share with your group, and pray for one another in this practice.
l070.title: Selflessness: Entering Fullness and Victory
l070.subtitle: From the Limits of the Self-Centred Life into the Boundlessness of Selflessness
l070.partTitle: Unit 5 · The Road to Revival — Selflessness

sections.heading: Introduction: One Finger Can Hide a Mountain
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, good morning. This morning, I’d like you to begin with a very simple experiment.

Hold up one index finger, about ten centimetres in front of your eye, and then look out of the window. You’ll notice something strange: that one small finger blots out an entire building, a whole row of trees, even a whole mountain. The finger hasn’t grown, and the mountain hasn’t shrunk; the only thing that has changed is the distance — the finger is simply too close to your eye.

That is the truth about “self”.

“Self” isn’t big, yet it can block out the whole of God. “Self” isn’t tall, yet it can hide the entire sky. Because “self” sits so close to our eyes — so close that we take it for the whole world. Every morning when we wake, the first thing we think of is “me”; every night when we lie down, the last thing we can’t let go of is still “me”. We measure everything by how “I” feel, arrange everything by “my” plans, judge everything by what “I” gain or lose. And so God is right there, and we can’t see him; the way out is right in front of us, and we can’t reach it.

In the last lesson we thought together about the first part of “Selflessness — Entering Jesus’ Fullness and Victory”. Today is Part 2. This lesson takes us deeper still: not only to know that “self” is the enemy, but to see clearly that “self” is the root of the problem; that the self-centred life has no way through, while selflessness has a way; and that selflessness lets us die with Christ, live with Christ and reign with Christ.

Many Christians on the road of faith long for victory, long for freedom, long for peace — and yet they keep going round in circles of worry, wearing themselves out in comparison, getting hurt in rivalry, shedding tears over misunderstandings. We assume the problem lies in our circumstances: that difficult colleague, that inconsiderate family member, that job that never goes right, that body that won’t stay well. So we spend most of our lives adjusting our circumstances, and very few of us are willing to face a more painful fact — the problem often isn’t the circumstances at all. It’s “self”.

Please hear this sentence clearly: where there is “self”, there are problems; where there is selflessness, there are none. Because “self” is the root of the problem.

At first hearing that sounds harsh, but in fact it is the greatest grace. If the problem lay in our circumstances, we would be forever powerless, because circumstances have never been under our control. But if the problem lies in “self”, then in Christ there is a sure way out — because the Lord Jesus has already crucified our old self together with him on the cross.

Brothers and sisters, this morning I want to ask you a question: if “self” really stepped down, what would your life become?

May the Holy Spirit himself, this morning, move aside the finger that blocks our view, so that we may see afresh the true and living Jesus, so full of abundance.

sections.heading: Scripture Background: A Crucified Man Writes to People About to Be Tied Down
sections.html:
The theme verse for this lesson is Galatians 2:20. To grasp the real weight of this verse, we first need to know its author, its readers and their situation.

Galatians was written by the apostle Paul. His original name was Saul, a Jew of the tribe of Benjamin, born in Tarsus of Cilicia and educated in Jerusalem at the feet of Gamaliel, the most famous teacher of the law in his day (Acts 22:3). He described his former self like this: “concerning the righteousness which is in the law, found blameless” (Philippians 3:6). In other words, Saul was a man whose “self” had been built up enormously high — highly educated, highly zealous, highly moral, highly accomplished. And it was precisely this “self” that sent him to Damascus with letters to arrest Christians (Acts 9:1–2). One of the most devout men alive, because “self” was sitting on the throne, became the fiercest persecutor of the church.

Until the light on the Damascus road threw him from his horse and left him blind for three days. God used an experience of blindness to heal a deeper blindness. From that moment Saul began to learn a lesson that would take him a lifetime — selflessness.

Galatians was written somewhere between AD 48 and 55. It is the earliest of Paul’s letters, and the most fiery in tone. Its readers were the churches of Galatia, founded on Paul’s first missionary journey, in what is today south-central Turkey. These churches were made up largely of Gentiles who had once worshipped idols and who, on hearing the gospel, had received Jesus Christ by faith alone.

The trouble came later. A group of people followed Paul into Galatia; history calls them the “Judaizers”. They didn’t deny Jesus; they simply “added a little” to the gospel: to be saved, besides believing in Jesus, you must also be circumcised, keep the law of Moses, and observe days, months, seasons and years (Galatians 4:10). That sounds very devout, but it is actually terrifying — because it quietly shifts the foundation of salvation from “Christ’s finished work” to “my extra effort”.

Brothers and sisters, notice this: the essence of legalism is “self” turned religious. It dresses “self” in holy robes, puts a Bible in its hand and sits it down in the synagogue. It looks holy, but at the core it is still “I want to stand on my own, be justified by my own effort, be better than others on my own.” That’s why Paul says, “Are you so foolish? Having begun in the Spirit, are you now completed in the flesh?” (Galatians 3:3)

Galatians 2:20 was spoken in the middle of exactly this battle. Just before it, Paul tells how he rebuked Peter publicly in Antioch. Peter had been eating with the Gentile believers, but when some people came from James, he drew back and separated himself out of fear (Galatians 2:12). Paul points out that this was no small social slip; it meant they “didn’t walk uprightly according to the truth of the Good News” (Galatians 2:14). Then straight away Paul makes that great declaration: “For I, through the law, died to the law, that I might live to God. I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live …” (Galatians 2:19–20)

Notice three keys:

First, “I have been crucified with Christ” — in the original the verb is in the perfect tense. The perfect describes something already accomplished, whose effect continues to this day. This isn’t a goal we must strive to reach; it is a fact Christ has already accomplished, which we simply enter by faith. The old self isn’t something for us to “repair”; the old self is to be “put to death” — and it has already been crucified on the cross.

Second, “it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me.” Here “no longer I” does not mean the person has vanished or his personality has been erased. Paul goes straight on to say, “That life which I now live in the flesh” — the “I” is still there, the personality is still there, the gifts are still there; only someone else now sits on the throne. Selflessness is not having nothing; it is entering into the infinite and living out the infinite.

Third, “who loved me, and gave himself up for me.” The foundation of the whole verse is love. Selflessness isn’t self-harm, isn’t repression, isn’t trampling yourself underfoot. Selflessness is gladly handing yourself over because you have seen a Lord who gave himself up for you. Love comes first; only then does denying of self become possible.

Now look at our other theme verse, John 10:10. The Lord Jesus spoke it in his teaching on the “Good Shepherd”. He was facing the Pharisees — the religious leaders who had just thrown out of the synagogue the man whose blind eyes had been healed (John 9:34). The Lord said the thief comes to steal, kill and destroy, but he came that the sheep may have life, and have it abundantly. The Greek word behind “abundantly” is perissos — “beyond measure, overflowing, more than enough”.

Brothers and sisters, put these two verses side by side, and you’ll see the skeleton of this lesson:

Only when “self” is nailed to the cross (Galatians 2:20) can life overflow (John 10:10).

sections.heading: Key Point 1: “Self” Is the Root of the Problem
sections.html:
Much of the pain and struggle in our lives actually comes from “self” being magnified. The lesson gives us five mirrors. Please look into them:

Jealousy is because “I” want what someone else has;

Strife is because “I” want to get what’s mine;

Irritation is because “my” feelings have been offended;

Worry is because “I” want to control the future;

Disappointment is because “my” expectations have fallen through.

Five emotions, five outlets, but only one source — “me”.

James laid this bare long ago: “Where do wars and fightings among you come from? Don’t they come from your pleasures that war in your members? You lust, and don’t have. You murder and covet, and can’t obtain. You fight and make war. You don’t have, because you don’t ask.” (James 4:1–2) And again: “For where jealousy and selfish ambition are, there is confusion and every evil deed.” (James 3:16)

Notice how James makes his diagnosis. He doesn’t ask, “Who have you been quarrelling with?” He asks, “Where does this come from?” He doesn’t treat the symptoms; he looks for the root of the disease. And the root lies in “your pleasures that war in your members” — the “self” living within, which always wants more, always wants to be seen, always wants to win.

As long as “I” am still the centre, the problems will never end. Change your job, and the same frustration will come back with a different face; change your church, and the same friction will be played out again by a different cast; change your surroundings, and the same worry will set you the same exam under a different title. Because you packed up “self” and took it with you.

A Key from the Original: Deny Self, or Deny the Lord

The Lord Jesus said, “If anyone desires to come after me, let him deny himself, take up his cross, and follow me.” (Luke 9:23)

The Greek word behind “deny” is aparneomai, meaning “to disown completely, to cut off all connection, to say flatly, ‘I do not know this person.’” The same word appears in the New Testament in another scene we know well — the Lord Jesus said to Peter, “Most certainly I tell you that tonight, before the rooster crows, you will deny me three times.” (Matthew 26:34) That “deny” is exactly the same word.

Brothers and sisters, what a solemn and startling contrast. The same action, and only two possible objects to choose between: deny self, or deny the Lord. Before the rooster crowed, Peter chose the second; after Pentecost, he chose the first. Life offers no third option. Every day, in every decision, every time an emotion surges up, we are choosing between these two.

That is why the Lord speaks of taking up the cross daily, as the Chinese Union Version reads. The cross isn’t an ornament; it’s an instrument of execution. It isn’t worn on the chest; it’s carried on the shoulder. And when a man carried a cross out of the city, the whole city knew — this man is going to die.

An Everyday Illustration: The Program Always Running in the Background

Anyone who uses a computer or a phone has had this experience: you’ve hardly got any apps open, yet the device gets slower and slower, feels hot to the touch, and the battery drains fast. You open the task manager and discover a program running non-stop in the background, quietly eating up most of the memory and processing power.

“Self” is that background program.

It may not make a sound, but it is always running: What did he mean by that remark just now? Why was he the one praised, and not me? What will people think of me if I do this? What if I lose my job next year? We think we are serving, reading the Bible, praying — yet a large share of our energy is being quietly eaten up by this background program. No wonder we so often feel tired and fed up without being able to say why.

Selflessness means shutting that program down. Not smashing the device, but handing the resources back to the one they belong to.

Evidence from Psychology: The More We Look at Ourselves, the Less Happy We Are

In 1954 the American social psychologist Leon Festinger put forward his “theory of social comparison” (“A Theory of Social Comparison Processes”, Human Relations, 1954). He pointed out that people have an inner drive to keep comparing themselves with others in order to assess their own abilities and worth.
