The trouble is that comparing upwards makes us feel inferior, comparing downwards makes us proud — and either way our sense of worth is tied to other people, and we never find rest.

In 2002 the psychologists Nilly Mor and Jennifer Winquist published in Psychological Bulletin a meta-analysis covering more than two hundred studies. Their conclusion: “self-focused attention” is significantly and positively associated with negative mood, depression and anxiety. Put plainly: the more people focus their attention on themselves, the worse they feel.

As for worry, in 2020 Lucas LaFreniere and Michelle Newman published a study in the journal Behavior Therapy that tracked the worries recorded by people with generalised anxiety disorder. They found that about 91.4 per cent of those worries never came true.

Brothers and sisters, the numbers science has measured, the Lord Jesus spoke two thousand years ago: “Therefore don’t be anxious for tomorrow, for tomorrow will be anxious for itself. Each day’s own evil is sufficient.” (Matthew 6:34)

The British writer C. S. Lewis, writing about pride in Mere Christianity, says that pride leads to every other vice; it is the complete anti-God state of mind. He is right — because pride is “self” climbing onto God’s throne.

When Jesus Is the One Who Lives

The lesson says: for it is no longer “I” who live, but Jesus (Galatians 2:20). When Jesus is living in us, four things happen naturally:

First, I no longer need to compare myself with others, because the focus is no longer on me. Paul says, “Let’s not become conceited, provoking one another, and envying one another.” (Galatians 5:26) Comparison can’t stop because the focus is wrong. The 321 vision says it plainly: Jesus is the focal point — not ourselves, not other people, not our circumstances. When our eyes are on the Lord, the finger naturally moves away from the eye, and the mountain appears.

Second, I can forgive those who hurt me, because Jesus has already been wounded in my place. Forgiveness is hard because “I” feel a debt must be repaid by someone; but when I see that the Lord has already paid a far greater debt for me, I can afford to pay this one.

Third, I no longer chase the satisfactions of the flesh, because Jesus is my complete satisfaction. Augustine opens his Confessions by saying: you have made us for yourself, and our heart is restless until it rests in you. The emptiness in the human heart only God can fill; fill it with anything else and the hole only stretches wider.

Fourth, I no longer live in anxiety, because Jesus is able to rule over everything. Paul says, “In nothing be anxious, but in everything, by prayer and petition with thanksgiving, let your requests be made known to God. And the peace of God, which surpasses all understanding, will guard your hearts and your thoughts in Christ Jesus.” (Philippians 4:6–7)

Brothers and sisters, please remember this: “self” makes us see limits; selflessness makes us see Jesus.

The eyes of “self” are always counting: I only have five loaves and two fish; I only have this much time, this much money, these few gifts, this little strength. The eyes of selflessness see instead: once these five loaves and two fish are placed in the Lord’s hands, they can feed five thousand, with twelve baskets left over (Matthew 14:19–21). The same bread, different hands, a completely different ending.

Turn to Jesus, and so many things we thought had no solution find a way through in him. This is exactly what 321 calls a change of perspective — from man’s perspective to God’s, from an earthly perspective to a heavenly one, from a temporary perspective to an eternal one, from a worldly perspective to a godly one. Change the perspective, and the problem changes size.

sections.heading: Key Point 2: The Self-Centred Life Has No Way Through; Selflessness Has a Way
sections.html:
Jesus said, “I am the way, the truth, and the life. No one comes to the Father, except through me.” (John 14:6)

Notice the Lord’s words. He didn’t say, “I will point out a way,” nor, “I will teach you a method for walking.” He said, “I am the way.” The way isn’t outside him; the way is he himself. Which means that apart from him we aren’t simply walking more slowly — we aren’t on the road at all.

The setting of this verse is very tender. It is the Last Supper. The Lord has just washed the disciples’ feet, and has just foretold that Judas will betray him and Peter will deny him three times. The disciples’ hearts are in turmoil. The Lord says to them, “Don’t let your heart be troubled. Believe in God. Believe also in me.” (John 14:1) Thomas asks, “Lord, we don’t know where you are going. How can we know the way?” (John 14:5) And the Lord’s answer is this declaration that spans two thousand years.

Brothers and sisters, Thomas wanted a route map; the Lord gave himself. We are so often the same: we ask God for guidance, for answers, for methods, for steps — and God wants to give us himself. Because “self” wants a map, so that “I” can stay in the driver’s seat; God wants companionship, so that he can lead the way.

Where Our Own Way Leads

When we insist on going “our own way”, we end up in a dead end. That isn’t scaremongering; the Bible says so plainly: “There is a way which seems right to a man, but in the end it leads to death.” (Proverbs 14:12)

Notice the words “seems right to a man”. People who walk into a dead end didn’t think they were making a mistake at the start; on the contrary, they felt perfectly reasonable, perfectly sure, perfectly logical. That is exactly what makes “self” so dangerous — it never beats a drum and announces, “I’m going to hurt you.” It always says gently, “You ought to think of yourself.”

God says through Isaiah, “‘For my thoughts are not your thoughts, and your ways are not my ways,’ says Yahweh. ‘For as the heavens are higher than the earth, so are my ways higher than your ways, and my thoughts than your thoughts.’” (Isaiah 55:8–9)

As far as the heavens are from the earth, so much higher are God’s ways than ours. And yet, brothers and sisters, to hold on to one idea that “I think is right”, we would often rather bang our heads against a wall for ten years than turn the corner.

Here is a modern picture. We’ve all used satellite navigation on our phones. Sat-nav can only take you to your destination if it first knows “where you are now”. If the location signal drifts and puts you three streets away, then however detailed the map and however powerful the processor, it will only take you to the wrong place.

“Self” is that false location. It makes us calculate every stretch of life’s road from a false starting point. So it isn’t that God’s map is wrong; it’s that our coordinates are off. Selflessness means honestly pressing “recalibrate” and saying: Lord, here I am. I don’t know the way. You are the way.

The Witness of History: Moving Ourselves out of the Centre

In 1543 the Polish astronomer Nicolaus Copernicus published On the Revolutions of the Heavenly Spheres. For more than a thousand years before that, astronomers had calculated the planets’ orbits with the earth at the centre of the universe. To explain the strange way the planets seem to “go backwards”, they had to add circles upon circles, piling up an ever more complicated system of “epicycles”. The more the theory was patched, the bigger it grew — and the messier.

What Copernicus did, put simply, was one thing: he moved the earth out of the centre and put the sun back there. With that one move, problems that had tangled astronomers for a millennium suddenly fell into place.

Brothers and sisters, can you hear it? This is the astronomers’ version of selflessness. Many people’s lives grow more and more complicated, the patches more and more chaotic — not because they haven’t tried hard enough, but because the centre is in the wrong place. When we move “self” out of the centre and put Jesus back there — when we let Jesus be King — many problems that have tangled us for years come loose in that very moment.

Evidence from Psychology: The Illusion of Control

In 1975 the psychologist Ellen Langer, then at Yale, published her famous study “The Illusion of Control” in the Journal of Personality and Social Psychology. She found that in situations governed purely by chance, as long as participants picked their own lottery ticket numbers or did the handling themselves, they clearly overestimated their chances of winning — and were even willing to ask a higher price before selling back the ticket they had chosen.

People aren’t really in control; they only think they are. And that “thinking” is the breeding ground of anxiety, and the most stubborn stronghold of “self”. We grip the steering wheel tight, palms sweating, when deep down we know very well whose hands the car is really in.

Three Men Who Laid Themselves Down

So often in life it is only at the moment we “lay ourselves down” that we truly see God’s way. The Bible gives us three witnesses.

The first is Moses. At forty, Moses was the man in Egypt’s royal palace who “was instructed in all the wisdom of the Egyptians” and “was mighty in his words and works” (Acts 7:22). In his own hot-blooded strength he killed an Egyptian, wanting to rescue his own people — and the very next day his own people threw it back in his face, and he had to flee to the wilderness of Midian (Exodus 2:11–15). Forty years passed, and the former prince became an old shepherd tending his father-in-law’s flock. And there, in the burning bush at Horeb, God called him. This time Moses said, “O Lord, I am not eloquent, neither before now, nor since you have spoken to your servant; for I am slow of speech, and of a slow tongue.” (Exodus 4:10) God’s answer was: “Who made man’s mouth? … Isn’t it I, Yahweh?” (Exodus 4:11)

Brothers and sisters, at forty Moses had eloquence, ability and zeal, yet couldn’t save a single person; at eighty Moses was slow of speech, slow of tongue and unsure of himself, yet God used him to lead out two million. The difference wasn’t ability; the difference was whether “self” had been laid down. And it was this same Moses, who had laid himself down, who could later ask God on the mountain, “Please show me your glory.” (Exodus 33:18) And God made all his goodness pass before him.

The second is Joshua. He stood before Jericho, a fortified city with walls of great height and thickness. A military commander’s instinct would surely be to survey the terrain and draw up tactics. Scripture records that Joshua lifted up his eyes and looked, “and behold, a man stood in front of him with his sword drawn in his hand.” Joshua asked him, “Are you for us, or for our enemies?” The man answered, “No; but I have come now as commander of Yahweh’s army.” And Joshua fell on his face to the earth and worshipped (Joshua 5:13–14).

Notice Joshua’s question and the commander’s answer. Joshua asked, “Whose side are you on?” The commander said, “No.” God never joins our side; God calls us to join his. That “No” cut short Joshua’s strategy; and the moment he fell down in worship, God told him the strangest tactic in the history of human warfare — march round the city for seven days, seven times on the seventh day, then blow the trumpets and shout (Joshua 6:3–5). And the walls fell down. Only by laying down his own strategy did he experience God’s victory.

The third is Peter. He was a professional fisherman who had toiled all night and caught nothing. And the Lord Jesus — a carpenter’s son — said to him, “Put out into the deep, and let down your nets for a catch.” Simon answered, “Master, we worked all night, and took nothing; but at your word I will let down the net.” (Luke 5:4–5)

“But at your word” — those few words are selflessness. The catch was so great that the nets were close to breaking; both boats were filled until they began to sink. Peter fell down at Jesus’ knees and said, “Depart from me, for I am a sinful man, Lord.” But the Lord said, “Don’t be afraid. From now on you will be catching people alive.” And Scripture goes on: “When they had brought their boats to land, they left everything, and followed him.” (Luke 5:8, 10–11)

Think about it: that was the biggest catch Peter ever landed in his life, and at that very moment he left everything. Because at last he had seen a Lord far more worth gaining than fish. Only by laying down his own nets did he become a fisher of people.

Selflessness Is Active Obedience

Brothers and sisters, please don’t misunderstand: selflessness isn’t passive waiting; it is active obedience.

Moses laid down his eloquence, yet he really did walk into Pharaoh’s palace; Joshua laid down his strategy, yet he really did march round the city for seven days; Peter laid down his nets, yet he really did put out into the deep. Selflessness doesn’t mean doing nothing. Selflessness means no longer doing what “self” wants to do, and giving everything to doing what the Lord wants me to do.

The 321 vision reminds us that the Path of Serving has an order: Spirit — the Holy Spirit is my guide; Understanding — the Bible is my standard; Life — Jesus is my role model; Service — let Jesus be King; God — let Jesus receive all the glory. Many people jump straight to “Service” and stay busy all their lives without ever passing through “Spirit, Understanding, Life”. That is serving with “self”: the more you do, the more tired you get, and the more tired you get, the more bitter.

That’s why 321 says: life first, then relationships, then ministry. When life is right, relationships come right; when relationships are right, ministry won’t wound people.

When we are willing to let Jesus lead, even if what lies ahead looks like a dead end, God can make a way. He says, “Behold, I will do a new thing. It springs out now. Don’t you know it? I will even make a way in the wilderness, and rivers in the desert.” (Isaiah 43:19)

Brothers and sisters, notice where God makes his way: not on the plain, but in the wilderness; not by the riverbank, but in the desert. God loves to make a way in the very place where people say “impossible”, because there no one can take the glory for himself.

sections.heading: Key Point 3: Selflessness Lets Us Die, Live and Reign with Christ
sections.html:
To choose selflessness is to let “self” die to the law, die to the world and die to sin. Scripture spells out each of these three deaths clearly in three places.

Dying to the law: “Therefore, my brothers, you also were made dead to the law through the body of Christ, that you would be joined to another, to him who was raised from the dead, that we might produce fruit to God.” (Romans 7:4)

Dying to the world: “But far be it from me to boast, except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, through which the world has been crucified to me, and I to the world.” (Galatians 6:14)

Dying to sin: “Thus consider yourselves also to be dead to sin, but alive to God in Christ Jesus our Lord.” (Romans 6:11)

Three deaths loosen three chains.

Dying to the law loosens the chain of “I have to perform to be worth anything.” Someone who has died to the law no longer needs to earn God’s smile with good marks, because he now belongs to the Lord who was raised from the dead.

Dying to the world loosens the chain of “I can only stand if others approve of me.” Someone who has died to the world is no longer held hostage by rankings, likes and other people’s verdicts, because between him and the world there now stands a cross.

Dying to sin loosens the chain of “I can’t help it.” Someone who has died to sin is no longer sin’s slave, because a master has no authority to give orders to a dead man.

So the lesson says: when “self” dies, we are set free! No longer bound by the world’s values, no longer enslaved by sin’s temptations, no longer held hostage by people’s opinions.

The Lord Jesus himself said, “You will know the truth, and the truth will make you free.” And again, “If therefore the Son makes you free, you will be free indeed.” (John 8:32, 36)

Evidence from Science: Death Turns Out to Be Part of Life’s Design

In 1972 three pathologists, John Kerr, Andrew Wyllie and Alastair Currie, published a paper in the British Journal of Cancer that gave a name to a phenomenon: “apoptosis”. The word is taken from Greek and originally means “the falling of petals or leaves”.

They found that a great many cells in the human body go to their death actively, following a set programme. This isn’t disease; it’s design. In the embryo our hands start out like a webbed paddle, and it is precisely because the cells between the fingers die off on schedule that five fingers separate. The immune system relies on apoptosis to clear away faulty cells. And when this programme fails — when cells that should die refuse to die and keep multiplying — that is cancer.

Brothers and sisters, hear the spiritual echo clearly: in the body God made, it is “what should die refusing to die” that is the disease. A Christian whose old self refuses to die won’t have a fuller life — only a more swollen one.

The Lord Jesus stated this principle long ago: “Most certainly I tell you, unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains by itself alone. But if it dies, it bears much fruit.” (John 12:24)

A grain of wheat that refuses to die can stay intact, beautiful and safe — but it will only ever be one grain. Its intactness is its poverty.

The German theologian Dietrich Bonhoeffer, in The Cost of Discipleship, wrote words still quoted today: when Christ calls a man, he bids him come and die. That isn’t pessimism; it is the shortest road to resurrection.

Dying Together in Order to Live Together

Paul says, “But if we died with Christ, we believe that we will also live with him.” (Romans 6:8)

Selflessness lets us rise together with Christ and enter the power of his resurrection. Paul has already explained this mystery a few verses earlier: “We were buried therefore with him through baptism into death, that just as Christ was raised from the dead through the glory of the Father, so we also might walk in newness of life.” (Romans 6:4)

Notice that dying together isn’t the end; it’s a passageway. Behind the Christian’s cross there is always an empty tomb. The world is afraid of death, so it clings desperately to itself; Christians know there is a resurrection, so they dare to let go.

More wonderful still, Scripture says we also “sit with him in the heavenly places”. Ephesians 2:5–6 records: “even when we were dead through our trespasses, made us alive together with Christ—by grace you have been saved—and raised us up with him, and made us to sit with him in the heavenly places in Christ Jesus,”

In the Greek, three verbs in a row here begin with the prefix syn (“together”): made alive together, raised together, seated together. Three “togethers”, like a three-stage rocket, carrying someone who was dead in trespasses and sins all the way to a seat in heaven.

Pay special attention to the last action — “sit”. In the culture of the Bible, servants stand and masters sit; to sit on a throne means to reign. So this means we are not only saved; we reign together with Christ.

Paul says to Timothy, “If we endure, we will also reign with him.” (2 Timothy 2:12) The Lord Jesus says to the church in Laodicea, “He who overcomes, I will give to him to sit down with me on my throne, as I also overcame, and sat down with my Father on his throne.” (Revelation 3:21)

Brothers and sisters, see this spiritual law clearly: someone who won’t let Jesus reign as King within him cannot reign together with Jesus either. Because there is only one throne. If “self” sits on it, the Lord can only stand outside the door and knock; if the Lord sits on it, we sit with him in the heavenly places.

This is the very heart of 321: let Jesus be King, let Jesus receive all the glory. Humility overcomes pride; selflessness overcomes Satan. Pride is leaving our originally intended position and seizing rights, wanting to take God’s place; humility is laying down our rights and returning to our originally intended position — letting man be man and letting God be God. Satan’s fall long ago was his attempt to raise his own throne above God’s (Isaiah 14:13–14); and his greatest temptation for us today is still the same move — you can be your own master.

A Life of Reigning Together: Doing What We See the Father Doing

When we let Jesus reign within us, we are able to do what we see the Father doing.

The Lord Jesus himself lived this way. He said, “Most certainly, I tell you, the Son can do nothing of himself, but what he sees the Father doing. For whatever things he does, these the Son also does likewise.” (John 5:19)

Think deeply about that: the Lord who had power to raise the dead and calm wind and waves actually said that he “can do nothing of himself”. It wasn’t that the Lord Jesus lacked power; it was that he didn’t use his own power to do his own thing. This is the most perfect model of selflessness, and it is what 321 means by “Jesus is my role model”.

So service no longer comes from the flesh, but from the Holy Spirit.

Service in the flesh has some clear marks: the more you do, the more tired you get and the more you resent it, and afterwards you care a great deal whether anyone noticed or said thank you. Service in the Spirit can be tiring too, but it is a joyful tiredness; afterwards there is peace in your heart, and you don’t care who gets the applause — only that the Lord gets the glory.

The Lord said, “I am the vine. You are the branches. He who remains in me and I in him bears much fruit, for apart from me you can do nothing.” (John 15:5) The branch doesn’t have to be anxious about bearing fruit; the branch only has to stay joined to the vine. Stay joined, and fruit comes naturally; come loose, and however hard you strain, you’ll only snap yourself off.

A life like this is just as Jesus said: “Most certainly I tell you, he who believes in me, the works that I do, he will do also; and he will do greater works than these, because I am going to my Father. Whatever you will ask in my name, I will do it, that the Father may be glorified in the Son.” (John 14:12–13)

Notice the reason and the purpose the Lord gives. The reason is “because I am going to my Father” — the Lord ascended and the Holy Spirit came down, so the work of one man became the work of millions. The purpose is “that the Father may be glorified in the Son” — the greater works aren’t for building a greater self, but for displaying a greater glory.

Brothers and sisters, the selfless life is Jesus living himself out again within us — so that the Father is glorified, people are blessed, and life is victorious.

sections.heading: Integrating the 321 Vision: A Map of the Selfless Life
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, this lesson is really the most central lesson of the whole 321 vision. Let’s lay it out as a map of life.

The Three Foundations, the Two Core Values, the Goal

The Three Foundations are: Jesus is my role model, the Bible is my standard, the Holy Spirit is my guide.

Jesus is my role model — he said, “the Son can do nothing of himself” (John 5:19); that is the role model of selflessness. Though he existed in the form of God, he “emptied himself, taking the form of a servant” (Philippians 2:7); that is the road of selflessness.

The Bible is my standard — when “self” says, “I feel it ought to be this way,” the Bible says, “There is a way which seems right to a man, but in the end it leads to death” (Proverbs 14:12). We don’t decide right and wrong by our feelings; we decide right and wrong by God’s word.

The Holy Spirit is my guide — “For as many as are led by the Spirit of God, these are children of God.” (Romans 8:14) A selfless person isn’t without direction; he has handed the steering wheel to the Holy Spirit.

The Two Core Values are: let Jesus be King, let Jesus receive all the glory. This is exactly the conclusion of this lesson’s third key point — there is only one throne; either “self” sits on it, or the Lord does.

The Goal is: establish God’s system. As selfless people multiply, families become God’s families, churches become God’s churches, and workplaces become a witness for God. God’s system isn’t established by organisation; it is established by selfless lives, one at a time.

The Old Self Is Self-Centred; the New Self Is Selfless

The 321 vision says: the self-centred life is the root of humanity’s fall; pride is the root of the problem.

Look at Genesis 3. In the serpent’s words to the woman lies hidden the deadliest temptation of all: “you will be like God, knowing good and evil.” (Genesis 3:5) “Like God” — that is the prototype of “self”: I want to sit in that seat; I want to define for myself what is good and what is evil.

So pride is leaving our originally intended position and seizing rights, wanting to take God’s place; humility is laying down our rights and returning to our originally intended position — letting man be man and letting God be God.

And pride provokes pride, and both sides lose; humility draws out humility, and both sides win. Even physics bears witness to this: Newton’s third law of motion says that every action has an equal and opposite reaction. However hard you push the other person, they push back just as hard. Husbands and wives quarrelling, co-workers clashing — almost all of it is a demonstration of this law. But humility is different — humility doesn’t create a reaction; humility absorbs it. “A gentle answer turns away wrath, but a harsh word stirs up anger.” (Proverbs 15:1)

Remember too: selflessness is not having nothing; it is entering into the infinite and living out the infinite. A drop of water in the palm of your hand soon dries up; a drop of water placed in the ocean takes on the vastness of the ocean. Selflessness doesn’t evaporate the drop; it places it in the ocean. “I” no longer live, but Christ lives in me.

The Fivefold Change and the Priority of Relationships

The 321 vision says the fivefold change is in mindset, life, daily living, relationships and ministry. Change the mindset and you change the life; change the life and you change daily living.

Today’s lesson starts precisely with mindset. When your mindset shifts from “the problem is my circumstances” to “the problem is self”, your life begins to loosen; once your life loosens, your reactions in daily living change; once your daily living changes, relationships are healed; and once relationships are healed, ministry bears real fruit.

That’s why 321 stresses: life first, then relationships, then ministry. People matter more than tasks; relationships matter more than things.

Relationships also have an order: first with God, then with ourselves, then with others, and last with things. Many people get stuck at the third level all their lives — busy sorting out their relationships with others, without first making peace with God or with themselves. The more they sort, the more tangled it gets. A selfless person first comes back before God; once settled before God, the way he sees people grows gentle.

A Change of Perspective

The key to the 321 vision is a change of perspective: from man’s perspective to God’s, from an earthly perspective to a heavenly one, from a temporary perspective to an eternal one, from a worldly perspective to a godly one.

Paul says, “If then you were raised together with Christ, seek the things that are above, where Christ is, seated on the right hand of God. Set your mind on the things that are above, not on the things that are on the earth.” (Colossians 3:1–2)

Brothers and sisters, since he has already “raised us up with him, and made us to sit with him in the heavenly places” (Ephesians 2:6), why do we still calculate our little gains and losses with earthly eyes? Someone sitting on the mountaintop doesn’t get angry over who took one step more at the foot of the mountain.

The 920 Practice and 235 Relationships

The 920 practice says: every person connected with us is our “2”; with each of them we are to practise living out the selfless life — the “0” — so as to bear the fruit of the Spirit in all nine of its expressions.

“But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith, gentleness, and self-control. Against such things there is no law.” (Galatians 5:22–23)

Notice: it isn’t nine fruits; it is “one fruit, nine expressions”. And not one of the nine can be squeezed out by “self”. Try squeezing out gentleness at the very moment you’ve been offended — all you’ll squeeze out is a fake smile. The fruit of the Spirit is the product of the “0”: when I step back to zero, the Holy Spirit has room, and the fruit grows.

So the hardest person to get along with in your life today isn’t your problem; they are your “2”. The situation that sends your blood pressure up isn’t your disaster; it’s your training ground.

235 relationships says: become a “2” with a selfless person, as spiritual companions to each other; build a “3”, becoming spiritual parents and spiritual children; and go on to become a “5”, a fivefold-ministry team of spiritual comrades.

Brothers and sisters, let me ask an honest question: without selflessness, can you truly become a “2” with anyone? Put two self-centred people together and you don’t have companions; you have a combination that will explode sooner or later. Only selflessness brings oneness; only oneness makes a team; only a team can establish God’s system.

Finally, 321 reminds us: rely on the heart and the Holy Spirit, not on the brain and ourselves; rely on the heart and you’ll be joyful, rely on the brain and you’ll be troubled. “Keep your heart with all diligence, for out of it is the wellspring of life.” (Proverbs 4:23)

sections.heading: Putting It into Practice: Making Selflessness an Everyday Habit
sections.html:
The lesson gives us three very concrete practices. Let’s take them one at a time, and use 321’s eight stages of changing our mindset — Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication — to take each one deeper.

Practice 1: When emotions surge up, first ask yourself, “Is this ‘me’ reacting, or is Jesus reigning?”

Emotions are the most honest dashboard there is. People can pretend; emotions can’t. When the blood rushes to your head, when the words are already on the tip of your tongue, when your finger is about to hit “send” — that is the very instant “self” shows itself.

In that instant, give yourself three seconds and ask that one question. That one question will pull you out of “reaction mode” and back into “reigning mode”.

Use the eight stages to take it deeper: Information is hearing this question today. Revelation is when, after one of your outbursts, the Holy Spirit suddenly lets you see that it wasn’t someone else’s fault — “self” had been stepped on. Conviction is admitting in your heart, “Lord, that really was me.” Implementation is asking this question every time an emotion surges up, starting tomorrow. Evaluation is looking back each evening at how many times you asked it and how many times you forgot. Correction is identifying the times and the people with whom you most easily lose ground, and praying especially for them. Repetition is not giving up for forty days in a row. Multiplication is teaching this practice to your spouse, your children or a spiritual companion.

Practice 2: When facing a challenge, don’t rush into action; first pray, “Lord, you are my way.”

The two words “self” loves most are “hurry up”. Hurry up and reply, hurry up and fix it, hurry up and prove I’m right. But the Bible says, “Trust in Yahweh with all your heart, and don’t lean on your own understanding. In all your ways acknowledge him, and he will make your paths straight.” (Proverbs 3:5–6)

In front of every challenge, stop for thirty seconds first, and speak John 14:6 out as a prayer: “Lord, you are my way, my truth and my life.”

Here is how the eight stages go: Information and Revelation — you do it once and discover that those thirty seconds really changed the outcome. Conviction and Implementation — you apply it to the most urgent matter of all. Evaluation and Correction — you note down the two different endings, rushing into action versus praying first. Repetition — you let it become a reflex. Multiplication — you lead your small group to pray this way together.

Practice 3: Each day, practise one small act of selflessness: let go of one insistence, forgive one person, hand over one area of control.

Don’t start by taking on the biggest one. Spiritual muscle is built starting with light weights.

Let go of one insistence — perhaps simply letting the other person choose the restaurant tonight, or choosing not to say, “I told you so.”

Forgive one person — not waiting until it feels right, but making the decision by an act of will, and then praying blessing over that person. Psychology has researched forgiveness extensively. A meta-analysis by Everett Worthington’s team at Virginia Commonwealth University, published in the Journal of Consulting and Clinical Psychology (2014), found that forgiveness interventions significantly reduced participants’ depression and anxiety and increased their hope. It turns out that the first person forgiveness heals is the one who forgives.

Hand over one area of control — the thing you’ve never felt safe entrusting to anyone else, actually hand it over; the family member you’ve always worried about, actually hand them over to God. “casting all your worries on him, because he cares for you.” (1 Peter 5:7)

Here is how the eight stages go: Information and Revelation show you how tightly you’ve been gripping. Conviction makes you willing to loosen your hold. Implementation is choosing one thing today. Evaluation and Correction is reviewing each week which kind is hardest to let go. Repetition is making “one small death a day” a habit. Multiplication is telling your story, so that others dare to let go too.

A Gentle Reminder

When “I” step down, Jesus steps up. When Jesus is Lord, there will be a way through everything.

sections.heading: Closing and Call: Let Jesus Be King, Let Jesus Receive the Glory
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, today we have walked through three key points together.

First, “self” is the root of the problem — jealousy, strife, irritation, worry, disappointment: five rivers, one source.

Second, the self-centred life has no way through; selflessness has a way — Moses laid down his eloquence, Joshua laid down his strategy, Peter laid down his nets, and God made a way in the wilderness and rivers in the desert.

Third, selflessness lets us die, live and reign with Christ — dying to the law, dying to the world, dying to sin; made alive together with him, raised together with him, seated together with him in the heavenly places.

So the lesson’s conclusion could not be clearer: selflessness is not the self disappearing; it is letting Jesus reign completely within us.

Please don’t be afraid of this word. Selflessness doesn’t make you worthless; it moves your worth from a foundation that will collapse onto a rock that will never be shaken. Selflessness isn’t losing yourself; it is finding your true self — the self created in the image of God and bought back at great price by the Lord’s precious blood.

When we choose selflessness, we choose a life of freedom, victory and glory.

This morning, the Lord may be knocking gently at one particular door of your heart: perhaps a relationship you’ve held on to for a long time and won’t let go; perhaps a name you still refuse to forgive; perhaps a plan you’re clutching tightly and don’t dare hand over; perhaps simply the “me” that won’t admit defeat every morning.

The Lord doesn’t want to take anything from you. The Lord wants to sit in the place that has always belonged to him.

Let us lay ourselves down every day, enter the fullness of Jesus, and live out a victorious life that no longer relies on self but relies wholly on the Lord.

May all the glory go to Jesus, for he is worthy.

keyVerses: “I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me. That life which I now live in the flesh, I live by faith in the Son of God, who loved me, and gave himself up for me.” (Galatians 2:20)
“The thief only comes to steal, kill, and destroy. I came that they may have life, and may have it abundantly.” (John 10:10)
declarations: Please declare with me:
Lord Jesus, you are my way, my truth and my life.
I choose to lay myself down and let you reign as King within me.
It is no longer I who live, but you;
It is no longer my way I walk, but yours.
I declare that the selfless life is the victorious life!
practices: When emotions surge up, first ask yourself
When facing a challenge, don’t rush into action; first pray
Practise one small act of selflessness each day
prayer: Dear Lord Jesus, we thank you.

You loved me and gave yourself up for me; you have already crucified my old self with you on the cross. Lord, forgive me — so often I climb down from the cross by myself and lift myself back onto the throne. I hold my little “self” up before my eyes, blocking your face, and then blame the world for being so dark.
Lord, please move that finger aside. May your Holy Spirit shine on me, and let me see that behind jealousy, strife, irritation, worry and disappointment, the real name is “me”.

Lord, today I choose selflessness. I hand you the steering wheel, I hand you control, I hand you the person I have never been willing to forgive, and I hand you the road that has never led me anywhere. You are the way, the truth and the life; no one comes to the Father except through you.
Reign as King within me, so that I no longer serve in the flesh, but do what I see the Father doing. Make me bear the fruit of the Spirit, and live out the selfless life with every “2” around me.
Lord, may you receive all the glory; may your kingdom come, may your will be done on earth as it is in heaven.
In the holy name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen.
discussion: Of these five — jealousy, strife, irritation, worry, disappointment — which shows up in you most often? Honestly identify the “me” behind it: is it my face, my rights, my plans, or my sense of security? Remind one another and pray for one another with James 3:16: “For where jealousy and selfish ambition are, there is confusion and every evil deed.”

Moses laid down his eloquence, Joshua laid down his strategy, Peter laid down his nets. Share: what is the hardest thing for you to let go of right now? If you really let it go, how do you believe God would make a way for you? Strengthen one another with Isaiah 43:19: “I will even make a way in the wilderness, and rivers in the desert.”
